options: Making a material misstatement on the license application
Demonstrating untrustworthiness or incompetency
Having lower annual sales volume than others in the office
Publishing dishonest or misleading advertising
questions.explanation: Listed grounds include violating Article 12-A, a material misstatement in the application, fraud or fraudulent practices, dishonest or misleading advertising, untrustworthiness or incompetency, and Human Rights Law violations committed as a licensee. Low production is a business issue, not misconduct.

questions.q: Instead of revoking or suspending a license, DOS may impose a fine. What is the maximum fine under RPL §441-c?
questions.explanation: §441-c allows DOS to impose a fine of up to $2,000 instead of revoking or suspending a license. Half of collected fines goes to the anti-discrimination in housing fund. $1,000 is an older figure that still appears in some study materials.

questions.q: DOS revokes a salesperson's license. When may she next become eligible for a broker's or salesperson's license?
options: One year after the date of the revocation
Immediately, by paying a reinstatement fee
Only after a new 77-hour course, at any time
Two years after the date of the revocation
questions.explanation: Under §441-c(4), a licensee whose license is revoked cannot be relicensed as a broker or salesperson until one year after the revocation date. Revocation is not cured by simply paying a fee.

questions.q: After receiving notice that DOS has suspended his license, what must a broker do with his license and pocket card?
options: Return them to DOS within five days, or file an affidavit if lost
Return them at the next renewal date, along with the renewal fee
Surrender them to the local Board of Realtors within thirty days
Keep them, but stop displaying them until the suspension ends
questions.explanation: Licenses and pocket cards must be returned to DOS within five days after notice of revocation or suspension. If they were lost or destroyed, the licensee files an affidavit instead. Displaying a revoked or suspended broker license is also prohibited.

questions.q: DOS revokes Broker Kim's license. What happens to the licenses of the salespersons associated with her?
options: They are unaffected, since each salesperson holds their own license
They are converted to inactive status until their next renewal
They are revoked as well, with a one-year bar on relicensing
They are suspended until each salesperson changes association
questions.explanation: Under RPL §441-d, revoking or suspending a broker's license suspends the license of each associated salesperson until the salesperson changes association or the broker's suspension ends. It does not count as a revocation of the salespersons' own licenses.

questions.q: A salesperson misrepresents a property's flood history. The broker did not know about it and gained nothing from it. When can the salesperson's violation be cause for suspending or revoking the broker's license?
options: Only if the broker had supervised the salesperson for under a year
Only if the broker knew of it, or kept the deal's proceeds after notice
Always, because a broker is strictly liable for every salesperson act
Never, because only the salesperson can be disciplined for the act
questions.explanation: RPL §442-c says a salesperson's violation is not cause to discipline the broker unless the broker had actual knowledge of it or kept the benefits of the wrongly negotiated transaction after notice of the misconduct. The broker's own supervision duties still apply separately.

questions.q: Before DOS holds a hearing to suspend a salesperson's license, what notice does RPL §441-e require?
options: Notice published in a newspaper of record for two consecutive weeks
Written notice of the charges at least 10 days before the hearing, also sent to her broker
Written notice to the salesperson only, mailed at least 30 days before the scheduled hearing date
A phone call to the salesperson at least 5 days before the hearing date
questions.explanation: DOS must notify the licensee in writing of the charges at least 10 days before the hearing and give her an opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel. When the licensee is a salesperson, DOS must also notify her broker by certified mail.

questions.q: A broker is fined and suspended by DOS after a hearing. How may he obtain court review of that determination?
options: File a federal civil-rights suit, which is the only available route to review
Bring an Article 78 proceeding under the Civil Practice Law and Rules
Appeal directly to the State Board of Real Estate for a new hearing
Ask the local Board of Realtors to review the DOS determination
questions.explanation: RPL §441-f makes DOS licensing and disciplinary actions reviewable through an Article 78 proceeding under the CPLR. Article 78 is how New York courts review the actions of state and local agencies.

questions.q: A homeowner files a complaint, and DOS decides not to discipline the broker. Under RPL §441-f, can the homeowner seek court review of that decision?
options: Yes, as a person aggrieved, through an Article 78 proceeding
No, because a refusal to discipline is final and unreviewable
Yes, but only by bringing a criminal complaint against DOS
No, because only the licensee may ever challenge a DOS decision
questions.explanation: §441-f covers DOS's refusal to revoke, suspend, fine, or reprimand as well as its decisions to do so. Review may be sought by the applicant, the disciplined licensee, or the person aggrieved through an Article 78 proceeding.

questions.q: Without being told to by the seller, a seller's agent declines to tell a buyer the lowest price the seller would accept. Which fiduciary duty is the agent fulfilling?
options: Accounting
Obedience
Confidentiality
Reasonable care
questions.explanation: Keeping the client's bargaining position private is confidentiality. Because the seller gave no instruction, obedience is not the duty involved.

questions.q: A listing agent promptly deposits a buyer's earnest money and keeps exact records of it. Which fiduciary duty does this best reflect?
options: Accounting
Loyalty
Disclosure
Obedience
questions.explanation: Accounting means safeguarding, recording, and accounting for money and property entrusted to the agent. Mishandling deposits violates both this duty and the escrow rules.

questions.q: A seller tells her listing agent not to show the house to any family with children. The agent should:
options: Comply, because the duty of obedience is owed to the seller
Comply, but only if the seller puts the instruction in writing
Comply, because the seller may choose who enters her own home
Refuse, because obedience covers only lawful instructions
questions.explanation: Obedience applies only to lawful instructions. Excluding families with children is familial-status discrimination, so the agent must refuse.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296

questions.q: A seller's agent is working with an unrepresented buyer (a customer). What does the agent owe that buyer?
options: Undivided loyalty and confidentiality of the buyer's position
Honest, fair dealing and disclosure of known material facts
The same full fiduciary duties owed to the seller
Only the information the seller authorizes
questions.explanation: Fiduciary duties go to the client (the seller). A customer is still owed honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known facts that materially affect the property's value or desirability.

questions.q: A seller tells his agent to keep quiet about a known basement leak that floods every spring. A buyer customer asks whether there are water problems. The agent should:
options: Disclose the leak; confidentiality never covers hiding known defects
Stay silent, because the duty of confidentiality is owed to the seller
Say there are no problems, since the buyer is only a customer, not a client
Refer the buyer to the seller's attorney and say nothing further
questions.explanation: Confidentiality protects the client's bargaining position. It never allows hiding a known material defect or making a false statement. An instruction to conceal is unlawful and must be refused.

questions.q: A buyer's agent will be paid through a split of the listing broker's fee, which comes from the seller's proceeds. Whom does the buyer's agent represent?
options: The seller, because the seller's proceeds fund the commission
Both parties, as an automatic dual agent sharing one fee
The buyer, because who pays does not decide who is represented
Neither party, acting only as a neutral transaction facilitator
questions.explanation: Representation depends on the agency relationship, not on who pays. Sharing a commission does not, by itself, create agency with the seller.

questions.q: A buyer signs the acknowledgment on the New York agency disclosure form. By doing so, the buyer has:
options: Entered a binding buyer-agency agreement with the broker
Acknowledged receiving the disclosure, not hired the broker
Agreed to pay the broker's commission if a purchase closes
Automatically consented to any dual agency that may arise
questions.explanation: The form states 'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT.' Signing confirms only that the buyer received it. A representation agreement is a separate document.

questions.q: When must a listing agent give the agency disclosure form to the seller of a single-family home?
options: At the first open house held for the property
When the first written offer arrives from a buyer
At or before the closing, with the other documents
Before entering into the listing agreement
questions.explanation: A seller's agent must give the seller the disclosure before the listing agreement is signed. A buyer's agent must give it to the buyer before a buyer-agency agreement.

questions.q: A seller's agent meets a prospective buyer at an open house and starts discussing the buyer's budget and housing needs. When must the agent give this buyer the disclosure form?
options: Before the buyer makes a written offer
Only if the buyer asks for it
After the buyer signs a purchase contract
At this first substantive contact
questions.explanation: The disclosure goes to the other party at the first substantive contact. A casual greeting doesn't count, but discussing the buyer's finances and needs does.

questions.q: Which transaction is NOT covered by the RPL § 443 agency disclosure requirement?
options: Sale of an owner-occupied two-family house
Sale of a vacant, unimproved building lot
Sale of a condominium unit in a high-rise
Sale of a cooperative apartment's shares
questions.explanation: Section 443 covers 1-4 family residential property and condo/co-op units. It does not cover unimproved land. The agent's general agency and honesty duties still apply.

questions.q: A licensee is helping a landlord rent out a residential apartment. Which agency disclosure form applies?
options: DOS-1736, the buyer and seller disclosure form
DOS-2156, the fair housing notice
DOS-1735, the landlord and tenant disclosure form
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
questions.explanation: DOS-1735 covers landlord/tenant relationships and DOS-1736 covers buyers and sellers. The fair housing notice and the PCDS are separate documents and do not replace the agency disclosure.

questions.q: A buyer refuses to sign the acknowledgment on the agency disclosure form. The licensee should:
options: Make a written declaration of the refusal and keep it at least three years
Stop working with the buyer, since the form must be signed to proceed
Tell the broker verbally about the refusal; no written record is needed
Sign the buyer's name with the buyer's verbal permission and continue
questions.explanation: A refusal does not cancel the disclosure duty. The licensee prepares a written declaration of the facts (under oath or affirmation) and keeps it, like signed acknowledgments, for at least three years.

questions.q: A New York broker may act as a dual agent in a sale only if:
options: The broker tells the buyer about the dual role orally
Both the buyer and the seller give informed written consent
The seller consents, since the seller pays the commission
Both clients are handled within the broker's own office
questions.explanation: Dual agency requires informed consent in writing from both principals. Each side gives up the right to undivided loyalty, so oral or one-sided consent is not enough.

questions.q: Can a buyer or seller consent to dual agency before a specific dual-agency situation arises?
options: No, consent is valid only after a specific property is chosen
No, dual agency is prohibited in New York sales
Yes, but only by telling the broker orally
Yes, advance informed consent can be given on the disclosure form
questions.explanation: The DOS form has checkboxes for advance informed consent to dual agency, with or without designated sales agents. The agent should still explain the arrangement when it actually happens.

questions.q: With informed written consent, a dual-agent broker designates Salesperson A for the buyer and Salesperson B for the seller. Which statement is correct?
options: The broker remains a dual agent; neither designee gives undivided loyalty
The broker stops being a dual agent once the sales agents are designated
Each designated agent gives full undivided loyalty to his or her client
The designated agents must be associated with different brokerages
questions.explanation: Designated sales agents advocate for their assigned clients, but the broker is still a dual agent. The NY form says designated agents cannot provide undivided loyalty. Some other states treat this differently, but New York does not.

questions.q: Salesperson Kim of ABC Realty has a buyer-agency agreement with Lee. Lee wants to buy a house listed by another ABC Realty salesperson. What is ABC Realty's position?
options: There is no conflict, because different salespersons handle each side
Kim may continue as Lee's agent with no further consent
ABC would be a dual agent and needs both parties' informed written consent
The listing salesperson automatically becomes Lee's agent
questions.explanation: The agency relationship is with the brokerage, not the individual salesperson. A firm representing both sides is a dual agent no matter which associates handle each side, so written informed consent is required.

questions.q: Without either party's written consent, a listing salesperson secretly advises the buyer on how low to offer. Which statement is correct?
options: It is allowed if the seller ends up accepting the buyer's offer anyway
It is allowed because the buyer is only a customer, not a client
It is undisclosed dual agency, which a successful closing does not cure
It is designated agency, which requires no written consent from either party
questions.explanation: Acting for both sides without informed written consent is undisclosed dual agency and a breach of loyalty to the seller. It can lead to DOS discipline and loss of the commission even if the sale closes.

questions.q: A listing agent engages a broker's agent from a different firm to help find a buyer. If the broker's agent misrepresents the property, who has liability for the broker's agent's acts, according to the NY disclosure form?
options: The listing agent who directs the broker's agent
The seller, because the broker's agent works for the seller
The buyer, because the buyer relied on the statement
No one, because broker's agents owe no duties
questions.explanation: The form says the seller cannot direct a broker's agent and has no vicarious liability for its acts. The listing agent who engages and directs the broker's agent carries that liability.

questions.q: How does a seller's subagent differ from a broker's agent?
options: A subagent represents the buyer; a broker's agent represents the seller
Only a subagent's acts can make the seller vicariously liable
A subagent must belong to the listing firm; a broker's agent need not
They are the same role, described under two interchangeable names
questions.explanation: A subagent is the seller's agent through the listing broker, so the seller can be vicariously liable for its acts. A broker's agent answers to the engaging agent, and the seller has no vicarious liability for it.

questions.q: Which event terminates a listing agency relationship by operation of law?
options: The listing being entered into the MLS
A buyer's agent showing the property
The seller hiring an attorney for closing
The death of the seller-principal
questions.explanation: Death or incapacity of the principal (or destruction of the property) ends the agency by operation of law. The other events are ordinary parts of a transaction.

questions.q: A listing expires without a sale. A buyer then asks the former listing agent what the seller's bottom-line price was. The agent should:
options: Disclose it, since all agency duties ended with the listing
Keep it confidential, because that duty survives the agency's end
Disclose it only if the buyer signs a buyer-agency agreement
Disclose it if the seller has not relisted the property
questions.explanation: Confidentiality continues after the agency ends. The former agent may not use or reveal the ex-client's confidential bargaining information.

questions.q: A seller's agent helps an unrepresented buyer fill in an offer form and describes the home's features. Does this, by itself, make the agent the buyer's agent?
options: Yes; helping fill in the offer form creates buyer agency
Yes; the agent automatically becomes a dual agent at that point
No; helping a customer does not by itself create buyer agency
No; but the agent must stop assisting the buyer immediately
questions.explanation: A seller's agent may give an unrepresented buyer factual help and stay the seller's agent. To avoid accidentally creating agency, the agent should explain their role and not coach the buyer's negotiating strategy.

questions.q: Which arrangement most closely fits a universal agency?
options: A broad power of attorney over all of the principal's affairs
An exclusive right to sell listing on one single-family home
A management agreement for a single apartment building
A salesperson's association with a sponsoring broker
questions.explanation: A universal agent may do anything the principal could lawfully delegate, usually under a broad power of attorney. A management agreement is the trap: it creates continuing but limited (general) authority over one property.
questions.citation: General agency law; GOL Art. 5, Title 15 (powers of attorney)

questions.q: Under a typical exclusive right to sell listing, the broker is a special agent. This means the broker ordinarily may NOT:
options: Sign a binding sale contract in the seller's name
Advertise the property to the public
Show the property to prospective buyers
Cooperate with other brokers as the listing allows
questions.explanation: A special agent is hired for one task, finding a ready, willing and able buyer, and cannot bind the principal to a contract without separate authority. Marketing, showing and authorized cooperation are within the listing's scope.

questions.q: A sponsored salesperson's relationship to the sponsoring broker is best described as:
options: Special agency limited to one transaction
Universal agency over all of the broker's affairs
General agency covering ongoing brokerage work
No agency, since the salesperson is a contractor
questions.explanation: The broker authorizes the salesperson to perform a continuing range of brokerage acts, which is general agency. Independent-contractor tax status does not erase the agency or the broker's supervision duty.

questions.q: An owner hires a broker to run her 40-unit building: collect rents, sign routine leases within set guidelines, and hire repair vendors. The broker is most likely a:
options: Special agent
Universal agent
Dual agent
General agent
questions.explanation: Ongoing authority to handle a range of matters for one principal, including binding her to routine leases, is general agency. It is not universal because it covers only the building's management, not all of her affairs.

questions.q: Ranked from MOST to LEAST authority, the three classifications of agency are:
options: General, universal, special
Universal, general, special
Special, general, universal
Universal, special, general
questions.explanation: Universal agents can do all the principal can delegate; general agents handle a range of matters in a defined area; special agents perform one specific act. A typical listing broker is the least-authority type, a special agent.

questions.q: Before a long deployment, Dana signs a power of attorney authorizing her brother only to sell her Albany condo and sign its closing papers. His authority is best described as:
options: Universal agency, as any power of attorney confers
Special agency limited to that one sale
General agency over all of Dana's financial affairs
Implied agency, because no listing was signed
questions.explanation: A power of attorney is only as broad as its terms; this one covers a single transaction, so it creates special agency. The trap is assuming every power of attorney makes the holder a universal agent.
questions.citation: General agency law; GOL Art. 5, Title 15

questions.q: A seller and a broker sign an exclusive listing stating the broker's duties, the term, and the commission. The agency was created by:
options: Implied agreement
Express agreement
Ratification
Estoppel
questions.explanation: Express agency is created by words, written or oral, that state the relationship; a signed listing is the clearest example. Implied agency, by contrast, is inferred from conduct when nothing was stated.

questions.q: A seller's agent repeatedly coaches an open-house visitor on bidding strategy and which inspection items to use as leverage, and she relies on the advice. The greatest risk is that:
options: An implied buyer agency arises, creating undisclosed dual agency
The listing agreement becomes void by operation of law
The agent becomes a broker's agent for the open-house visitor
The visitor must pay the agent a separate buyer's commission
questions.explanation: Conduct that shows the agent advising and advocating for the buyer can create an implied agency; because the agent already represents the seller, the result is undisclosed dual agency. A broker's agent works for another agent, not the consumer, so that distractor misuses the term.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443 (dual agency needs informed written consent)

questions.q: Without authority, a listing agent tells a buyer the dining set is included. The seller later learns of this, approves the promise, and signs a contract including the set. This illustrates agency by:
options: Ratification
Estoppel
Express grant
Operation of law
questions.explanation: Ratification occurs when a principal approves, after the fact, an act the agent had no authority to perform. Estoppel instead rests on a third party's reasonable reliance on the principal's conduct, not on later approval.

questions.q: An owner knows a licensee is telling buyers she is his listing agent, though no listing exists. He never corrects this, and a buyer relies on it. A court is most likely to find agency by:
options: Ratification
Express agreement
Gratuitous consent
Estoppel
questions.explanation: When a principal's silence or conduct lets a third party reasonably believe an agency exists, the law can bar the principal from denying it (agency by estoppel, from ostensible authority). Ratification would require the owner to approve a specific act after the fact.

questions.q: What is the key difference between agency by ratification and agency by estoppel?
options: Ratification needs the principal's later approval of an act
Estoppel needs a signed writing; ratification can be oral
Ratification arises only by operation of law after death
Estoppel binds the agent alone and never the principal
questions.explanation: Ratification turns on the principal approving an unauthorized act after it happens; estoppel turns on a third party's reasonable reliance on the principal's conduct. Neither depends on a signed writing, and estoppel binds the principal.

questions.q: As a favor and for no fee, a broker agrees to find a buyer for a friend's house. Which statement is correct?
options: No agency exists, because no fee will be paid to the broker
The broker owes only honesty and fair dealing, not loyalty
The friend is only a customer rather than a client
The broker still owes the friend full fiduciary duties
questions.explanation: Gratuitous agency is still agency: consent to act for the principal creates the fiduciary duties, whether or not a fee is paid. Compensation does not determine whether representation exists.

questions.q: A cooperating broker accepts an offer of subagency and is paid a share of the listing broker's commission. Whom does the subagent represent?
options: The seller, through the listing broker
The buyer the subagent brings to the sale
The listing broker alone, not the seller
No one, because the split is a referral fee
questions.explanation: A subagent is an agent of the agent and owes the original principal, the seller, the same fiduciary duties as the listing broker. Working for the listing agent but not the seller describes a broker's agent instead.

questions.q: A seller's written instructions require 24 hours' notice before any showing. A salesperson shows the house on one hour's notice to an out-of-town buyer. Which duty was breached?
options: Obedience
Accounting
Confidentiality
Reasonable care
questions.explanation: Obedience requires following the principal's lawful instructions, and a notice requirement for showings is lawful. Good intentions about a likely buyer do not excuse ignoring it.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of obedience)

questions.q: A listing agent learns the seller must relocate quickly and arranges for her spouse's LLC to buy the home, without telling the seller of the connection. Which duty is most directly breached?
options: Obedience
Accounting
Loyalty
Confidentiality
questions.explanation: Undisclosed self-dealing puts the agent's interest ahead of the client's, the core breach of loyalty. An agent buying directly or through a relative or entity must fully disclose the interest first.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of loyalty)

questions.q: A listing agent receives an offer well below asking and does not pass it along, believing the seller would reject it. The agent has breached the duty of:
options: Accounting
Obedience
Disclosure
Confidentiality
questions.explanation: Offers are material facts the client must receive; the decision to reject belongs to the seller, not the agent. Obedience is the trap: no seller instruction was involved.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of disclosure)

questions.q: A buyer's agent learns from public records that the seller's home is in foreclosure, suggesting the seller may accept a quick, lower offer. What should the agent do?
options: Keep it private as a courtesy to the seller
Share it with the buyer client as a material fact
Share it only if the seller's agent agrees
Disclose it only after a contract is signed
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent owes the buyer full disclosure of material facts, including facts that affect negotiating leverage. The seller is a customer to this agent, so there is no duty to protect the seller's bargaining position.
questions.citation: RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form (buyer's agent fiduciary duties)

questions.q: To show the buyer is serious, a buyer's agent tells the listing agent the client is preapproved for $150,000 more than the offer. Which duty did the buyer's agent violate?
options: Accounting
Reasonable care
Confidentiality
Disclosure
questions.explanation: The client's financial capacity is confidential bargaining information, and revealing it weakens the client's position. Disclosure runs to the client, so it is not the duty breached here.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of confidentiality)

questions.q: A salesperson keeps a buyer's $10,000 deposit check in a desk drawer for two weeks, then has it deposited in the broker's operating account. Which duty is most directly implicated?
options: Confidentiality
Obedience
Accounting
Loyalty
questions.explanation: Accounting requires safeguarding entrusted funds, handling them promptly, and keeping them in a proper escrow account, not mixed with business funds. Placing a deposit in the operating account is commingling.

questions.q: A buyer client asks whether a recorded utility easement will prevent her from building a garage. The buyer's agent best meets the duty of reasonable care by:
options: Assuring her that utility easements never limit building
Telling her the seller must remove the easement
Advising her to skip the title review to save time
Recommending that an attorney review the easement
questions.explanation: Reasonable care includes recognizing the limits of one's expertise and referring legal questions to an attorney. Assuring a client about a legal effect the agent has not verified is the trap.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of reasonable care)

questions.q: Which seller instruction must the listing agent refuse to follow?
options: Show the home only on weekends after 12 noon
Do not place any for-sale sign on the front lawn
Tell buyers the 25-year-old roof was just replaced
Send every offer to the seller by email right away
questions.explanation: Obedience extends only to lawful instructions; a false statement about the roof would be misrepresentation. Limits on showing times, signage, and how offers are delivered are lawful and must be followed.
questions.citation: General agency law (obedience limited to lawful instructions)

questions.q: Which duty does a seller's agent owe the seller but NOT an unrepresented buyer?
options: Honesty
Fair dealing
Undivided loyalty
Disclosure of known material defects
questions.explanation: Loyalty and the other fiduciary duties run only to the client. Customers are still owed honesty, fair dealing, and disclosure of known material facts affecting value or desirability.

questions.q: A buyer's agent steers a client away from a home that fits her needs because the listing firm offers a lower cooperating fee. This breaches the duty of:
options: Loyalty
Accounting
Confidentiality
Obedience
questions.explanation: Loyalty requires placing the client's interests ahead of the agent's own compensation. Choosing homes to show based on the fee rather than the buyer's needs reverses that priority.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of loyalty)

questions.q: Under New York's agency disclosure form, in dealings with a buyer, a seller's agent should disclose known facts that materially affect the property's:
options: Seller's lowest acceptable price
Seller's reasons for selling
Buyer's ability to obtain financing
Value or desirability
questions.explanation: The form directs a seller's agent dealing with a buyer to disclose known facts materially affecting value or desirability, except as otherwise provided by law. The seller's price floor and motives stay confidential.

questions.q: Under New York's agency disclosure form, in dealings with the seller, a buyer's agent should disclose known facts that materially affect:
options: The buyer's top price for the property
The buyer's ability or willingness to perform
The buyer's reasons for choosing this home
The value of other homes the buyer has seen
questions.explanation: The form's mirror-image rule: a buyer's agent should disclose facts materially affecting the buyer's ability and/or willingness to perform, consistent with its duties to the buyer. Value or desirability is the seller's-agent version of the rule.

questions.q: A buyer customer asks the listing agent, 'Will the seller take $20,000 less?' The seller has privately said yes. The best response is:
options: 'No, the seller won't take a penny less than list.'
'I can't share that; please submit your best offer.'
'Yes, the seller has already agreed to that price.'
'The seller would probably accept even less than that.'
questions.explanation: The agent must keep the seller's price confidential but may not lie to the buyer. Saying the seller won't budge is the trap: it protects the seller with a false statement, which is misrepresentation.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: A buyer works only with a salesperson who is a subagent of the seller. Who in the transaction represents the buyer's interests?
options: No one, unless the buyer hires an agent
The subagent, because the buyer chose him
The listing broker, acting as dual agent
The seller's attorney, by default
questions.explanation: A subagent represents the seller, so a buyer working only with one is an unrepresented customer. Choosing which licensee to work with does not make that licensee the buyer's agent.

questions.q: In agency terms, a customer is a party who:
options: Has signed a listing with the broker
Receives services but is not represented
Owes the agent fiduciary duties
Is represented by a designated agent
questions.explanation: A customer deals with the agent without an agency relationship and is owed honesty and fair dealing, not fiduciary duties. A client is the represented principal.

questions.q: Under RPL §443, which licensee could act as a broker's agent for the seller?
options: A salesperson employed by the listing broker's own firm
A buyer's agent at a cooperating firm working for a buyer
A licensee at a different firm engaged by the listing agent
The seller's own real estate attorney at the closing
questions.explanation: A broker's agent cooperates with or is engaged by the listing agent but does not work for the same firm. A salesperson in the listing firm is the trap; that person acts within the seller's agency, not as a broker's agent.

questions.q: A seller wants to cooperate with other firms but limit her own liability for their misstatements. The listing should authorize cooperation through:
options: Subagents only, under a blanket offer
Subagents and dual agents from other firms
Any licensee, since a seller is never liable
Broker's agents and buyer's agents, not subagents
questions.explanation: Under the disclosure form, sellers have no vicarious liability for a broker's agent, and a buyer's agent works for the buyer; a subagent's acts can be imputed to the seller. Rejecting subagency is how a seller limits that exposure.

questions.q: How should a licensee determine whether a cooperating broker represents the seller or the buyer?
options: By which party ultimately pays the commission
By the actual agreement and the disclosed role
By the cooperating broker's MLS membership
By which party first contacted the broker
questions.explanation: Representation comes from the agency agreement and disclosed role. Payment source, MLS participation, and who called first do not decide whom a cooperating broker represents.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: Salesperson Rosa works for the listing broker and shows that listing to unrepresented buyers. Whom does Rosa represent?
options: The seller, through her broker
The buyers, as their default agent
Neither party, acting as a facilitator
Both parties, acting as a dual agent
questions.explanation: The listing belongs to Rosa's broker, and Rosa acts for the broker, so she represents the seller. New York has no neutral facilitator role on the disclosure form, and dealing with buyers does not create dual agency.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: A seller wants to give showing instructions directly to a broker's agent from another firm. Under New York's disclosure form, the proper channel is:
options: Through the listing agent, who directs the broker's agent
Directly to the broker's agent in a signed written memo
Through the buyer, who then passes them along to the agent
Only through private remarks posted in the MLS listing
questions.explanation: The form says the seller cannot instruct or direct the broker's agent; the listing agent does, and so bears liability for the broker's agent's acts. Direct instruction from the seller would undercut that structure.

questions.q: A buyer's agent from Firm B shows Firm A's listing. What does the buyer's agent owe the seller?
options: Undivided loyalty, since the seller pays the fee
Full fiduciary duties, as the seller's subagent
Honesty, fair dealing, and reasonable skill and care
No duties at all, since the seller is not a client
questions.explanation: The form says a buyer's agent dealing with the seller should use reasonable skill and care, deal honestly, fairly and in good faith, and make the required disclosures. Fiduciary duties run only to the buyer, even if the fee comes from the seller.

questions.q: A buyer's agent in Buffalo engages a licensee from a Rochester firm to help locate homes there for the buyer client. The Rochester licensee is best described as:
options: A subagent of the seller
A designated sales agent
A dual agent for both sides
A broker's agent for the buyer
questions.explanation: A licensee from a different firm engaged by a buyer's agent to help locate property for that buyer is a broker's agent for the buyer. Designated sales agents exist only within one firm's consented dual agency.

questions.q: In a dual agency with designated sales agents, the buyer's designated agent may:
options: Share the seller's bottom line with the buyer
Act without supervision from the broker
Promise the buyer undivided loyalty
Advocate for and negotiate on behalf of the buyer
questions.explanation: With informed written consent, each designated agent represents and advocates for an assigned client in negotiations, under the broker's supervision. Undivided loyalty is still unavailable because the broker remains a dual agent.

questions.q: Which licensee can serve as a designated sales agent?
options: The principal broker of the dual-agent firm itself
A salesperson from a cooperating firm in the deal
An associate broker supervised by the firm's broker
An unlicensed assistant employed by the firm
questions.explanation: A designated sales agent is a salesperson or associate broker working under the supervision of the broker who represents both clients. The supervising principal broker is the dual agent and cannot also be a designee.

questions.q: A broker acting as a consensual dual agent without designated agents is asked by the buyer, 'What's the least the seller will take?' The broker should:
options: Answer, since dual agency waives confidentiality
Answer only if the seller is not present
Give an estimate based on the listing file
Decline, since each party's price stays confidential
questions.explanation: A dual agent must not reveal one principal's confidential information, such as price, to the other. Consent to dual agency gives up undivided loyalty, not confidentiality.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: A firm's buyer client wants to see a home listed by the same firm, and the seller refuses to consent to dual agency. Which option remains lawful?
options: The firm acts as dual agent, since the buyer consented
The firm appoints designated agents without the seller's consent
The firm treats the seller as a customer for this sale
The firm keeps the seller, and the buyer may seek other representation
questions.explanation: Dual agency, with or without designated agents, needs informed written consent from both parties. Without the seller's consent the firm cannot represent both sides; keeping the seller while the buyer gets other representation for this purchase is lawful.

questions.q: A broker acts as an undisclosed dual agent. Which consequence is most likely?
options: No consequence, if both parties were treated fairly
A fine, but only if the price was below the list price
Automatic conversion into a designated agency
License discipline and possible loss of the commission
questions.explanation: Undisclosed dual agency violates the license law and breaches both fiduciary relationships, exposing the broker to DOS discipline and forfeiture of the commission. Fair treatment or a good result does not cure the lack of consent.

questions.q: A broker wants to collect a fee from both the buyer and the seller in the same sale. This is permitted only if:
options: The combined fee stays under 6 percent
The broker's client knows and consents
The broker uses designated agents
The buyer's fee is paid at closing
questions.explanation: Under 19 NYCRR §175.7, a broker must make clear which party it acts for and may not take compensation from more than one party without the full knowledge and consent of the broker's client. Commission rates are negotiable, not capped by state law.

questions.q: Two designated agents in one firm represent opposite sides. The seller's designated agent asks the buyer's designated agent how high the buyer will go. The buyer's designated agent should:
options: Answer, since both work for the same broker
Answer only if the broker approves it
Refuse and keep the buyer's confidences
Answer, since designated agency waives confidentiality
questions.explanation: Designated agents advocate for their own clients and should keep those clients' confidences, even from colleagues. Sharing a broker does not make one client's bargaining information available to the other side.

questions.q: Before obtaining consent to dual agency, the agent must explain to the buyer and seller that:
options: The commission rate is fixed by state regulation
Designated agents would restore full undivided loyalty
The broker may share either party's price with the other
Each will give up the right to undivided loyalty
questions.explanation: The form requires the dual agent to explain that it acts for the other party and that consenting gives up undivided loyalty. Even designated agents cannot provide undivided loyalty.

questions.q: A listed house burns to the ground before any offer is accepted. How does this affect the listing agency?
options: It continues until the stated expiration date
It ends by operation of law, as the subject is destroyed
It ends only after the seller sends written notice
It automatically becomes a vacant-land listing
questions.explanation: Destruction of the subject matter makes performance impossible and terminates the agency by operation of law. No notice or new agreement is needed, and a listing of the land would require a new agreement.

questions.q: Halfway through a six-month exclusive listing, the seller revokes the broker's authority without cause. Which statement is correct?
options: The revocation is void until the term expires
The agency ends with no possible liability
The agency ends, but the seller may owe damages
Only the Department of State can end it
questions.explanation: A principal has the power to revoke an agent's authority at any time, but not always the right; revoking without cause can breach the listing contract. The agency still ends; the seller may owe damages or expenses.
questions.citation: General agency law (revocation: power vs. right)

questions.q: The salesperson who took a listing leaves her firm to join a competitor. What happens to the listing?
options: It moves with the salesperson to the new firm
It stays with the broker, who is the seller's agent
It ends automatically by operation of law
It becomes an open listing with both firms
questions.explanation: The listing contract is between the seller and the broker; the salesperson acted only for the broker. The salesperson's departure does not transfer or end it.

questions.q: A sole-proprietor broker holds a listing. Which event would end the listing by operation of law?
options: The death of the sole-proprietor broker
The death of the salesperson who took the listing
A sale of the house next door
The seller's move to another state
questions.explanation: Death of either the principal or the agent ends a personal agency by operation of law; here the broker is the agent. A salesperson is not a party to the listing, so the salesperson's death does not end it.

questions.q: A broker learns the seller insists on hiding a known defect from buyers and withdraws from the listing. This termination is best called:
options: Revocation by the principal
Ratification by the agent
Renunciation by the agent
Termination by operation of law
questions.explanation: An agent who gives up the agency renounces it; revocation is when the principal ends it. Withdrawing rather than taking part in concealment protects the broker from joining a misrepresentation.

questions.q: After a listing expires, the broker still holds the seller's house keys and a $500 marketing deposit owed back to the seller. Which duty requires their return?
options: Confidentiality
Accounting
Obedience
Loyalty
questions.explanation: Accounting requires an agent to account for and return the principal's money and property, and that duty continues after the agency ends. Confidentiality also survives, but it covers information, not keys or funds.
questions.citation: General agency law (fiduciary duty of accounting)

questions.q: While showing a listing, a salesperson falsely tells a buyer the home is on city sewer. Who may be held liable?
options: Only the salesperson, since the broker made no statement
Only the broker, since the salesperson acts for the firm
Only the seller, since he owns the home being shown
The salesperson and, vicariously, the sponsoring broker
questions.explanation: The salesperson is liable for her own misrepresentation, and the broker can be vicariously liable for acts of a licensee working on its behalf. The broker's liability adds to the salesperson's; it does not replace it.
questions.citation: General agency law (respondeat superior / vicarious liability)

questions.q: Vicarious liability means a person is liable for:
options: Only his own intentional wrongdoing in the transaction
Any unpaid debt of any party to the transaction
The acts of those acting with authority on his behalf
Defects already disclosed on the condition disclosure
questions.explanation: Vicarious liability imputes an agent's wrongful acts, done within the agency, to the principal. It is why a seller is exposed to a subagent's misstatements but not, under the NY form, to a broker's agent's.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: A seller's subagent at a cooperating firm misrepresents the home's school district to a buyer. Can the buyer pursue the seller?
options: No, only the listing broker can ever be liable
No, unless the seller personally made the statement
Yes, a principal is vicariously liable for subagents
Yes, but only if the seller paid the subagent directly
questions.explanation: A subagent acts for the seller, so its misrepresentations within the agency can be imputed to the seller. The disclosure form's no-vicarious-liability rule applies to broker's agents, not subagents.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: Which statement by a listing agent is most likely puffing rather than misrepresentation?
options: 'This kitchen gets the best light on the block.'
'The roof was replaced in the summer of 2022.'
'Annual property taxes here are $6,200.'
'The lot is legally zoned for two families.'
questions.explanation: Puffing is exaggerated opinion that a reasonable buyer would not treat as fact. Roof age, tax amount, and zoning are verifiable facts, so a false version of any of them is misrepresentation.

questions.q: Which set of facts best describes actionable fraud?
options: A knowingly false material statement, relied on, causing loss
An honest opinion of value that later proves too high
A true statement that the buyer later misunderstands
A sincere prediction that prices will rise next year
questions.explanation: Fraud requires a knowingly false statement or concealment of a material fact, justifiable reliance, and resulting damage. Honest opinions, true statements, and predictions lack the knowing falsity of a present fact.

questions.q: A listing agent enters 2,400 square feet in the MLS from the seller's guess, without checking records that show 1,850. A buyer relies on the figure. Which is the most accurate characterization?
options: Puffing, because square footage is merely an opinion figure
No breach at all, since the seller supplied the number
Fraud, but only if the buyer was the agent's own client
Negligent misrepresentation; the agent should have verified
questions.explanation: An agent who states a material fact carelessly, when readily available records would have shown it was wrong, can be liable for negligent misrepresentation. Passing along the seller's number is no defense when the agent had reason to verify it.

questions.q: Before showings, a listing agent has fresh paint applied over a ceiling stain from an active roof leak and says nothing. This is best described as:
options: Puffing
Fraud by active concealment
Permissible staging
Innocent misrepresentation
questions.explanation: Deliberately hiding a known material defect is fraud by concealment, even without a spoken lie. Staging improves appearance; it may not hide a defect the agent knows exists.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: To hurry a buyer, a listing agent says, 'We have three other offers,' when there are none. This is:
options: Acceptable puffing about the strength of market demand
Misrepresentation that breaches honesty to the buyer
Proper loyalty to the seller who wants a quick sale
Allowed as long as the seller approved the statement
questions.explanation: Inventing competing offers is a false statement of fact, not opinion, and violates the honesty owed to customers. Loyalty to the seller never permits lying, and a seller's approval does not make it lawful.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: A buyer customer asks the listing agent whether the septic system has ever failed. The agent does not know. The best response is:
options: Say it never failed, since no failure was reported
Say she doesn't know and offer to ask the seller
Say septic history is confidential seller information
Say she is barred from answering septic questions
questions.explanation: Honesty means not stating facts the agent doesn't know; saying 'I don't know' and following up is correct. Defect history is a material fact, not protected confidential information.
questions.citation: General agency law; RPL §443; DOS-1736 disclosure form

questions.q: A seller's agent knowingly gives a buyer customer a false flood-zone status, reasoning that the buyer is not her client. Which statement is correct?
options: She is liable, since honesty is owed to customers too
She is protected, since her duties run only to clients
She is liable only if the buyer signed a contract
She is protected if the seller told her to say it
questions.explanation: Agents owe customers honesty and fair dealing; 'not my client' is never a license to misrepresent. A seller's instruction to lie is unlawful and is no defense.

questions.q: A salesperson meets a couple who want her firm to represent them in finding a house to buy. When must she give them the agency disclosure form?
options: Before they sign an agreement for her firm to act as their buyer's agent
After they sign the buyer agency agreement, within 3 business days
When they make their first written offer on a specific property
At the closing, together with the final commission statement
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent must provide the form to the buyer before entering into an agreement to act as the buyer's agent and obtain a signed acknowledgment. Waiting until an offer is too late: by then the buyer has already shared confidential needs and finances without understanding the relationship.

questions.q: Salesperson Ortiz represents a buyer under a written agreement. She calls the owner of a for-sale-by-owner single-family home and begins discussing a showing and the owner's terms. What does RPL §443 require of Ortiz regarding the owner?
options: Nothing, because only a seller's own agent must disclose to a seller
Provide the disclosure form to the owner at this first substantive contact
Provide the form only if the owner later agrees to pay her commission
Provide the form to the owner after the contract of sale is signed
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent must give the form to the seller (or seller's agent) at the first substantive contact with the seller and obtain a signed acknowledgment. The duty runs to the other party too, and it does not depend on who pays the commission.

questions.q: A buyer's agent from Firm X arranges a showing through the listing agent at Firm Y. Under RPL §443, from whom may the buyer's agent obtain the signed acknowledgment on the seller's side?
options: Only from the sponsoring broker of the buyer's agent's firm
Only from the seller personally, never the listing agent
From either the seller or the seller's listing agent
From the buyer, who signs on behalf of both principals
questions.explanation: The statute directs a buyer's agent to obtain a signed acknowledgment from the seller, landlord, or the listing agent. The trap is assuming the seller must always sign personally; when a listing agent is involved, that agent may acknowledge receipt.

questions.q: A listing agent gets a call from a buyer's agent at another firm who wants details about the listing for her client. Under RPL §443, to whom may the listing agent provide the disclosure form at this first substantive contact?
options: To no one, because the buyer already has an agent
Only to the buyer, in person, at a showing
Only to the seller, who forwards it to the buyer
To the buyer or to the buyer's agent
questions.explanation: A seller's agent must provide the form to a buyer, buyer's agent, tenant, or tenant's agent at the first substantive contact. A buyer having her own agent does not excuse the listing agent's disclosure of whom it represents.

questions.q: At an open house, a visitor signs the guest register, walks through quickly, and leaves after asking only what year the house was built. Has a first substantive contact occurred that requires the agency disclosure form?
options: Not yet; a brief walk-through with a general question is not substantive
Yes; signing the open house register is itself the first substantive contact
Yes; any visitor who enters a listed home must sign the form at the door
Not yet; disclosure is required only once a written offer is presented
questions.explanation: Substantive contact begins when the conversation turns to the visitor's specific needs, finances, motivation, or a possible offer, not with a casual walk-through or general question. The 'written offer' choice is wrong because disclosure must come at the first substantive discussion, well before any offer.

questions.q: A caller asks a listing salesperson only whether a ranch house is still available and what the asking price is. What does RPL §443 require at this point?
options: Immediate mailing of the form, since any phone call is a substantive contact
Nothing yet, because general listing questions are not substantive contact
An oral reading of the full form, followed by the caller's verbal consent
A sworn declaration stating that the caller did not sign the acknowledgment
questions.explanation: Answering general questions such as availability and price is not a first substantive contact, so the form is not yet due. A refusal declaration applies only when a party who has been given the form refuses to sign the acknowledgment.

questions.q: During a phone call, a prospective buyer starts telling a listing salesperson her maximum price and how urgently she must move. What is the salesperson's best course?
options: Tell the caller she is neutral and will help both sides get a fair price
Keep gathering the information, since phone calls are exempt from §443
Explain that she represents the seller, then deliver the form for acknowledgment
Wait until the buyer submits an offer, then provide the disclosure form
questions.explanation: Once the buyer's finances and motivation come up, the contact is substantive, so the seller's agent must disclose her role and provide the form for signed acknowledgment. Claiming neutrality is a misrepresentation: as the seller's agent she owes the seller full disclosure of what the buyer says.

questions.q: A buyer with no agent walks into a brokerage and asks a salesperson to show her three listed homes that afternoon. The firm represents the sellers of all three. When must the salesperson give her the DOS-1736?
options: Not at all, because the buyer remains a customer, not a client
After the showings, if the buyer wants to make an offer on one
Only if the buyer later signs a buyer agency agreement with the firm
Now, at this first substantive meeting, before showing the homes
questions.explanation: A seller's agent must provide the form to a buyer at the first substantive contact, and a walk-in who asks to see specific homes has reached that point. Unrepresented customers are exactly the people the form is meant to inform; the 'before agreement' timing applies only if the firm becomes her buyer's agent.

questions.q: Which property's sale is covered by the RPL §443 agency disclosure requirement?
options: A unit in a 300-unit condominium tower
An eight-unit rental apartment building
A vacant two-acre lot zoned for one house
A small office building with two tenants
questions.explanation: Residential real property under §443 means property improved by a one-to-four-family dwelling or by condominium or cooperative apartments, regardless of building size. An eight-unit rental building exceeds four units and is not a condo or co-op, so it is outside the definition.

questions.q: A buyer plans to build a single-family home on a vacant lot. Does that intended use bring the lot's sale under RPL §443?
options: Yes; land intended for a residence counts as residential real property
No; unimproved land is excluded even if a home will be built on it
Yes, but only if the lot is in a subdivision with a recorded plat
No, unless the buyer will finance the purchase with a mortgage
questions.explanation: The statute's definition expressly excludes unimproved real property upon which dwellings are to be constructed. The buyer's plan to build does not convert raw land into covered residential property.

questions.q: A licensee lists two properties: a four-family house and a five-family house, neither of them a condo or co-op. For which does RPL §443 require the agency disclosure form?
options: Both, since each is residential
The five-family house only
The four-family house only
Neither, since both produce rent
questions.explanation: Coverage stops at one-to-four-family dwellings (plus condo and co-op units). A five-family house is residential in use but falls outside the statutory definition; producing rent does not remove the four-family house from coverage.

questions.q: A licensee is selling the shares and proprietary lease for a cooperative apartment. Does RPL §443 apply?
options: Yes, but only if the co-op building has four or fewer units
No; co-op shares are personal property, not real property
No; the co-op board's approval replaces the disclosure
Yes; co-op apartments are expressly included
questions.explanation: §443 expressly covers condominium and cooperative apartments, in a building of any size. Although co-op ownership is technically shares plus a lease, the statute names co-op apartments, so the disclosure applies.

questions.q: A licensee represents the seller of a vacant commercial lot. Which disclosure applies at first substantive contact with a prospective buyer?
options: The fair housing disclosure (DOS-2156), but not the agency form
The agency disclosure form (DOS-1736), but not the fair housing form
Both the agency disclosure form and the fair housing disclosure
Neither form, because commercial land is exempt from both rules
questions.explanation: The agency form is limited to 1–4-family residential and condo/co-op units, so vacant commercial land is outside §443. The fair housing disclosure under 19 NYCRR §175.28 applies to all real property, including commercial and vacant land.

questions.q: Under RPL §443, the agency disclosure requirement does NOT apply to a licensee who:
options: Works only with buyers and never takes listings from sellers
Works with a party, by agreement, in a capacity other than as an agent
Is a salesperson rather than a broker or associate broker
Shows homes only as a cooperating agent on another firm's listings
questions.explanation: Subdivision 5 excludes a licensee who works with a buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord under agreed terms in a capacity other than as an agent. Salespersons, buyer's agents, and cooperating agents acting as agents remain fully covered.

questions.q: A licensee represents a landlord leasing retail space in a strip mall. Is the DOS-1735 landlord/tenant disclosure required?
options: Yes, because any lease over three years must include the form
Yes; DOS-1735 applies to every lease negotiated by a licensee
No; DOS-1735 covers only residential real property leasing
No, because only sales of property, never leases, require it
questions.explanation: §443 applies only to transactions involving residential real property, so a retail lease is outside it. Leases are not exempt as such: residential leasing within the definition does require DOS-1735.

questions.q: What statement appears prominently at the top of both New York agency disclosure forms?
options: Read carefully before signing any listing
This form must be reviewed by an attorney
This form creates an agency relationship
This is not a contract
questions.explanation: Both DOS-1736 and DOS-1735 are headed 'THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT.' The forms explain relationships; they do not themselves create an agency or bind the signer.

questions.q: The DOS-1736 lists the fiduciary duties a seller's agent owes the seller. Which is NOT one of them?
options: Impartiality toward buyer and seller
Undivided loyalty to the seller
Accounting for funds and property
Confidentiality of seller information
questions.explanation: The form lists reasonable care, undivided loyalty, confidentiality, full disclosure, obedience, and duty to account. Impartiality between the parties is the opposite of a seller's agent's role.

questions.q: According to the DOS-1736, in dealings with a buyer, a seller's agent should disclose:
options: The lowest price the seller has said he would accept for the property
Known facts materially affecting the property's value or desirability
Every fact the agent knows about the seller's finances and motives
Only those facts the seller has authorized in writing to be released
questions.explanation: The form says a seller's agent dealing with a buyer should use reasonable skill and care, deal honestly and in good faith, and disclose known facts materially affecting value or desirability, except as otherwise provided by law. The seller's bottom price and motives stay confidential.

questions.q: According to the DOS-1736, in dealings with the seller, a buyer's agent should disclose known facts materially affecting:
options: The buyer's reasons for choosing this particular home
The highest price the buyer is prepared to pay
The buyer's ability or willingness to perform the contract
The commission split agreed with the listing broker
questions.explanation: A buyer's agent should disclose facts materially affecting the buyer's ability and/or willingness to perform, to the extent not inconsistent with fiduciary duties to the buyer. The buyer's top price is confidential client information.

questions.q: A buyer working with her own buyer's agent receives one DOS-1736 from that agent and another from the listing agent. Why?
options: The listing agent's form is a counteroffer that requires her signature
The second form cancels the first and makes the listing agent her agent
Two forms are needed whenever the price is more than $1 million
Each agent assisting in the transaction may be required to present one
questions.explanation: The form itself warns that a consumer may receive more than one disclosure because the law may require each agent assisting in the transaction to present it. Receiving the listing agent's form discloses that agent's seller relationship; it does not change who represents the buyer.

questions.q: A seller asks his listing agent whether the sale will trigger capital gains tax. The DOS-1736 itself advises consumers that for legal or tax advice they should:
options: Consult a professional in that field
Rely on the listing agent's opinion
Ask the Department of State in writing
Ask the buyer's agent for a second view
questions.explanation: The form states that a real estate agent is qualified to advise about real estate, and that for legal, tax, or other advice the consumer should consult a professional in that field.

questions.q: Which relationship can a licensee NOT indicate by checking a box on the DOS-1736?
options: Broker's agent for the buyer
Transaction broker or facilitator
Dual agent with designated sales agents
Seller's agent for the seller
questions.explanation: The form's boxes cover seller's agent, buyer's agent, broker's agent (for either side), dual agent, and dual agent with designated sales agents. New York's form has no transaction-broker or facilitator category.

questions.q: On the DOS-1736, whose signature appears on the acknowledgment line?
options: The sponsoring broker of the licensee's firm
The licensee who presented the form
The buyer or seller who received the form
A notary public witnessing the delivery
questions.explanation: The buyer and/or seller sign to acknowledge receipt of a copy; the licensee prints his or her name and firm in the 'provided to me by' section. No notary is involved in ordinary delivery.

questions.q: Which pair of agent roles is described on DOS-1735 but not on DOS-1736?
options: Designated sales agent and dual agent
Seller's agent and buyer's agent
Broker's agent and dual agent
Landlord's agent and tenant's agent
questions.explanation: DOS-1735, the landlord and tenant form, defines landlord's agent and tenant's agent. Broker's agent, dual agent, and dual agent with designated sales agents appear on both forms.

questions.q: Salesperson Pat works for the same firm as the listing agent and helps find a buyer for the listing. Under the §443 definitions, is Pat a broker's agent?
options: No; a broker's agent does not work for the listing agent's firm
Yes; any licensee who assists the listing agent is a broker's agent
Yes, as long as Pat receives part of the commission from the seller
No; only a licensed broker, not a salesperson, can be a broker's agent
questions.explanation: A broker's agent cooperates with or is engaged by a listing, buyer's, or tenant's agent but does not work for the same firm. Pat is simply part of the listing firm; 'agent' under §443 includes salespersons, so the license-type choice is wrong.

questions.q: After a seller signs the acknowledgment on the agency disclosure form, what must the agent do with it?
options: File the original with the Department of State within 10 days
Give the seller a copy and keep a copy at least three years
Keep it only until the listing agreement expires or is cancelled
Return it to the seller and keep no copy, since it isn't a contract
questions.explanation: The agent must give the party a copy of the signed acknowledgment and maintain a copy for not less than three years. The form is not filed with DOS, and 'not a contract' does not mean no record is required.

questions.q: Before signing an exclusive right to rent, a landlord refuses to sign the acknowledgment on the DOS-1735 the agent just gave him. Which document must the agent prepare?
options: A letter to DOS requesting a waiver of the acknowledgment requirement
A note on the form initialed by the agent and a second licensee as witness
A written declaration of the facts of the refusal, made under oath or affirmation
A new form marked 'refused' and mailed to the landlord for signature
questions.explanation: When a seller, buyer, landlord, or tenant refuses to sign, the agent must set forth under oath or affirmation a written declaration of the facts of the refusal and keep a copy for at least three years. An initialed note or witness signature is not the statutory declaration.

questions.q: A prospective buyer refuses to sign the acknowledgment after the seller's agent explains the form. Which statement is correct?
options: The agent may treat the form as never given and need not record it
The agent must stop all contact with the buyer until the buyer signs
The refusal makes the buyer a client of the seller's agent by law
The agent records the refusal as required and may keep working with her
questions.explanation: A refusal is handled by the sworn or affirmed written declaration, retained for three years; it does not bar further dealings. The refusal changes nothing about representation, and it cannot simply be ignored.

questions.q: Which document sets the commission and term of a seller's listing?
options: The listing agreement with the broker
The DOS-1736 agency disclosure form
The seller's property condition disclosure
The DOS-2156 fair housing disclosure
questions.explanation: Compensation and duration are contract terms set in the listing agreement. The agency disclosure form only explains relationships and is 'not a contract'; the PCDS and fair housing form serve other purposes.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the agency disclosure form with a buyer agency agreement?
options: The form sets the buyer's fee; the agreement only explains agency roles
The form explains possible relationships; the agreement creates binding terms
Both are contracts, but only the agreement must be signed by the buyer
Signing either one obligates the buyer to pay the firm a commission
questions.explanation: The disclosure form informs the consumer about agency relationships and its signature only acknowledges receipt. The buyer agency agreement is the contract that sets duties, duration, and compensation.

questions.q: Does compliance with RPL §443 replace the common law of agency in New York residential transactions?
options: Yes; the form replaces any duties arising from an agent's conduct
Yes; once the form is signed, only its listed duties apply
No; §443 does not limit or alter common-law agency duties
No, but the common law applies only to commercial transactions
questions.explanation: The statute expressly states that nothing in §443 limits or alters the common law of agency for residential transactions. Delivering the form satisfies a disclosure duty but does not displace fiduciary obligations or agency created by conduct.

questions.q: A seller gave advance informed consent to dual agency when she listed. Later, a buyer client of the same firm wants to make an offer. What has the seller's advance consent accomplished?
options: The firm may now act for both sides without explaining dual agency
The buyer's consent is no longer needed for the firm to act
The seller regains the right to undivided loyalty from the firm
The seller's written consent to dual agency is already in place
questions.explanation: Advance consent indicated on the form supplies the seller's informed written consent ahead of time, so the in-house offer can proceed once the buyer also consents in writing. Dual agency still means giving up undivided loyalty and requires the dual agent's careful explanation to both parties.

questions.q: According to the disclosure form, by consenting to dual agency the buyer and seller give up their right to:
options: Undivided loyalty from the broker
Confidentiality of all information
Honest and fair dealing by the broker
Reasonable care and skill by the broker
questions.explanation: The form explains that by consenting to dual agency the buyer and seller give up their right to undivided loyalty. Honest dealing and reasonable care are still owed, and a dual agent must not disclose one party's confidential information to the other.

questions.q: Under RPL §443, advance consent to dual agency with designated sales agents is written informed consent that:
options: Names both designated agents and sets each one's commission split
Names the agent appointed to represent that consenting party
Lets the broker choose a designee after the contract is signed
Transfers the listing to another firm if dual agency arises
questions.explanation: The statute defines it as written informed consent indicating the name of the agent appointed to represent that seller/landlord or buyer/tenant as a designated sales agent. The other side's designee need not be known yet, and commission splits are not part of it.

questions.q: Broker-owner Diaz personally holds a listing. A buyer client of her salesperson Lee wants the home. Both parties consent to dual agency with designated sales agents, and Lee is designated for the buyer. Who may be designated to represent the seller?
options: Lee, who can serve as designee for both sides
Diaz, because she personally took the listing
Another salesperson or associate broker at the firm
A broker's agent from a different firm
questions.explanation: A designated sales agent is a salesperson or associate broker working under the supervising broker; the broker remains the dual agent and cannot be a designee. One person cannot be the designee for both sides, and a broker's agent by definition works for another firm.

questions.q: With both parties' informed written consent, the broker designates Salesperson Ruiz to represent the buyer. During negotiations, Ruiz may:
options: Negotiate for both principals at the same time
Share the seller's bottom line with the buyer
Give the buyer undivided loyalty like a single agent
Advocate for the buyer on price and terms
questions.explanation: The form states the buyer's designated sales agent functions as the buyer's agent, representing and advocating for the buyer in negotiations. Ruiz still cannot provide undivided loyalty, and must not reveal the seller's confidential information.

questions.q: According to the disclosure form, what must a dual agent carefully explain to both the buyer and the seller?
options: That the agent is also acting for the other party
That the agent guarantees each a fair market price
That the agent may disclose either party's bottom line
That neither party may seek independent legal advice
questions.explanation: The form requires a dual agent to explain carefully to both parties that the agent is acting for the other party as well, and the possible effects, including loss of undivided loyalty. Revealing either side's bottom line would breach confidentiality.

questions.q: Salesperson Kay lists a condo, and her own buyer client wants to buy it. Both give informed written consent to dual agency. Which statement is accurate?
options: Kay must withdraw, because one licensee can never serve both parties
The firm acts as dual agent; Kay cannot give either one undivided loyalty
Kay becomes a designated sales agent for both principals at once
Kay may keep advocating fully for the buyer, since the buyer came first
questions.explanation: With both parties' informed written consent, New York permits dual agency, including one licensee working with both sides, but neither party receives undivided loyalty. Designated agency requires two different designees, one per party.

questions.q: Firm Q has an exclusive right to rent an apartment in a two-family house and also represents a tenant who wants that unit. What is required for Firm Q to represent both?
options: Only the tenant's consent, since tenant agency came first
Only the landlord's consent, since the landlord pays the fee
Informed written consent of both landlord and tenant
No consent, because dual agency rules apply only to sales
questions.explanation: A dual agent includes one acting as tenant's agent and landlord's agent in the same transaction, and DOS-1735 requires both parties' informed written consent. Who pays or who signed first does not substitute for either consent.

questions.q: When listing, a seller leaves the advance informed consent boxes on the DOS-1736 unchecked. What is the effect?
options: The seller has automatically consented to dual agency with designees
The listing agreement is void, because dual agency consent is mandatory
The firm must refer all in-house buyers to the Department of State
The firm cannot act as dual agent unless the seller later consents in writing
questions.explanation: Advance consent is optional. Without it, the firm may act as a dual agent only if the seller (and the buyer) later gives informed written consent; the listing itself remains valid.

questions.q: A landlord's agent meets a prospective tenant to show a co-op unit available for rent, and they discuss the tenant's move-in date and budget. What must the agent do?
options: Give DOS-1735 now and get the tenant's signed acknowledgment
Give DOS-1736, since co-op units are treated as sales property
Give no form, because tenants never receive agency disclosures
Give DOS-1735 only after the tenant has signed the lease
questions.explanation: A landlord's agent must provide the disclosure to a tenant at the first substantive contact and obtain a signed acknowledgment; discussing budget and timing is substantive. For a rental, the landlord/tenant form (DOS-1735) is the correct one even for a co-op unit.

questions.q: A renter asks a salesperson to sign an exclusive agreement to find her an apartment in a three-family house. When must the salesperson give her DOS-1735?
options: After the tenant agency agreement is signed
Before entering into the tenant agency agreement
When the tenant applies for a specific unit
When the lease is signed and the fee is paid
questions.explanation: A tenant's agent must provide the form to the tenant before entering into an agreement to act as the tenant's agent, and obtain a signed acknowledgment. Giving it after the agreement reverses the required order.

questions.q: In New York City, a salesperson lists an apartment under an agreement with the landlord. A tenant rents it without hiring any agent of her own. Who may be charged the listing agent's fee?
options: The tenant and landlord, split equally
The tenant, who benefited from the showing
The landlord, who engaged the listing agent
Whoever the lease names, if the tenant agrees
questions.explanation: Under the NYC FARE Act, effective June 11, 2025, a broker fee for an agent who represents the landlord cannot be passed on to the tenant. The landlord who hired the listing agent pays, and a lease clause shifting the fee does not make it lawful.

questions.q: According to DOS-1735, in dealings with a prospective tenant, a landlord's agent should:
options: Disclose the landlord's minimum acceptable rent if asked
Advocate for the lowest rent the landlord would accept
Keep material defects confidential at the landlord's request
Deal honestly and disclose known material facts about the property
