questions.explanation: The form says a landlord's agent dealing with a tenant should exercise reasonable skill and care, deal honestly, fairly and in good faith, and disclose known facts materially affecting value or desirability. The landlord's minimum rent remains confidential.

questions.q: An owner rents the upstairs unit of her two-family house directly to a tenant, with no licensee involved. Must she give the tenant DOS-1735?
options: No; the duty falls on licensees acting as agents, not on owners
Yes; every residential landlord must give tenants DOS-1735
Yes, but only if the lease term is longer than one year
No, unless the building is a condominium or co-op unit
questions.explanation: §443 imposes the disclosure duty on agents, meaning licensees acting in a fiduciary capacity. An owner dealing directly with a tenant has no agency relationship to disclose.

questions.q: A seller's elderly father died of natural causes in the house last year. Under RPL §443-a, this fact is:
options: A material defect that must appear on the PCDS
Not a material defect or fact under the statute
A material fact the seller's agent must disclose
A latent defect that lets a buyer rescind later
questions.explanation: §443-a provides that the property being the site of a death by natural or accidental causes is not a material defect or fact. No cause of action arises for failing to disclose it.

questions.q: A buyer who is making a bona fide offer wants to know whether a homicide ever occurred in the house. Under RPL §443-a, how may the buyer seek the information?
options: Request a police report through the seller's listing broker
Demand an oral answer that the seller must give within 10 days
Submit a written inquiry, delivered to the seller's agent
Ask DOS to order the seller to disclose under oath
questions.explanation: A buyer may, when negotiating or making a bona fide offer, submit a written inquiry; the buyer or buyer's agent gives it to the seller's agent, or to the seller if there is none. The seller may choose whether to respond.

questions.q: After a buyer's written inquiry about a past suicide in the house, the seller tells the listing agent she does not want to answer. What should the agent do?
options: Report the seller to DOS for withholding facts
Answer the inquiry herself from what she knows
Withdraw from the listing until the seller answers
Respect it, since the seller may choose not to respond
questions.explanation: The statute lets the seller choose whether to respond, and the seller's agent reports information only with the seller's consent and subject to privacy laws. Answering on her own would violate the seller's choice and her confidentiality duty.

questions.q: A house was raided years ago as an illegal drug lab, and the listing agent knows chemical residue was never cleaned up. How should the residue be treated?
options: As a physical condition the agent must disclose, not exempt stigma
As exempt stigma, since the property was the site of a felony
As a fact a buyer may learn only through a written inquiry
As confidential, because the seller did not cause the crime
questions.explanation: §443-a covers only the stigma of the crime itself, not physical conditions it left behind. Known contamination materially affects value and safety, so the seller's agent must disclose it; labeling it 'stigma' does not hide a defect.
questions.citation: RPL §443-a(1)(b); common-law duty to disclose known material defects

questions.q: Under RPL §443-a, the fact that a prior owner had AIDS is:
options: A material fact the listing agent must disclose to buyers
Not a material fact, and privacy laws limit any disclosure
Disclosable only if the buyer asks orally at a showing
A defect that must be noted on the property condition form
questions.explanation: An owner or occupant having HIV/AIDS, or another disease highly unlikely to be transmitted through occupancy, is not a material defect or fact. Any response to a written inquiry is subject to the seller's consent and applicable privacy laws.

questions.q: An agent is leasing apartments in a 60-unit rental building where a tenant died last year. Does RPL §443-a protect the agent from a claim for not disclosing the death?
options: No; §443-a applies only to sales, never to leases
No; §443-a follows §443 and covers only one-to-four-family homes
Yes; §443-a covers sales and leases regardless of number of units
Yes, but only if the death occurred more than three years ago
questions.explanation: Unlike the §443 agency form, §443-a applies to property offered for sale or lease, including residential property regardless of the number of units. The fine distinction is that the two sections have different scopes.

questions.q: Under RPL §443-a, an agent's failure to disclose that a property was the site of a suicide is:
options: Grounds for a fine only if the sale closes
Grounds for license suspension for a first offense
A misdemeanor if the buyer asked in writing
Not grounds for disciplinary action against the licensee
questions.explanation: The statute provides that failing to disclose a §443-a fact to a transferee is not grounds for disciplinary action against a licensed broker or salesperson, and no cause of action arises from it.

questions.q: A town passes a local law requiring sellers' agents to disclose any death in a house within the past 10 years. How does RPL §443-a affect it?
options: §443-a preempts the inconsistent local law
The local law controls within that town
Both apply; the stricter rule always wins
The local law applies only to co-op units
questions.explanation: §443-a states that it preempts any local law inconsistent with its provisions. A local mandate to disclose deaths conflicts with the state rule that a death is not a material fact.

questions.q: At a showing, a buyer casually asks the listing agent, 'Did anyone die in this house?' A prior owner died there. What is the agent's best response?
options: Say no one died, since a death is not a material fact
Avoid any false answer and explain the written-inquiry route
Disclose the full details immediately without the seller
Refuse to continue showing the house to this buyer
questions.explanation: §443-a removes a duty to volunteer the fact, not the duty of honesty, so the agent must not lie. The statutory route is a written inquiry to the seller's agent, and the seller decides whether to answer.

questions.q: In Stambovsky v. Ackley, a New York court let a buyer rescind a purchase because the seller had:
options: Hidden a structural defect behind newly painted drywall
Failed to tell the buyer a prior owner had died in the house
Publicly promoted the house as haunted but did not tell the buyer
Refused to answer a written inquiry about a past felony
questions.explanation: The seller had reported poltergeists in national and local publications, creating the house's haunted reputation, and then kept silent with an out-of-town buyer, so the court allowed rescission. A death alone would not be a material fact under §443-a.

questions.q: A buyer's home inspection revealed a failing septic system, and that buyer walked away. The listing agent now shows the house to a new buyer customer. What must the agent do?
options: Keep quiet unless the seller gives written permission
Keep quiet, since the report belonged to the first buyer
Disclose it only if the new buyer orders an inspection
Disclose the known septic failure to the new buyer
questions.explanation: Once the agent knows of a material defect, it must be disclosed to buyers no matter how the agent learned of it. Confidentiality protects a client's private information, not concealment of physical defects.
questions.citation: RPL §443(4) (seller's agent duty to buyer); common-law misrepresentation

questions.q: A seller tells his listing agent he has accepted a job in Ohio and must sell within 60 days. A buyer customer asks why the seller is moving. The agent should:
options: Decline to share it, since the seller's motivation is confidential
Reveal the deadline, since it is a material fact about the property
Reveal it, since a seller's agent owes buyers full disclosure
Reveal it, but only after the buyer signs the disclosure form
questions.explanation: The seller's motivation and deadline are confidential information that would weaken his negotiating position; they are not facts about the property's value or desirability. Full disclosure is owed to the client, not to the customer.

questions.q: A buyer tells her buyer's agent she would pay up to $25,000 more than her offer. The listing agent asks whether the buyer can go higher. The buyer's agent should:
options: Disclose it, as a fact about ability to perform
Keep the buyer's top price confidential
Disclose it, since honesty to the seller requires it
Disclose it if the seller pays the buyer's agent
questions.explanation: The buyer's maximum price is confidential client information. A buyer's agent's disclosure duty to the seller covers facts on the buyer's ability or willingness to perform only to the extent not inconsistent with fiduciary duties to the buyer, and who pays the fee does not change loyalty.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the RPL §443 agency disclosure form?
options: To disclose the physical condition of the property to buyers
To create a binding agency contract with the brokerage firm
To tell consumers whom the agent represents and what that means
To notify consumers of their rights under fair housing laws
questions.explanation: The form advises consumers of the nature of the agent's relationship and the rights and obligations it creates so they can make informed choices. Property condition and fair housing have their own separate disclosures.

questions.q: Which New York deed gives the grantee the greatest protection, containing covenants of seisin, quiet enjoyment, against encumbrances, further assurances, and warranty of title?
options: Full covenant and warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts
Quitclaim deed
Referee's deed
questions.explanation: The full covenant and warranty deed carries all five statutory covenants and is the strongest deed for a grantee. A bargain and sale deed with covenants only promises the grantor did nothing to encumber the property.

questions.q: In a typical New York residential sale, the seller's deed states only that the grantor has not done anything to encumber the property. Which deed is this?
options: Full covenant and warranty deed
Bargain and sale deed without covenant against grantor's acts
Bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts
Quitclaim deed
questions.explanation: The bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts implies the grantor holds title and promises only that the grantor has not encumbered it. It is the deed most commonly used in NY residential closings, but it gives no warranty against defects created by earlier owners.

questions.q: A title search shows a former owner's nephew may have a claim to a parcel. To clear the cloud, the nephew is asked to sign a deed giving up whatever interest he may have, with no warranties at all. Which deed fits?
options: Full covenant and warranty deed
Quitclaim deed
Executor's deed
Bargain and sale deed with covenants
questions.explanation: A quitclaim conveys only whatever interest the grantor actually has, if any, and makes no promises about title. That is why it is used to remove clouds on title; it does not guarantee clear title.

questions.q: After a court-ordered mortgage foreclosure sale, the deed to the successful bidder is signed by an officer appointed by the court. What type of deed is it?
options: Executor's deed
Quitclaim deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
Referee's deed
questions.explanation: In NY, foreclosure and partition sales are conducted by a court-appointed referee, who conveys by a referee's deed. The referee does not personally warrant title.

questions.q: A homeowner dies leaving a will that names her brother to settle the estate. The brother sells the house to a buyer. What type of deed will he most likely use?
options: Executor's deed
Referee's deed
Administrator's quitclaim deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
questions.explanation: The person named in a will to handle the estate is the executor, who conveys estate real property by an executor's deed. An administrator is appointed by the court only when there is no will (or no executor able to serve).
questions.citation: NY RPL § 258 (statutory forms of deeds); NY EPTL

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required for a deed to be valid in New York?
options: The grantor's signature
An adequate legal description
The grantee's signature
Delivery and acceptance
questions.explanation: A conveyance of real property must be in writing and subscribed by the grantor; the grantee normally does not sign. The grantee must, however, accept the delivered deed.

questions.q: A seller signs and delivers a deed to a buyer, but the deed is never acknowledged before a notary. What is its status?
options: Void, because acknowledgment is required for a deed to be valid
Valid between the parties, but it cannot be recorded until acknowledged
Valid and fully recordable as it stands, without any acknowledgment
Voidable at the option of the grantee only, until it is notarized
questions.explanation: Acknowledgment is a requirement for recording, not for validity. An unacknowledged deed can transfer title between the parties but cannot be recorded, so it gives no constructive notice.

questions.q: A mother signs a deed conveying her house to her son, then locks it in her own safe-deposit box and keeps the only key. The son finds the deed after her death. When did title pass to the son?
options: At the moment the mother signed and dated the deed
Automatically at the moment of the mother's death
When the son recorded the deed in the county clerk's office after finding it
Never through that deed, because it was never delivered
questions.explanation: A deed transfers title only when it is delivered with present intent to pass title and accepted. Signing and keeping control of the deed is not delivery, and recording cannot cure a failure of delivery.
questions.citation: Common-law delivery and acceptance requirement; NY RPL Article 8

questions.q: What is the main legal effect of recording a deed with the county clerk?
options: It gives constructive notice of the grantee's interest to the world
It makes an otherwise invalid or undelivered deed valid
It is the legal act that transfers title to the grantee
It guarantees that the title is free of all defects, liens, and claims
questions.explanation: Recording protects the grantee by giving constructive notice to later purchasers and lenders. Title passes on delivery and acceptance; recording does not validate a defective deed or guarantee title.

questions.q: An owner sells a lot to Ana, who does not record. The owner then sells the same lot to Ben, who pays value, knows nothing of Ana's deed, and records first. Who prevails under New York's recording act?
options: Ana, because her deed was delivered and accepted first
Ana and Ben, who become tenants in common of the lot
Ben, as a good-faith purchaser for value who recorded first
Ana, because a deed is valid between parties without recording
questions.explanation: NY is a race-notice state: an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith purchaser for value whose deed is recorded first. Ana's remedy is against the seller.

questions.q: Under New York's recording act, a later buyer who records first will NOT defeat an earlier unrecorded deed if the later buyer:
options: Financed the purchase with a mortgage
Knew of the earlier conveyance when buying
Received a bargain and sale deed
Closed without ordering a survey of the parcel
questions.explanation: Recording-act protection goes only to purchasers in good faith for value. A buyer with actual knowledge of the prior deed is not in good faith, even if that buyer records first.

questions.q: A buyer finances a purchase and the lender requires a lender's (mortgagee's) title policy. Which statement is accurate?
options: The lender's policy protects both the lender and the buyer for the full price
Every lender requires the buyer to also purchase a separate owner's policy
The owner's policy must be renewed and repaid each year to stay in force
The lender's policy protects only the lender; an owner's policy protects the buyer
questions.explanation: A lender's policy insures the lender's lien, and its coverage generally declines as the loan is paid down. An owner's policy is optional, is paid once at closing, and protects the owner (and heirs) for as long as they hold title.

questions.q: A standard owner's title policy issued without a survey reading would most likely exclude coverage for:
options: An encroachment that an accurate survey would have revealed
A forged deed from an earlier owner in the chain of title
A recorded judgment lien that the title searcher missed
A deed signed years ago by a prior owner who was a minor
questions.explanation: Title insurance covers specified title risks such as forgery, missed recorded liens, and incapacity of prior grantors. Survey matters like encroachments are standard exceptions unless a survey is provided and the exception is removed.

questions.q: A condensed history summarizing every recorded deed, mortgage, lien, and other instrument affecting a parcel is called:
options: The chain of title
A certificate of occupancy
An abstract of title
A title insurance policy
questions.explanation: An abstract of title is a summary of all recorded documents affecting the property. The chain of title is narrower: the sequence of ownership transfers from owner to owner. Distinguish the two.

questions.q: A title search shows a recorded deed from Adams to Baker and a recorded deed from Cole to Diaz, but no recorded deed from Baker to Cole. This is best described as:
options: An encroachment revealed by the public record of the deeds
A gap in the chain of title that must be cured before closing
A lis pendens that has been filed against the property
A normal record that requires no further action by the buyer
questions.explanation: A missing link between owners is a gap (break) in the chain of title. It is typically cured by obtaining and recording the missing deed, a quitclaim, or a court action to quiet title.
questions.citation: NY RPAPL Article 15 (action to determine claims to real property)

questions.q: A legal description begins at a fixed point, runs along stated directions and distances, and must return to that same starting point. Which method is this?
options: Rectangular (government) survey
Lot and block
Street address
Metes and bounds
questions.explanation: Metes and bounds describes boundaries by courses and distances from a point of beginning and must close back at that point. It is widely used in New York, often along with tax map or lot-and-block references.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (legal descriptions)

questions.q: Which method of legal description is NOT used for land in New York?
options: The rectangular (government) survey system
Metes and bounds
Lot and block on a filed subdivision map
Tax map section, block, and lot
questions.explanation: The rectangular survey system of townships and sections is used in federal public-land states, not in New York. NY relies on metes and bounds and on references to filed maps and tax maps.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (legal descriptions)

questions.q: For how long must a claimant's possession continue before title may be acquired by adverse possession in New York?
options: 5 years
15 years
10 years
20 years
questions.explanation: NY requires actual, open and notorious, exclusive, continuous, and hostile possession under a claim of right for 10 years. Long use alone is not enough; every element must be proven.

questions.q: For 12 years, a neighbor's hedge and a small fence have stood 18 inches over the boundary line. Can the neighbor claim that strip by adverse possession in New York?
options: Yes, because the 10-year statutory period has already run
No; fences and hedges are de minimis encroachments deemed permissive
Yes, but only after the neighbor records a notice of the adverse claim
No, because adverse possession in New York requires 20 years
questions.explanation: Since 2008, NY law treats de minimis non-structural encroachments such as fences, hedges, and shrubbery as permissive and not adverse. Simply passing the 10-year mark does not create title.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of voluntary alienation of real property?
options: The state takes the land for a highway through eminent domain
A lender forecloses after the owner defaults
Land passes to the state by escheat
An owner deeds her house to her daughter as a gift
questions.explanation: Voluntary alienation is a transfer the owner chooses, such as by deed or will. Eminent domain, foreclosure, escheat, and adverse possession are involuntary transfers.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (voluntary and involuntary alienation)

questions.q: In a will, a gift of real property is called a:
options: Devise
Bequest
Legacy
Codicil
questions.explanation: A devise is a gift of real property by will, made to a devisee. A bequest or legacy is a gift of personal property, and a codicil is an amendment to a will.
questions.citation: NY Estates, Powers and Trusts Law (EPTL) — wills

questions.q: A New York resident dies intestate, survived by a spouse and two children. How is the estate distributed?
options: The spouse receives the entire estate; the children receive nothing
The children share the entire estate equally; the spouse takes nothing
Spouse receives $50,000 plus half the balance; the children share the rest
The spouse and each of the two children receive one-third of the estate
questions.explanation: Under NY intestacy rules, a surviving spouse with issue takes $50,000 plus one-half of the residue, and the issue take the remainder. The spouse takes everything only when there are no surviving issue.

questions.q: Which covenant in a full covenant and warranty deed is the grantor's promise to sign any additional documents later needed to perfect the grantee's title?
options: Covenant of quiet enjoyment
Covenant of further assurances
Covenant of seisin
Covenant against encumbrances
questions.explanation: Further assurances obligates the grantor to execute whatever later instruments are needed to cure the title. Quiet enjoyment is a different promise: that the grantee will not be disturbed by someone with superior title.

questions.q: Which pair of deed covenants are 'present' covenants, meaning they are breached, if at all, at the moment the deed is delivered?
options: Seisin and against encumbrances
Quiet enjoyment and warranty
Further assurances and warranty
Quiet enjoyment and further assurances
questions.explanation: Seisin (grantor owns the estate conveyed) and against encumbrances (no undisclosed liens) speak to title as it stands at delivery. Quiet enjoyment, further assurances, and warranty are future covenants that protect the grantee going forward.

questions.q: After closing, a buyer learns of a judgment lien filed against the owner who held title before the seller. The seller gave a bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts. Does the buyer have a claim against the seller under the deed?
options: Yes; the covenant protects against every lien filed by any prior owner
Yes; every New York deed implies a full warranty of title
No; bargain and sale deeds never contain any covenants at all
No; the covenant covers only encumbrances the seller created or allowed
questions.explanation: The covenant against grantor's acts promises only that the grantor has not done or suffered anything to encumber the property; a predecessor's lien is outside it. The trap is treating it like a full warranty, which would reach defects from before the seller's ownership.
questions.citation: RPL §258 (statutory bargain and sale deed with covenant)

questions.q: A buyer wants a deed under which the seller would be answerable for title defects that arose even before the seller owned the property. Which deed provides that?
options: Bargain and sale deed with covenant against grantor's acts
Executor's deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
Quitclaim deed
questions.explanation: The full covenant and warranty deed warrants title against all lawful claims, whenever they arose. A bargain and sale deed with covenant reaches only problems created during the grantor's own ownership.

questions.q: How does a bargain and sale deed without covenants differ from a quitclaim deed?
options: The quitclaim gives the grantee more protection against prior liens
Only the bargain and sale deed implies the grantor holds title
The bargain and sale deed warrants title against all persons forever
Only the quitclaim deed may be recorded with the county clerk
questions.explanation: A bargain and sale deed purports to convey the land itself, implying the grantor has title, though it gives no warranties. A quitclaim releases only whatever interest the grantor may have, if any, so it is the weaker deed, not the stronger one.

questions.q: Which statement about a quitclaim deed is accurate?
options: It conveys full ownership if the grantor in fact holds full title
A quitclaim can convey only a leasehold, never ownership
A quitclaim deed cannot be recorded in New York
A quitclaim guarantees no liens arose while the grantor owned
questions.explanation: A quitclaim transfers whatever interest the grantor actually has, which can be complete ownership. What it lacks is any warranty; it does not promise freedom from liens, even ones the grantor created.

questions.q: Raymond dies without a will. The Surrogate's Court issues letters of administration to his daughter, who then sells his house. What deed will she most likely sign?
options: Executor's deed
Referee's deed
Full covenant and warranty deed
Administrator's deed
questions.explanation: A court-appointed administrator of an intestate estate conveys by administrator's deed. An executor's deed is used when the decedent left a will naming an executor, who receives letters testamentary.
questions.citation: SCPA; EPTL; general NY conveyancing practice

questions.q: The New York statutory form of executor's deed customarily contains which covenant?
options: That the grantor warrants the title forever against all persons
That the grantor is seized of the property in fee simple
That the grantor has not done anything to encumber the property
That the grantor will defend against every claim of prior owners
questions.explanation: An executor acts in a representative capacity and typically gives only a covenant against the grantor's own acts. Full warranty and seisin covenants belong to the full covenant and warranty deed.

questions.q: Two siblings who co-own inherited land cannot agree on a sale. One sues for partition, and the court orders the property sold at auction. Who signs the deed to the winning bidder?
options: Both siblings, by bargain and sale deed
A referee appointed by the court
The executor of the parents' estate
The county clerk where the land lies
questions.explanation: Court-ordered sales, such as partition and foreclosure sales, are conveyed by a referee's deed signed by the court-appointed referee. The siblings do not sign because the conveyance is made under the court's judgment, not their agreement.

questions.q: A recorded deed misspells the buyer's surname and transposes two digits in the lot number. What is the usual way to fix the record?
options: The original grantor signs and records a correction deed
The buyer files an amended TP-584 that rewrites the deed
The county clerk edits the recorded deed at the buyer's request
The seller sells the property again for a second purchase price
questions.explanation: A correction deed from the same grantor to the same grantee fixes clerical errors in a prior deed without making a new sale. Transfer tax forms and the clerk's records do not alter a deed's contents.

questions.q: Which sequence ranks these New York deeds from MOST to LEAST protection for the grantee?
options: Bargain and sale with covenant; full covenant; quitclaim; bargain and sale without covenant
Full covenant; bargain and sale without covenant; bargain and sale with covenant; quitclaim
Quitclaim; bargain and sale without covenant; bargain and sale with covenant; full covenant
Full covenant; bargain and sale with covenant; bargain and sale without covenant; quitclaim
questions.explanation: Protection shrinks as covenants drop away: all five covenants, then only the covenant against grantor's acts, then no covenants but an implied claim of title, then a quitclaim that claims nothing.

questions.q: New York statutory deed forms include a clause in which the grantor agrees to hold the sale proceeds as a trust fund to be applied first to paying the cost of any improvement. This clause comes from:
options: The recording act
The General Obligations Law
The Lien Law
The Tax Law transfer tax article
questions.explanation: Lien Law §13 requires the grantor's trust-fund covenant so that contractors who improved the property are paid from the proceeds. The recording act deals with priority and notice, not proceeds.

questions.q: A 17-year-old who inherited a lot signs a deed selling it to a neighbor. What is the status of the deed?
options: Void from the moment it is signed
Voidable at the minor's option
Fully valid once it is recorded
Valid only if the grantee is also a minor
questions.explanation: A grantor must have legal capacity; in New York a person under 18 is a minor, and a minor's conveyance can be disaffirmed. It is voidable rather than void, and recording does not cure lack of capacity.
questions.citation: General contract and property law (capacity; age of majority 18)

questions.q: Which deed is void because of a problem with the grantee?
options: A deed naming a grantee who died before the deed was delivered
A deed naming a 12-year-old child as the sole grantee
A deed naming two grantees without stating their shares
A deed naming a grantee who never signed the instrument
questions.explanation: A grantee must be a living person or existing entity capable of taking title when the deed is delivered. Minors can receive title, unspecified shares are presumed equal, and grantees need not sign.
questions.citation: General property law (essential elements of a deed)

questions.q: The words 'does hereby grant and release unto the party of the second part' form which part of a deed?
options: The habendum clause
The consideration recital
The acknowledgment
The granting clause
questions.explanation: The granting clause contains the words of conveyance showing present intent to transfer. The habendum clause ('to have and to hold') defines the estate the grantee takes.

questions.q: A deed's habendum clause states that the grantee is 'to have and to hold the premises for and during her natural life.' What estate does the grantee receive?
options: A fee simple absolute
A leasehold for years
A life estate
An easement in gross
questions.explanation: The habendum clause defines the extent of the estate granted; 'for and during her natural life' limits it to a life estate. Fee simple would read 'to the grantee, her heirs and assigns forever.'

questions.q: A deed recites a consideration of 'ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration,' though the buyer actually paid $540,000. What is the effect?
options: The deed is void because the recital must match the price
None; the deed is valid and nominal recitals are customary
The deed is voidable by the grantee until corrected
The deed must be re-signed before the clerk will record it
questions.explanation: Nominal consideration recitals are standard in New York deeds, and the true price is reported on the TP-584 and RP-5217 filed with the deed. A mismatch between the recital and the price does not affect validity.

questions.q: A father signs and delivers a deed giving his cabin to his adult daughter. She pays nothing. Is the conveyance effective?
options: Yes; a properly executed and delivered gift deed is valid
No; a deed is void unless the grantee pays fair value
No; a gift of land must instead be made by will
Only after the daughter pays the transfer tax due
questions.explanation: Payment is not required to transfer title by gift; capacity, a proper writing, execution, delivery, and acceptance are what matter. The catch is that a donee is not a purchaser for value, so the recording act gives her less protection.

questions.q: Two sisters own a duplex as tenants in common. Only one sister signs a deed conveying 'the property' to a buyer. What does the buyer receive?
options: The entire property, because one owner signed
Nothing, because the whole deed is void
The entire property once the deed is recorded
Only the signing sister's undivided interest
questions.explanation: A grantor can convey only what she owns, so the buyer becomes a tenant in common with the non-signing sister. Recording cannot transfer an interest the grantor never held.

questions.q: Under New York law, must a deed be witnessed to be valid?
options: Yes; two witnesses must sign alongside the grantor's signature
Yes; one witness and a notary must both sign the deed itself
No; witnesses are not required for the deed to be valid
Only when the grantee is a corporation or limited liability company
questions.explanation: A New York deed needs no attesting witnesses to be valid between the parties. To be recorded, it must be acknowledged before a notary or other officer, or proved by a subscribing witness if one signed.

questions.q: An owner conveys 40 acres 'EXCEPT the two-acre homesite in the northeast corner.' What does this language do?
options: It creates a new easement over the two acres for the grantor
It keeps the two-acre homesite out of the conveyance
It gives the grantor a life estate in the entire 40 acres
It restricts how the grantee may use all 40 acres
questions.explanation: An exception withholds part of the described land from the grant, so the grantor keeps the homesite outright. A reservation, by contrast, creates a new right (like an easement) in land that is conveyed.

questions.q: Ruth sells her farm, but the deed gives Ruth a permanent right of way across the farm to reach her adjoining lot. This provision is best described as:
options: A reservation of an easement in favor of the grantor
An exception that keeps the driveway land out of the sale
A revocable license that the buyer may cancel
A quitclaim of the driveway back to the grantor
questions.explanation: A reservation creates a new interest, here an easement, for the grantor in land that does pass to the buyer. An exception would have excluded the strip from the conveyance entirely, leaving Ruth as owner rather than easement holder.

questions.q: Why would a seller's deed list a recorded utility easement in a 'subject to' clause?
options: To terminate the utility easement as of the closing date
To make the buyer's lot the dominant estate for the easement
To make the easement enforceable against owners for the first time
So the buyer takes title burdened by it without a covenant breach
questions.explanation: 'Subject to' language discloses existing encumbrances the grantee accepts, so the grantor is not liable for them under the deed's covenants. It neither creates nor ends the easement.

questions.q: An acknowledgment on a deed primarily serves to:
options: Transfer title to the grantee at the moment the notary signs
Give the public constructive notice of the conveyance's terms
Verify the signer's identity and voluntary act, allowing recording
Guarantee the grantee that the title is free of all liens
questions.explanation: The grantor declares before a notary or other officer that the signature is genuine and voluntary, which makes the deed eligible for recording. Title passes by delivery, and constructive notice comes from recording, not acknowledgment.

questions.q: Which sequence shows the correct order of events in a typical New York conveyance?
options: Grantor signs; deed is recorded; grantor acknowledges; deed is delivered and accepted
Grantor signs; grantor acknowledges; deed is delivered and accepted; deed is recorded
Deed is recorded; grantor signs; deed is delivered and accepted; grantor acknowledges
Grantor acknowledges; deed is delivered and accepted; deed is recorded; grantor signs
questions.explanation: The grantor executes and acknowledges the deed, title passes on delivery and acceptance, and the grantee then records to protect against later claimants. A clerk will not record a deed that has not been acknowledged (or proved by a subscribing witness).

questions.q: At what point does title pass from the grantor to the grantee?
options: When the deed is delivered and accepted
When the grantor signs and dates the deed
When the deed is recorded by the clerk
When the state transfer tax is paid
questions.explanation: Delivery with present intent to transfer, plus acceptance, passes title. Recording is not required for the transfer itself; it protects the grantee against later purchasers.

questions.q: A seller signs a deed and hands it to her own attorney with instructions to hold it until she decides whether to go through with the sale. Has the deed been delivered?
options: Yes; handing a deed to any attorney counts as legal delivery
Yes; delivery occurred as soon as the deed was notarized
Yes; the attorney is an officer of the court, so it counts
No; she kept control, so there was no intent to pass title
questions.explanation: Delivery requires the grantor to give up control with intent that title pass now. Her own agent holding it subject to her further decision is not delivery; a true escrow with irrevocable instructions would be different.

questions.q: After a valid closing, the buyer hands the original deed back to the seller, who tears it up. Who owns the property?
options: The seller, because the deed itself no longer exists
No one, until a court action quiets the title to it
The buyer, since title passed when the deed was delivered
The buyer, but only if the deed was already recorded
questions.explanation: Once title has passed, destroying or returning the paper does not reconvey the land; only a new conveyance by the buyer would. Recording is irrelevant to the transfer between these two parties.

questions.q: A grandmother mails a signed deed for a lakefront lot to her grandson as a surprise. He learns the lot is contaminated, refuses it, and mails the deed back. What is the result?
options: The grandson owns it, since delivery alone passes title
Title never passed, because acceptance is required
The grandson owns it until he deeds it back
The lot escheats to the state as abandoned
questions.explanation: A conveyance needs both delivery and acceptance. Acceptance of a beneficial deed is usually presumed, but an express refusal defeats it, so title stays with the grandmother.

questions.q: Owner sells to Ana, who does not record right away. Owner then sells the same lot to Ben, who pays value and knows nothing of Ana. Ana records before Ben does. Who prevails under New York law?
options: Ana, because Ben did not record first
Ben, because he bought in good faith for value
Ben, because his deed was the later conveyance
Ana and Ben share the lot as tenants in common
questions.explanation: New York's recording act is race-notice: a later good-faith purchaser for value wins only if he also records first. Ben lost the race to the clerk's office, so Ana's earlier deed stands.

questions.q: New York's recording statute is best classified as which type?
options: Pure race
Pure notice
Grace period
Race-notice
questions.explanation: Under RPL §291 a later buyer must both purchase in good faith for value (no notice) and record first. A pure race statute ignores notice; a pure notice statute ignores who records first.

questions.q: An owner sells a lot to Pia, who does not record. The owner then gives the same lot to his nephew as a gift. The nephew knows nothing of Pia and records at once. Who prevails?
options: The nephew, because he recorded first without notice
The nephew, because a gift deed outranks a sale
Pia, since only purchasers for value are protected
Pia and the nephew share the lot equally
questions.explanation: RPL §291 protects a later grantee who pays valuable consideration, acts in good faith, and records first. A donee pays nothing, so recording first does not let him defeat Pia's earlier deed.

questions.q: Quinn buys a lot, never records, and builds and moves into a house there. The seller later sells the same lot to Ross, who records first but never visits the property. Who most likely prevails?
options: Ross, because he was the first to record his deed
Quinn, because her possession put Ross on inquiry notice
Ross, because Quinn never recorded her deed at all
Neither, so title stays with the original seller
questions.explanation: A buyer is charged with what a reasonable inspection would reveal, and open possession by someone other than the seller is notice of that person's rights. With notice, Ross is not a good-faith purchaser, so recording first does not help him.
questions.citation: RPL §291; general NY law on possession as notice

questions.q: A forger records a deed purporting to transfer Ellen's house to himself, then sells it to an innocent buyer who records. What does the buyer receive?
options: No title, because a forged deed is void even when recorded
Good title, because the buyer recorded in good faith
Good title once one year passes after recording
Half of the title shared with the owner, Ellen
questions.explanation: Recording gives notice of a document but cannot validate a forgery; the forger had nothing to convey. The recording act protects against prior unrecorded conveyances, not against forged ones.

questions.q: To give constructive notice, a deed to a house in Albany County must be recorded with which office?
options: The NYS Department of State
The NYS Department of Taxation
The local town assessor
The Albany County Clerk
questions.explanation: Outside New York City, conveyances are recorded with the county clerk of the county where the land lies. The assessor receives sale data from the RP-5217 but is not the recording office.

questions.q: Owner sells to Carla, who does not record. Owner then borrows from a bank that knows nothing of Carla, takes a mortgage on the same property, and records it first. Is the bank protected by the recording act?
options: No; the act protects only buyers who take full ownership
No; a mortgage is a lien and can never outrank a deed
Yes; a good-faith mortgagee for value that records first wins
Yes, but only if the bank also takes possession
questions.explanation: The recording act treats a mortgage as a conveyance and a mortgagee for value as a purchaser. The bank lent in good faith and recorded first, so its mortgage has priority over Carla's unrecorded deed.

questions.q: Form TP-584, filed when a deed is recorded, is primarily the:
options: Real property transfer report for assessors
Combined real estate transfer tax return
Property condition disclosure statement
Agency disclosure acknowledgment
questions.explanation: The TP-584 reports and pays the New York State real estate transfer tax and includes related certifications. Sale data for assessors goes on the RP-5217.

questions.q: The sale information on Form RP-5217 is used mainly by:
options: Assessors and the state Office of Real Property Tax Services
The IRS, to compute the seller's capital gains
The Department of State, to track licensee commissions
The lender, to set the property's appraised value
questions.explanation: The Real Property Transfer Report gives assessors and ORPTS sale prices and conditions used in assessment and equalization work. It is not a federal tax filing or a licensing record.

questions.q: Who must sign the main affirmation on Form TP-584 in a typical sale?
options: Only the grantor, as the seller
Only the grantee, as the buyer
Only the closing attorney or agent
Both the grantor and the grantee
questions.explanation: The TP-584 is signed by both parties to the conveyance. The seller alone signs the separate personal income tax certification section.

questions.q: For the sale of a single-family house in Brooklyn, the deed, transfer tax returns, and RP-5217NYC are prepared and filed through:
options: eAccessNY, the state licensing portal
The NYS Department of State's filing office
ACRIS, the city's online land records system
The local tax assessor's walk-in office
questions.explanation: In New York City, deeds and related tax forms are prepared and recorded through ACRIS with the Department of Finance's City Register. eAccessNY is the DOS licensing system, unrelated to recording.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code; NYC Department of Finance (ACRIS)

questions.q: A house sells for $437,250. What New York State real estate transfer tax is reported on the TP-584, and who normally pays it?
options: $1,749, paid by the seller
$1,750, paid by the seller
$1,748, paid by the buyer
$4,372.50, paid by the buyer
questions.explanation: The tax is $2 per $500 or fraction: 437,250 ÷ 500 = 874.5, which rounds up to 875 units; 875 × $2 = $1,750, paid by the grantor. $1,749 skips the round-up, $1,748 rounds down, and $4,372.50 wrongly applies a 1% rate.

questions.q: A woman dies without a will and with no living relatives who qualify as heirs. Her house passes to the State of New York by:
options: Escheat, a form of involuntary alienation
Devise, a form of voluntary alienation
Eminent domain, a form of involuntary alienation
Dedication, a form of voluntary alienation
questions.explanation: When no one is entitled to inherit, property escheats to the state; the owner did not choose this, so it is involuntary. Eminent domain is a taking of a living owner's land for public use with just compensation.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an example of involuntary alienation?
options: A lender forecloses and a referee conveys the house
A county condemns land for a highway widening
A county takes title for unpaid real property taxes
An owner deeds land to a buyer after accepting an offer
questions.explanation: A sale by deed is the owner's own choice, so it is voluntary alienation. Foreclosure, condemnation, and tax foreclosure all transfer title by operation of law without the owner's consent.

questions.q: The state takes 0.4 acre of a farm to widen a highway and pays the owner just compensation. How is the owner's loss of title classified?
options: Voluntary alienation, because the owner was paid
Escheat, because the state takes title
Involuntary alienation through condemnation
Accretion, because the boundary shifts
questions.explanation: Condemnation under the power of eminent domain transfers title without the owner's consent, so it is involuntary even though compensation is paid. Escheat applies only when an owner dies without heirs.
questions.citation: NY Eminent Domain Procedure Law; US Const. 5th Amend.

questions.q: A title search comes back clean, but for 15 years a neighbor has openly driven across the seller's side yard to reach a garage. Why might the search have missed this?
options: A prescriptive easement can exist without any recorded document
Easements must be recorded to be valid in New York
Title searches never review more than ten years of records
Driveway rights are only listed on the tax bill
questions.explanation: Rights acquired by long use, such as a prescriptive easement, arise without a recorded instrument, so a records search cannot reveal them; an inspection or survey may. Easements are not invalid merely because they are unrecorded.

questions.q: A buyer relied on an abstract of title showing no problems. After closing, a deed in the chain turns out to have been forged. What does this illustrate?
options: An abstract automatically makes the abstractor the new owner's insurer
An abstract summarizes the records but does not insure against hidden defects
A forged deed is valid once it has been recorded for one year
The buyer's mortgage lender becomes liable to the buyer for the loss
questions.explanation: An abstract only condenses what the public records show; a forgery looks normal on the record. Protection against hidden risks such as forgery comes from a title insurance policy, not from recording or the abstract itself.

questions.q: Which description best defines marketable title?
options: Title that is subject to no easements, liens, or restrictions of any kind
Title that has been held by the same family for at least ten years
Title free from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept
Title that the buyer's lender has already appraised and approved
questions.explanation: Marketable title is free from reasonable doubt about its validity, so a reasonably prudent, informed buyer would accept it. It need not be free of every easement or restriction, especially those the contract allows.

questions.q: A contract says the buyer takes title subject to recorded utility easements that do not interfere with the use of the house. The title report shows such an easement. Can the seller still deliver the title the contract requires?
options: No, because any easement makes title unmarketable
No, unless the utility company first releases the easement
Yes, but only if the seller credits the buyer its value
Yes, because the buyer agreed to take title subject to it
questions.explanation: Marketability is measured against the contract. An encumbrance the buyer expressly agreed to accept does not breach the seller's title obligation, so no release or credit is required.
questions.citation: General contract and real property law

questions.q: Before closing, the title company sends a report listing the liens that must be paid off and the items it will not insure. What is this document?
options: A title report or commitment
An abstract of title
An owner's title policy
A survey reading report
questions.explanation: The title report (commitment) states the insurer's requirements and exceptions before the policy is issued. The owner's policy is issued at or after closing, and an abstract is only a summary of the records.

questions.q: How long does an owner's title insurance policy generally protect the insured?
options: For the term of the mortgage loan, which is usually 30 years
For as long as the insured or the insured's heirs hold an interest
For one year, renewable on each anniversary of the closing date
For ten years, matching the adverse possession period in New York
questions.explanation: An owner's policy has no expiration date and no renewal premium; coverage continues while the insured or heirs keep an interest. The loan term limits only the lender's policy.

questions.q: A buyer finances $400,000 of a $500,000 purchase. How does the lender's title policy usually work?
options: It covers the full $500,000 price, and the buyer is the insured party
It covers $100,000, the amount of the buyer's down payment
It covers up to the loan amount and ends once the loan is paid off
It continues to protect the lender after the loan has been paid off
questions.explanation: A lender's policy is written for the loan amount ($400,000), protects only the lender, and its coverage shrinks as the debt is paid down and ends when the loan is satisfied. The buyer's equity is protected only by an owner's policy.

questions.q: Three years after closing, a neighbor builds a shed that extends onto the insured owner's lot. Will the owner's title policy cover this?
options: Yes, because the policy covers all boundary problems forever
Yes, because the policy follows the land rather than the owner
No, because title policies never cover encroachments
No, because the problem arose after the policy date
questions.explanation: Title insurance covers defects existing on the policy date, not problems created later. Some encroachments that existed at closing can be covered, so saying the policy never covers encroachments is too broad.

questions.q: After closing, a person with a valid claim to the property surfaces because a prior deed in the chain was signed by someone who lacked legal capacity. The buyer has an owner's policy. What should the buyer expect?
options: The insurer will defend the title and pay covered losses up to the policy amount
The buyer must sue the prior grantor alone because policies exclude capacity issues
The policy is void because the defect existed before the policy was issued
The county clerk must refund the recording fees and void the deed
questions.explanation: Defects that predate the policy and are not shown in the records, such as a grantor's incapacity, are exactly what title insurance covers; the insurer defends and pays covered losses up to the policy amount.

questions.q: Which item is a typical standard exception in a title insurance policy?
options: A forged deed that appears earlier in the chain of title
Rights of parties in possession not shown by the public records
An error by the county clerk in indexing a recorded deed
A claim by a prior owner's heir who was never disclosed
questions.explanation: Standard exceptions remove matters a records search cannot reveal but an inspection could, such as rights of people in possession. Forgery, indexing errors, and missing heirs are classic covered hidden risks.

questions.q: In a typical New York residential sale, who customarily pays the premiums for both the owner's and the lender's title policies?
options: The seller
The listing broker
The buyer
The lender
questions.explanation: In New York, the buyer customarily pays for both the owner's (fee) policy and the lender's (mortgage) policy, though the contract may allocate costs differently. The seller customarily pays the transfer tax, not the title premiums.

questions.q: A seller bought her house with an owner's title policy. She now sells to a buyer. Does her policy protect the buyer?
options: Yes; the policy transfers with the deed
Yes, but only for defects found within one year
No, unless the seller adds the buyer as a co-insured
No; the buyer needs a new owner's policy in his own name
questions.explanation: An owner's policy protects the named insured (and heirs), not later buyers, so each purchaser obtains a new policy. The seller may keep limited protection for her warranty obligations, but coverage does not pass with the deed.

questions.q: A mortgage on a property was paid in full years ago, but no satisfaction was ever recorded. How is this best described, and how is it cured?
options: A cloud on title, cured by recording a satisfaction of mortgage
A valid lien, which can be cured only by a foreclosure sale
An easement, which is cured by recording a release of easement
A gap in the chain of title, cured by a corrective deed
questions.explanation: An undischarged but paid mortgage is a cloud: it appears on the record and casts doubt on title. Recording a satisfaction from the lender (or its successor) clears it.

questions.q: A title search shows that a former owner's heirs may have a claim, but they cannot be located to sign quitclaim deeds. Which remedy can clear title?
options: A notice of pendency
An action to quiet title
A survey reading
A new abstract of title
questions.explanation: When adverse claimants cannot be found or will not sign, the owner can sue to quiet title (RPAPL Article 15) to have a court determine the claims. A notice of pendency only announces litigation; it does not resolve anything.

questions.q: A neighbor has met every element of adverse possession for more than ten years, but the deed records still show the original owner. What gives the neighbor recordable, marketable title?
options: Recording an affidavit of possession alone
Paying the property taxes for one more year
A court judgment in a quiet title action
Obtaining a new survey of the disputed strip
questions.explanation: Title may vest by adverse possession without any document, but to make it marketable the possessor obtains a judgment determining the claim (RPAPL Article 15), which can be recorded. An affidavit or survey alone does not change record title.

questions.q: To measure a lot's height for a flood-zone review, a surveyor starts from a nearby government brass disk with its elevation stamped on it. Which statement correctly describes the terms involved?
options: A datum is a permanent corner marker; a benchmark is the lot's tax map number
A datum is the deed's point of beginning; a benchmark is the final closing course
A datum is a bearing such as N 60° E; a benchmark is a filed subdivision plat
A datum is the base level for elevations; a benchmark is a marker of known height
questions.explanation: A datum is the reference plane (based on mean sea level) from which elevations are measured. A benchmark is a permanent marker, usually set by a government survey, whose elevation above the datum is known, so surveyors can measure nearby heights from it. A point of beginning, bearings, and plats concern horizontal boundaries, not elevation.

questions.q: A deed reads "thence north 200 feet to an iron pipe." A surveyor finds the original iron pipe 204 feet away. Which generally controls?
options: The location of the iron pipe
The stated distance of 200 feet
An average of the two measurements
Whichever result gives the buyer more land
questions.explanation: When a monument conflicts with a stated distance, the monument generally controls because it is the physical evidence of what the parties intended. Courses and distances are given less weight than monuments.
questions.citation: General rules of construction for legal descriptions

questions.q: What does a course reading of S 30° W mean?
options: Start facing west and turn 30 degrees toward the south
Start facing south and turn 30 degrees toward the west
Start facing south and turn 30 degrees toward the east
Start facing north and turn 30 degrees toward the west
questions.explanation: Bearings always start from north or south and turn toward east or west, so S 30° W means 30 degrees west of due south. Starting from west reverses the reading; the angle is measured off the north–south line.

questions.q: A boundary line runs N 60° E from corner A to corner B. What is the bearing of the same line run from B back to A?
options: N 60° W
S 60° E
S 60° W
S 30° W
questions.explanation: Reversing a line keeps the angle and flips both letters: N becomes S and E becomes W, so N 60° E becomes S 60° W. Flipping only one letter, or changing the angle to its complement, gives a different line.

questions.q: A New York City deed identifies a parcel as "Borough of Queens, Block 1450, Lot 22." These numbers come from which source?
options: A township-and-range grid
The metes-and-bounds courses in the deed
The zoning map
The city's tax map
questions.explanation: Borough, block, and lot numbers come from the tax map used for assessment, a standard way to identify parcels in NYC. New York does not use the township-and-range (rectangular survey) grid.
questions.citation: NYC tax map; general real property law

questions.q: A deed describes land as "Lot 14 as shown on the map of Maple Ridge Estates, filed in the County Clerk's Office as Map No. 3127." Which description method is this?
options: Reference to a recorded plat (subdivision map)
Metes and bounds from a point of beginning
Rectangular (government) survey system
Assessor's appraisal card reference
questions.explanation: Identifying a lot by its number on a subdivision map filed with the county clerk is a recorded plat (lot-and-block) description. It does not list courses and distances, so it is not metes and bounds.

questions.q: When a title company performs a "survey reading," what does it do?
options: Sends its own surveyor to restake all four corners of the lot
Compares the survey with the deed description and lists encroachments
Checks the survey for compliance with the local zoning code
Calculates the property's assessed value from the survey's acreage
questions.explanation: In a survey reading, the title company reviews the survey against the deed description and lists any encroachments, discrepancies, or easements as exceptions in the title report. It does not resurvey the land or decide zoning compliance.

questions.q: A rectangular parcel measures 660 feet by 330 feet. How many acres does it contain?
options: 2.5 acres
4.5 acres
5 acres
50 acres
questions.explanation: Area = 660 × 330 = 217,800 sq ft; 217,800 ÷ 43,560 sq ft per acre = 5 acres. Dividing by 48,400 (a mis-remembered acre) gives 4.5, and halving the area as if it were a triangle gives 2.5.
questions.citation: Real estate math: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft

questions.q: A metes-and-bounds description encloses a triangular lot with a base of 400 feet and a perpendicular height of 217.8 feet. How many acres is the lot?
options: 2 acres
0.5 acre
4 acres
1 acre
questions.explanation: Triangle area = ½ × 400 × 217.8 = 43,560 sq ft; 43,560 ÷ 43,560 = 1 acre. Forgetting the ½ gives 87,120 sq ft, or 2 acres.
questions.citation: Real estate math: 1 acre = 43,560 sq ft

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a requirement for acquiring title by adverse possession in New York?
options: Paying the property taxes on the land
Possession that is hostile and under a claim of right
Possession that is open and notorious
Possession that is exclusive and continuous
questions.explanation: New York requires possession that is hostile under claim of right, actual, open and notorious, exclusive, and continuous for 10 years. Paying taxes can be evidence but is not a required element, unlike in some other states.

questions.q: Since the 2008 amendments, how does RPAPL §501 define a "claim of right" for adverse possession?
options: Possession of the land for at least ten years without any objection
A reasonable basis for the belief that the property belongs to the possessor
Written permission from the record owner to occupy and use the land
Payment of the property taxes on the land for the full statutory period
questions.explanation: RPAPL §501(3) defines claim of right as a reasonable basis for believing the property belongs to the adverse possessor. Permission would defeat hostility, and ten years is the time period, not the state of mind.

questions.q: A man moves onto a vacant lot knowing it belongs to his neighbor, whose name and address are on the deed records, and builds a garden shed and fence enclosing it. Eleven years pass, all after 2008. Is his adverse possession claim likely to succeed?
options: Yes, because the enclosure stood for more than the ten-year period
Yes, because building improvements on the land proves a claim of right
No, because he had no reasonable basis to believe the land was his
No, because adverse possession in New York requires at least 20 years
questions.explanation: After the 2008 amendments, a possessor must have a reasonable basis for believing he owns the land; a knowing intruder lacks this claim of right when the record owner can be found. The 10-year period alone is not enough.

questions.q: Under RPAPL §501(3), claim of right is NOT required when:
options: The possessor has paid the property taxes on the land for at least five years
The possessor's fence has fully enclosed the land for the entire period
The possessor has occupied the land openly for more than twenty years
The record owner cannot be found in county records or located by reasonable means
questions.explanation: The statute excuses claim of right only where the owner(s) throughout the statutory period cannot be ascertained in the county clerk's or register's records and located by reasonable means. Taxes, fencing, or longer possession do not substitute for it.

questions.q: For 12 years, a homeowner has regularly mowed and raked a strip of the neighbor's lawn next to the boundary. What is the effect under New York law?
options: The mowing is deemed permissive and non-adverse
The homeowner now owns the strip by adverse possession
The homeowner has acquired a prescriptive easement to the strip
The neighbor must compensate the homeowner for the maintenance
questions.explanation: RPAPL §543(2) deems lawn mowing and similar maintenance across a boundary line permissive and non-adverse, so it cannot support an adverse possession claim. A prescriptive easement also requires hostile use, which is missing here.

questions.q: Under RPAPL §522 as amended in 2008, land not held under a written instrument is treated as adversely possessed only where:
options: The possessor recorded an affidavit of possession with the county clerk
Acts open enough to notify a diligent owner, or a substantial enclosure
The possessor was assessed and billed for the land's property taxes
The possessor obtained a building permit for improvements on the land
questions.explanation: RPAPL §522 now requires either acts sufficiently open to put a reasonably diligent owner on notice or protection by a substantial enclosure. Recording an affidavit, paying taxes, or getting permits is not the statutory test.

questions.q: A claimant's 10 years of qualifying possession were completed in 2005, but she does not sue until 2026. Which law governs whether she acquired title?
options: The 2008 amendments, because the lawsuit was filed afterward
Neither, because her claim is barred by waiting more than 10 years
The law before 2008, because title vested when the 10 years ran
The 2008 amendments, but only for possessions on enclosed land
questions.explanation: Adverse possession title vests automatically when the statutory period ends, and courts apply the pre-2008 law to title that vested before the amendments took effect (July 7, 2008). Delay in suing does not undo title that has already vested.
questions.citation: RPAPL §501; L. 2008, ch. 269; Franza v. Olin, 73 A.D.3d 44 (4th Dept 2010)

questions.q: Possessor A occupies a strip openly and adversely for 6 years, then sells his house and his claim to B, who continues the same possession for 5 more years. What is the likely result?
options: B must start a new 10-year period running from the day he bought
The claim fails because an adverse possession claim cannot be sold
B needs 20 years in total because ownership of the house changed
B can add A's time to his own, giving 11 years toward the 10-year period
questions.explanation: Successive possessors in privity, such as a seller and a buyer, may "tack" their periods: 6 + 5 = 11 years, which exceeds the 10-year requirement. A break in privity or possession would restart the clock.

questions.q: A man dies intestate. Who is appointed by the Surrogate's Court to settle his estate?
options: An administrator
An executor
A devisee
A court-appointed referee
questions.explanation: With no will, the Surrogate's Court issues letters of administration to an administrator. An executor is named in a will and receives letters testamentary.

questions.q: What is probate?
options: The transfer of a decedent's property to the State when no heirs exist
The court process of proving a will valid and authorizing the executor
The division of an estate among the heirs when there is no will
The recording of the executor's deed with the county clerk's office
questions.explanation: Probate takes place in the Surrogate's Court, which validates the will and issues letters testamentary to the executor. Transfer to the State with no heirs is escheat; distribution with no will is intestate succession.

questions.q: A will leaves "my house to my niece and my car and savings account to my nephew." Which statement uses the terms correctly?
options: The niece receives a bequest; the nephew is a devisee
Both the niece and the nephew are devisees
The niece is a devisee; the nephew receives a bequest
Both the niece and the nephew are administrators
questions.explanation: A gift of real property by will is a devise, made to a devisee; a gift of personal property such as a car or money is a bequest (legacy). Administrators manage estates without wills; they are not recipients.

questions.q: A testator types his will, signs it at the end, and has one friend sign as a witness. Is the will properly executed under New York law?
options: Yes, because a typed will needs only a single attesting witness
Yes, because the testator signed at the end of the document
No, because every will must also be notarized to be valid
No, because at least two attesting witnesses are required
questions.explanation: EPTL §3-2.1 requires the testator to sign at the end and at least two attesting witnesses to sign within a 30-day period. Notarization is not a requirement for a will's validity.

questions.q: A New York homeowner who is not in military service and not at sea writes her entire will by hand, signs it, and has no witnesses. Is it valid in New York?
options: No; such wills are valid only in narrow wartime or at-sea situations
Yes; handwritten wills are valid in New York if they are signed and dated
Yes, but only to pass property worth less than $50,000 in total
No; handwritten wills become valid only if later notarized by a clerk
questions.explanation: New York recognizes holographic (handwritten, unwitnessed) wills only when made by armed forces members, or people serving with or accompanying them, during war or armed conflict, or by mariners at sea (EPTL §3-2.2). An ordinary homeowner's unwitnessed handwritten will is not validly executed; a will needs two attesting witnesses under EPTL §3-2.1.

questions.q: A man dies intestate, survived by his wife and his parents, but no children. Who inherits his estate?
options: His wife and his parents share equally
His wife takes everything
His parents take everything
His wife takes $50,000 and his parents take the rest
questions.explanation: Under EPTL §4-1.1, a spouse with no surviving issue takes the entire estate; parents inherit only when there is no spouse and no issue. The $50,000-plus-half rule applies only when issue survive.

questions.q: A woman dies without a will and without any spouse, descendants, parents, or other relatives entitled to inherit. What happens to her real property?
options: It passes to the town where it is located by eminent domain
It goes to her closest neighbor by adverse possession
It escheats to the State of New York
It remains ownerless until someone records a deed
questions.explanation: When no one is entitled to inherit, the property passes to the State by escheat. Eminent domain is a taking with compensation, and adverse possession requires 10 years of qualifying possession.

questions.q: An owner dies with no will. Her only relative is a first cousin. Will her house escheat?
options: Yes, because only spouses and children can inherit
Yes, because dying without a will always triggers escheat
No, because the house goes to the town automatically
No, because a cousin can qualify as a distributee
questions.explanation: Dying intestate does not by itself cause escheat; property escheats only if no distributee survives. Under EPTL §4-1.1, first cousins can inherit when no closer relatives survive.

questions.q: A husband's will leaves his entire estate to a charity and nothing to his wife. Under New York law, what can she do?
options: Claim an elective share: the greater of $50,000 or one-third of the net estate
Nothing, because a properly executed will always controls who inherits
Take the entire estate, because a spouse can never be disinherited at all
Claim one-half of the estate as her share under tenancy by the entirety
questions.explanation: EPTL §5-1.1-A gives a surviving spouse a right of election to take the greater of $50,000 or one-third of the net estate. A spouse can be partly disinherited, but not below the elective share without a valid waiver.

questions.q: The State needs a strip of a farm to widen a highway, and the owner refuses to sell. What can the State do?
options: Take it without payment under its police power
Acquire it by condemnation and pay just compensation
Wait for the strip to escheat to the State
Rezone the strip as a public highway without compensation
questions.explanation: Eminent domain lets government take private property for public use through condemnation, but just compensation, usually fair market value, must be paid. Police power and zoning regulate use; they do not transfer title.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amend.; NY Const. art. I §7; Eminent Domain Procedure Law

questions.q: A county takes the front 30 feet of a commercial lot for a road, and the smaller remaining parcel loses value because its parking is cut in half. What compensation may the owner seek?
options: Only the value of the 30-foot strip that was actually taken
Only the relocation costs for moving the business elsewhere
Value of the strip taken plus severance damages to the remainder
Nothing, because a partial taking is not compensable at all
questions.explanation: In a partial taking, just compensation includes the value of the part taken and the decrease in value of the remaining land (severance or consequential damages). Limiting the award to the strip alone ignores the remainder's loss.
questions.citation: Eminent Domain Procedure Law; NY Const. art. I §7

questions.q: A town's sewer project repeatedly floods a private lot, making it unusable, but the town never started a condemnation proceeding. What claim may the owner bring?
options: An action to quiet title
A petition for escheat
An action for partition
Inverse condemnation
questions.explanation: Inverse condemnation is a suit by an owner when government action effectively takes property without formal condemnation, seeking just compensation. Quiet title resolves competing ownership claims, and partition divides co-owned land.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amend.; NY Const. art. I §7

questions.q: Which of the following is a freehold estate?
options: Life estate
Estate for years
Periodic tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
questions.explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple and life estates) are ownership interests of indefinite duration. Estates for years, periodic tenancies, tenancies at will, and tenancies at sufferance are leasehold (less-than-freehold) estates.

questions.q: A deed conveys land "to the Town of Clifton so long as the land is used as a public park." If the town stops using it as a park, what happens?
options: The grantor must first sue to exercise a right of re-entry
The town keeps title, because use conditions in deeds are void
Title automatically returns to the grantor (possibility of reverter)
The town's interest converts into a leasehold held from the grantor
questions.explanation: Words of duration such as "so long as" or "while" create a fee simple determinable, which ends automatically when the condition is broken. A fee on condition subsequent ("but if") requires the grantor to act.

questions.q: A deed conveys a lot to a buyer "but if alcohol is ever sold on the premises, the grantor may re-enter and reclaim the property." Alcohol is later sold. What is the result?
options: Title reverts to the grantor automatically on the sale
The buyer keeps title until the grantor acts to reclaim it
The deed is void from the date it was delivered
The buyer's estate becomes a leasehold estate
questions.explanation: "But if" or "provided that" language creates a fee simple on condition subsequent. Breach gives the grantor a right of re-entry (reacquisition), but the estate does not end until the grantor exercises it.

questions.q: An owner deeds a house "to Beth for life, then to Carlos." What interest does Carlos hold while Beth is alive?
options: A reversion
A life estate pur autre vie
A leasehold estate
A remainder
questions.explanation: A future interest held by a third party who takes when the life estate ends is a remainder (Carlos is the remainderman). If the property were to return to the original grantor instead, the grantor's interest would be a reversion.

questions.q: An owner deeds land "to Dana for the life of Eli." Dana dies while Eli is still living. What happens to the estate?
options: It passes to Dana's heirs or devisees until Eli dies
It ends immediately at Dana's death, since Dana was the holder
It reverts to the grantor at the moment of Dana's death
It becomes a fee simple absolute owned by Dana's heirs
questions.explanation: A life estate pur autre vie is measured by the life of someone other than the holder (here Eli). It continues for Eli's lifetime, so it passes to Dana's estate if Dana dies first.

questions.q: A residential tenant's one-year lease expired, and the tenant remains in possession without the landlord's consent. This tenant has a:
options: Tenancy at will
Periodic (month-to-month) tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
Estate for years
questions.explanation: A tenancy at sufferance is a holdover after a lawful tenancy ends, without the landlord's consent; it is not a new agreed lease. A tenancy at will exists with the landlord's permission. Self-help eviction is still prohibited.

questions.q: Which of the following is a general lien?
options: A mortgage
A docketed money judgment
A mechanic's lien
A real property tax lien
questions.explanation: A general lien attaches to all of the debtor's property within its reach, such as a judgment lien on all real property in the county. Mortgages, mechanic's liens, and property tax liens are specific liens on one parcel.

questions.q: A creditor wins a money judgment and dockets it with the clerk of the county where the debtor owns two houses. What is the effect?
options: It is a lien only on the specific property named in the lawsuit
It is a lien on the debtor's personal property, but not on real estate
It attaches to a house only when the debtor later tries to sell it
It is a lien on his real property in that county, generally for 10 years
questions.explanation: A docketed judgment is a general lien on the debtor's real property in that county, generally for 10 years. It is involuntary and is not limited to a single parcel.

questions.q: A property has a mortgage recorded in 2019, a judgment lien docketed in 2021, and unpaid 2026 real property taxes. Which lien generally has first priority?
options: The real property tax lien
The mortgage, because it was recorded first
The judgment lien, because it is a general lien
They share equally, in proportion to their amounts
questions.explanation: Real property tax and special assessment liens generally take priority over other liens regardless of when those were recorded. "First recorded wins" does not override tax-lien priority.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Tax Law (tax lien priority)

questions.q: A contractor finishes a kitchen renovation on an owner-occupied single-family house on March 1. Under the NY Lien Law, the notice of mechanic's lien must be filed within:
options: 8 months after completion of the work
30 days after completion of the work
4 months after completion of the work
1 year after completion of the work
questions.explanation: For a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien must be filed within 4 months after the work is completed or the materials are last furnished. The 8-month period applies to other property.

questions.q: A supplier last delivered materials to an office building renovation on January 10. Under the NY Lien Law, the deadline to file a mechanic's lien is generally:
options: 4 months after the final furnishing of materials
8 months after the final furnishing of materials
90 days after the final furnishing of materials
2 years after the final furnishing of materials
