questions.explanation: For property other than a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien must be filed within 8 months after the final performance of work or final furnishing of materials. The 4-month period is only for single-family dwellings.

questions.q: A buyer's title search reveals a notice of pendency (lis pendens) filed against the property. What does it mean?
options: A final judgment of foreclosure has already been entered against it
The property has unpaid real estate taxes that are now a lien
A neighbor holds a recorded easement over part of the lot
A lawsuit affecting title to or possession of the property is pending
questions.explanation: A notice of pendency warns that litigation affecting the property is pending. Anyone who later acquires an interest takes subject to the outcome. It is a cloud on title, not a judgment or a tax lien.

questions.q: The owner of a rear lot has a recorded right-of-way over the driveway on the front lot. The front lot is sold. What happens to the right-of-way?
options: It continues, and the new owner of the front lot takes subject to it
It ends, because easements are personal to the original parties
It continues only if the new owner signs a new easement agreement
It converts into a revocable license held by the rear owner
questions.explanation: This is an easement appurtenant: the rear lot is the dominant tenement and the front lot is the servient tenement. Appurtenant easements run with the land when either parcel is sold.
questions.citation: NY common law of easements; NY RPL § 291 (recording)

questions.q: An electric utility holds the right to run power lines across a farm. The utility owns no adjoining land. This right is best described as:
options: An easement appurtenant
An easement by necessity
An easement in gross
A license
questions.explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity rather than a neighboring parcel, so there is no dominant tenement. Commercial easements in gross, like utility easements, are interests in land, unlike a revocable license.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (easements)

questions.q: An owner sells the back half of his land, leaving the buyer's parcel with no access to any public road except across the seller's remaining land. What right does the law give the buyer?
options: An easement in gross
An easement by necessity
A license coupled with an interest
An encroachment
questions.explanation: When a parcel is landlocked as a result of dividing commonly owned land, the law implies an easement by necessity across the grantor's remaining land. It lasts as long as the necessity exists.

questions.q: For 11 years, a neighbor has openly and continuously used a path across your land, without permission and without any claim from you. What has the neighbor most likely acquired?
options: Title to the path by adverse possession
A license that you may revoke at any time
An easement in gross
An easement by prescription
questions.explanation: Open, notorious, continuous, and hostile use for 10 years in NY creates a prescriptive easement, which is a right of use, not ownership. Adverse possession requires exclusive possession and transfers title.
questions.citation: NY common law of prescriptive easements (10-year period, CPLR § 212(a))

questions.q: A homeowner verbally tells her neighbor he may fish in her pond whenever he likes. Which statement is true?
options: It is a revocable personal permission, not an interest in land
It is an oral easement appurtenant that runs with the land
It becomes a permanent easement after one year of regular use
It is an easement in gross that the neighbor may sell to others
questions.explanation: A license is personal permission to do something on another's land; it is not an interest in real property. It can generally be revoked and ends on the death of either party or the sale of the land.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (licenses)

questions.q: A survey shows that a neighbor's garage extends two feet onto the buyer's lot. This is an example of:
options: An easement appurtenant
A license
An encroachment
A lis pendens
questions.explanation: An encroachment is an unauthorized intrusion of an improvement onto another's land. It is typically revealed by a survey, not a title search, and it is a common standard exception in title policies.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (encroachments)

questions.q: Local zoning allows two-family houses, but a recorded deed restriction limits a lot to one single-family house. What may the owner build?
options: A two-family house, because zoning overrides private restrictions
Only a single-family house, because the stricter restriction applies
A two-family house, if the owner obtains a building permit
Anything allowed by zoning once the deed is 10 years old
questions.explanation: Private deed restrictions and public zoning both apply, so the owner must satisfy whichever is more restrictive. A building permit does not override a valid private restriction.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (deed restrictions and zoning)

questions.q: In the MARIA test for whether an item is a fixture, the letters stand for:
options: Market value, Age, Removability, Insurability, Appraisal method
Method of payment, Assessment, Rights, Inspection, Agreement
Material used, Attachment, Reasonableness, Improvement, Agreement
Method of annexation, Adaptability, Relationship, Intention, Agreement
questions.explanation: Fixture analysis considers how the item is attached, whether it is adapted to the property, the relationship of the parties, their intention, and any agreement. A specific written agreement or exclusion carries great weight.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (fixtures)

questions.q: A seller installed custom-fitted built-in bookcases and a dining room chandelier. The contract of sale is silent about them. At closing they:
options: Pass to the buyer as fixtures, since the contract does not exclude them
Remain the seller's personal property, which the seller may remove
Pass to the buyer only if they were listed in the property advertisement
May be removed by the seller if they were paid for separately
questions.explanation: Items permanently attached or adapted to the property are presumed fixtures that pass with the real property. A seller who wants to keep one should exclude it in the written contract before signing.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (fixtures)

questions.q: A restaurant tenant bolted commercial ovens to the floor for its business. What are the tenant's rights at the end of the lease?
options: They became the landlord's property when they were bolted down
It may remove them at any time, even years after the lease ends
It may remove them before the lease ends, repairing damage from removal
They must stay unless the landlord pays the tenant for them
questions.explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for its business remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed by the end of the lease, with any damage repaired. Items left behind may become the landlord's property by accession.
questions.citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (trade fixtures)

questions.q: What most clearly distinguishes a freehold estate from a leasehold estate?
options: A freehold can always be passed to heirs by will
A freehold can be created only by a recorded deed
A freehold lasts for an indefinite period of time
A freehold is classified as personal property
questions.explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple and life estates) have no fixed ending date; leaseholds run for a fixed term, a repeating period, or at will. A life estate is a freehold yet cannot be willed by the life tenant, so inheritability is not the test.
questions.citation: General real property law (estates in land)

questions.q: A tenant's interest under a ten-year commercial lease is traditionally classified as:
options: A freehold estate, since the term exceeds one year
A life estate measured by the tenant's business
A fee simple determinable that ends with the lease
A leasehold estate, treated as personal property
questions.explanation: A lease of any length creates a leasehold (nonfreehold) estate, historically called a chattel real and treated as personal property. A long term does not convert it into a freehold.

questions.q: A buyer takes fee simple absolute title to a vacant lot. Which of the following can still limit how the buyer uses it?
options: Nothing, since this fee carries no limits at all
Local zoning and recorded deed restrictions
Only restrictions the buyer personally signed
Only the seller's retained right of re-entry
questions.explanation: Fee simple absolute is the broadest estate, but it remains subject to government powers such as zoning and to private restrictions of record. A seller retains no right of re-entry in an absolute fee; that belongs to a fee on condition subsequent.
questions.citation: General real property law (fee simple absolute)

questions.q: Which deed wording most clearly creates a fee simple determinable?
options: "to the church, but if services stop, grantor may re-enter"
"to the church and its successors and assigns forever"
"to the church for the life of its current pastor"
"to the church for as long as services are held there"
questions.explanation: Durational words such as "so long as," "while," or "until" mark a determinable fee. "But if ... may re-enter" is the language of a fee on condition subsequent, "forever" gives a fee simple absolute, and "for the life of" creates a life estate.

questions.q: The grantor's future interest after a fee simple determinable is called a ____, while the grantor's interest after a fee simple on condition subsequent is a ____.
options: right of re-entry; possibility of reverter
remainder; reversion
reversion; remainder
possibility of reverter; right of re-entry
questions.explanation: A determinable fee is followed by a possibility of reverter, so title returns automatically. A fee on condition subsequent is followed by a right of re-entry (power of termination), which the grantor must exercise. Remainder and reversion follow life estates.

questions.q: An owner deeds a house "to my sister for life" and the deed says nothing more. When the sister dies, who owns the house?
options: The owner or the owner's heirs, by reversion
The sister's heirs, as remaindermen
The State of New York, by escheat
The sister's executor, by survivorship
questions.explanation: When no remainderman is named, the future interest stays with the grantor as a reversion and returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs. The sister held only a life estate, so she had nothing to pass to her heirs.

questions.q: Grace holds a life estate measured by her own life and sells it to Hal. Grace later dies while Hal is still alive. What happens to Hal's interest?
options: It continues for the rest of Hal's life
Hal now owns fee simple since he paid value
It passes to Hal's heirs when Hal dies
It ends, and the remainderman or reversioner takes
questions.explanation: A life tenant can transfer only what she holds. Hal bought an estate measured by Grace's life (pur autre vie), so it ends at Grace's death. The trap is assuming the buyer's own life becomes the measuring life.

questions.q: Without the remainderman's consent, a life tenant tears down a sound barn and clear-cuts the woodlot for timber. The remainderman's best claim is for:
options: Partition
Adverse possession
Waste
Breach of seisin
questions.explanation: A life tenant must not damage or deplete the property in a way that harms the future interest; destroying a sound building and stripping timber is waste. Partition divides co-owned property and does not apply between a life tenant and a remainderman.
questions.citation: General real property law (waste); RPAPL Article 8 (actions for waste)

questions.q: A life tenant lets the roof leak for years and makes no ordinary repairs, and the framing rots. This is best described as:
options: Permissive waste
Voluntary waste
Constructive eviction
Functional obsolescence
questions.explanation: Waste by neglect, such as failing to make ordinary repairs, is permissive waste. Voluntary (affirmative) waste is a deliberate harmful act, like demolishing a building.

questions.q: Absent any restriction in the granting deed, which action may a life tenant take without the remainderman's consent?
options: Sell the property in fee simple to a buyer
Lease the property for the duration of the life estate
Demolish the house to build a larger one
Leave the property to a friend by will
questions.explanation: A life tenant may possess, lease, mortgage, or sell the life estate itself, but any lease ends when the measuring life ends. She cannot convey a fee she does not own, commit waste, or will away an interest that ends at death.

questions.q: While a life estate is in effect, who is ordinarily responsible for paying the real property taxes?
options: The life tenant
The remainderman
The original grantor
Both, in equal shares
questions.explanation: The life tenant has possession and the income from the property, so ordinary carrying costs such as property taxes and routine repairs fall on the life tenant. The remainderman has no current possession.
questions.citation: General real property law (life tenant duties)

questions.q: An owner deeds a cottage "to Ira for as long as Ira's mother lives." Ira holds:
options: A life estate measured by Ira's life
An estate for years
A fee simple determinable
A life estate pur autre vie
questions.explanation: An estate measured by the life of someone other than the holder (here, Ira's mother) is a life estate pur autre vie. "For as long as" sounds determinable, but an estate that must end at a person's death is a life estate, not a fee.

questions.q: While a life estate is in effect, the remainderman:
options: May share occupancy with the life tenant
Owns a future interest that may be sold now
Has no property interest of any kind yet
Must pay the property taxes each year
questions.explanation: A remainderman has a present ownership of a future interest, which can be sold or mortgaged, but no right to possession until the life estate ends. Possession and ordinary carrying costs belong to the life tenant.

questions.q: A widow asks whether she has a dower right in a house her late husband owned in his own name in New York. The correct response is that:
options: Dower gives her a life estate in one-third
Dower is abolished; she may have a right of election
Dower applies only to the marital residence
Dower applies if she claims it within six months
questions.explanation: New York abolished dower and curtesy. A surviving spouse is protected instead by the statutory right of election against the deceased spouse's will. The one-third life estate describes historic common-law dower.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT available to a married couple or a surviving spouse in New York today?
options: Curtesy
Tenancy by the entirety
Right of election
Joint tenancy
questions.explanation: Curtesy, the historic life estate of a husband in his deceased wife's land, has been abolished in New York along with dower. Married couples may hold title as tenants by the entirety or joint tenants, and a surviving spouse has a right of election.

questions.q: New York's homestead exemption primarily:
options: Gives a surviving spouse a life estate in the home
Lowers school taxes on owner-occupied homes
Bars any foreclosure of a primary residence
Shields some home equity from judgment creditors
questions.explanation: The homestead exemption protects a limited amount of equity in a principal residence from being taken to satisfy money judgments. It is not a surviving-spouse life estate (New York does not recognize one) and is not the STAR school tax program.

questions.q: A homeowner defaults on a mortgage he signed when buying his primary residence. Does the homestead exemption prevent the lender's foreclosure?
options: Yes; a primary residence can never be foreclosed
No; it does not defeat a mortgage he gave voluntarily
Yes, if he has lived there for at least ten years
No, because it covers only vacant investment land
questions.explanation: The exemption limits what unsecured money-judgment creditors can reach; it does not cancel a lien the owner voluntarily granted as security for the purchase loan. It applies to a principal residence, not vacant land.

questions.q: A tenant signs a lease running from March 1 to August 31 of the same year. This lease creates:
options: A periodic tenancy
An estate for years
A tenancy at will
A tenancy at sufferance
questions.explanation: Any lease with a definite beginning and ending date is an estate for years, even when the term is shorter than a year. A periodic tenancy has no fixed end and renews period to period.

questions.q: Which of the following estates ends upon the death of either the landlord or the tenant?
options: A tenancy at will
An estate for years
A month-to-month tenancy
A fee simple absolute
questions.explanation: A tenancy at will rests on the parties' continuing consent, so it ends when either party dies. An estate for years and a periodic tenancy survive the death of either party and bind the estate.
questions.citation: General real property law (tenancy at will)

questions.q: What separates a tenant at sufferance from a trespasser?
options: The tenant at sufferance first entered lawfully
The tenant at sufferance has a written lease
The tenant at sufferance owes no rent at all
The tenant at sufferance has the owner's consent
questions.explanation: A tenant at sufferance came into possession under a valid tenancy and stayed after it ended without the owner's consent. A trespasser never had a right to enter. Continuing consent would make it a tenancy at will, not sufferance.

questions.q: A tenant's one-year lease expires, the tenant stays, and the landlord accepts the next monthly rent payment. Absent another agreement, New York law generally treats the tenancy as:
options: A renewal for another full year
A tenancy at sufferance
A month-to-month tenancy
A tenancy at will with no notice
questions.explanation: New York does not apply the common-law rule that accepting rent renews the lease for a full term; a holdover whose rent is accepted is generally a month-to-month tenant. Acceptance of rent shows consent, so it is no longer sufferance.

questions.q: An owner lets her nephew live in a spare house with no set term and no fixed rental period, until either of them decides to end it. This is:
options: An estate for years
A tenancy at will
A tenancy at sufferance
A life estate
questions.explanation: Possession with the owner's consent but no fixed term or period is a tenancy at will. Sufferance requires a holdover without consent, and an estate for years needs a definite term.

questions.q: A deed conveys land "to Ana and Ben," who are not married to each other, with no other language. Under New York law they hold title as:
options: Joint tenants
Tenants by the entirety
Tenants in common
Owners in severalty
questions.explanation: New York presumes a tenancy in common when real property goes to two or more persons unless the instrument expressly declares a joint tenancy. Naming two grantees alone does not create survivorship.

questions.q: A deed conveys a house "to Carla and Dev," who are married to each other, and says nothing about the form of ownership. They hold title as:
options: Tenants in common
Tenants by the entirety
Joint tenants
Owners in severalty
questions.explanation: A disposition to persons married to each other creates a tenancy by the entirety unless the instrument expressly declares a tenancy in common or joint tenancy. The tenancy-in-common default applies only to unmarried co-grantees.

questions.q: Three unrelated friends own a cabin as joint tenants with right of survivorship. One dies, leaving a will that gives everything to her son. Who owns the cabin?
options: The son and both friends, one-third each
The son alone, under the terms of the will
The two surviving friends, one-half each
The friends and the son as tenants in common
questions.explanation: Survivorship operates at the moment of death, so the deceased joint tenant's interest passes to the surviving joint tenants and never enters her estate. A will cannot override it: 1 ÷ 2 survivors gives each one-half.

questions.q: Eva, Finn, and Gia own land as joint tenants. Eva sells her interest to Hugo. Later Finn dies. Who owns the land, and how?
options: Gia two-thirds and Hugo one-third, as tenants in common
Gia and Hugo one-half each, as joint tenants
Gia owns all of it by right of survivorship
Gia, Hugo, and Finn's heirs one-third each
questions.explanation: Eva's sale severed her one-third, so Hugo holds 1/3 as a tenant in common; Finn and Gia stayed joint tenants as to the other 2/3. When Finn died, Gia took his share by survivorship: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 for Gia, with Hugo still holding 1/3.
questions.citation: General real property law (severance of joint tenancy)

questions.q: The four unities traditionally required to create a joint tenancy are:
options: Possession, interest, time, and marriage
Possession, consent, title, and recording
Possession, interest, time, and title
Interest, title, survival, and severalty
questions.explanation: Joint tenants must take equal interests (interest), by the same deed (title), at the same time (time), with equal rights to possess the whole (possession). Marriage is the added fifth unity for a tenancy by the entirety.

questions.q: Two investors take title to a building as tenants in common, and one paid 70% of the price. Which statement is true?
options: The law requires them to hold equal half shares
The larger investor alone may occupy the building
Each one's share passes to the other at death
Their shares may be unequal, such as 70% and 30%
questions.explanation: Tenants in common may hold unequal undivided shares, but each has the right to possess the whole property. Unequal shares are a key contrast with joint tenancy, and there is no survivorship among tenants in common.
questions.citation: General real property law (tenancy in common)

questions.q: A tenancy by the entirety requires the four unities of a joint tenancy plus:
options: A valid marriage between the owners
A recorded survivorship affidavit
Equal financial contributions
Use as the couple's primary home
questions.explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is available only to spouses, so marriage is the fifth unity. It does not depend on who paid what or on the property being the couple's residence.

questions.q: A married couple owns their home as tenants by the entirety and later divorces. Absent an agreement or court order, they then generally own it as:
options: Joint tenants with survivorship
Tenants by the entirety until death
The higher earner, in severalty
Tenants in common
questions.explanation: Divorce ends the marriage that a tenancy by the entirety requires, and in New York the former spouses generally become tenants in common, with no survivorship. Title does not pass automatically to either spouse alone.
questions.citation: Stelz v. Shreck, 128 N.Y. 263 (1891); general real property law (tenancy by the entirety)

questions.q: A wife holds her home with her husband as tenants by the entirety. She wants to sell over his objection. Which statement is correct?
options: She may sell the whole house since she paid most of it
She cannot convey the whole or force a partition alone
She may force a partition sale as any co-owner can
She may end the survivorship by deeding to herself
questions.explanation: A tenancy by the entirety protects each spouse's survivorship right; one spouse cannot unilaterally convey the entire property or compel partition while the marriage lasts. Who paid more does not change that.
questions.citation: General real property law (tenancy by the entirety)

questions.q: Two tenants in common cannot agree whether to sell their jointly owned lot. Either of them may ask a court to:
options: Declare a reversion to the grantor
Convert it to a tenancy by the entirety
Grant one owner an easement by necessity
Order a partition by division or sale
questions.explanation: A partition action lets a co-owner end the co-ownership: the court divides the land physically or, if that is impractical, orders a sale and divides the proceeds.

questions.q: A corporation with 500 shareholders takes title to a warehouse. How is the warehouse owned?
options: As tenants in common among the shareholders
As joint tenants among the board members
In severalty, by the corporation as one entity
In common by the officers who signed the deed
questions.explanation: A corporation is a single legal person, so property titled in its name is owned in severalty. Shareholders own stock in the corporation, not undivided interests in its real estate.
questions.citation: General real property law (ownership by entities)

questions.q: Investors want to own a rental building with personal protection from the business's debts while managing it themselves. The form most often chosen is:
options: A general partnership
A joint tenancy
A tenancy in common
A limited liability company
questions.explanation: An LLC lets members participate in management while generally shielding their personal assets from the company's debts. General partners, joint tenants, and tenants in common have no such entity shield.

questions.q: When real estate is placed in a trust, legal title is held by the:
options: Beneficiary
Trustor
Trustee
Executor
questions.explanation: The trustor (settlor) creates the trust; the trustee holds legal title and manages under the trust instrument; the beneficiary receives the benefits (equitable interest). An executor administers a decedent's estate, not a trust.

questions.q: Several investors join together to buy, build, and sell one specific subdivision, then disband. This arrangement is best described as:
options: A real estate investment trust
A tenancy by the entirety
A joint venture
A housing cooperative
questions.explanation: A joint venture combines parties for a single project of limited duration. A REIT is an ongoing investment vehicle owning many properties, and a tenancy by the entirety is available only to spouses.

questions.q: An owner signs a five-year lease of her building. Which right in her bundle of rights does she temporarily transfer to the tenant?
options: Disposition
Possession
Legal title
Escheat
questions.explanation: A lease transfers possession (and use) for the term while the owner keeps title and the right of disposition, meaning she can still sell the building subject to the lease. Escheat is a government power, not an owner's right.
questions.citation: General real property law (bundle of rights)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT part of a private owner's traditional bundle of rights?
options: Right of exclusion
Right of escheat
Right of enjoyment
Right of disposition
questions.explanation: The bundle includes possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition. Escheat is a government power under which property passes to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
questions.citation: General real property law (bundle of rights)

questions.q: A homeowner cuts down a tree in the yard and stacks the logs for firewood. The logs are now:
options: Personal property, since they were severed
Real property, since they grew on the land
Fixtures, since they remain on the parcel
Trade fixtures belonging to the homeowner
questions.explanation: A growing tree is part of the real property, but severance converts it into personal property (chattel). Logs merely lying on the ground are not attached, so they are not fixtures.
questions.citation: General real property law (real vs. personal property)

questions.q: A tenant farmer plants an annual crop, but the lease ends without the tenant's fault before harvest. The doctrine that may allow the tenant to come back and harvest is:
options: Accretion
Severalty
Escheat
Emblements
questions.explanation: Emblements are annual crops produced by labor; a tenant whose tenancy ends through no fault of their own before harvest may generally enter to harvest them. Accretion concerns soil deposited by water.

questions.q: A railroad sells a developer the right to build an office tower over its tracks while keeping the tracks in use. The developer has acquired:
options: Air rights
Riparian rights
Subsurface rights
An easement by necessity
questions.explanation: Air rights, the right to use the space above the surface, can be sold separately from the land. Subsurface rights concern the area below the surface, and riparian rights concern flowing water.

questions.q: An owner sells farmland but keeps the right to extract the natural gas beneath it. The owner has:
options: Created a tenancy in common with the buyer
Retained the littoral rights to the land
Reserved the subsurface (mineral) rights
Kept a life estate in the surface only
questions.explanation: Surface and subsurface rights can be separated; reserving the gas leaves the seller with mineral rights while the buyer owns the surface. Littoral rights concern land bordering lakes or seas.

questions.q: A house sits on the shore of Lake George. The owner's rights to access and use the lake water are called:
options: Littoral rights
Riparian rights
Percolating rights
Avulsion rights
questions.explanation: Littoral rights belong to owners of land bordering stationary bodies of water such as lakes and seas. Riparian rights belong to owners bordering flowing water such as rivers and streams.

questions.q: A spring flood suddenly cuts a new channel for a stream, abruptly tearing away part of a farm. This sudden change is called:
options: Accretion
Reliction
Avulsion
Alluvion
questions.explanation: Avulsion is a sudden, perceptible loss or shift of land caused by water. Accretion is the gradual buildup of soil (the deposit itself is alluvion), and reliction is land exposed as water gradually recedes.
questions.citation: General real property law (water-related land changes)

questions.q: A village levies a charge against a home to pay for new sidewalks along its frontage. If unpaid, the resulting lien is best classified as:
options: Voluntary and general
Involuntary and specific
Voluntary and specific
Involuntary and general
questions.explanation: A special assessment lien arises by law without the owner's consent (involuntary) and attaches only to the benefited parcel (specific). Calling it general confuses it with a judgment or federal tax lien, which reach all of a debtor's property.
questions.citation: General real property law (special assessment liens)

questions.q: The IRS files a notice of federal tax lien against a taxpayer who owes unpaid income tax. How is this lien classified?
options: Voluntary and general
Voluntary and specific
Involuntary and specific
Involuntary and general
questions.explanation: A federal tax lien arises by operation of law (involuntary) and attaches to all of the taxpayer's property and rights to property (general). The trap is treating it like a property tax lien, which is specific to one parcel.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between liens and encumbrances?
options: Every encumbrance is a lien, but only some liens are encumbrances
Liens and encumbrances are two names for the same interest
Every lien is an encumbrance, but some encumbrances are not liens
An encumbrance must be recorded, while a lien never needs recording
questions.explanation: An encumbrance is any interest that burdens title or use; a lien is the money-claim type of encumbrance. Easements, restrictions and encroachments are encumbrances that secure no debt, so not every encumbrance is a lien.

questions.q: A homeowner borrows against her house and signs a home equity mortgage. This lien is:
options: Involuntary, because the bank can foreclose without her consent
General, because it reaches all property she owns
Statutory, because the Lien Law creates it on signing
Voluntary and specific, attaching only to the mortgaged parcel
questions.explanation: The owner chooses to give the mortgage (voluntary), and it secures the debt only with the described property (specific). The foreclosure remedy does not make the lien involuntary; how a lien is created decides that label.

questions.q: A plumber files a notice of mechanic's lien against a client's building. Under the NY Lien Law, when must the plumber serve a copy of the notice on the owner?
options: Within 4 months after filing the notice
Within 10 days after the last day of work
At least 30 days before filing the notice
Within 5 days before or 30 days after filing
questions.explanation: Lien Law §11 requires service on the owner within 5 days before or 30 days after the notice of lien is filed. The 4-month figure is the filing deadline for a single-family dwelling, not the service window.

questions.q: A contractor files a notice of lien and serves the owner properly, but never files proof of service with the county clerk. What is the result after 35 days from filing?
options: The lien stays valid but cannot be foreclosed until proof is filed
The notice terminates as a lien
The lien converts into a general lien on the owner's property
The owner must post a bond to keep the lien from expanding
questions.explanation: Lien Law §11 says failure to file proof of service within 35 days after the notice of lien is filed terminates the notice as a lien. Proper service alone is not enough; the filing of proof is what preserves it.

questions.q: A notice of mechanic's lien was filed on May 12, 2026, against an office building. If the lienor does nothing further, when does it stop being a lien?
options: November 12, 2026, six months after filing
January 12, 2027, eight months after filing
May 12, 2027, one year after filing
May 12, 2036, ten years after filing
questions.explanation: Lien Law §17 limits a mechanic's lien to one year after filing unless a foreclosure action with a notice of pendency is filed or the lien is extended. Ten years is the judgment-lien period, and eight months is a filing deadline, not a duration.

questions.q: A contractor's lien on a single-family house will expire in three weeks. The contractor is not ready to sue to foreclose. How can the lien be extended?
options: Only by an order of a court of record
By filing an extension with the county clerk
By re-serving the owner with a new notice
By recording a second notice of lien
questions.explanation: Lien Law §17 bars extension by simple filing for a lien on a single-family dwelling; it may only be extended by court order. For other property, filing an extension with the county clerk within the first year is allowed.

questions.q: A supplier holds a mechanic's lien on a 20-unit apartment building. Before the first year runs out, the supplier files an extension with the county clerk. For how long does that filed extension continue the lien?
options: Six months from the original expiration
No more than one year from its filing
Until the building is sold or refinanced
Ten years, like a docketed judgment
questions.explanation: Under Lien Law §17, a filed extension cannot continue the lien for more than one year from the extension's filing; after that, a foreclosure action or a court order is needed. Liens do not ride along until a sale, and the 10-year period belongs to judgments.

questions.q: An owner wants to sell a building that has a $23,600 mechanic's lien on it. To discharge the lien by bond under the Lien Law, the bond must be at least:
questions.explanation: Lien Law §19(4) requires a bond equal to 110% of the lien: $23,600 × 1.10 = $25,960. $23,600 omits the 10% cushion, $27,140 uses 115%, and $35,400 uses 150%.

questions.q: An owner posts a proper bond and obtains discharge of a mechanic's lien. What is the effect?
options: The lienor loses all right to be paid for the work
The lien is moved to the owner's other real estate
The lien stays on title until the claim is resolved
The claim shifts to the bond and the land is freed
questions.explanation: Discharging a lien by bond releases the real property; the lienor's claim is now secured by the bond instead. The lienor does not lose its claim; it simply must pursue the bond rather than the land.

questions.q: A contractor finishes renovating an owner-occupied two-family house on February 2. What is the deadline to file a notice of mechanic's lien?
options: 8 months after completion, since it is not a single-family dwelling
4 months after completion, since the owner lives in the house
90 days after completion, the same as any residential job
1 year after completion, the life of a mechanic's lien
questions.explanation: Lien Law §10's shorter 4-month window applies only to a single-family dwelling; a two-family house falls under the general 8-month deadline. Owner occupancy does not trigger the 4-month rule, and one year is how long a filed lien lasts.

questions.q: A contractor starts work on January 5. A bank records a mortgage on the property on February 1. The unpaid contractor files a notice of lien on April 2. Under NY law, which has priority?
options: The lien, because it relates back to the January 5 start of work
The mortgage, because it was recorded before the notice was filed
The lien, because mechanic's liens always outrank mortgages
Neither, because the two share any foreclosure proceeds equally
questions.explanation: Lien Law §13 gives a mechanic's lien priority over interests not recorded when the notice of lien is filed; a mortgage recorded earlier stays ahead. NY measures from the filing of the notice, not the start of work, which is the relation-back trap from other states.

questions.q: An owner's renovation contract with a general contractor is $40,000. The job is complete and the owner has paid $34,000 in good faith. An unpaid subcontractor then files a $10,000 lien. What is the most the lien can recover against the owner's property?
questions.explanation: Under Lien Law §4, a subcontractor's lien cannot exceed the amount earned and unpaid on the owner's contract when the notice is filed: $40,000 − $34,000 = $6,000. The full $10,000 claim ignores this cap, and $4,000 wrongly subtracts $6,000 from $10,000.

questions.q: A home improvement contract includes a clause, signed before any work begins, in which the contractor gives up any right to file a mechanic's lien. This clause is:
options: Void as against public policy
Enforceable if the owner paid a deposit
Valid only if it is notarized and recorded
Binding on subcontractors but not the contractor
questions.explanation: Lien Law §34 voids any agreement waiving the right to file or enforce a mechanic's lien. The statute does allow a written waiver delivered at or after payment for the work, but an advance waiver in the contract is unenforceable.

questions.q: A contractor who is owed $8,000 knowingly files a notice of lien claiming $19,000. If a court finds the amount was willfully exaggerated, the likely result is that:
options: The lien is reduced to $8,000 and stays in force
The lien remains valid until the owner posts a bond
The lien is void and the contractor may owe damages
The contractor must refile within 30 days at $8,000
questions.explanation: Under Lien Law §§39 and 39-a, a willfully exaggerated lien is void, and the lienor can be liable for damages, including the cost of discharging it. A court does not simply trim the amount when the exaggeration was willful.

questions.q: A retail tenant hires a contractor to install new storefront lighting. The landlord did not request or consent to the work. If the tenant does not pay, the contractor's lien can attach to:
options: The landlord's fee title to the building
The tenant's leasehold interest only
The landlord's other properties in the county
Nothing, because tenants cannot contract for work
questions.explanation: A tenant is an "owner" of its leasehold under Lien Law §2, and §3 gives a lien on an owner's interest for work done with that owner's consent or at its request. Without the landlord's affirmative consent, the lien reaches only the tenant's leasehold, not the landlord's fee.

questions.q: A judgment against Ruth was docketed in Albany County in 2023. In 2025, she buys a house in Albany County. What is the status of the house?
options: The judgment is a lien on the house
The house is exempt because it was bought later
A new lawsuit is needed to reach the house
The lien attaches only if Ruth agrees in writing
questions.explanation: A docketed judgment is a general lien on the debtor's real property in that county, including property acquired later during the 10-year lien period. No new suit or consent is needed for the lien to attach.

questions.q: A creditor's judgment is docketed in Westchester County, but the debtor also owns a cabin in Ulster County. How can the creditor obtain a lien on the cabin?
options: Record a lis pendens against the debtor's home
File a mechanic's lien in Ulster County
Wait; a docketed judgment reaches every county
Docket a transcript of the judgment in Ulster County
questions.explanation: A judgment is a lien only on real property in a county where it is docketed, so the creditor must docket it with the Ulster County clerk. A judgment does not automatically reach every county, and a lis pendens does not create a money lien.

questions.q: A notice of pendency (lis pendens) is filed against a property. Under the CPLR, how long does it remain effective?
options: 1 year, renewable by filing an extension
10 years, like a docketed money judgment
Until the property is sold to a new owner
3 years, extendable by court order for good cause
questions.explanation: CPLR §6513 makes a notice of pendency effective for 3 years from filing, and a court may extend it for a like period on a showing of good cause. One year is the mechanic's lien period and 10 years is the judgment-lien period.

questions.q: A buyer closes on a lot one month after a neighbor filed a notice of pendency in a boundary lawsuit against the seller. The buyer never searched title. How is the buyer affected?
options: The buyer is bound by the outcome of the lawsuit
The buyer takes free because he lacked actual notice
The suit is dismissed because the owner has changed
The seller alone bears the risk of the suit's result
questions.explanation: A filed notice of pendency is constructive notice, so a later purchaser is bound by the judgment as if a party to the suit. Lack of actual knowledge does not protect a buyer who could have found the filing in a title search.

questions.q: Before trial, a court orders a defendant's real property held so that it will be available if the plaintiff later wins a money judgment. This is called:
options: A writ of execution
An attachment
A lis pendens
A satisfaction
questions.explanation: An attachment is a prejudgment remedy that seizes or holds property to secure a possible judgment. A writ of execution comes after judgment to enforce it, and a lis pendens only gives notice of a suit affecting title.

questions.q: A notice of federal tax lien was filed against an owner in 2023. In 2026, the owner fails to pay the year's real property taxes. Which lien generally has priority against the house?
options: The federal tax lien, because federal claims always come first
The federal tax lien, because its notice was filed earlier
Neither; they share proceeds in proportion to the amounts
The real property tax lien, despite being later in time
questions.explanation: Federal law yields to local real property tax and special assessment liens that have priority under local law, even when the federal notice was filed first. The trap is assuming either federal status or first-in-time filing beats the property tax lien.

questions.q: A bank's mortgage was recorded in 2020. In 2024, the IRS files a notice of federal tax lien against the homeowner. Which interest generally has priority on the house?
options: The bank's mortgage, recorded before the tax lien notice
The federal tax lien, because it is a government claim
The federal tax lien, because it is a general lien
Whichever creditor first starts a foreclosure action
questions.explanation: A federal tax lien is not valid against a holder of a security interest, such as a mortgagee, until the notice of federal tax lien is filed, so the earlier mortgage stays ahead. Unlike local real property taxes, a federal tax lien gets no special priority over prior recorded mortgages.

questions.q: Lot A's owner holds a recorded easement to use a driveway that crosses Lot B to reach the street. Which statement is correct?
options: Lot B is the dominant estate
Lot A is the servient estate
Lot B is the servient estate
Neither lot is dominant or servient
questions.explanation: The servient estate bears the burden of the easement; Lot B's land is crossed, so it is servient. Lot A benefits from the easement, which makes it the dominant estate.

questions.q: An owner sells the front half of her land but, in the deed to the buyer, keeps for herself the right to keep crossing the front half to reach her well. Her right was created by:
options: Reservation in the deed
Prescription
Implication from necessity
An oral license
questions.explanation: When a grantor conveys land but keeps an easement over it for her own use, the easement is created by reservation. Prescription requires years of adverse use, and a license is a revocable permission, not an interest in land.

questions.q: A single owner's two lots were served by an underground sewer line running from the rear house across the front lot, with a visible cleanout cap. He sells the front lot without mentioning the line. The rear lot most likely has:
options: An easement in gross held by the sewer district
No right, because the deed did not mention the line
A license that the new front-lot owner may revoke
An implied easement based on the prior use
questions.explanation: When one owner's land is divided, an apparent, continuous use that is necessary for the retained parcel's enjoyment can create an easement by implication. The deed's silence does not defeat it, and the rear lot's right is appurtenant, not in gross.
questions.citation: General real property law (easements by implication)

questions.q: A landlocked parcel received an easement by necessity across a neighbor's land. Years later, the county builds a public road along the parcel's back line. What is the likely effect?
options: The easement continues permanently because it was recorded
The easement ends because the necessity has ended
The easement becomes an easement in gross for the county
The neighbor must now pay for the parcel's road frontage
questions.explanation: An easement by necessity lasts only as long as the necessity that created it; once the parcel has its own public access, the easement ends. An express easement by grant would not end this way.
questions.citation: General real property law (easements by necessity)

questions.q: The owner of a dominant parcel buys the servient parcel that his driveway easement crosses. What happens to the easement?
options: It is extinguished by merger
It becomes a license he may revoke
It continues as a separate right
It converts to an easement in gross
questions.explanation: An easement is a right in another's land. When one person owns both the dominant and the servient parcels, the easement ends by merger, and it does not revive merely if the parcels are later separated.
questions.citation: General real property law (termination of easements)

questions.q: A recorded right-of-way created by deed has not been used for 15 years, but its owner has done nothing else to show an intent to give it up. Under NY law, the easement:
options: Ended automatically after 10 years of nonuse
Became a license that either party may revoke
Is still in effect, because nonuse alone does not end it
Passed by prescription to the servient owner
questions.explanation: An easement created by grant is not lost by nonuse alone; abandonment requires an intent to abandon shown by clear acts. The 10-year figure is the adverse possession period, which requires adverse acts by the servient owner, not just nonuse.
questions.citation: General real property law (abandonment of easements)

questions.q: A dominant owner no longer needs a utility path across a neighbor's yard and wants to end the easement permanently. The cleanest way is to:
options: Stop using the path for one full year
Give the neighbor a written release and record it
Tell the neighbor orally that the path is no longer needed
Let the neighbor build a fence across the path
questions.explanation: A written release from the dominant owner to the servient owner, recorded, terminates the easement and clears the record. Oral statements and brief nonuse do not reliably end a recorded easement.
questions.citation: General real property law (termination of easements)

questions.q: What is the key difference between an easement by prescription and title by adverse possession?
options: Prescription requires 20 years, adverse possession 10
Adverse possession needs no hostile use; prescription does
Prescription gives title, adverse possession only use
Prescription gives a right to use; adverse possession gives title
questions.explanation: Both require open, notorious, continuous and hostile use for the 10-year statutory period in NY, but prescription yields only an easement, while adverse possession transfers ownership.

questions.q: For 12 years a neighbor has walked across Dan's yard to reach a lake. When the use began, the neighbor asked Dan, who said, "Sure, go ahead." Does the neighbor have a prescriptive easement?
options: No, because the use was permissive rather than hostile
Yes, because the use lasted more than 10 years
Yes, because Dan never revoked the permission
No, because a path to a lake cannot be an easement
questions.explanation: Prescription requires hostile use, meaning use without the owner's permission. Use that began with permission is a license, and the passage of time alone does not convert it into an easement.

questions.q: A homeowner lets her neighbor park a boat in her side yard, with no written agreement. She then sells the house. What is the neighbor's right to keep parking there?
options: It continues because it is an easement appurtenant
It continues for 10 years from when it began
It ends, because the license does not bind the buyer
It ends only after the buyer gives 30 days' notice
questions.explanation: Informal permission to use land is a license: a personal, generally revocable privilege, not an interest in land. A license ends when the licensor sells the property or revokes it, so the buyer is not bound.

questions.q: A landowner grants a gravel company the right to enter her land and remove sand and gravel. This right is best described as:
options: A license
An easement appurtenant
A profit (profit à prendre)
An encroachment
questions.explanation: A profit is the right to enter another's land and take something from it, such as gravel, timber or minerals. A plain easement allows use but not removal of resources, and a license is a revocable permission rather than an interest in land.

questions.q: A subdivision's recorded declaration bars detached garages. A new owner starts building one. A neighbor who owns a lot bound by the same declaration most likely may:
options: Do nothing, since only the town enforces such limits
Ask the building inspector to revoke the owner's deed
Seek a court injunction to stop the construction
Reclaim the lot under a possibility of reverter
questions.explanation: Restrictive covenants under a common subdivision plan run with the land and may be enforced by other benefited lot owners, usually by injunction. Private deed restrictions are separate from zoning, and a covenant breach does not cause a reversion of title.

questions.q: A 1940s deed in a buyer's chain of title contains a covenant barring sale to members of a certain race. Today this covenant is:
options: Enforceable only against buyers who knew of it
Unenforceable under fair housing law
Binding until removed by a vote of neighbors
Valid if no one has challenged it in 50 years
questions.explanation: Racially restrictive covenants cannot be enforced by courts and violate federal and state fair housing laws. They remain void regardless of buyer knowledge, neighbor votes, or how long they sat unchallenged.
questions.citation: Shelley v. Kraemer (1948); Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. §3604

questions.q: A neighbor's hedge has grown two feet over the property line for 14 years. The neighbor now claims the strip by adverse possession. Under NY law, the hedge encroachment is:
options: Enough for title, since 10 years have passed
Enough only if the neighbor also paid the taxes
Deemed permissive and not adverse
Converted into an easement by prescription
questions.explanation: RPAPL §543 deems de minimis non-structural encroachments, such as fences, hedges, plantings and sheds, permissive and non-adverse. Without hostility, the 10-year period does not ripen into title or a prescriptive easement.

questions.q: Custom-cut storm windows made for a house are stored in the basement when the sale closes. The contract is silent. How are they most likely treated?
options: As the seller's personal property because they are unattached
As fixtures that convey, since they were adapted to the house
As the seller's property unless the buyer pays separately
As trade fixtures the seller may remove within 30 days
questions.explanation: Under the adaptation factor, items made specifically for a particular building are generally treated as fixtures even when temporarily detached. Physical attachment is only one factor; intention shown by adaptation controls here.

questions.q: A tenant and an owner each mount an identical wall air-conditioner. Which fixture factor most explains why the tenant's unit is more likely to remain personal property?
options: The relationship of the parties
The method of annexation
The adaptability of the item
The cost of the item
questions.explanation: Courts presume a tenant installs items for its own use and intends to remove them, while an owner's improvements are presumed permanent. The attachment method is identical here, so the parties' relationship is the deciding factor.

questions.q: A seller's dining room chandelier is wired into the ceiling. The signed contract states, "Seller excludes the dining room chandelier." At closing, the chandelier:
options: Must stay, because it is wired in as a fixture
Belongs to the buyer unless a bill of sale is signed
Must stay unless the seller installs a substitute
May be removed by the seller under the agreement
questions.explanation: A written agreement between the parties overrides the other fixture tests. Even a firmly attached item may be excluded, though the seller should leave the wiring safely capped.

questions.q: A bakery tenant's lease expires and the tenant moves out, leaving its bolted-down display cases and ovens. No lease clause addresses them. Who generally owns them now?
options: The tenant, who may return to remove them at any time
The tenant, until the landlord pays their fair value
The landlord, by accession
The next tenant of the space
questions.explanation: Trade fixtures remain the tenant's personal property only if removed by the end of the tenancy; items left behind generally become the landlord's property by accession. The tenant has no open-ended right to return for them.

questions.q: A life tenant plants a field of corn in May and dies in July, before the harvest. Who is generally entitled to harvest the crop?
options: The life tenant's estate
The remainderman alone
The county where the land lies
Whoever first cuts the crop
questions.explanation: Under the doctrine of emblements, a tenant whose estate ends unexpectedly through no fault of its own, such as the end of a measuring life, may enter to harvest annual crops it planted. The remainderman takes the land but not that crop.

questions.q: Which is generally treated as personal property rather than part of the real estate?
options: An apple orchard
A planted wheat crop
A stand of oak trees
Perennial shrubbery
questions.explanation: Annual crops produced by labor (fructus industriales), such as wheat, are generally treated as personal property. Trees, orchards and perennial plantings (fructus naturales) are part of the real property.

questions.q: Under New York's statute of frauds, which agreement must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged to be enforceable?
options: A lease of an apartment for six months
An agreement for a salesperson to show a home on Saturday
A contract for the sale of a single-family house
A month-to-month rental of a garage space
questions.explanation: GOL § 5-703 requires contracts for the sale of real property (and leases longer than one year) to be in a writing subscribed by the party to be charged. Leases of one year or less, like a six-month or month-to-month rental, may be oral.

questions.q: Before the tenant moves in, a landlord and tenant orally agree to a two-year lease of a store. The landlord then refuses to honor it. The oral lease is best described as:
options: Unenforceable, because a lease for more than one year must be in writing
Void, because a lease can never be created orally
Fully enforceable, because both parties clearly agreed to it
Voidable only at the tenant's option because the tenant relied on it
questions.explanation: A lease for more than one year falls within the statute of frauds, so this oral two-year lease cannot be enforced in court. Trap: it is unenforceable, not void — oral leases of one year or less are perfectly valid.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an essential element of a valid real estate contract?
options: Competent parties who have legal capacity to contract
Consideration exchanged between the buyer and seller
A lawful object or purpose for the agreement
Recording in the county clerk's office
questions.explanation: A valid contract needs competent parties, mutual assent (offer and acceptance), consideration, and a lawful object, and a real estate sale contract must also be in writing. Recording gives constructive notice to the public; it is not required for the contract to be valid between the parties.
questions.citation: General contract law; NY GOL § 5-703; NY RPL § 291 (recording)

questions.q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy a vacant lot from an adult seller. The contract is:
options: Void from the start because minors cannot sign contracts
Voidable at the minor's option
Voidable at the seller's option only
Valid and binding on both parties because both signed
questions.explanation: In New York a person under 18 is a minor (infant). A minor's contract is generally voidable by the minor, who may disaffirm it, while the adult remains bound if the minor chooses to go through with it. Trap: voidable, not void.

questions.q: Two parties sign a contract whose stated purpose is to sell a building to be used for an illegal gambling operation. The contract is:
options: Void, because it lacks a lawful object
Voidable at the buyer's option
Valid but unenforceable until the buyer obtains a license
Valid, because transferring real property is itself legal
questions.explanation: A contract for an illegal purpose lacks the essential element of a lawful object, so it is void — it has no legal effect, and neither party can enforce it. Voidable contracts (such as those induced by fraud or a minor's contract) are valid until one party disaffirms.

questions.q: A buyer and a seller sign a written purchase contract in which the buyer promises to pay $410,000 and the seller promises to convey title. This contract is best described as:
options: Implied and unilateral
Express and unilateral
Express and bilateral
Implied and bilateral
questions.explanation: It is express because the terms are stated in words (written or oral), and bilateral because each side exchanges a promise for a promise. An implied contract arises from conduct, and a unilateral contract is a promise given in exchange for an act.

questions.q: A seller tells area brokers she will pay a $5,000 bonus to whichever cooperating agent first brings a buyer who closes. No agent promises to do anything. This arrangement is best described as:
options: A bilateral contract binding on every broker who hears it
An executed contract as soon as it is announced
A void contract for lack of any consideration
A unilateral contract, accepted only by performance
questions.explanation: A unilateral contract is a promise in exchange for an act: only the seller is bound, and an agent accepts by actually producing the buyer who closes. No agent is obligated to try, which is why it is not bilateral.

questions.q: A purchase contract has been signed by both buyer and seller, and the closing is scheduled for next month. Right now the contract is:
options: Executed, because both parties have signed it
Executory, because performance is still to come
Unilateral, because only the seller still has to act
Implied, because the closing terms are still pending
questions.explanation: An executory contract has obligations still to be performed; it becomes executed only when both sides have fully performed (here, at closing). Trap: 'executed' does not mean 'signed.'

questions.q: A buyer offers $500,000. The seller replies, 'I'll take $520,000.' The buyer declines. The next day the seller says, 'Fine, I accept your $500,000 offer.' What is the legal status?
options: No contract yet; the seller's statement is only a new offer the buyer may accept or reject
A binding contract at $500,000, because the seller accepted the buyer's exact original terms
A binding contract at $520,000, because that was the last price either party stated
A binding contract at $500,000, but the buyer may cancel within three days of the acceptance
questions.explanation: A counteroffer is a rejection of the original offer and terminates it. The buyer's $500,000 offer no longer exists to be accepted, so the seller's later 'acceptance' is only a new offer that the buyer is free to accept or reject.

questions.q: A buyer hands a salesperson a $20,000 earnest money check payable to the brokerage. What should the salesperson do?
options: Deposit it in the salesperson's own personal account and hold it there until closing
Keep it safely in a locked desk drawer at the office until the closing date is near
Promptly turn it over to the supervising broker for deposit in a separate escrow account
Give it directly to the seller, since the earnest money belongs to the seller once signed
questions.explanation: A salesperson must promptly turn over funds belonging to others to the supervising broker, who must keep them in a separate special (escrow) account. Mixing client money with personal or business money is commingling, and using it is conversion — both are prohibited.

questions.q: A buyer signs a binding purchase contract with no remaining contingencies, then changes her mind and refuses to close. She demands her earnest money back. Generally:
options: She is automatically entitled to a full refund because the deal never actually closed
The broker must refund it to her within 30 days, as required by the license law
The broker may keep the full deposit as its earned commission on the failed sale
No automatic refund; the contract's default terms decide who gets the deposit
questions.explanation: An earnest-money refund is not automatic just because the buyer changes her mind. Once contingencies are satisfied or have expired, the contract's default and liquidated damages terms decide who gets the deposit. The broker holds it in trust and cannot simply keep it as a commission.

questions.q: A contract's mortgage contingency gives the buyer until June 1 to get a loan commitment. The buyer applies promptly and in good faith but is denied, and gives the seller written notice on May 25 as the contract requires. The buyer most likely may:
options: Be forced to close with cash because loan denial is the buyer's risk
Cancel the contract and recover the deposit under the contingency
Cancel only if the seller agrees to waive the deadline
Keep the contract alive indefinitely until some loan is approved
questions.explanation: A mortgage contingency lets a buyer who makes a good-faith application and is denied cancel and get the deposit back, as long as the buyer follows the clause's notice and deadline terms. Missing the deadline or not applying in good faith can lose that protection.

questions.q: An upstate contract filled out by a salesperson has an attorney approval clause with a three-business-day review period. Neither party's attorney sends written disapproval within the period. What is the result?
options: The contingency is deemed waived and the contract is binding
The contract automatically terminates for lack of approval
The salesperson's broker must approve the contract instead
The parties automatically get 30 more days to obtain approval
questions.explanation: A standard attorney approval clause says the contingency is deemed waived unless an attorney sends written disapproval by the deadline. The clause lets licensees fill in a form contract without engaging in the unauthorized practice of law, while still giving each side's attorney a chance to review it.
questions.citation: NY Judiciary Law § 478 (unauthorized practice of law); standard attorney-approval clause

questions.q: A contract says that if the buyer defaults, the seller may keep the buyer's 10% down payment as the seller's sole remedy. This provision is a(n):
options: Specific performance clause
Rescission clause
Liquidated damages clause
Acceleration clause
questions.explanation: Liquidated damages are an amount the parties agree to in advance as compensation for a breach — often the earnest money. Specific performance forces completion of the sale, rescission cancels the contract and restores both parties, and acceleration is a mortgage clause.

questions.q: A seller signs a valid sale contract, then refuses to close because she got a higher offer. The buyer wants the property itself, not money. The buyer should sue for:
options: Liquidated damages
Rescission
A deficiency judgment
Specific performance
questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy in which a court orders the breaching party to perform. Courts grant it in real estate cases because every parcel is unique. Rescission would cancel the deal, which is the opposite of what this buyer wants.

questions.q: After signing, a buyer discovers the seller knowingly lied about the house being connected to public sewer. The buyer wants to cancel and put both parties back where they were before the contract, including return of the deposit. This remedy is:
options: Specific performance
Rescission
Novation
Liquidated damages
questions.explanation: Fraud or misrepresentation makes a contract voidable by the injured party, who may seek rescission: the contract is canceled and each party is restored to its pre-contract position. Novation substitutes a new contract or party; it does not unwind the deal.

questions.q: Under an exclusive right to sell listing, the owner finds a buyer on her own (a coworker) and sells during the listing term without the broker's help. The broker is:
options: Entitled to the commission, because the broker is paid no matter who sells
Not entitled to anything, because the owner found the buyer herself
Entitled to half the commission by law
Entitled only to reimbursement of advertising costs
questions.explanation: Under an exclusive right to sell, the listing broker earns the agreed commission if the property sells during the term, no matter who finds the buyer — including the owner. That is the key difference from an exclusive agency listing.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an exclusive agency listing from an exclusive right to sell listing?
options: Under exclusive agency, the broker is paid even if the owner sells on her own
Exclusive agency lets the owner list with several brokers at the same time
Exclusive agency must be oral, while exclusive right to sell must be written
Under exclusive agency, the owner owes no commission if she finds the buyer herself
questions.explanation: Exclusive agency names one broker but reserves the owner's right to sell on her own without owing a commission; under exclusive right to sell, the broker is paid regardless. Listing with several brokers at once is an open listing. NY regulations require exclusive listing agreements to include an explanation of this difference.

questions.q: An owner gives open listings to three brokers. Broker B is the procuring cause of the sale. Who earns a commission?
options: All three brokers, split equally
The first broker who signed a listing
Only Broker B
No broker, because open listings cannot be enforced
questions.explanation: In an open listing, only the broker who is the procuring cause of the sale earns the commission. If the owner sells the property herself, she owes no one.

questions.q: A tenant's lease gives the tenant a right of first refusal to buy the building. Which statement is correct?
options: The tenant can force the landlord to sell at a set price at any time during the lease
The tenant can match a bona fide offer the landlord is willing to accept, but cannot force a sale
The tenant is obligated to buy the building if the landlord decides to sell
A right of first refusal and an option to purchase are the same thing
questions.explanation: A right of first refusal only lets the holder match terms if the owner decides to sell; it cannot force a sale. An option, by contrast, lets the optionee (who pays consideration) compel the sale at a set price within the option period — the optionor is bound, the optionee is not.
questions.citation: General contract law (options and rights of first refusal)

questions.q: A buyer assigns her purchase contract to her brother with the seller's consent, but no agreement releasing the buyer is signed. If the brother fails to close:
options: The original buyer is automatically released because the seller consented
The seller can sue only the brokerage
The contract is void because real estate contracts cannot be assigned
The original buyer generally remains liable, because only a novation releases her
questions.explanation: In an assignment, the assignor generally stays secondarily liable if the assignee does not perform. A novation replaces the old contract or party with a new one and releases the original party. Consenting to an assignment is not the same as agreeing to a release.

questions.q: In parts of downstate New York, a licensee may prepare a binder. Which statement about a binder is most accurate?
options: A written outline of key terms that can be enforceable if it contains all essential terms
It is the title insurance policy that the title company delivers to the buyer at closing
It can never be enforced, because only a contract prepared by an attorney is binding
It replaces the deed and transfers title to the buyer once all parties have signed it
questions.explanation: A binder is a written outline of the main terms, often signed by the parties, after which attorneys draft the formal contract of sale. A binder may lack essential terms such as contingencies, but one that has all the required elements can be an enforceable contract.

questions.q: Under contract law, the element that exists when one party's offer is accepted on exactly its terms is usually called:
options: Mutual assent, or a meeting of the minds
Consideration, or a bargained-for exchange
Legal capacity of both parties
Legality of the contract's object
questions.explanation: Offer plus unqualified acceptance produces mutual assent (a meeting of the minds). Consideration is a separate element: the exchange of value, not the agreement itself.

questions.q: A seller's listing advertises her house 'for $600,000.' A buyer emails the listing agent, 'I accept your $600,000 price.' The seller has signed nothing further. Generally:
options: A contract exists, because the buyer accepted the exact advertised price
A contract exists once the listing agent receives the buyer's email
No contract exists, because an advertised price is an invitation to negotiate
A contract exists, but only the buyer can enforce it against the seller
questions.explanation: Advertisements and listing prices invite offers; they are not offers that can be accepted. The buyer's email is itself an offer, and the seller is free to accept, counter, or reject it.

questions.q: A buyer signed an installment land contract at age 17. After turning 18, she kept making the monthly payments for two years without objecting. The contract is most likely:
options: Still voidable at her option at any time she chooses
Void, because she lacked capacity when she signed it
Ratified by her conduct and now binding on her
Unenforceable until a court approves the original signing
questions.explanation: A minor's contract is voidable, but continuing to perform for a substantial time after reaching majority (18 in New York) ratifies it. The 'void' trap confuses a minor's contract with one lacking any legal effect.

questions.q: A 16-year-old and an adult sign a contract under which the minor will buy the adult's vacant lot. Before closing, the adult changes his mind. Which statement is correct?
options: Either party may disaffirm because the contract is void
The adult may disaffirm at any time before the closing
Neither party may disaffirm once both have signed
The adult is bound; only the minor may disaffirm
questions.explanation: Voidability protects the minor only: the minor may disaffirm, but the adult party stays bound. Calling the contract void is the trap; it is voidable, and only at the minor's option.

questions.q: Which of the following contracts is generally VOID rather than merely voidable?
options: One signed by a 17-year-old buyer of a building lot
One the buyer signed after the seller's fraudulent statement
One signed by a person a court had already declared incompetent
One a seller signed while too intoxicated to understand it
questions.explanation: Under the traditional rule, a contract made by someone already adjudicated incompetent is void. Minority, fraud, and intoxication make a contract voidable by the protected party, so it stays valid unless that party chooses to avoid it.

questions.q: At a party, a seller signs a sale contract while so intoxicated that he cannot understand what he is signing. When sober the next morning, he promptly objects. The contract is most likely:
options: Void from the start for both parties
Valid, since he chose to drink
Voidable by the buyer only
Voidable by the seller
questions.explanation: Intoxication severe enough to prevent understanding makes a contract voidable by the impaired party, who must act promptly once sober. It is not automatically void, and the sober buyer has no right to avoid it.

questions.q: Each of the following ends an offer EXCEPT:
options: The offeror's death before any acceptance
A counteroffer made by the offeree
The passing of the offer's stated deadline
The offeree asking whether the price is firm
questions.explanation: A mere inquiry about the terms does not reject or change the offer, so the offer survives. Death of the offeror, a counteroffer (which acts as a rejection), and lapse of time all terminate an offer.

questions.q: A buyer offers $475,000 with a June 30 closing. The seller signs the offer but crosses out 'June 30,' writes 'July 15,' and initials the change. The seller has made:
options: A counteroffer that the buyer may accept or reject
A binding acceptance, because the change is minor
A binding acceptance on the original June 30 date
An acceptance that binds unless the buyer objects
questions.explanation: Acceptance must match the offer exactly; changing any term, even a closing date, is a counteroffer that rejects the original offer. No contract exists until the buyer accepts the July 15 date.

questions.q: Under the mailbox rule, an acceptance sent by a method the offer authorizes is generally effective when it is:
options: Received by the offeror
Sent by the offeree
Read by the offeror
Acknowledged by the offeror
questions.explanation: The mailbox (dispatch) rule makes a properly sent acceptance effective on dispatch, even before it arrives. Receipt is the rule for revocations, which is the usual trap.

questions.q: A seller mails a revocation of her offer on Monday. The buyer, who has not heard anything, mails an acceptance on Tuesday. The buyer receives the revocation Wednesday, and the seller receives the acceptance Thursday. Generally:
options: A contract was formed Tuesday, when the acceptance was mailed
No contract exists, because the revocation was mailed first
No contract exists, because the revocation arrived Wednesday
A contract was formed Thursday, when the acceptance arrived
questions.explanation: A revocation is effective only when received (Wednesday), but an acceptance is effective when dispatched (Tuesday). The acceptance took effect first, so the contract was formed Tuesday.

questions.q: An offer states, 'Your acceptance is effective only when I actually receive your signed copy.' The buyer mails the signed copy Monday; it arrives Friday. On Wednesday the offeror phones the buyer and revokes. Generally:
options: A contract was formed Monday, when the buyer mailed the signed copy
No contract, since the offer required receipt and the revocation came first
A contract was formed Friday, when the signed copy reached the offeror
No contract, because a written offer cannot be revoked by telephone
questions.explanation: The offeror controls the offer and may require receipt, displacing the dispatch rule. The Wednesday revocation reached the buyer before the acceptance reached the offeror, so the offer was gone when it arrived.

questions.q: Unless an offer has been made irrevocable (for example, by a paid option), an offeror may generally revoke it:
options: Only after giving the offeree 24 hours' notice
Only if the offer contained a stated deadline
At any time up until the scheduled closing
At any time before the acceptance takes effect
questions.explanation: An ordinary offer can be withdrawn any time before acceptance becomes effective. Once acceptance takes effect a contract exists, so revoking afterward (up to closing) would be a breach, not a revocation.

questions.q: A buyer pays an owner $5,000 for the right to buy his land for $300,000 at any time within 90 days. On day 30, the owner announces he is withdrawing the offer. The owner:
options: May withdraw if he returns the buyer's $5,000 payment
Cannot withdraw; the paid option holds the offer open for 90 days
May withdraw, because the buyer has not yet agreed to buy
May withdraw with written notice, since options are revocable
questions.explanation: Because the buyer gave consideration for the promise to keep the offer open, the option is a binding contract for its 90-day term. Refunding the money does not undo the bargain the owner already made.

questions.q: A buyer's offer says, 'If I don't hear from you by Friday, I'll treat your silence as acceptance.' The seller never responds. Generally:
options: No contract exists, because silence is ordinarily not acceptance
A contract formed Friday when the stated deadline passed
A contract formed, but only the buyer is bound by it
