questions.q: A foreclosure sale brings $380,000. Referee fees and sale costs are $12,000, the first mortgage judgment is $250,000, and a properly joined second mortgage is owed $90,000. How much surplus remains for the former owner?
questions.explanation: $380,000 - $12,000 costs - $250,000 first mortgage - $90,000 second mortgage = $28,000. Skipping the costs gives $40,000, and skipping the junior lien gives $118,000; junior lienholders are paid from surplus before the owner.

questions.q: A buyer takes title subject to the seller's existing mortgage. Later the loan defaults and the foreclosure sale leaves a deficiency. Who is personally liable for it?
options: The buyer, as the current owner
The seller, who signed the note
Both of them, jointly and severally
Neither, since only the lien remains
questions.explanation: Taking subject to a mortgage puts the property at risk but adds no personal promise, so the original borrower remains liable on the note. A buyer who formally assumes the loan, by contrast, takes on personal liability.

questions.q: With the lender's consent, a buyer formally assumes the seller's mortgage, but the lender signs no release. If a deficiency later arises, who may be liable?
options: Only the seller, because he signed the original note
Only the buyer, because assumption releases the seller
Neither one, because assumed loans are nonrecourse
The buyer primarily, with the seller secondarily liable
questions.explanation: An assuming buyer becomes primarily liable, but the original borrower is not released unless the lender agrees. Believing assumption alone frees the seller is the classic trap.

questions.q: A seller lets a buyer assume her mortgage and wants to be completely free of the debt. She should obtain:
options: A satisfaction of mortgage signed by the buyer
A subordination agreement from the lender
A novation or written release from the lender
A recorded lis pendens against the property
questions.explanation: A novation substitutes the new borrower for the old one, and a release from the lender ends the seller's liability. A satisfaction is given by a lender at payoff, not by a buyer, and the loan here is not paid off.

questions.q: A buyer pays $340,000 and assumes the seller's $212,500 loan balance. The lender charges a 1% assumption fee on the assumed balance. Ignoring other costs, how much cash does the buyer need?
After a homeowner pays off her mortgage in full, New York law requires the lender to present a satisfaction for recording (or deliver it as requested) within:
options: 30 days
10 days
90 days
6 months
questions.explanation: New York requires the mortgagee to arrange for the satisfaction to be recorded, or delivered on written request, within 30 days of payoff, with escalating statutory penalties for delay. Waiting 90 days or longer would already violate the deadline.

questions.q: A seller paid off a mortgage years ago, but a title search shows it still open of record. Which recorded document most directly clears it?
options: A notice of pendency
A subordination agreement
A satisfaction of mortgage
An assignment of mortgage
questions.explanation: A recorded satisfaction (certificate of discharge) shows the lien was paid and released. An assignment would only transfer the mortgage to a new holder, leaving it open.

questions.q: In a New York foreclosure, the notice of pendency (lis pendens) filed with the county clerk mainly serves to:
options: Transfer title to the lender until the auction
Create a money judgment against the borrower
Give constructive notice of the lawsuit to later buyers
Schedule the mandatory settlement conference
questions.explanation: A notice of pendency warns anyone later dealing with the property that a suit affects it, binding later purchasers and lenders as if they were parties. It is not a judgment, a debt lien, or a title transfer.

questions.q: Unless extended by court order, a notice of pendency filed in New York generally remains effective for:
options: 1 year from filing
90 days from filing
3 years from filing
10 years from filing
questions.explanation: A notice of pendency lasts three years from filing and can be extended for good cause. It does not last indefinitely, so long-running cases must extend it.

questions.q: Before starting a foreclosure action on a home loan, a New York lender must send the borrower a pre-foreclosure notice at least how long before filing?
options: 30 days
90 days
60 days
120 days
questions.explanation: RPAPL §1304 requires the notice at least 90 days before the lender commences the action. The 120-day figure is a separate federal servicing rule on delinquency before a first foreclosure filing, not the New York notice period.

questions.q: Which item must the RPAPL §1304 90-day pre-foreclosure notice include?
options: At least five housing counseling agencies serving the county
The scheduled date and place of the referee's foreclosure auction
The deficiency amount the court will award after the sale
A current appraisal of the home by a certified appraiser
questions.explanation: RPAPL §1304 requires the notice to list at least five housing counseling agencies serving the county where the property is located, along with statutory warning language. No sale date exists yet because no action has even been filed.

questions.q: A lender files a foreclosure action on a borrower's home loan without having properly mailed the 90-day pre-foreclosure notice. What is the likely result?
options: The court simply adds 90 days to the eventual sale date
The action can be dismissed for lack of a condition precedent
The lender pays a small fine and the case continues
The mandatory settlement conference is skipped
questions.explanation: Proper service of the RPAPL §1304 notice is a condition precedent to commencing the action, and courts dismiss cases that do not strictly comply. Lateness is not cured by adding time or paying a fee.

questions.q: In a residential foreclosure of an owner-occupied home loan, the mandatory settlement conference under CPLR 3408 requires both sides to:
options: Accept a modification written by the judge
Agree to a short sale before the case proceeds
Waive any later deficiency judgment claims
Negotiate in good faith toward a resolution
questions.explanation: CPLR 3408 requires the parties to negotiate in good faith toward a mutually agreeable resolution, such as a modification, and lets the court sanction bad faith. The court does not impose a particular deal or force a deficiency waiver.

questions.q: When is the first mandatory settlement conference generally held in a New York residential foreclosure?
options: Before the 90-day pre-foreclosure notice is sent
After the referee's sale but before deed delivery
Only if the borrower requests one in writing
Within 60 days after proof of service is filed
questions.explanation: CPLR 3408 calls for the conference within 60 days after the plaintiff files proof of service of the summons and complaint. It happens during the lawsuit, so it cannot precede the 90-day notice or follow the sale.

questions.q: Along with the summons and complaint in a residential foreclosure, New York requires the borrower to receive a separate notice titled:
options: Notice of Default and Election to Sell
Notice of Intent to Accelerate the Loan
Your Rights After the Referee's Sale
Help for Homeowners in Foreclosure
questions.explanation: RPAPL §1303 requires the 'Help for Homeowners in Foreclosure' notice to be delivered with the summons and complaint. A notice of default and election to sell belongs to nonjudicial foreclosure states, not New York's court process.

questions.q: After a judgment of foreclosure and sale in New York, who typically conducts the public auction?
options: The lender's loan servicer
A trustee named in the mortgage
A referee appointed by the court
The borrower's listing broker
questions.explanation: New York foreclosure is judicial: the court appoints a referee to sell the property at public auction and deliver a referee's deed. A trustee sale is the nonjudicial deed-of-trust process used in other states.

questions.q: A New York borrower's equity of redemption allows her to:
options: Buy the home back within one year after the sale
Cancel the mortgage within three days of signing
Force the lender to accept a deed in lieu instead
Pay off the debt and keep the home before the sale
questions.explanation: The equity of redemption lets the borrower pay the full debt and costs to stop the foreclosure up until the sale. New York has no post-sale statutory redemption period, and the three-day right is the TILA rescission right on certain refinances.
questions.citation: RPAPL §1351 (judgment of foreclosure and sale); RPAPL Article 13

questions.q: Which protection does New York NOT give a borrower facing residential foreclosure?
options: A 90-day pre-foreclosure notice before suit is filed
A statutory right to redeem after the referee's sale
A mandatory settlement conference on a home loan
Credit for fair market value in a deficiency motion
questions.explanation: New York has no statutory redemption period after the referee's sale; the equity of redemption ends at the sale. The other three are real protections under RPAPL §1304, CPLR 3408, and RPAPL §1371.

questions.q: Before the foreclosure sale, a borrower wants to pay off the entire debt to keep her home. She owes $218,000 principal, $9,400 accrued interest, and $6,150 in allowed costs. She has missed 9 payments of $1,620. What must she pay to redeem?
questions.explanation: Redemption means paying the full debt: $218,000 + $9,400 + $6,150 = $233,550. Leaving out the costs gives $227,400, and $14,580 (9 x $1,620) is just the missed payments, not a full payoff.
questions.citation: New York equity of redemption; RPAPL Article 13

questions.q: A foreclosure judgment is $288,000, and referee fees and costs add $7,500. The home sells at auction for $245,000; the court finds fair market value is $236,000. What is the maximum deficiency judgment?
questions.explanation: The borrower is credited with the higher of the sale price or fair market value, here the $245,000 sale price. $288,000 + $7,500 - $245,000 = $50,500. Using the lower $236,000 value gives $59,500, and leaving out costs gives $43,000.

questions.q: In computing a New York deficiency judgment, the borrower is credited with:
options: The higher of the auction price or fair market value
The lower of the auction price or fair market value
The auction price only, regardless of market value
The price the borrower originally paid for the home
questions.explanation: RPAPL §1371 subtracts the higher of the sale price or the court-determined fair market value, preventing a lender from buying cheaply and suing for an inflated shortfall. Using the lower figure is the trap.

questions.q: A foreclosing lender wants a deficiency judgment. Under RPAPL §1371, it must move for one within:
options: 90 days after the referee's deed is delivered
30 days after the judgment of foreclosure
1 year after the auction is held
6 years after the borrower's default
questions.explanation: The motion must be made within 90 days after the sale is completed by delivery of the referee's deed. The clock runs from deed delivery, not from the judgment or the auction gavel.

questions.q: The referee's deed was delivered four months ago, and the foreclosing lender never moved for a deficiency judgment. What is the borrower's remaining liability on the mortgage debt?
options: The full shortfall, collectible within six years
None; the sale proceeds count as full satisfaction
Half the shortfall, as a statutory compromise
The shortfall minus the home's market value
questions.explanation: If no deficiency motion is made within 90 days of deed delivery, the sale proceeds are deemed full satisfaction of the mortgage debt and no deficiency can be recovered. The lender cannot simply sue later on the note.

questions.q: A lender accepts a deed in lieu of foreclosure on a home that also has a recorded home equity line held by another bank. The lender generally takes title:
options: Free of the junior lien, which ends automatically
Free of all liens, since the transfer was voluntary
With the junior lien converted to an unsecured debt
Subject to the junior lien, which is not wiped out
questions.explanation: A deed in lieu is a voluntary conveyance, not a foreclosure, so it does not extinguish junior liens. That is why lenders often refuse a deed in lieu when other liens exist and foreclose instead.

questions.q: In a short sale, the:
options: Seller closes within 30 days of listing the property
Buyer assumes the seller's loan at a reduced balance
Lender accepts sale proceeds that are less than the payoff
Court sets a minimum bid for the foreclosure auction
questions.explanation: A short sale is a sale where the lender agrees to release its lien for less than the full amount owed. It is a private sale, not a court auction, and the buyer gets new financing or pays cash rather than assuming the loan.

questions.q: A salesperson lists a home whose sale price will not cover the mortgage payoff. Which step is essential before the closing can occur?
options: Filing a notice of pendency to protect the buyer
Recording a satisfaction before the contract is signed
Getting the lender's written approval of the sale terms
Getting the Department of State to approve the price
questions.explanation: Because the proceeds will not pay off the loan, the lien can be released only if the lender approves the short sale in writing. A satisfaction comes only after the lender is paid or agrees to accept less.

questions.q: A short-sale seller asks her salesperson whether the leftover loan balance disappears automatically when the sale closes. The best response is:
options: Not necessarily; review the lender's written terms with a lawyer
Yes; state law cancels any balance left after a short sale
Yes, but only if the buyer pays the full price in cash
No; the buyer becomes liable for the remaining balance
questions.explanation: Releasing the lien does not automatically release personal liability; whether the shortfall is waived depends on the lender's written approval and law, which calls for legal advice. A salesperson should not promise forgiveness.
questions.citation: General mortgage law; short-sale approval terms

questions.q: A permanent change to a loan's original terms, such as a lower rate or a longer term, to make payments affordable is a:
options: Forbearance plan
Deed in lieu
Short sale
Loan modification
questions.explanation: A loan modification permanently changes the note's terms so the borrower can keep the home. Forbearance is the common trap: it only temporarily reduces or suspends payments.

questions.q: After a job loss, a lender lets a borrower make reduced payments for six months, with the skipped amounts to be repaid later. This arrangement is:
options: A loan modification
Forbearance
A novation
A subordination
questions.explanation: Forbearance temporarily reduces or suspends payments, and the missed amounts are repaid afterward; the loan's terms are not permanently rewritten. A modification would permanently change the loan terms.

questions.q: A company promises to stop a homeowner's foreclosure if she pays a $2,500 fee before it contacts her lender. Under federal rules, such an up-front fee is generally:
options: Permitted if the fee is disclosed in writing in advance
Prohibited until she signs an agreement with her lender
Permitted if the company offers a money-back guarantee
Permitted if the fee is below the state's maximum cap
questions.explanation: Federal Regulation O bars mortgage assistance relief providers from collecting fees until the homeowner has signed an agreement with the lender incorporating the offered relief. Disclosure or a refund promise does not make an advance fee lawful, and New York's distressed property consultant law adds its own protections.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly orders a typical New York residential foreclosure?
options: Lawsuit filed, 90-day notice, judgment, settlement conference, referee sale
90-day notice, lawsuit filed, settlement conference, judgment, referee sale
90-day notice, lawsuit filed, judgment, referee sale, settlement conference
Lawsuit filed, settlement conference, referee sale, judgment, 90-day notice
questions.explanation: The RPAPL §1304 notice must come at least 90 days before suit; the CPLR 3408 conference occurs early in the case; then the court enters a judgment of foreclosure and sale; the referee then auctions the property. A conference after the sale is too late to help.

questions.q: A mortgaged home in default appears vacant and abandoned before the foreclosure is finished. New York's 'zombie property' law places the duty to maintain it on:
options: The mortgagee or its loan servicer
The town code enforcement office
The listing broker of record
The neighboring property owners
questions.explanation: Under the 2016 zombie property law, the lender or servicer must inspect and maintain vacant, abandoned residential property while the loan is in default. The duty is the lender's, not the town's, the broker's, or the neighbors'.

questions.q: Which activity takes place in the PRIMARY mortgage market?
options: Freddie Mac buys a pool of loans from a savings bank
An investor buys mortgage-backed securities from a dealer
Ginnie Mae guarantees payments on a mortgage security
A savings bank lends money directly to a homebuyer
questions.explanation: The primary market is where loans are originated: a lender makes the loan directly to the borrower. Buying existing loans or securities backed by them, and guaranteeing those securities, are secondary-market activities.
questions.citation: General mortgage market principles (primary vs. secondary market)

questions.q: A company takes loan applications and matches borrowers with lenders for a fee, but the loans are funded with the lenders' money, not its own. This company is acting as a:
options: Mortgage banker
Mortgage broker
Savings association
Secondary-market purchaser
questions.explanation: A mortgage broker arranges loans between borrowers and lenders without funding them. A mortgage banker originates and funds loans with its own (or borrowed) money, often selling them later on the secondary market.
questions.citation: General mortgage lending principles; NY Banking Law Art. 12-D (mortgage brokers and bankers)

questions.q: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are best described as:
options: Congressionally chartered government-sponsored enterprises
Divisions of HUD that insure loans for low-income buyers
Federal Reserve banks that set national mortgage rates
State agencies that license New York mortgage brokers
questions.explanation: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are government-sponsored enterprises chartered by Congress (and under FHFA conservatorship since 2008). The HUD-related distractor describes FHA's insurance role and Ginnie Mae's place within HUD, not Fannie or Freddie.
questions.citation: Federal National Mortgage Association Charter Act; Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation Act

questions.q: A conventional loan whose amount is above the limit Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac may purchase is called a:
options: Conforming loan
Package loan
Jumbo loan
Bridge loan
questions.explanation: A loan exceeding the conforming loan limit is a jumbo (nonconforming) loan. A conforming loan is one that meets Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac guidelines, including the loan limit.
questions.citation: Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac conforming loan limits set by FHFA

questions.q: Which statement about a conventional mortgage loan is accurate?
options: It is not insured or guaranteed by a government agency
It must be a fixed-rate loan with a 30-year term
It always requires a down payment of at least 20%
It must be sold to Fannie Mae after closing
questions.explanation: 'Conventional' means the loan is not FHA-insured or VA-guaranteed. Conventional loans can be fixed or adjustable, can be made with less than 20% down (usually with PMI), and may be kept or sold.

questions.q: A buyer with a credit score of 640 wants the smallest down payment allowed on an FHA-insured purchase loan. What is the minimum down payment?
options: 0% of the purchase price
3.5% of the purchase price
10% of the purchase price
20% of the purchase price
questions.explanation: FHA requires a minimum 3.5% down payment for borrowers with credit scores of 580 or higher (10% for scores of 500–579). Zero down is a VA feature, not FHA.
questions.citation: HUD Single Family Housing Policy Handbook 4000.1

questions.q: An FHA borrower pays an up-front and an annual mortgage insurance premium (MIP). Whom does the MIP primarily protect?
options: The borrower, if she becomes disabled or unemployed
The seller, if the buyer fails to close on time
The lender, against loss if the borrower defaults
The title insurer, against defects in the title
questions.explanation: FHA mortgage insurance protects the lender against loss on default; the borrower pays for it. It is not credit disability or unemployment coverage for the borrower.

questions.q: A homeowner bought with an FHA loan in 2021, putting 3.5% down on a 30-year term. After extra principal payments, her balance is now 77% of the original value, yet she is still billed the annual MIP. What is the best explanation?
options: It ends only after she pays a 1% cancellation fee
The lender failed to apply the HPA's 78% PMI rule
It can end only after a new appraisal of the home
Her annual MIP is payable for the life of the loan
questions.explanation: For FHA loans endorsed since June 3, 2013 with less than 10% down, the annual MIP lasts for the life of the loan; refinancing out of FHA is the usual way to end it. The Homeowners Protection Act's 78% automatic termination applies to private mortgage insurance on conventional loans, not FHA MIP, and no reappraisal or fee cancels it.
questions.citation: Homeowners Protection Act of 1998, 12 U.S.C. §4901 et seq.; HUD Mortgagee Letter 2013-04

questions.q: Which document shows a lender that a veteran is eligible for a VA-guaranteed home loan and states the veteran's entitlement?
options: Certificate of Occupancy
Certificate of Eligibility
Loan Estimate
Commitment letter
questions.explanation: The VA's Certificate of Eligibility (COE) confirms eligibility and entitlement. A certificate of occupancy concerns a building's legal use, and a Loan Estimate is a TRID cost disclosure.

questions.q: An eligible veteran with full entitlement buys a home for a price equal to its appraised value. What minimum down payment does the VA require?
options: No down payment
3.5% of the purchase price
5% of the purchase price
10% of the purchase price
questions.explanation: VA-guaranteed loans can be made with no down payment when the price does not exceed the appraised value and the veteran has full entitlement. The 3.5% figure is the FHA minimum.

questions.q: Which VA borrower is generally exempt from paying the VA funding fee?
options: A first-time VA borrower who makes no down payment at all
A veteran who is buying a home priced above the appraised value
A veteran receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability
A veteran whose spouse is also a co-borrower on the loan
questions.explanation: Veterans receiving compensation for a service-connected disability are exempt from the funding fee. A first-time zero-down VA borrower pays the fee; making no down payment actually puts the borrower in the highest fee tier.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes a VA-guaranteed loan from a typical low-down-payment conventional loan?
options: The VA itself funds the loan from Treasury money
The interest rate is fixed by the VA for all lenders
The borrower must have owned a home in the past
No monthly mortgage insurance premium is charged
questions.explanation: The VA guaranty substitutes for mortgage insurance, so VA loans carry no monthly mortgage insurance even with no down payment (there is a one-time funding fee instead). Private lenders make the loans; the VA does not set a single rate, and no prior homeownership is required.

questions.q: A buyer makes a 15% down payment on a conventional loan. Which is the most likely result?
options: The lender will require FHA mortgage insurance
The lender will require private mortgage insurance
The loan must be guaranteed by the VA instead
The buyer will be charged a VA funding fee
questions.explanation: A 15% down payment means an 85% loan-to-value ratio. Conventional lenders typically require PMI when the LTV exceeds 80%. FHA MIP and the VA funding fee apply only to government-backed loans.
questions.citation: General conventional lending practice; Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac mortgage insurance requirements

questions.q: Under the Homeowners Protection Act, a conventional borrower with a good payment history may ask in writing to cancel PMI when the principal balance reaches what percentage of the original value?
questions.explanation: The borrower may request cancellation at 80% of original value (with a good payment history and other conditions). The 78% figure is the separate point at which PMI terminates automatically without a request.

questions.q: A buyer paid $400,000 for a home that appraised at $410,000 and took a conventional loan of $360,000 with PMI. Under the Homeowners Protection Act, at what principal balance may she first request that the PMI be canceled?
questions.explanation: 'Original value' is the lesser of the sale price or the appraised value, so $400,000 × 80% = $320,000. Using the appraisal gives $410,000 × 80% = $328,000; $312,000 is the 78% automatic-termination point; $288,000 wrongly applies 80% to the loan amount.

questions.q: A borrower's 30-year conventional loan carries PMI, and her balance has not yet reached the 78% automatic-termination point. If she is current on payments, what is the latest point at which the Homeowners Protection Act requires her PMI to end?
options: When the loan is paid off in full
After the tenth year of the loan
When the home's market value doubles
Halfway through the amortization period
questions.explanation: The HPA's final-termination rule ends PMI at the midpoint of the amortization period (year 15 of a 30-year loan) if the borrower is current, even if the LTV thresholds were not met. Rising market value does not by itself trigger termination.

questions.q: In an adjustable-rate mortgage, the fixed percentage the lender adds to the index to set the interest rate is the:
options: Index
Margin
Periodic cap
Floor
questions.explanation: Rate = index + margin. The margin stays the same for the life of the loan, while the index moves with the market; caps and floors limit how far the rate can move.

questions.q: Which characteristic should the index of an adjustable-rate mortgage have?
options: It is a rate the lender sets based on its own costs
It is a percentage that never changes during the loan
It is a published rate that the lender does not control
It is the borrower's credit score converted to a rate
questions.explanation: An ARM index is an independent, published market rate (for example, a Treasury yield or SOFR) outside the lender's control. A fixed percentage that never changes describes the margin, not the index.
questions.citation: Truth in Lending Act / Regulation Z, 12 C.F.R. §1026.19(b)

questions.q: An ARM began at 5.00% with caps of 2% per adjustment and 5% over the initial rate for the life of the loan. The current rate is 8.50%. At the next adjustment the index is 7.75% and the margin is 2.75%. What is the new rate?
questions.explanation: Index + margin = 7.75% + 2.75% = 10.50%, and the periodic cap allows 8.50% + 2% = 10.50%, but the lifetime cap is 5.00% + 5% = 10.00%. The lowest limit controls, so the rate is 10.00%. Choosing 10.50% ignores the lifetime cap.
questions.citation: ARM rate adjustment principles (index + margin, subject to caps)

questions.q: An adjustable-rate loan has a payment cap but no interest rate cap. Rates rise sharply, and the capped payment no longer covers the interest due. What happens?
options: The lender must absorb the unpaid interest permanently
The loan converts automatically to a fixed-rate loan
The borrower receives a refund of the excess interest
The unpaid interest is added to the principal balance
questions.explanation: When a payment cap holds the payment below the interest due, the shortfall is added to the balance, which is negative amortization. The loan balance grows even though the borrower pays on time.
questions.citation: General ARM principles; Regulation Z, 12 C.F.R. §1026.19(b)

questions.q: An ARM is offered at a discounted initial rate of 3.99%. The current index is 4.10% and the margin is 2.50%. What is the fully indexed rate?
questions.explanation: Fully indexed rate = index + margin = 4.10% + 2.50% = 6.60%. Adding the margin to the teaser rate (3.99% + 2.50% = 6.49%) is the common mistake; the teaser rate is not part of the formula.

questions.q: A borrower chooses a 5/1 hybrid adjustable-rate mortgage. How does the interest rate behave?
options: Adjusting every 5 years for the life of the loan
Fixed for the first 5 years, then adjusting once a year
Fixed for 5 years, then due in full as a balloon
Adjusting once a year, capped at 5% per change
questions.explanation: In a 5/1 ARM, the first number is the initial fixed period (5 years) and the second is the adjustment frequency afterward (every 1 year). It is not a balloon loan, and the numbers do not describe caps.

questions.q: An investor takes a $250,000 interest-only loan at 6.6% annual interest with the full principal due at the end of 5 years. What is the monthly payment?
questions.explanation: $250,000 × 6.6% = $16,500 per year; $16,500 ÷ 12 = $1,375.00 per month. $16,500 is the annual figure; $4,166.67 divides the principal by 60 months; $5,541.67 adds that principal to the interest, which an interest-only loan does not do.

questions.q: A buyer's payments are calculated as if the loan would be repaid over 30 years, but the entire remaining balance comes due at the end of year 7. This is a:
options: Balloon mortgage
Fully amortizing mortgage
Reverse mortgage
Growing-equity mortgage
questions.explanation: Payments that do not fully repay the loan by the due date leave a large final balloon payment. A fully amortizing loan's regular payments retire the entire debt by the end of the term.

questions.q: Which statement about an FHA-insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) is accurate?
options: The borrower must be at least 62 and keep paying taxes and insurance
The borrower must make monthly principal and interest payments
The loan comes due as soon as the borrower turns 85 years old
The lender takes title to the home on the day the loan closes
questions.explanation: HECM borrowers must be at least 62, require no monthly loan payments, and keep title, but must still pay property taxes, homeowners insurance, and upkeep. The loan generally comes due when the last borrower dies, sells, or permanently moves out, not at a set age.

questions.q: A builder's construction loan is paid off when the house is finished by a long-term permanent loan. That permanent loan is often called a:
options: Bridge loan
Takeout loan
Blanket loan
Wraparound loan
questions.explanation: The permanent (takeout) loan replaces the short-term construction loan when work is complete. A bridge loan instead covers a gap between buying one property and selling another.

questions.q: A builder has a $300,000 construction loan at 9% annual interest, interest-only on funds advanced. So far $120,000 has been paid out in draws. What is this month's interest payment?
questions.explanation: Interest is charged only on money disbursed: $120,000 × 9% = $10,800 per year; $10,800 ÷ 12 = $900 per month. $2,250 charges interest on the full $300,000; $1,350 uses the $180,000 not yet drawn.
questions.citation: Construction loan draw principles; interest calculation

questions.q: A couple has signed a contract to buy a new home, but their current home has not sold yet. They need short-term funds for the new down payment, secured by their existing home. Which loan fits?
options: Blanket loan
Package loan
Takeout loan
Bridge loan
questions.explanation: A bridge (swing) loan provides short-term funds secured by the current property until it sells. A blanket loan covers several parcels under one mortgage, and a package loan includes personal property.

questions.q: A buyer of a furnished condominium finances the unit together with the furniture and appliances under one mortgage. This is a:
options: Blanket mortgage
Wraparound mortgage
Package mortgage
Open-end mortgage
questions.explanation: A package mortgage covers both the real property and personal property such as furniture and appliances. A blanket mortgage covers multiple parcels of real property.

questions.q: Before a seller agrees to give a buyer a wraparound mortgage, which provision in the seller's existing mortgage is most important to check?
options: Whether it contains a defeasance clause
Whether its interest rate is fixed or adjustable
Whether it was recorded in the county clerk's office
Whether it contains a due-on-sale (alienation) clause
questions.explanation: A wraparound leaves the original loan in place. If that loan has a due-on-sale clause, the transfer can let the original lender accelerate the entire balance. A defeasance clause only governs release of the lien on payoff.
questions.citation: General mortgage principles (wraparound financing, alienation clause)

questions.q: A buyer purchased a $525,000 home with a $420,000 loan and paid $6,300 in discount points. How many points did she pay?
questions.explanation: Points are a percentage of the loan amount: $6,300 ÷ $420,000 = 0.015 = 1.5 points. Dividing by the price ($6,300 ÷ $525,000 = 1.2) is the common mistake; 0.15 and 15 misplace the decimal.
questions.citation: Discount point calculation (1 point = 1% of the loan amount)

questions.q: A Loan Estimate shows a note rate of 6.25% and an APR of 6.48%. Why is the APR higher?
options: It also reflects points and other finance charges over the loan term
It adds the property taxes and homeowners insurance to the rate
It is the highest rate the loan could ever reach after adjustments
It includes the buyer's down payment as part of the cost of credit
questions.explanation: The APR expresses the total cost of credit as a yearly rate, so prepaid finance charges such as points and origination fees raise it above the note rate. Taxes, insurance escrows, and the down payment are not finance charges.
questions.citation: Truth in Lending Act; Regulation Z, 12 C.F.R. §§1026.4, 1026.22

questions.q: For a loan secured by real estate, which charge is excluded from the finance charge used to calculate the APR?
options: Discount points paid to the lender
A bona fide, reasonable appraisal fee
A loan origination fee
A mortgage broker's fee
questions.explanation: Regulation Z excludes bona fide and reasonable real-estate-related fees such as appraisal, title examination, and credit report fees from the finance charge. Points, origination fees, and mortgage broker fees are finance charges.

questions.q: A home-loan ad states 'Monthly payments of only $1,890.' Under Regulation Z, which disclosures must the ad now include?
options: The lender's NMLS number, the APR, and closing costs
The property taxes, the insurance, and the HOA dues
The prepayment penalty, the late fee, and the APR
The down payment, the repayment terms, and the APR
questions.explanation: A payment amount is a triggering term. Once a trigger appears, the ad must also state the down payment amount or percentage, the terms of repayment, and the APR (and whether the rate may increase).

questions.q: Which statement may appear in a mortgage advertisement by itself WITHOUT triggering additional Regulation Z disclosures?
options: Repay over 360 monthly payments
Only $2,000 down to move in
Rates as low as 6.75% APR
Finance charges under $1,000
questions.explanation: Stating the APR alone does not trigger further disclosures; a rate must be stated as an APR. The number of payments, the down payment amount, and the finance charge amount are all triggering terms.

questions.q: A homeowner refinances the mortgage on her principal residence with a new lender. She signs on a Thursday and receives all required disclosures and rescission notices that day. With no federal holiday that week, her right to rescind runs until midnight of which day?
options: Monday
Tuesday
Sunday
Wednesday
questions.explanation: For rescission, business days are all calendar days except Sundays and federal holidays. Counting Friday, Saturday, and Monday, the third business day is Monday. Choosing Tuesday wrongly skips Saturday.

questions.q: Under the Truth in Lending Act, which of these loans does NOT carry a three-day right of rescission?
options: A home equity loan secured by the borrower's principal residence
A first mortgage used to buy the borrower's principal residence
A refinance of a principal residence with a different lender
A home equity line of credit on the borrower's principal residence
questions.explanation: Rescission applies to certain non-purchase credit secured by the borrower's principal dwelling. A residential mortgage transaction that finances the purchase of the home is exempt.

questions.q: A lender refuses to count an applicant's steady public assistance income when deciding whether she qualifies, although she documents that it is reliable. Which federal law does this most directly violate?
options: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
Community Reinvestment Act
Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
questions.explanation: ECOA prohibits credit discrimination because an applicant's income comes from a public assistance program. HMDA is a reporting law, CRA addresses community credit needs, and RESPA governs settlement costs and kickbacks.
questions.citation: Equal Credit Opportunity Act, 15 U.S.C. §1691(a)(2); Regulation B, 12 C.F.R. §1002.6(b)(5)

questions.q: Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Regulation B, a lender that denies a completed mortgage application generally must notify the applicant of the action within:
options: 30 days
3 business days
10 days
60 days
questions.explanation: Regulation B requires notice of action taken within 30 days after receiving a completed application, including a statement of reasons (or the right to request them) for an adverse action. Three business days is a TRID timing rule, not ECOA.

questions.q: Which law requires many mortgage lenders to collect and report data on loan applications, including the property's location and the applicant's race, ethnicity, and sex, so regulators can spot possible redlining?
options: Community Reinvestment Act
Truth in Lending Act
Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
questions.explanation: HMDA is a data-reporting law that helps reveal lending patterns such as redlining. The CRA evaluates how well depository institutions meet community credit needs but is not the application-data reporting statute.
questions.citation: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, 12 U.S.C. §2801 et seq.; Regulation C

questions.q: Federal regulators rate a bank on how well it meets the credit needs of its entire community, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, and consider that record when the bank applies to open a branch. Which law is this?
options: Community Reinvestment Act
Home Mortgage Disclosure Act
Equal Credit Opportunity Act
Homeowners Protection Act
questions.explanation: The CRA directs regulators to assess depository institutions' records of meeting community credit needs, consistent with safe and sound operation, and to weigh that record on applications such as branches and mergers. It does not guarantee any applicant a loan.
questions.citation: Community Reinvestment Act, 12 U.S.C. §2901 et seq.

questions.q: A lender uses qualifying ratios of 28% for housing expense and 36% for total debt. An applicant earns $7,500 a month and has $650 a month in car and student loan payments. What is the maximum monthly housing payment (PITI) she qualifies for?
questions.explanation: Housing limit: $7,500 × 28% = $2,100. Total-debt limit: $7,500 × 36% = $2,700 − $650 = $2,050. The lower figure controls, so $2,050. Choosing $2,100 ignores the back-end ratio; $1,450 wrongly subtracts the debts from the housing limit.
questions.citation: Qualifying ratio principles (front-end and back-end ratios)

questions.q: A lender's housing expense (front-end) ratio compares:
options: Total monthly debts to gross monthly income
Monthly PITI to take-home pay after taxes
The loan amount to the property's value
Monthly PITI to gross monthly income
questions.explanation: The front-end ratio is housing expense (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) divided by gross monthly income. Total debt to gross income is the back-end ratio, and loan amount to value is the LTV ratio.

questions.q: A buyer's projected PITI is $2,450 a month. The lender's housing expense ratio is 28%. What minimum gross ANNUAL income does the buyer need?
questions.explanation: $2,450 ÷ 0.28 = $8,750 per month; $8,750 × 12 = $105,000 per year. $8,750 is the monthly figure; $81,666.67 wrongly uses 36%; $8,232 multiplies by 28% instead of dividing.

questions.q: How does a mortgage preapproval generally differ from a prequalification?
options: Preapproval follows a credit check and verified application
Preapproval is a binding promise to fund at any interest rate
Preapproval is based only on what the buyer says in a talk
Preapproval is issued by the seller's broker, not by a lender
questions.explanation: A prequalification is an informal estimate based on unverified information the buyer provides. A preapproval comes after an application, credit report, and verification of income and assets, producing a conditional commitment, but it is still not an unconditional promise to fund.

questions.q: A lender making a high-cost home loan under New York Banking Law §6-l wants to add a single-premium credit life insurance policy to the loan balance. This is:
options: Allowed if the borrower initials the policy
Prohibited for a high-cost home loan
Allowed if the premium is under 2% of the loan
Required for borrowers over age 62
questions.explanation: Section 6-l bars financing single-premium credit life, disability, unemployment, or similar insurance into a high-cost home loan. Coverage paid monthly is treated differently; a signature or initials does not cure a financed single premium.

questions.q: A lender offers a New York high-cost home loan with a 'payment option' that lets the borrower pay less than the interest due each month. Under Banking Law §6-l, this feature is:
options: Permitted, because the borrower chooses the option
Permitted, if the loan also offers a full payment
Prohibited, because it allows negative amortization
Prohibited only when the loan is a jumbo loan
questions.explanation: High-cost home loans may not have payment schedules that cause the balance to grow, and a payment option that permits negative amortization counts as prohibited even if a fully amortizing option is also offered.

questions.q: At application for a New York high-cost home loan, what must the lender or mortgage broker give the borrower?
options: A completed appraisal showing the home's value supports the loan
A certificate that the loan carries no prepayment penalty at all
A signed promise to refinance later at a lower rate without fees
A notice recommending financial counseling, with a list of counselors
questions.explanation: Section 6-l requires a written notice that the borrower should consider financial counseling before signing, along with a list of counselors provided by the NYS Department of Financial Services.

questions.q: Which statement about subprime lending is accurate?
options: Any loan to a borrower with a low credit score is predatory and unlawful
Subprime loans must be insured by FHA before they can be made in New York
Subprime loans are not illegal by themselves; abusive terms make lending predatory
Subprime loans are conforming loans sold to Fannie Mae at a discount
questions.explanation: 'Subprime' describes credit risk and pricing, not illegality. Lending becomes predatory through practices such as hidden fees, loan flipping, equity stripping, or lending without regard to the ability to repay.
questions.citation: General predatory lending principles; NY Banking Law §6-l

questions.q: Which governmental power is the legal basis for a municipality's zoning ordinance?
options: Police power
Eminent domain
Escheat
Taxation
questions.explanation: Zoning is an exercise of the police power: regulating private property use to protect public health, safety, morals and general welfare. Eminent domain takes property (with compensation); escheat transfers property of an owner who dies without heirs or a will.
questions.citation: NY Town Law § 261; NY Village Law § 7-700

questions.q: A town downzones an area, reducing permitted density, and an owner's lot loses some market value. What is the general rule on compensation?
options: Just compensation is always owed for any loss in market value caused by a zoning change
The town must buy the lot at its pre-rezoning appraised value whenever the owner demands
No compensation is owed for a valid regulation unless it goes so far as to be a taking
The owner may ignore the new zoning until compensation is paid in full
questions.explanation: A valid police-power regulation does not require payment merely because it reduces value. Compensation is required for a taking under eminent domain, or where regulation is so severe that courts treat it as a regulatory taking.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amendment; NY Const. Art. I § 7

questions.q: The State acquires part of a farm by condemnation to widen a highway. Which pair of requirements must the taking satisfy?
options: Owner consent and a fair hearing
Public use and just compensation
Public use and a majority vote of neighbors
A recorded deed and owner consent
questions.explanation: Eminent domain lets government take private property without the owner's consent, but only for a public use and upon payment of just compensation. Consent is exactly what condemnation does not require.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amendment; NY Const. Art. I § 7; NY Eminent Domain Procedure Law

questions.q: In an eminent domain taking, just compensation is generally measured by:
options: The owner's original purchase price plus the cost of any improvements made since
The assessed value currently shown for the property on the municipal tax roll
The cost the government expects to incur to build the planned public project
The fair market value of the property taken, considering its highest and best use
questions.explanation: Just compensation is generally the property's fair market value at the time of the taking, considering its highest and best use. Purchase price and assessed value are not the measure.
questions.citation: NY Eminent Domain Procedure Law; NY Const. Art. I § 7

questions.q: An owner in a residential-only district wants to open a retail store. Because retail is not a permitted use there, what must the owner show the zoning board of appeals to obtain relief?
options: Practical difficulty balanced against detriment to the neighborhood
That the store would earn more than the house currently does
That a majority of adjoining owners signed letters of support
Unnecessary hardship, including no reasonable return from any permitted use
questions.explanation: A use variance requires unnecessary hardship: no reasonable return under any permitted use (shown by competent financial evidence), a unique hardship, no change to neighborhood character, and a hardship that is not self-created. Merely wanting a more profitable use is insufficient.

questions.q: A homeowner wants to build a deck that would extend 6 feet into a required rear-yard setback. What type of relief is needed?
options: A use variance
An area variance
A rezoning of the district
A nonconforming use certificate
questions.explanation: A setback is a dimensional requirement, so relief is an area variance. The ZBA balances the benefit to the applicant against any detriment to the health, safety and welfare of the neighborhood.

questions.q: When deciding an area variance, how does New York law treat a difficulty that the applicant created?
options: It is relevant but does not by itself preclude granting the variance
It automatically requires the board to deny the area variance request
It is irrelevant, and the board may not consider it in deciding the variance
It converts the request into a use variance with a stricter hardship test
questions.explanation: For an area variance, self-created difficulty is one factor in the balancing test and does not necessarily bar relief. Trap: for a use variance, the hardship must not be self-created.

questions.q: A town's zoning ordinance lists day-care centers as allowed in residential districts if specified conditions on parking and lot size are met. A provider seeking approval needs:
options: A use variance
An area variance
A special use permit
A spot zoning amendment
questions.explanation: A special use permit authorizes a use the ordinance already contemplates for the district, once its conditions are met. It is not a variance, because the use is not prohibited.

questions.q: A gas station has operated legally on a corner since before the area was zoned residential. Under the new zoning, the station:
options: May generally continue as a lawful nonconforming use
Must close immediately because it is now an illegal use
Automatically receives a use variance from the zoning board
May expand freely because it existed before the zoning
questions.explanation: A use that was lawful before a zoning change may generally continue as a nonconforming use. That status does not authorize unlimited expansion, and it is not the same as an illegal use.
questions.citation: NY zoning law: nonconforming use doctrine (local zoning ordinance)

questions.q: Which statement about a lawful nonconforming use is generally accurate?
options: It may be enlarged or extended at any time without any approval from the town
It may be changed to any other nonconforming use without zoning board review
It may be lost if abandoned or discontinued for the period set by the ordinance
It automatically becomes a permitted use after ten years of continuous operation
questions.explanation: Ordinances typically restrict expansion or change of a nonconforming use and terminate it if the use is discontinued or abandoned for a stated period. The goal is to phase nonconforming uses out over time.
questions.citation: NY zoning law: nonconforming use doctrine (local zoning ordinance)

questions.q: A city council rezones one owner's small lot to commercial, solely for that owner's benefit, while all surrounding land stays residential and the change conflicts with the comprehensive plan. This is:
options: Cluster zoning, which is generally valid
Spot zoning, which is generally invalid
Incentive zoning, which is generally valid
A lawful area variance by the council
questions.explanation: Spot zoning singles out a small parcel for a classification different from the surrounding area, for private benefit and inconsistent with the comprehensive plan. Courts generally strike it down.
questions.citation: NY Town Law § 263 (zoning in accordance with comprehensive plan)

questions.q: A developer groups homes on smaller lots and leaves the rest of the tract as permanent open space, without exceeding the density a conventional subdivision would allow. This is:
options: Spot zoning
Downzoning
A use variance
Cluster zoning
questions.explanation: Cluster development concentrates buildings to preserve open space while keeping overall density no greater than a conventional layout. The planning board may approve it when authorized by the town board.

questions.q: A developer plans to divide a 40-acre parcel into 25 building lots. Before lots are sold, the developer generally must obtain:
options: A use variance from the zoning board of appeals
A certificate of occupancy for each lot
A deed restriction approved by the assessor
Subdivision plat approval from the planning board
questions.explanation: Subdivision regulations require planning board approval of the plat (lots, streets, utilities, drainage) before it is filed and lots are sold. Variances and COs address different issues.

questions.q: Outside New York City, which code sets statewide minimum construction and fire-safety standards that local building departments enforce?
options: The Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law
The Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code
The State Environmental Quality Review Act
The Multiple Residence Law of New York
questions.explanation: The Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code sets minimum construction and fire-safety standards. Municipalities enforce it through permits and inspections; New York City has its own construction codes.

questions.q: What does a certificate of occupancy (CO) indicate?
options: The building was inspected and may be legally occupied for its stated use
The property has clear, marketable title insured against all defects
The owner has permission to begin construction on the lot
The building is free of every physical defect and needs no repairs
questions.explanation: A CO is issued after completed work is found to comply with approved plans and applicable codes, allowing legal occupancy for the stated use. It does not guarantee title or the absence of every defect.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; local building code

questions.q: A contractor has just received a building permit for a new house. A buyer under contract asks whether they can move in once the walls are up. The best answer is:
options: Yes; a building permit also authorizes occupancy once the framing inspection is passed
Yes; occupancy is legally allowed as soon as the buyer closes and takes title to the house
No; a permit only authorizes construction; occupancy generally needs a certificate of occupancy
No; occupancy additionally requires a new variance from the zoning board of appeals
questions.explanation: A building permit is issued before work starts and authorizes construction. A certificate of occupancy (or equivalent) is issued after completion and inspection, and that is what allows legal occupancy.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; local building code

questions.q: Under New York's town zoning enabling law, zoning regulations must be adopted:
options: In accordance with a comprehensive plan
Only after a vote of all property owners
Only with approval from the Department of State
In accordance with each owner's deed restrictions
questions.explanation: Town Law requires zoning to be made in accordance with a comprehensive (master) plan, which guides long-term land use, transportation and community facilities.

questions.q: Under SEQR, the lead agency determines a proposed project may have a significant adverse environmental impact. What happens next?
options: It issues a negative declaration and the project proceeds without further review
The project is automatically denied and may not be resubmitted
It issues a positive declaration and an environmental impact statement is required
The application is transferred to the Department of State for a decision
questions.explanation: A positive declaration means an EIS must be prepared. A negative declaration means no significant adverse impact, so no EIS. Not every project requires an EIS.

questions.q: Under SEQR, an action classified as Type II:
options: Is presumed likely to require an environmental impact statement
Has been determined not to require further environmental review
Must be reviewed by the Adirondack Park Agency
May proceed only after a positive declaration is issued
questions.explanation: Type II actions (e.g., many routine actions and minor residential construction) are listed as not requiring SEQR review. Type I actions are more likely to require an EIS; unlisted actions get case-by-case review.

questions.q: A buyer plans to build a home on private land inside the Adirondack Park. In addition to local approvals, the buyer should check whether a permit is needed from:
options: The New York State Board of Real Estate
The Federal Housing Administration
The county tax assessor's office
The Adirondack Park Agency
questions.explanation: The Adirondack Park Agency regulates land use and development on private land within the Park through its own land-use plan and permit system, in addition to local rules.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 27 (Adirondack Park Agency Act)

questions.q: A buyer wants to fill and build on land near a freshwater wetland. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only local zoning applies, because wetlands are governed solely by the town or village
No wetland permit is needed once the buyer closes and holds a recorded deed to the land
Only federal law applies, because New York State does not regulate freshwater wetlands
State, federal and local rules may each apply; get a current jurisdictional determination
questions.explanation: NYS DEC regulates freshwater wetlands under ECL Article 24 (including adjacent areas), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers regulates fill under the Clean Water Act, and localities may add rules. Get a current determination rather than assuming.
questions.citation: NY ECL Article 24; Clean Water Act § 404

questions.q: Zoning allows two-family homes in a district, but a recorded deed restriction on a lot limits it to one single-family home. Which rule controls?
options: The zoning, because public law always overrides private covenants
The deed restriction, because the more restrictive rule governs
Neither, because the two conflict and cancel each other out
Whichever was recorded or enacted more recently
questions.explanation: When zoning and a private deed restriction differ, the more restrictive one controls. An owner must satisfy both, so the single-family limit applies.
questions.citation: NY zoning law; restrictive covenants (deed restrictions)

questions.q: A county acquires and later sells a parcel through a foreclosure proceeding because the owner left real property taxes unpaid for several years. Which government power underlies this process?
options: Taxation
Police power
Eminent domain
Escheat
questions.explanation: The power to tax includes the power to enforce the tax lien against the land, ultimately through tax foreclosure. Eminent domain is a trap: it involves a taking for public use with just compensation, not collection of unpaid taxes.
questions.citation: N.Y. Real Property Tax Law Article 11 (tax enforcement)

questions.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes eminent domain from a police power regulation such as zoning?
options: Eminent domain may be used only to acquire vacant land
Eminent domain requires paying the owner just compensation
Police power may be exercised only by the State itself
Police power rules apply only to commercial property
questions.explanation: Eminent domain transfers property to the government for public use and requires just compensation; a valid police power regulation restricts use without compensation. Police power is commonly delegated to localities, so the State-only option is wrong.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. Amend. V; N.Y. Const. art. I, §7; Eminent Domain Procedure Law

questions.q: A state flood-control project permanently floods part of a private farm, but the State never started a condemnation proceeding. The owner's lawsuit seeking payment for the land effectively taken is generally called:
options: A partition action
A quiet title action
An inverse condemnation claim
A specific performance suit
questions.explanation: When government action effectively takes property without formal condemnation, the owner may sue for just compensation in inverse condemnation. A quiet title action resolves competing ownership claims and does not seek compensation from the government.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. Amend. V; N.Y. Const. art. I, §7 (just compensation)

questions.q: The State condemns a 40-foot strip along the front of a commercial lot for a road project, eliminating most of the remaining parcel's parking and lowering its value. Compensation for the lost value of the land the owner keeps is called:
options: Liquidated damages
A special assessment
Consequential rent
Severance damages
questions.explanation: In a partial taking, the owner is paid for the part taken plus severance damages for the decline in value of the remainder. A special assessment is the reverse: a charge imposed on owners for a public improvement that benefits their land.
questions.citation: N.Y. Eminent Domain Procedure Law; general law of just compensation

questions.q: Each of the following is generally an exercise of the police power EXCEPT:
options: Condemning a house for a new state highway
Enforcing a local building and fire code
Adopting a town zoning ordinance
Imposing rent regulation on apartments
questions.explanation: Building codes, zoning and rent regulation restrict how property is used to protect health, safety and welfare, which is police power. Taking title to a house for a highway is eminent domain, which requires just compensation.
questions.citation: General law of police power and eminent domain

questions.q: Why is the 1926 U.S. Supreme Court decision in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co. important to land-use law?
options: It required compensation whenever zoning reduces property value
It upheld comprehensive use-district zoning as a valid police power
It struck down zoning that separates homes from industry
It created the public-use test for eminent domain takings
questions.explanation: Euclid upheld a village ordinance dividing land into separate use districts as a reasonable police power regulation; traditional district zoning is still called Euclidean zoning. It did not require compensation for value lost to zoning.
questions.citation: Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., 272 U.S. 365 (1926)

questions.q: Under a cumulative (pyramid) zoning ordinance, a builder proposes a single-family house in a light-industrial district. The house is generally:
options: Prohibited unless the builder obtains a use variance
Allowed only if it qualifies as a nonconforming use
Permitted, because higher uses may locate in lower districts
Permitted only after the district is formally rezoned
questions.explanation: Cumulative zoning ranks uses, with single-family residential at the top, and lets a higher use locate in a district zoned for a lower use. The use-variance option describes exclusive zoning, where only the district's listed uses are allowed.

questions.q: Which statement best describes exclusive (non-cumulative) zoning?
options: Any use ranked higher than the district's use may locate there as of right
The zoning board selects the uses for each lot when a permit is requested
Each district permits only one structure per lot regardless of the use proposed
Only a district's listed uses are allowed, so homes can be barred from industrial zones
questions.explanation: Exclusive zoning allows only the designated uses in each district, even keeping homes out of industrial zones to protect industrial land and prevent conflicts. Letting higher uses locate in lower districts is the definition of cumulative zoning, the opposite approach.

questions.q: A city designates a historic district that sits on top of portions of existing residential and commercial districts. It adds façade-review rules but leaves each base district's permitted uses unchanged. This technique is:
options: An overlay zone
A floating zone
Spot zoning
A buffer zone
questions.explanation: An overlay zone is superimposed on the underlying base districts and adds requirements, such as historic, flood or watershed rules, without replacing the base zoning. A floating zone is described in the ordinance text but not mapped until applied to a specific parcel.
questions.citation: General principles of zoning (overlay districts); N.Y. General City Law §20 (city zoning power)

questions.q: A village zoning ordinance describes a "senior housing district" with detailed standards, but the district appears nowhere on the zoning map. The village board will apply it to a particular parcel only after an owner applies and meets the standards. This is:
options: An overlay zone
A floating zone
A cumulative zone
An incentive zone
questions.explanation: A floating zone is defined in the text and floats until the legislative body lands it on a qualifying parcel by amending the map; New York's highest court upheld this technique in Rodgers v. Village of Tarrytown. An overlay zone is already mapped over base districts.
questions.citation: Rodgers v. Village of Tarrytown, 302 N.Y. 115 (1951)

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes a planned unit development (PUD) from a typical cluster subdivision?
options: A PUD must contain only detached single-family homes on standard-sized lots
A cluster subdivision may exceed the district's density with no approval needed
A PUD can mix uses and building types under one master plan for the whole tract
A cluster subdivision always combines retail, office and residential uses
questions.explanation: A PUD treats the tract as a single planned unit and may combine housing types, commercial uses and open space with flexible standards. Cluster development usually rearranges the permitted housing onto smaller lots to preserve open space, without exceeding the conventional density.
questions.citation: N.Y. Town Law §278 (cluster development); general PUD principles

questions.q: A town zoning ordinance lets a developer build more floor area than the district normally permits if the developer provides a public plaza and a community meeting room. This technique is:
options: Spot zoning
Exclusive zoning
Amortization
Incentive zoning
questions.explanation: Incentive zoning grants bonuses, such as added density or floor area, in exchange for specified community benefits or amenities. Spot zoning is a trap: it singles out one parcel for special treatment that conflicts with the comprehensive plan.

questions.q: A city ordinance requires every new residential building above a set size to reserve a percentage of its units as permanently affordable to lower-income households. This is:
options: Inclusionary zoning
Exclusionary zoning
Cluster zoning
Overlay zoning
questions.explanation: Inclusionary zoning requires or encourages affordable units within market-rate development, often paired with a density bonus; New York City's Mandatory Inclusionary Housing program is an example. Exclusionary zoning is the opposite: rules that effectively keep lower-income households out.
questions.citation: General principles of zoning; NYC Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (Zoning Resolution)

questions.q: A 30-acre tract is zoned for a base density of 2 dwelling units per acre. The town's incentive zoning provisions grant a 20% density bonus if the developer dedicates a public park. How many units may be built if the park is provided?
options: 60 units
72 units
66 units
80 units
questions.explanation: Base density = 30 acres × 2 units = 60 units; bonus = 60 × 20% = 12; total = 60 + 12 = 72 units. A common mistake is adding 20 units (60 + 20 = 80) by treating the percentage as a unit count.

questions.q: An inclusionary zoning rule requires 25% of the units in a new 120-unit building to be affordable. How many units may be offered at market rate?
options: 30 units
95 units
90 units
96 units
questions.explanation: Affordable units = 120 × 25% = 30; market-rate units = 120 − 30 = 90. The 30-unit distractor is the affordable count, not the market-rate count.

questions.q: Under Town Law §267-b(2), an applicant for a use variance must prove unnecessary hardship. Which of the following is NOT one of the required showings?
options: No reasonable return is possible under the current zoning
The hardship is unique to the property, not the district
The use will not alter the neighborhood's essential character
The proposed use would earn more than the current use
questions.explanation: The four elements are no reasonable return, a unique hardship, no change to essential neighborhood character, and a hardship that is not self-created. Showing that a new use would simply be more profitable does not establish unnecessary hardship.

questions.q: A use-variance applicant claims that the property cannot yield a reasonable return. How must that claim generally be proven?
options: With competent financial evidence covering each permitted use
With the owner's testimony that a store would earn more
With proof that the current use alone is no longer profitable
With letters from neighbors who support the proposed use
questions.explanation: The statute requires that the lack of reasonable return be substantial and shown by competent financial evidence, and courts require that showing for every use the district permits. Proving only that the current use is unprofitable is insufficient, since other permitted uses might still produce a return.

questions.q: An investor buys a lot zoned residential, knowing the zoning, and pays a price that assumes commercial use. The investor then seeks a use variance for a store. The board will most likely find the hardship:
options: Unique, because the price paid was unusually high
Self-created, which generally defeats a use variance
Irrelevant, because the zoning board ignores the purchase
Self-created, but generally no bar to a use variance
questions.explanation: Buying with knowledge of the restriction makes the hardship self-created, and a self-created hardship is one of the grounds that defeats a use variance. The last option confuses this with an area variance, where self-creation is relevant but not necessarily a bar.

questions.q: Every residential lot along a busy state highway corridor suffers the same traffic noise, making homes there hard to rent profitably. Owners seek relief so they can operate businesses. The more appropriate remedy is generally:
options: A use variance for each owner, because the hardship is shared
An area variance for each lot, because noise is dimensional
A rezoning by the town board, because the hardship is not unique
A special use permit, which the building inspector can issue
questions.explanation: A use variance requires a hardship unique to the parcel; a problem shared by a substantial part of the district calls for legislative rezoning instead. Granting individual use variances for a district-wide condition would effectively rezone the area through the ZBA.
questions.citation: N.Y. Town Law §267-b(2)(b)(2); Town Law §§264-265 (zoning amendments)

questions.q: An applicant asks the ZBA for a 20-foot reduction in a front-yard setback. The board finds that an 8-foot reduction would fully address the applicant's need while better protecting the neighborhood. The board should generally:
options: Grant the full 20 feet because the applicant requested it
Deny the variance because the request was larger than needed
Refer the application to the town board for a rezoning vote
Grant only the minimum relief that is necessary and adequate
questions.explanation: Town Law §267-b directs the board to grant the minimum variance it deems necessary and adequate while preserving neighborhood character and public health, safety and welfare. An oversized request does not require outright denial; the board may grant less than requested.

questions.q: When deciding an area variance, the zoning board of appeals primarily weighs:
options: The benefit to the applicant against the detriment to the community
The added tax revenue against the applicant's construction cost
The applicant's profit against the return from permitted uses
The neighbors' opinions against the building inspector's opinion
questions.explanation: Town Law §267-b(3) sets a balancing test: the benefit to the applicant versus the detriment to the health, safety and welfare of the neighborhood or community, using five listed factors. Comparing returns from permitted uses belongs to the use-variance standard.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the statutory factors a ZBA considers for an area variance?
options: Whether the benefit can be achieved by another feasible method
Whether every permitted use would fail to earn a reasonable return
Whether the requested variance is substantial
Whether physical or environmental conditions will be harmed
questions.explanation: The area-variance factors are: undesirable change or detriment to nearby properties, feasible alternatives, substantiality, adverse physical or environmental effects, and self-created difficulty. The reasonable-return showing is part of the use-variance standard.

questions.q: A zoning ordinance requires a 20-foot side yard. An owner proposes an addition that would leave only 15 feet. Measured against the requirement, how large is the requested relief?
questions.explanation: Relief = 20 − 15 = 5 feet; 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, or 25% of the requirement. Dividing by the proposed 15 feet (5 ÷ 15 = 33%) uses the wrong base; 75% is the portion of the yard that remains.

questions.q: The zoning ordinance requires a minimum lot size of 10,000 square feet in a single-family district. An owner of a 9,000-square-foot lot wants to build one single-family house. What relief is needed?
options: A use variance, because the lot cannot be used as zoned
A special use permit, because the house is a listed use
A rezoning, because the lot falls below the district minimum
An area variance, because lot size is a dimensional requirement
questions.explanation: A single-family house is a permitted use there; only the dimensional lot-area rule is not met, so the request is for an area variance. A use variance is needed only to allow a use the district prohibits.
questions.citation: N.Y. Town Law §267(1) (definitions of use and area variances)

questions.q: A private school wants to locate in a residential district where the ordinance lists schools as allowed by special use permit. Compared with a use variance, what is the key difference?
options: The applicant must meet the ordinance's stated standards, not prove unnecessary hardship
The applicant must show no reasonable return from every use the district permits
The applicant needs approval from the State rather than a local board
The permit is issued automatically once a fee is paid, without any review
questions.explanation: A special use permit authorizes a use the legislative body has already found appropriate in the district if specified conditions are met, so no hardship showing is required. Proving no reasonable return is the use-variance burden.

questions.q: A planning board grants a special use permit for a day-care center, conditioned on limited drop-off hours and landscaped screening along a neighbor's line. These conditions are generally:
options: Invalid, because special permit uses may not carry conditions
Valid, if reasonable and directly related to the use's impacts
Valid only if the applicant later consents to them in court
Invalid, because only the town board may impose any conditions
questions.explanation: The statute lets the authorized board impose reasonable conditions that are directly related and incidental to the proposed use. The condition power is not reserved to the town board; it belongs to whichever board is authorized to grant the permit.

questions.q: A ZBA grants an area variance on the condition that it expires automatically when the current owner sells the house. This condition is generally:
options: Valid, because variances are personal to the applicant
Valid, because the board may impose any condition it likes
Invalid, because a variance runs with the land, not the owner
Invalid, because area variances can never carry conditions
questions.explanation: Zoning regulates the use of land, not the person who owns it, so New York courts treat a variance as running with the land and strike conditions tied to a particular owner. Boards may impose reasonable land-related conditions, so the never-carry-conditions option overstates the rule.
questions.citation: Matter of St. Onge v. Donovan, 71 N.Y.2d 507 (1988); Town Law §267-b(4)

questions.q: A lawful nonconforming auto-repair shop sits in a residential district. The owner wants to add two service bays, doubling the building's size. Generally:
options: The expansion is allowed because the use was grandfathered
The expansion is allowed if the owner has owned it a decade
The building inspector must approve it as a matter of course
Nonconforming status alone does not authorize the expansion
questions.explanation: A nonconforming use is tolerated so it can continue, but the policy is to let it wither, not grow; enlargement is generally restricted and usually needs whatever relief the ordinance requires. "Grandfathered" does not mean unlimited expansion rights.
questions.citation: General law of nonconforming uses; local zoning ordinance

questions.q: A lawful nonconforming delicatessen in a residential district is sold, and the buyer continues to run the same deli. Generally, the buyer:
options: May continue the use, because nonconforming status runs with the land
Loses the right, because the protection was personal to the seller
Must apply for a use variance within one year after the closing
May continue the use only until the seller's original lease ends
questions.explanation: A lawful nonconforming use attaches to the property, so a change of ownership alone does not end it. It can still be lost by abandonment or discontinuance, or limited by amortization, under the ordinance.

questions.q: A town amends its sign law to give owners of existing nonconforming billboards seven years to remove them, so they can recover their investment. This approach is called:
options: Spot zoning
Amortization
Inverse condemnation
Downzoning
questions.explanation: Amortization terminates a nonconforming use after a set grace period, and New York courts generally uphold it when the period is reasonable in light of the owner's investment. Inverse condemnation is a lawsuit by an owner seeking compensation for an uncompensated taking.
questions.citation: Matter of Harbison v. City of Buffalo, 4 N.Y.2d 553 (1958)

questions.q: An ordinance provides that a nonconforming use discontinued for one year may not be resumed. A nonconforming warehouse sits vacant for 14 months, though the owner insists it always meant to reopen. Under New York law, generally:
options: The right survives, because the owner never intended to abandon
The right survives until the owner sells the warehouse to another
The right is lost, because the period ran regardless of intent
The right is lost only after a court enters a judgment of abandonment
questions.explanation: Where an ordinance sets a discontinuance period, New York's highest court has held that the nonconforming right ends when the period runs, without proof of intent to abandon. The intent option states the common-law abandonment test that such ordinances displace.
questions.citation: Matter of Toys "R" Us v. Silva, 89 N.Y.2d 411 (1996)

questions.q: The owner of a lawful nonconforming machine shop in a residential district wants to convert it into a nightclub. Generally:
options: Any nonconforming use may replace another as of right
The conversion is allowed if the nightclub is quieter
The change is allowed once the shop has run for ten years
