A different nonconforming use is not allowed as of right
questions.explanation: Nonconforming rights generally protect only the use that existed; changing to a different nonconforming use usually requires approval, while a change to a conforming use is allowed. Zoning aims to phase nonconforming uses out, not swap one for another.
questions.citation: General law of nonconforming uses; local zoning ordinance

questions.q: After its updated comprehensive plan calls for medical services along a corridor, a town board rezones one corridor parcel to allow a medical office. Neighbors call it spot zoning. Generally:
options: A small rezoning consistent with the comprehensive plan is usually valid
Any rezoning that affects a single parcel is automatically invalid
Rezoning one parcel is valid only if the owner pays compensation
A town board may never rezone a parcel after an owner has applied
questions.explanation: Spot zoning is invalid when a parcel is singled out for a use inconsistent with the comprehensive plan for the owner's benefit. A rezoning of a small parcel that carries out the plan and serves the general welfare is generally upheld.
questions.citation: N.Y. Town Law §§263, 272-a; general law of spot zoning

questions.q: A town's comprehensive plan designates a residential street for future commercial use, but the zoning map still shows the street as single-family residential. A buyer wants to open a shop there now. Generally:
options: The plan controls, so the shop may open without further approvals
The current zoning controls until the town board actually rezones
The plan designation entitles the buyer to a use variance on request
The zoning board of appeals must rezone the street to match the plan
questions.explanation: A comprehensive plan guides future land-use decisions, while the zoning ordinance is the enforceable law; changing the zoning map is a legislative act of the town board. The ZBA grants relief and interprets the ordinance but cannot rezone.

questions.q: The building inspector denies a permit, interpreting the zoning ordinance against an owner. Under the Town Law, the owner generally must file an appeal to the zoning board of appeals within:
options: 30 days after the decision is filed
10 days after the decision is filed
60 days after the decision is filed
4 months after the decision is filed
questions.explanation: Town Law §267-a(5)(b) allows an appeal to the ZBA within 60 days after the administrative official's determination is filed. The 30-day figure is the deadline to seek court review of a ZBA decision under Town Law §267-c.

questions.q: A neighbor wants to challenge a town ZBA's grant of a use variance in court. The Article 78 proceeding generally must be started within:
options: 4 months after the decision is filed with the town clerk
62 days after the board's public hearing has closed
1 year after the variance holder receives a permit
30 days after the decision is filed with the town clerk
questions.explanation: Town Law §267-c requires an Article 78 proceeding within 30 days after the ZBA decision is filed in the town clerk's office. Four months is the general Article 78 limitation period, which this shorter zoning-specific deadline overrides; 62 days is the board's time to decide after the hearing.

questions.q: A town ZBA has seven members. Five attend a meeting, and they vote 3–2 to grant an area variance. Generally, the variance:
options: Is not granted, because a majority of all seven members is needed
Is granted, because a majority of the members present voted yes
Is granted, because the vote met the quorum of four members
Is not granted, because every variance requires a unanimous vote
questions.explanation: Town Law §267-a(13) requires the concurring vote of a majority of the members of the board, meaning the full membership: 4 of 7. Three votes is a majority of those present but not of the board, so the motion fails.

questions.q: Owners of 20% or more of the land immediately adjacent to an area proposed for rezoning, extending 100 feet from it, file a valid written protest. The town board has seven members. What is the minimum number of yes votes needed to adopt the change?
options: 4 votes
6 votes
5 votes
7 votes
questions.explanation: A valid protest under Town Law §265 requires the favorable vote of at least three-fourths of the town board's members: 7 × 3/4 = 5.25, rounded up to 6. Four votes is the ordinary simple majority of 7, which the protest raises.

questions.q: A court reviews a ZBA's denial of an area variance in an Article 78 proceeding. The court will generally:
options: Hold a new hearing and decide the variance on its own judgment
Overturn the denial whenever it would have weighed the factors differently
Uphold the denial if it has a rational basis supported by the record
Send the application to the town board for a final legislative vote
questions.explanation: Courts defer to a ZBA's quasi-judicial decision unless it is illegal, arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion, so a rationally based decision stands. A court does not substitute its own judgment for the board's.

questions.q: A town planning board has signed a developer's approved final subdivision plat. The developer then waits three months before doing anything else with it. What is the risk under the Town Law?
options: Nothing, because the planning board's signature is the last step and approval never lapses
The planning board must file the plat itself, so the developer's delay has no effect
The approval expires if the plat is not filed with the county clerk within 62 days of signing
The plat must be re-approved only if the developer later sells lots to out-of-state buyers
questions.explanation: A signed final plat must be filed in the county clerk's office within 62 days or the approval expires. The trap is treating the board's signature as the final step; filing is what puts the plat on record.

questions.q: Before a town planning board signs a final subdivision plat, the subdivider has not yet built the required streets, drains and water lines. What may the board accept instead of completed construction?
options: A performance bond or other security guaranteeing the improvements
A recorded deed restriction barring resale of lots for five years
A variance from the zoning board of appeals for each unbuilt street
A certificate of occupancy for the first house in the subdivision
questions.explanation: The Town Law lets the board require that improvements be installed or that their installation be guaranteed by a performance bond or other security. A ZBA variance relieves zoning rules; it does not secure unbuilt infrastructure.

questions.q: A planning board finds that a new subdivision will create a need for recreation land, but no part of the tract is suitable for a park. Under the town subdivision law, the board may:
options: Deny the plat, because every subdivision must contain its own park site
Take a park site from the developer by eminent domain without payment
Ignore recreation needs, because only the county may consider them
Require a money payment in lieu of parkland, kept for recreational purposes
questions.explanation: When a suitable park cannot be properly located on the plat, the board may require a fee in lieu of parkland, to be used for park and recreational purposes. Taking land without payment would violate the just-compensation requirement.

questions.q: A developer owns 30 acres. Streets, drainage and other required improvements will use 25% of the land, and zoning requires a 2-acre minimum lot size. What is the maximum number of conforming building lots?
options: 12 lots
11 lots
15 lots
10 lots
questions.explanation: Usable land = 30 × (1 − 0.25) = 22.5 acres; 22.5 ÷ 2 = 11.25, so only 11 lots can meet the 2-acre minimum. Rounding up to 12 creates an undersized lot, and 15 forgets to deduct the 25% for improvements (30 ÷ 2).
questions.citation: General subdivision and zoning density principles

questions.q: A subdivider plans to sell eight 1-acre residential lots served by private wells and septic systems. Before the lots are offered for sale, the water supply and sewage disposal plans generally must be approved by:
options: The local zoning board of appeals as part of a use variance
The state or county health department under the Public Health Law
The Department of State's Division of Licensing Services
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's land sales office
questions.explanation: Public Health Law Article 11 treats a tract divided into five or more residential lots of five acres or less as a realty subdivision whose water and sewage plans need health-department approval before sale. Licensing Services regulates brokers and salespersons, not septic design.

questions.q: A village board wants to impose stricter construction standards than the Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code requires. Under the Executive Law, the village generally:
options: May adopt them by simple resolution with no state agency involvement at all
Can never impose any standard stricter than the Uniform Code's minimums
Needs approval only from its own zoning board of appeals before adoption
May do so only with approval from the State Fire Prevention and Building Code Council
questions.explanation: A local government may adopt more restrictive building standards, but they take effect only after the State Code Council approves them as reasonably necessary. The trap is assuming the Uniform Code is either an absolute ceiling or freely changeable by local vote.

questions.q: Outside New York City, a homeowner restoring an old house cannot meet one specific Uniform Code construction requirement and wants relief from it. Who generally decides the request?
options: A Department of State regional board of review
The town or village zoning board of appeals
The county clerk who records the deed
The planning board that approved the plat
questions.explanation: Variances from the Uniform Code are decided through the Department of State's code variance process, by regional boards of review. A ZBA grants relief from zoning rules, not from building-code requirements.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 18; 19 NYCRR Part 1205

questions.q: In New York City, which body primarily issues building permits and certificates of occupancy?
options: The NYS Department of State, under the Uniform Code
The NYC Department of Finance, under the Real Property Tax Law
The NYC Department of Buildings, under the NYC Construction Codes
Each borough's planning board, under the Town Law
questions.explanation: New York City is outside the Uniform Code system; it has its own Construction Codes enforced by the NYC Department of Buildings. The Department of Finance handles assessment and taxes, not construction approvals.
questions.citation: NYC Administrative Code Title 28 (NYC Construction Codes)

questions.q: A buyer is purchasing a Brooklyn row house built in 1925. The city has no certificate of occupancy on file, and the use and occupancy have not changed since construction. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The house must be vacated until the owner obtains a new CO
No one- or two-family home in NYC has ever needed a CO
NYC generally did not require a CO for buildings erected before 1938
The seller may substitute a sworn affidavit for the missing CO
questions.explanation: NYC began requiring certificates of occupancy in 1938, so older buildings without later changes in use, egress or occupancy usually have none. Saying no one- or two-family home ever needs a CO is wrong: homes built after 1938 do.
questions.citation: NYC Department of Buildings certificate of occupancy rules

questions.q: An owner converts a legal two-family house into a three-family house. Regarding the certificate of occupancy, the owner generally needs:
options: A new or amended CO reflecting the changed use and occupancy
Nothing more, because the original CO runs with the land forever
Only a written notice to the tenant who will occupy the new unit
A recorded deed restriction in place of an updated certificate
questions.explanation: A CO certifies a particular lawful use and occupancy; adding a dwelling unit changes both, so an amended or new CO is required (after any zoning approval). The original CO covers only the two-family use it describes.
questions.citation: NY Uniform Code (19 NYCRR Part 1203); NYC Construction Codes

questions.q: The lower floors of a new apartment building are finished and safe, but work on the roof deck is incomplete. The building department may let residents move into the finished portion by issuing a:
options: Certificate of nonconforming use
Conditioned negative declaration
Renewed building permit
Temporary certificate of occupancy
questions.explanation: A temporary CO allows lawful occupancy of completed, safe portions while remaining work is finished within a set time. A conditioned negative declaration is a SEQR environmental finding and has nothing to do with occupancy.
questions.citation: NY Uniform Code (19 NYCRR Part 1203); NYC Construction Codes

questions.q: Under the SEQR regulations, an action that is subject to SEQR but appears on neither the Type I list nor the Type II list is classified as:
options: An exempt action
An Unlisted action
A ministerial action
A Type III action
questions.explanation: Anything not listed as Type I or Type II is an Unlisted action and still needs a determination of significance. There is no Type III category; exempt and ministerial actions are separate concepts.

questions.q: Compared with an Unlisted action, a Type I action under SEQR:
options: Never requires an EIS because it was screened in advance
Is more likely to require an EIS and calls for a Full EAF
Is excused from review by any lead agency at all
May be approved before any environmental assessment
questions.explanation: Type I actions are those more likely to have significant impacts and require an EIS, and the Full Environmental Assessment Form must be used for them. The pre-screened category that needs no further review is Type II, not Type I.

questions.q: After reviewing the environmental assessment form, a lead agency concludes the proposed project will not have any significant adverse environmental impact. The agency issues a:
options: Positive declaration, so a draft EIS follows
Findings statement, followed by a final EIS
Type II listing that removes it from review
Negative declaration, so no EIS is required
questions.explanation: A negative declaration ends SEQR review without an EIS. A positive declaration is the opposite finding, and a findings statement comes only at the end of an EIS process.

questions.q: A conditioned negative declaration under SEQR may be issued for:
options: Unlisted actions only, with conditions that eliminate significant impacts
Type I actions only, provided a full EIS is also prepared afterward
Type II actions only, such as one single-family home on an approved lot
Any ministerial permit that a building inspector issues without discretion
questions.explanation: A conditioned negative declaration is limited to Unlisted actions where mitigation conditions remove all potentially significant impacts; it may not be used for Type I actions. Type II and ministerial actions need no determination of significance at all.

questions.q: Place these SEQR steps in their usual order for an action that receives a positive declaration: (1) draft EIS and public comment; (2) environmental assessment form; (3) final EIS; (4) agency findings statement.
questions.explanation: The EAF comes first and supports the determination of significance; a positive declaration leads to a draft EIS with public comment, then a final EIS, and finally the agency's written findings before it decides. Findings never precede the final EIS.

questions.q: Why does issuing a routine building permit, where the inspector must approve it once code requirements are met, generally not trigger SEQR review?
options: Building permits are issued only by federal agencies, outside SEQR
SEQR applies only inside the Adirondack and Catskill parks
SEQR covers discretionary agency decisions, not purely ministerial acts
SEQR reviews private developers' choices, not agency approvals
questions.explanation: SEQR applies to discretionary actions of state and local agencies; official acts of a ministerial nature involving no discretion are excluded. SEQR applies statewide and specifically to agency actions, so the other choices reverse the rule.

questions.q: Filling a wetland that qualifies as a 'water of the United States' generally requires a federal Clean Water Act Section 404 permit issued by:
options: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers
The Federal Emergency Management Agency
The Department of Housing and Urban Development
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
questions.explanation: Section 404 permits for discharging dredged or fill material are issued by the Army Corps of Engineers, with EPA oversight. FEMA administers flood mapping and flood insurance, not wetland fill permits.

questions.q: A Long Island homeowner wants to build a dock and walkway across a salt marsh along a bay. Which New York State program is most directly involved?
options: DEC's freshwater wetlands permit program
The Adirondack Park Agency shoreline rules
The State Energy Conservation Construction Code
DEC's tidal wetlands permit program
questions.explanation: Salt marshes along bays and other tidal waters are regulated under the Tidal Wetlands Act administered by DEC. The freshwater wetlands program covers inland, non-tidal wetlands.
questions.citation: ECL Article 25 (Tidal Wetlands Act); 6 NYCRR Part 661

questions.q: A buyer plans a garage on dry ground about 80 feet from a regulated tidal wetland, with no work in the marsh itself. Which statement is most accurate?
options: No state permit can be required because no wetland vegetation will be disturbed
The project may still need a DEC permit because regulated adjacent areas extend beyond the wetland
Only the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers could regulate work done on dry upland
A permit is required only if the garage will have plumbing or a septic system
questions.explanation: New York's tidal wetlands rules also regulate activities in the adjacent area landward of the wetland, generally up to 300 feet (150 feet in New York City) unless a 10-foot elevation contour or an existing substantial structure such as a road ends it sooner. The trap is assuming that staying out of the wet area avoids review.

questions.q: On FEMA flood insurance rate maps, a Special Flood Hazard Area is land that has:
options: A certainty of flooding exactly once every 100 years
At least a 1% chance of flooding in any given year
At least a 10% chance of flooding in any given year
Any past record of water seeping into a basement
questions.explanation: The SFHA is the area subject to the base or '100-year' flood, which means a 1% annual chance, not a flood on a 100-year schedule. Two such floods can occur in consecutive years.

questions.q: A house is located where the chance of flooding is 1% each year. Treating each year independently, what is the approximate chance of at least one flood during a 30-year mortgage?
options: Exactly 30%
About 1%
About 74%
About 26%
questions.explanation: Chance of no flood in 30 years = 0.99^30 ≈ 0.740, so the chance of at least one flood = 1 − 0.740 ≈ 0.26, or about 26%. Adding 1% × 30 = 30% overstates it, and 74% is the chance of no flood.
questions.citation: FEMA National Flood Insurance Program risk guidance (probability computation)

questions.q: A buyer is financing a house in a Special Flood Hazard Area with a mortgage from a federally regulated lender, in a community that participates in the NFIP. Federal law generally requires the buyer to:
options: Keep flood insurance on the building for the term of the loan
Obtain a SEQR negative declaration before the loan closes
Elevate the house above flood level before the loan can fund
Rely on the standard homeowners policy's flood coverage
questions.explanation: The mandatory purchase rule requires flood insurance for the life of a federally related loan secured by a building in an SFHA. Standard homeowners policies generally exclude flood, so they do not satisfy the requirement.
questions.citation: Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973 (42 U.S.C. §4012a)

questions.q: An oceanfront owner on Long Island wants to build within a mapped Coastal Erosion Hazard Area. Which statement is most accurate?
options: No permit is needed because all oceanfront land below the bluff is federal property
Only the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers may regulate any shoreline construction
A coastal erosion management permit is generally needed from DEC or an approved local program
The Adirondack Park Agency issues coastal erosion permits for the whole state
questions.explanation: The Coastal Erosion Hazard Areas Act requires permits for regulated activities in mapped erosion hazard areas, administered by DEC or by a locality with an approved program. The APA's jurisdiction is limited to the Adirondack Park.

questions.q: Under the Adirondack Park Agency's land use and development plan, which private land classification allows the greatest building density?
options: Rural Use
Low Intensity Use
Hamlet
Resource Management
questions.explanation: Hamlet areas are the park's growth centers and have no overall intensity limit. Resource Management is the most restrictive classification, and Rural Use and Low Intensity Use carry density limits.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law §805 (Adirondack Park Agency Act)

questions.q: Which Adirondack private land classification has the most restrictive overall intensity guideline, about one principal building per 42.7 acres?
options: Resource Management
Moderate Intensity Use
Rural Use
Industrial Use
questions.explanation: Resource Management allows roughly 15 principal buildings per square mile (640 ÷ 15 ≈ 42.7 acres each). Rural Use is less restrictive, at roughly 75 per square mile (about 8.5 acres each).

questions.q: State-owned Forest Preserve land in the Adirondack and Catskill parks is protected by the New York Constitution in which way?
options: It may be subdivided once the Adirondack Park Agency holds a hearing
It is subject to local zoning in the same way as private land nearby
It may be sold to private owners whenever DEC finds a public benefit
It must be kept forever wild and may not be sold, leased or exchanged
questions.explanation: The 'forever wild' clause bars the sale, lease or exchange of Forest Preserve lands and the sale or removal of their timber; changes require a constitutional amendment. APA hearings govern private development, not disposal of Forest Preserve land.

questions.q: How does land-use regulation of private land in the Catskill Park differ from that in the Adirondack Park?
options: The Adirondack Park Agency also controls all private land inside the Catskills
The Catskills have no regional agency like the APA; local and state rules apply
All Catskill Park land is owned by New York City and cannot be sold privately
Federal park rangers issue all building permits for land inside the Catskills
questions.explanation: The Adirondack Park Agency Act applies only to the Adirondack Park; private Catskill land is governed by local zoning plus state rules such as DEC permits, and in watershed areas New York City's watershed regulations. Much Catskill land is privately owned.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law Article 27 (APA Act, Adirondack Park only); NY Constitution Article XIV

questions.q: The State takes part of a property for a road widening. Appraisers value the whole property at $500,000 before the taking and the remaining land at $380,000 after the taking. The strip taken alone is worth $90,000. Using the before-and-after method, what is the owner's compensation?
questions.explanation: Compensation = before value − after value = $500,000 − $380,000 = $120,000. This includes the $90,000 strip plus $30,000 ($120,000 − $90,000) of severance damage to the remainder; paying only $90,000 ignores the remainder's loss in value.
questions.citation: NY Eminent Domain Procedure Law; partial-taking (direct and consequential damages) rule

questions.q: Under New York's Eminent Domain Procedure Law, an owner who wants to challenge the condemnor's published determination and findings, such as whether the project serves a public use, generally must file in:
options: The local zoning board of appeals, within one year of the public hearing
The Court of Claims, within six years after the condemnor's hearing
The county clerk's office, before the condemnor records a vesting map
The Appellate Division, within 30 days after the findings are published
questions.explanation: EDPL §207 gives the Appellate Division exclusive jurisdiction to review the determination and findings, with a 30-day filing deadline after publication. The Court of Claims hears compensation claims against the State, not the public-use challenge.

questions.q: The State offers an owner $400,000 for a parcel it is acquiring by eminent domain. The owner believes it is worth $550,000. Under the EDPL, the owner may generally:
options: Accept the $400,000 as an advance payment and still claim more
Either take $400,000 as full payment or forfeit all compensation
Refuse the offer and thereby block the State from taking title
Accept it only after the local assessor certifies the value
questions.explanation: The condemnor's offer may be accepted as an advance payment without waiving the right to seek additional compensation in court. Refusing the offer does not stop a lawful taking; it only affects payment timing.

questions.q: A new county airport runway brings constant low flights directly over a farm, making it unusable, but the county never started a condemnation proceeding. The owner sues for compensation. This claim is called:
options: Escheat
Adverse possession
Inverse condemnation
Spot zoning
questions.explanation: Inverse condemnation is an owner-initiated suit for compensation when government action effectively takes property without formal condemnation. Escheat is the passing of property to the State when no lawful heir or owner exists.
questions.citation: U.S. Const. 5th Amendment; NY Const. Art. I §7 (inverse condemnation doctrine)

questions.q: Zoning requires a 15-foot side yard; a recorded subdivision covenant requires 25 feet. The zoning board of appeals grants a variance allowing 10 feet. A neighbor who holds rights under the covenant sues to stop construction. What is the likely result?
options: The variance overrides the covenant because public law always controls
Both restrictions become void because they directly conflict with each other
The covenant remains enforceable; a variance does not release private restrictions
The neighbor must appeal to the ZBA instead of suing in court
questions.explanation: A ZBA can relax only public zoning rules; it has no power to waive a private covenant, which its beneficiaries enforce in court. The owner must satisfy both, so the stricter 25-foot covenant still applies.
questions.citation: Common law of restrictive covenants; NY Town Law §267-b (scope of variances)

questions.q: A deed conveys land 'on condition that' it be used only as a public library and reserves a right of re-entry to the grantor. If the land is later used as a store, the grantor's heirs may be able to:
options: Reclaim title to the land by exercising the right of re-entry
Collect only a small fine, payable to the municipality
Convert the owner's title into a year-to-year lease
Do nothing, because conditions cannot bind later owners
questions.explanation: A deed condition with a right of re-entry creates a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent, so a breach can cost the owner title. Breaching an ordinary restrictive covenant usually leads only to an injunction or damages.
questions.citation: Common law of estates (fee simple subject to a condition subsequent)

questions.q: An old deed for a subdivision lot contains a clause barring sale to members of a particular religion. Today that clause is:
options: Enforceable because it was recorded before 1968
Enforceable only by the homeowners association
Enforceable until the deed is next re-recorded
Unenforceable under Shelley v. Kraemer and fair housing laws
questions.explanation: Courts may not enforce discriminatory covenants (Shelley v. Kraemer, 1948), and the federal Fair Housing Act and NY Human Rights Law prohibit them. Recording before 1968 does not save them.
questions.citation: Shelley v. Kraemer, 334 U.S. 1 (1948); 42 U.S.C. §3604; NY Executive Law §296(5)

questions.q: A homeowners association's recorded declaration of covenants, conditions and restrictions bans front-yard sheds. A new owner says she never read it. Which statement is most accurate?
options: She is bound only if she personally signed the declaration at closing
She is bound, because the recorded declaration gives constructive notice
The ban is void, because only zoning may regulate accessory sheds
The ban ended automatically when the lot was sold to her
questions.explanation: Recorded covenants that run with the land bind later owners whether or not they read them, because recording gives constructive notice. Private restrictions may be stricter than zoning.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Law §291 (recording and notice); common law of covenants running with land

questions.q: The federal Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act requires a developer of a covered subdivision to give each buyer, before the contract is signed, a:
options: Condominium offering plan
Property report
Certificate of occupancy
Loan Estimate
questions.explanation: The Act requires a property report disclosing facts about the lots and the development. An offering plan is the NY Attorney General disclosure for condos and co-ops, and a Loan Estimate is a TRID mortgage disclosure.
questions.citation: Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act, 15 U.S.C. §1703; 12 CFR Part 1010 (Regulation J)

questions.q: After receiving the property report, a buyer signs a contract to buy an unimproved lot in a subdivision covered by the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act. The buyer may revoke the contract for any reason:
options: Within three business days after signing
At any time before the deed is recorded
Within 30 days after the first payment
Until midnight of the seventh day after signing
questions.explanation: The Act gives buyers a non-waivable right to revoke until midnight of the seventh day after signing. The three-day period is a trap borrowed from other federal consumer rules.

questions.q: A developer covered by the Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act never gives a buyer the required property report before the contract is signed. The buyer generally may revoke the contract within:
options: Two years after signing
Seven days after signing
Ninety days after signing
Ten years after signing
questions.explanation: When the property report was not provided before signing, the buyer may revoke within two years of signing. Seven days is the ordinary cooling-off period when the report was properly delivered.

questions.q: In which framing method do wall studs run continuously from the sill plate up to the roof line, creating hollow vertical channels that can spread fire unless firestops are installed?
options: Platform framing
Post-and-beam framing
Balloon framing
Modular framing
questions.explanation: Balloon framing uses long, continuous studs from the foundation sill to the rafters; without firestops the open wall cavities act like chimneys. Platform framing, the most common method today, builds each floor as a separate platform so studs stop at every level; post-and-beam uses heavy, widely spaced timbers.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (platform, post and beam construction)

questions.q: A buyer tours a house that has no basement and no crawl space; the concrete floor was poured directly on the ground at grade level. What type of foundation is this?
options: Slab-on-grade
Full basement
Crawl space
Pier and girder
questions.explanation: A slab-on-grade foundation is a concrete slab poured directly on prepared ground, often with plumbing or ducts embedded in or beneath it. A crawl space leaves a shallow open area under the floor, and a full basement provides a below-grade story.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (slab-on-grade construction)

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a footing in residential construction?
options: To anchor the wood sill plate and floor framing to the top of the foundation wall
To act as a vapor barrier that keeps ground moisture from rising through the basement slab
To carry roof loads down to the ceiling joists
To spread the building's weight over a wider soil area below the frost line
questions.explanation: The footing is the wide concrete base beneath foundation walls and columns; it distributes the structure's load over more soil and is set below the frost line to prevent heaving. Anchoring the wood framing to the foundation is the job of the sill plate and its anchor bolts.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (footing, foundation walls)

questions.q: A home inspector reports rot in the lowest horizontal wood member, which rests directly on top of the foundation wall and is secured with anchor bolts. Which component is damaged?
options: Ridge board
Sill plate
Header
Rafter
questions.explanation: The sill plate is the first wood member of the frame, bolted to the foundation; floor joists rest on it. A header spans a door or window opening, and the ridge board and rafters are roof components.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (sill plates)

questions.q: Which structural members slope from the ridge down to the exterior walls and support the roof sheathing?
options: Rafters
Floor joists
Studs
Girders
questions.explanation: Rafters are the sloped roof framing members. The common trap is joists: joists are horizontal members that support floors and ceilings, studs are vertical wall members, and girders are main beams that support joists.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (rafter, joists, studs, girder)

questions.q: A buyer compares two attics, one insulated to R-19 and the other to R-38. Which statement is correct?
options: The R-19 attic insulates better because a lower R-value means less heat escapes through the ceiling
R-value rates the BTU output of the furnace, not the insulation
Both insulate equally because R-value measures only the material's thickness
The R-38 attic insulates better because higher R-values mean more resistance to heat flow
questions.explanation: R-value measures a material's resistance to heat flow; the higher the R-value, the better the insulation. BTU is a separate measure of heat quantity used to rate heating and cooling equipment.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (R-value, insulation)

questions.q: A British thermal unit (BTU) is the amount of heat required to:
options: raise the temperature of one gallon of water by 1°F
raise the temperature of one pound of water by 1°F
raise the temperature of one cubic foot of air by 10°F
keep a 100-square-foot room at 68°F for one hour
questions.explanation: One BTU is the heat needed to raise one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit. Furnaces, boilers, and air conditioners are rated in BTUs (per hour); the gallon option is the common trap.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (BTU/British Thermal Unit)

questions.q: During a showing, a circuit breaker trips every time the seller runs the microwave and space heater at the same time. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The insulation's R-value is too low for the heating system
The breaker is defective, because properly working breakers never trip
The circuit is drawing more current (amps) than it is rated to carry
The home has too much amperage at the main service panel
questions.explanation: Circuit breakers (and older fuses) cut power when the current on a circuit exceeds its amperage rating, preventing overheated wiring; tripping under heavy load is the breaker doing its job. A licensee should note the condition and refer electrical evaluation to a licensed electrician rather than diagnose it.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (amperage, circuit breaker, fuse)

questions.q: What is the main function of the U-shaped trap installed beneath a sink drain?
options: It holds a water seal that keeps sewer gases from entering the home
It increases water pressure in the supply lines
It carries sewer gases up and out through the vent stack on the roof
It filters sediment and debris out of the drinking water supply
questions.explanation: The trap retains water that blocks sewer gas from backing up through the fixture. Venting gases through the roof and admitting air to the drain lines is the vent stack's job, and supply lines (under pressure) are a separate system from gravity drain-waste-vent lines.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (plumbing systems)

questions.q: A one-and-a-half-story house with a steep gable roof, dormer windows, and a symmetrical front with a center door best describes which architectural style?
options: Ranch
Split-level
Cape Cod
Colonial
questions.explanation: A Cape Cod is a compact 1½-story home with a steep roof and dormers that make the upper half-story usable. A Colonial has two full stories with a symmetrical facade, a Ranch is a single-story home, and a split-level has three or more levels offset by half-flights of stairs.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Construction (architectural styles)

questions.q: A developer wants to fill a freshwater wetland on a parcel in upstate New York. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only the local zoning board regulates wetlands, so no state or federal review applies
A federal Clean Water Act permit and a NYS DEC freshwater wetlands permit may both be required
Wetlands may be filled freely once the parcel is zoned residential
Wetland rules apply only to tidal areas on the coast, not inland parcels
questions.explanation: Filling wetlands can require a U.S. Army Corps of Engineers permit under Clean Water Act § 404 and a NYS DEC permit under the Freshwater Wetlands Act, plus any local review. Zoning does not override these rules, so get a current jurisdictional determination rather than assume no rules apply.
questions.citation: Clean Water Act § 404 (33 U.S.C. § 1344); NY ECL Article 24 (Freshwater Wetlands)

questions.q: A buyer is under contract to buy a single-family home built in 1962. Under the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule, the buyer must be given:
options: a lead-free certificate that the seller must obtain by having a certified inspector test all painted surfaces
a 3-day right to cancel the contract after receiving the seller's Property Condition Disclosure Statement
nothing, because the federal lead rule applies only to rental housing
a 10-day opportunity for a lead inspection or risk assessment, unless changed or waived in writing
questions.explanation: For pre-1978 target housing, the seller must disclose known lead information and reports, give the EPA pamphlet, and include the lead warning; the buyer gets a 10-day inspection/risk-assessment opportunity that can be changed by mutual written agreement or waived. The rule does not require the seller to test or remove lead.

questions.q: For the sale of pre-1978 housing, how long must the seller and the listing agent keep a copy of the signed lead-based paint disclosure and acknowledgment?
options: 1 year after closing
At least 3 years from the completion of the sale
6 years from the date of the listing agreement
Until the buyer resells the property
questions.explanation: The seller and any agent must keep the completed lead disclosure attachment for at least 3 years from the completion date of the sale. Lessors and agents likewise keep lease disclosures for 3 years from the start of the lease term.

questions.q: A radon test in the lowest lived-in level of a home reads 6.2 pCi/L. Which statement is accurate under EPA guidance?
options: Radon matters only in commercial buildings, so no action is needed for a home
The result is acceptable because EPA's action level for homes is 10 pCi/L
It exceeds EPA's 4 pCi/L action level, so professional mitigation is recommended
A retest is unnecessary because radon at that level can be detected by its smell
questions.explanation: EPA recommends fixing homes at 4 pCi/L or higher (and considering mitigation between 2 and 4). Radon is an odorless, invisible radioactive gas, so only testing reveals levels, and a reading below 4 is not a guarantee of no risk.
questions.citation: EPA, A Citizen's Guide to Radon (4 pCi/L action level)

questions.q: During a showing, a buyer notices crumbling insulation wrapped around old basement heating pipes and asks whether it is asbestos. What should the salesperson do?
options: Advise against disturbing it and recommend evaluation by a qualified asbestos professional
Break off a small sample herself and mail it to a testing lab to save the buyer the inspection fee
Assure the buyer it is safe because asbestos was banned from all residential products in 1978
Tell the seller to sweep it up and repaint the pipes before closing
questions.explanation: Crumbling (friable) asbestos can release dangerous fibers, and appearance alone cannot identify it, so the licensee should not sample or disturb it and should refer testing to qualified professionals. There is no blanket ban date that clears older materials.
questions.citation: EPA asbestos guidance; Clean Air Act asbestos NESHAP (40 CFR Part 61, Subpart M)

questions.q: Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation (UFFI) is an environmental concern primarily because it:
options: contains radioactive particles that enter through foundation cracks
leaks petroleum into the groundwater from buried tanks
contains PCBs like those used in older electrical transformers
can release formaldehyde gas into the indoor air
questions.explanation: UFFI, a foam insulation used mostly in the 1970s, can emit formaldehyde gas that irritates the eyes and lungs. Radon is the radioactive soil gas, PCBs are associated with older electrical equipment, and petroleum leaks come from storage tanks.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 7: Environmental Issues (UFFI)

questions.q: Before listing, a seller wants to paint over a damp, moldy basement wall. What is the best advice?
options: Painting is enough because federal law sets a maximum indoor mold level that a sealed wall will satisfy
Fix the moisture source and remediate properly; known material defects must not be concealed
Mold is never a disclosure issue because it is a naturally occurring substance found in every home
Have the buyer sign a waiver promising never to test for mold
questions.explanation: Mold grows from moisture, so lasting remediation starts with fixing the water source; painting over it hides the problem without solving it. There is no federal indoor mold limit that serves as a pass/fail standard, and concealing a known material defect can expose the seller and agent to liability.
questions.citation: EPA mold guidance; NY Labor Law Article 32 (mold assessment and remediation)

questions.q: A property inspection finds an abandoned underground heating-oil tank. What is the main environmental risk?
options: A corroded tank can leak petroleum into the soil and groundwater
The tank will emit radon gas into the living space
The tank lowers the R-value of the foundation walls
The tank violates the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule
questions.explanation: Aging steel tanks can corrode and leak oil, contaminating soil and groundwater and creating costly cleanup liability. NY law imposes strict liability for petroleum discharges, so buyers should have tanks evaluated, tested, or properly removed and closed.
questions.citation: NY Navigation Law Article 12 (petroleum discharges); NYS DEC tank regulations

questions.q: Under New York's Amanda's Law, carbon monoxide alarms are required in one- and two-family dwellings that:
options: are located within 1,000 feet of a highway, truck route, or other major source of vehicle exhaust
were built before the NYS Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code took effect in 1984
have a fuel-burning appliance or system that can emit carbon monoxide, or an attached garage
have more than three bedrooms or more than one sleeping floor
questions.explanation: Amanda's Law requires CO alarms in homes with a CO source, such as a fossil-fuel-burning furnace, boiler, water heater, or fireplace, or an attached garage. This is separate from the smoke-alarm requirement; CO is odorless, and an alarm means leave the building and call for help.

questions.q: A company buys an industrial site and later discovers contamination dumped by a prior owner decades ago. Under CERCLA (Superfund), the current owner:
options: is never liable because it did not cause the pollution
is liable only for the share of waste it personally dumped
is automatically protected as an innocent purchaser, with no prior investigation needed
can be held liable because liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive
questions.explanation: CERCLA can impose cleanup liability on current owners regardless of fault (strict), for the entire cleanup (joint and several), and for contamination that occurred before the law (retroactive). Innocent-landowner type defenses require 'all appropriate inquiry,' such as a Phase I assessment, before buying; they are not automatic.

questions.q: What distinguishes a Phase II Environmental Site Assessment from a Phase I?
options: Phase II is limited to reviewing historical records and interviewing owners
Phase II involves sampling and lab testing of soil, groundwater, or building materials
Phase II is the cleanup stage in which contamination is physically removed
Phase II is required for every residential sale in New York
questions.explanation: A Phase I is an investigative review (records, site reconnaissance, interviews) with no sampling; if it flags concerns, a Phase II samples and tests to confirm contamination. Remediation is a later, separate phase. These assessments are used mainly in commercial transactions.
questions.citation: ASTM E1527 / EPA All Appropriate Inquiries Rule (40 CFR Part 312)

questions.q: The seller of a covered single-family home in New York offers the buyer a $500 credit at closing instead of delivering a Property Condition Disclosure Statement. Under current law:
options: the credit is still an acceptable alternative to the statement as long as the buyer agrees to it in writing
the credit must now be given in addition to the statement, and both are due at or before the closing
the statement must be delivered before the buyer signs a binding contract, because the $500 credit was repealed in 2024
the seller may skip both because the statement became optional for all residential sellers in 2024
questions.explanation: Amendments effective March 20, 2024 repealed the old $500 credit, so covered sellers of 1-4 family homes must deliver the PCDS before the buyer signs a binding contract unless an exemption applies (condo and co-op units are not covered). The statement reflects the seller's actual knowledge and is not a warranty.

questions.q: A lakeside cottage sits on a series of isolated concrete columns that extend below the frost line, with beams spanning between them to carry the floor framing. What type of foundation is this?
options: Slab-on-grade foundation
Full basement foundation
Pier-and-beam foundation
Monolithic mat foundation
questions.explanation: Piers are isolated vertical supports, each on its own footing, with beams spanning between them; the area beneath is typically an open or enclosed crawl space. A slab or mat is one continuous concrete layer, not separate columns.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A buyer's inspector notes a white, chalky crust on the inside face of a concrete-block basement wall. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Water has moved through the masonry and left mineral salts behind
Subterranean termites have built tunnels across the block face
Radon gas has reacted with the concrete and stained its surface
The foundation has settled and the blocks are being crushed
questions.explanation: This is efflorescence: moisture migrating through masonry dissolves salts and deposits them as it evaporates, signaling a water-management issue to evaluate. Termite tubes are brown soil tunnels, and radon is colorless and leaves no visible residue.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A builder frames the first-floor walls, sets the second-floor joists and subfloor on top of them, and then raises the second-floor walls on that deck. Which framing method is this?
options: Balloon framing
Platform framing
Post-and-beam framing
Pole framing
questions.explanation: In platform (western) framing each story is built on its own floor platform, and that deck acts as a firestop between stories; it is the dominant modern method. Balloon framing uses studs that run continuously through both stories with no intermediate platform.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A buyer admires a home with widely spaced heavy timber columns, exposed ceiling beams, and large open rooms with few interior walls. Which framing method was most likely used?
options: Platform framing
Balloon framing
Light-gauge framing
Post-and-beam framing
questions.explanation: Post-and-beam framing carries loads on large members spaced far apart, which allows open interiors and exposed beams. Platform and balloon framing rely on many closely spaced light studs.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: When a wall is opened up for a new picture window, which framing member must span the top of the opening to carry the load from above around it?
options: Sole plate
Ridge board
Header
Collar tie
questions.explanation: A header (a lintel, in masonry) spans a window or door opening and transfers the load above to the studs at each side. The sole plate is the bottom horizontal member of a wall, not a span over an opening.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A buyer plans to remove an interior wall to open up the kitchen. In the attic, the ceiling joists end and overlap directly on top of that wall. What is the best advice?
options: Treat it as load-bearing until an engineer or architect plans the change
Remove it freely, because interior walls only divide space and carry no load
Remove it freely as long as the house has a gable roof rather than a hip roof
Cut out the studs and leave the top plate in place to carry the joists
questions.explanation: Joists that end or lap over a wall show it likely carries load from above, so removal needs a properly designed beam or header and generally a building permit. Interior walls can be bearing walls, and a top plate alone cannot span the opening.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A buyer measures a dry 2×4 stud in the garage and finds it is about 1½ by 3½ inches. What explains this?
options: The stud was trimmed on site to fit an unusual wall height
The lumber is defective and should be noted as a code violation
The stud is metric lumber that was mislabeled at the mill
2×4 is a nominal size; dressed lumber is smaller than its name
questions.explanation: Lumber is named by nominal dimensions; drying and surfacing (dressing) reduce a 2×4 to roughly 1½ × 3½ inches. The smaller actual size is standard, not a defect or code issue.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: Which component is the layer of plywood or oriented strand board (OSB) fastened to the outside of studs and rafters, beneath the siding and roofing?
options: Sheathing
Fascia
Flashing
Drywall
questions.explanation: Sheathing covers the exterior framing, adds rigidity, and provides a nailing base for siding and roofing. Flashing is metal or membrane at joints to shed water, and fascia is the trim board along the roof edge.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A homeowner wants to cut out the diagonal web members of the prefabricated roof trusses to create attic storage. Why is this a serious concern?
options: Truss webs only hold insulation and can be replaced with plywood
Removing webs is fine if the cut ends are nailed to the ceiling joists
Each truss is an engineered unit, and cutting any member can cause failure
Webs carry load only during construction and become redundant afterward
questions.explanation: A truss is a factory-engineered triangulated assembly whose members work together; cutting or altering one can compromise the roof unless an engineer designs the change. The webs are permanent structural members, not construction aids.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: Which roof has two different slopes on each of its two sides—a steep lower slope and a shallower upper slope—like a traditional barn?
options: Hip roof
Gambrel roof
Mansard roof
Saltbox roof
questions.explanation: A gambrel roof has two pitches on each of two sides with gable ends, the classic barn profile also seen on Dutch Colonial homes. A mansard also has a double slope, but on all four sides.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A roof slopes down toward the eaves on all four sides, with no vertical triangular wall at either end. Which style is it?
options: Gable roof
Shed roof
Gambrel roof
Hip roof
questions.explanation: A hip roof slopes on all four sides, so the eaves run around the entire house. A gable roof slopes on only two sides and leaves triangular gable-end walls; a shed roof has a single slope.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A 19th-century house has a roof with a double slope on all four sides; the steep, nearly vertical lower slope is pierced by dormers, creating a full top story. What is the roof, and which style is it associated with?
options: Mansard roof; Second Empire style
Gambrel roof; Dutch Colonial style
Hip roof; Prairie style
Gable roof; Greek Revival style
questions.explanation: A mansard roof has two slopes on all four sides, with the steep lower slope enclosing a usable top floor; it is the hallmark of the Second Empire style. A gambrel has a double slope on only two sides.

questions.q: A symmetrical gable roof spans 32 feet from outside wall to outside wall, and the ridge rises 8 feet above the top of the walls. What is the roof pitch, in inches of rise per 12 inches of run?
options: 3 in 12
6 in 12
8 in 12
4 in 12
questions.explanation: Run is half the span: 32 ÷ 2 = 16 ft. Rise ÷ run = 8 ÷ 16 = 0.5, and 0.5 × 12 = 6, so the pitch is 6 in 12. Using the full span gives 8 ÷ 32 × 12 = 3 in 12, a common error.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: An attic floor has existing insulation rated R-11. The owner adds 8 inches of blown cellulose rated R-3.5 per inch. What is the combined R-value?
questions.explanation: New layer: 8 × 3.5 = R-28. R-values of layers add: 11 + 28 = R-39. R-28 ignores the existing layer, R-14.5 adds only one inch (11 + 3.5), and R-88 wrongly multiplies 11 × 8.
questions.citation: General building science: R-values of layers in series are additive

questions.q: To fit a shallow wall cavity, an installer squeezes R-21 batts into a space only half their designed thickness. What is the effect?
options: The R-value doubles because the fibers become denser
The R-value stays R-21 because the material is unchanged
The R-value rises as long as a vapor retarder is added
The installed R-value drops below the rating on the label
questions.explanation: Batt insulation resists heat flow largely through trapped air, so compressing it lowers its installed R-value below the labeled rating. Denser is not better for batts, and a vapor retarder does not restore the lost thickness.
questions.citation: General building science; insulation must be installed per manufacturer specifications

questions.q: A buyer comparing replacement windows sees one rated U-0.27 and another rated U-0.45. Which statement is correct?
options: The U-0.27 window loses less heat, because a lower U-factor is better
The U-0.45 window insulates better, because a higher number is better
Both insulate equally; the U-factor measures only air leakage
The U-0.45 window is better, because U-factor equals R-value
questions.explanation: U-factor measures the rate of heat flow through the window, so lower is better—the opposite of R-value, where higher is better. Air leakage is a separate rating.

questions.q: Which window type is hinged on one side and swings outward, usually opened with a crank?
options: Double-hung window
Casement window
Awning window
Sliding window
questions.explanation: A casement window is side-hinged and cranks outward like a door. An awning window is hinged at the top and swings out from the bottom; double-hung sashes slide vertically.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: During a showing, a buyer notices condensation trapped between the two panes of a double-glazed window that cannot be wiped from either side. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The home's humidity is too low for winter
The window frame has been infested by termites
The seal of the insulated glass unit has failed
The low-E coating is working as intended
questions.explanation: Moisture between the panes means the sealed insulated glass unit has failed, letting humid air in and reducing insulating value. Condensation on the room-side surface relates to indoor humidity, not a failed seal.
questions.citation: General residential construction practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Construction and Environmental Issues)

questions.q: A home's boiler heats water that a circulator pump sends through baseboard convectors in each room. What type of heating system is this?
options: Forced warm-air system
Air-source heat pump system
Electric resistance baseboard system
Hydronic hot-water system
questions.explanation: Hydronic systems heat water in a boiler and circulate it through baseboards, radiators, or radiant tubing. A forced warm-air system uses a furnace to heat air and blow it through ducts.
questions.citation: General HVAC practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Major Systems)

questions.q: Which set of components would an inspector expect to find in a forced warm-air heating system?
options: Furnace, blower, supply ducts, and return-air registers
Boiler, circulator pump, expansion tank, and radiators
Boiler, steam piping, air vents, and cast-iron radiators
Ground loop, heat exchanger, and in-floor radiant tubing
questions.explanation: Forced warm-air systems heat air in a furnace and use a blower to push it through supply ducts, drawing it back through return registers. Boilers, circulators, and radiators belong to hot-water or steam systems.
questions.citation: General HVAC practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Major Systems)

questions.q: Which statement about an air-source heat pump is accurate?
options: It burns heating oil and distributes the heat through ducts
It moves heat with a refrigerant cycle and can reverse to cool
It heats water in a boiler for distribution to radiators
It cannot provide any useful heat once outdoor air is below 32°F
questions.explanation: A heat pump uses electricity to move heat with a refrigerant cycle—pulling heat from outdoor air in winter and reversing to remove heat from the house in summer. Modern cold-climate units still deliver heat well below freezing, so the old 'useless below 32°F' claim is wrong.
questions.citation: General HVAC practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Major Systems)

questions.q: A load calculation shows a house needs 42,000 BTU per hour of cooling. Air conditioners are sized in tons. What size unit is indicated?
options: 4.2 tons
2.8 tons
3.5 tons
3 tons
questions.explanation: One ton of cooling = 12,000 BTU/hr. 42,000 ÷ 12,000 = 3.5 tons. Dividing by 10,000 gives the wrong 4.2 tons, and dividing by 15,000 gives 2.8 tons.
questions.citation: HVAC industry standard: 1 ton of cooling = 12,000 BTU/hr

questions.q: A gas furnace has an input rating of 90,000 BTU per hour and an AFUE of 80%. About how much heat does it deliver to the house per hour?
questions.explanation: AFUE is the share of fuel energy delivered as usable heat: 90,000 × 0.80 = 72,000 BTU/hr. 18,000 BTU is the amount lost (90,000 × 0.20), and 112,500 wrongly divides 90,000 by 0.80.
questions.citation: HVAC industry standard: AFUE (annual fuel utilization efficiency)

questions.q: How does a home's water supply system differ from its drain-waste-vent (DWV) system?
options: Supply lines carry water under pressure; DWV lines rely on gravity
Supply lines rely on gravity; DWV lines are kept under pump pressure
Supply lines carry wastewater; DWV lines bring in fresh potable water
Both run under pressure, but DWV pipes use smaller copper tubing
questions.explanation: Supply piping delivers potable water under pressure from a well pump or municipal main, while drain lines slope so waste flows by gravity to the sewer or septic system, with vents admitting air. DWV piping is not pressurized.
questions.citation: General residential plumbing practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Major Systems)

questions.q: When a bathtub drains, the nearby sink gurgles and a sewer odor appears, even though the sink trap held water beforehand. Which plumbing component is most likely blocked?
options: The sink's P-trap
The main water shutoff valve
The vent stack
The water heater relief valve
questions.explanation: Vent pipes, usually exiting through the roof, admit air so draining water does not siphon fixture traps. A blocked vent lets drainage pull the water seal out of nearby traps, causing gurgling and sewer gas; the trap is the seal being lost, not the blockage.
questions.citation: General residential plumbing practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Major Systems)

questions.q: What is the purpose of the temperature-and-pressure (T&P) relief valve on a tank water heater?
options: To mix in cold water so the taps do not scald
To release water if temperature or pressure gets dangerously high
To shut off the gas supply when the pilot light goes out
To drain sediment from the bottom of the tank during service
questions.explanation: The T&P valve opens to discharge water if the tank's temperature or pressure exceeds safe limits, preventing a rupture or explosion. Shutting off gas when the pilot fails is the thermocouple's job, and sediment is flushed through the drain valve.
questions.citation: General residential plumbing practice (NYS salesperson syllabus: Major Systems)

questions.q: An inspector recommends ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) protection for the outlets beside the kitchen sink. What does a GFCI do?
options: It detects arcing in damaged wiring that could start a fire
It raises a circuit's capacity so more appliances can run
It converts 120-volt outlets to 240 volts for appliances
It cuts power when current leaks to ground, reducing shock risk
questions.explanation: A GFCI compares current leaving and returning on a circuit and shuts off within a fraction of a second if some leaks to ground—such as through a person—so it is used where water is present (kitchens, baths, outdoors, garages). Detecting dangerous arcing is the job of an AFCI.
questions.citation: National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), as referenced by the NYS Uniform Code

questions.q: Which device is designed mainly to prevent electrical fires by detecting dangerous arcing in damaged or loose wiring, and is commonly required for bedroom circuits?
options: Arc-fault circuit interrupter (AFCI)
Ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI)
Surge protective device (SPD)
Time-delay cartridge fuse
questions.explanation: An AFCI senses the electrical signature of arcing—from a nail through a cable or a loose connection—and trips before a fire starts; the code requires AFCI protection for bedroom and many other living-area circuits. A GFCI targets shock from ground faults, not arcing.
questions.citation: National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), as referenced by the NYS Uniform Code

questions.q: A 1,500-watt space heater and a 1,200-watt microwave run at the same time on one 120-volt, 20-amp kitchen circuit. How much current do they draw, and what happens?
options: 11.25 amps; the breaker will hold because the load is under 20 amps
22.5 amps; the breaker will likely trip because the load exceeds 20 amps
12.5 amps; the breaker will hold because only the heater draws power
27 amps; the breaker will likely trip because the load exceeds 20 amps
questions.explanation: Amps = watts ÷ volts. Total load = 1,500 + 1,200 = 2,700 W; 2,700 ÷ 120 = 22.5 A, above the 20-A rating, so the breaker will likely trip. Dividing by 240 V gives the wrong 11.25 A; dividing by 100 gives 27 A.
questions.citation: Ohm's law/power formula: watts = volts × amps

questions.q: A 1940s house still has its original 60-amp electrical service. Which statement is most accurate?
options: 60 amps describes the home's monthly electricity use
The service is ideal because fewer amps mean lower bills
It is likely inadequate for modern loads; 100–200 amps is typical today
The voltage must be raised to 480 volts to support modern appliances
questions.explanation: Service amperage describes capacity, not energy use (measured in kilowatt-hours). A 60-amp service is often too small for today's appliances; 100 amps is generally treated as a practical minimum, and 200 amps is common in newer homes.
questions.citation: National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), as referenced by the NYS Uniform Code

questions.q: An attached 19th-century row house in Brooklyn has a façade of brown sandstone, a tall exterior stoop leading to a raised parlor floor, and a flat roof. Which style best describes it?
options: Dutch Colonial
Ranch
Tudor
Brownstone
questions.explanation: Brownstones are attached urban row houses faced in brown sandstone, typically with a high stoop to the parlor floor and a flat or low-slope roof. Dutch Colonial and Tudor are detached styles with gambrel or steep cross-gabled roofs; a ranch is a one-story suburban style.

questions.q: A house features an asymmetrical façade, a round corner tower, a wraparound porch, and decorative spindle and bracket trim. Which architectural style is it?
options: Federal
Victorian (Queen Anne)
Greek Revival
Cape Cod
questions.explanation: Victorian houses, especially the Queen Anne type, are known for irregular asymmetrical shapes, towers or turrets, wraparound porches, and ornate trim. Federal and Greek Revival houses emphasize symmetry and classical restraint.

questions.q: The front door of a house opens onto a small landing; a short stair leads up to the main living level and another leads down to a partly below-grade lower level. Which style is this?
options: Center-hall Colonial
Story-and-a-half Cape Cod
Raised ranch (split entry)
Craftsman bungalow
questions.explanation: A raised ranch (split-entry or bi-level) has its front door on a landing between two stacked levels, with half-flights going up to the living floor and down to the partly below-grade level. A center-hall Colonial, a Cape Cod, and a bungalow are entered directly at the main floor.

questions.q: Under New York law, a licensed home inspector must give the client a written report of the findings no later than:
options: the day of the inspection
3 business days after the inspection
10 calendar days after the inspection
5 business days after the inspection
questions.explanation: RPL §444-g(3) requires the written report within five business days after the inspection, and it must identify which systems and components were observed. Three business days is a common confusion with other deadlines.

questions.q: The listing agent calls the buyer's licensed home inspector and asks for a copy of the inspection report to prepare the seller's response. What should the inspector do?
options: Refuse unless the buyer, as the client, expressly consents
Send it, because the listing agent is a licensed party
Send it, because all parties to the deal share the report
File it with the seller's attorney before sharing it
questions.explanation: A home inspector's duty runs to the client, and the report is confidential—it may not be disclosed without the client's express consent (RPL §444-g(1), (3)). Being a licensee or a party to the transaction does not entitle the listing agent to it.

questions.q: Which of the following is PROHIBITED for a licensed New York home inspector?
options: Showing the license number on every inspection report
Paying the buyer's agent a fee for each client referral
Stating which systems were observed in the written report
Recommending a structural engineer for a sagging beam
questions.explanation: RPL §444-g(4)(c) bars inspectors from paying any commission, referral fee, or kickback to the seller or to either party's agent for referrals. Showing the license number and identifying observed systems are required, and referring a structural issue to an engineer is proper because inspectors may not practice engineering.

questions.q: During an inspection, pencil-width tunnels of dried mud are found running up the concrete foundation wall to the wood sill. Which pest do they indicate?
options: Carpenter ants
Powderpost beetles
Subterranean termites
Carpenter bees
questions.explanation: Subterranean termites live in the soil and build mud shelter tubes to reach wood while staying moist and hidden. Carpenter ants, powderpost beetles, and carpenter bees do not build mud tubes.
questions.citation: General pest/wood-destroying insect identification (NYS salesperson syllabus: Environmental Issues)

questions.q: Which statement about carpenter ants is accurate?
options: They digest cellulose and eat wood the way termites do
They build mud tubes from the soil to reach wooden sills
They attack only dry hardwood flooring, not framing lumber
They hollow out wood for nests but do not actually eat it
questions.explanation: Carpenter ants excavate galleries in (often moist or damaged) wood to nest, pushing out coarse sawdust-like debris called frass, but they do not digest wood. Eating wood is a termite trait, and mud tubes signal subterranean termites.
questions.citation: General pest/wood-destroying insect identification (NYS salesperson syllabus: Environmental Issues)

questions.q: An inspector finds many tiny round holes in old floor joists, with small piles of fine, flour-like powder beneath them. Which wood-destroying insect is most likely responsible?
options: Powderpost beetles
Subterranean termites
Carpenter ants
Carpenter bees
questions.explanation: Powderpost beetle larvae tunnel inside wood and emerge as adults through small round exit holes, leaving fine, powdery frass. Carpenter bee holes are about half an inch wide, and carpenter ant debris is coarse and fibrous.
questions.citation: General pest/wood-destroying insect identification (NYS salesperson syllabus: Environmental Issues)

questions.q: Under the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule, which EPA pamphlet must a seller of a 1955 house give the buyer before the buyer is bound by the contract?
options: The Lead-Safe Certified Guide to Renovate Right
Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home
A Citizen's Guide to Radon
A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture, and Your Home
questions.explanation: Sellers and lessors of pre-1978 target housing must provide the EPA/HUD pamphlet 'Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home.' 'Renovate Right' is the trap: it is the pamphlet renovation contractors give under the separate RRP rule, not the sale/lease disclosure pamphlet.

questions.q: A landlord is renting a two-bedroom apartment in a 1940 building on a one-year lease. Under the federal lead disclosure rule, the landlord must do all of the following EXCEPT:
options: give the tenant the EPA lead hazard information pamphlet
disclose any known lead-based paint or hazards in the unit
give the tenant a 10-day opportunity to conduct a lead inspection
include the required lead warning statement in the lease
questions.explanation: Lessors must give the pamphlet, disclose known lead information and records, and attach the lead warning statement and acknowledgments. The 10-day inspection or risk-assessment opportunity is a right of purchasers only, so tenants do not receive it.

questions.q: Which of the following transactions is exempt from the federal lead-based paint disclosure requirements?
options: A 90-day summer rental of a 1920 cottage with no renewal option
A one-year lease of a two-bedroom apartment in a 1975 building
The resale of a two-bedroom co-op apartment in a 1970 building
The sale of a 1965 house to an investor who will never live there
questions.explanation: Leases of 100 days or less with no possible renewal or extension are exempt. The other choices all involve pre-1978 target housing (multi-bedroom units, not exempt 0-bedroom units); co-op transfers and sales to non-occupant investors are still covered.

questions.q: A listing agent learns that the seller of a 1950 home has a lead inspection report showing lead-based paint on the window trim. The seller tells the agent not to mention it because no law requires testing. What must the agent do?
options: Stay silent, since the seller was never required to test for lead
Disclose the report only if a buyer asks about lead in writing
Tell buyers to use their 10-day inspection right and say nothing else
Ensure the seller discloses the known lead paint and gives the buyer the report
questions.explanation: The rule does not require testing, but it does require disclosure of known lead-based paint and any available records or reports. Agents must ensure the seller complies; if the seller refuses, the agent cannot go along with the concealment.

questions.q: A contractor is hired to replace two windows in a 1960 house occupied by its owner. The work will disturb only about 4 square feet of painted surface. Under EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) rule:
options: the job is exempt because it disturbs less than 6 square feet of paint
the job is exempt because exterior work under 20 square feet is minor
the RRP rule applies only if a child under 6 lives in the house
the RRP rule applies because window replacement is never treated as minor repair
questions.explanation: The minor repair and maintenance exception (6 sq ft per interior room, 20 sq ft exterior) does not cover window replacement, so a certified firm must follow lead-safe work practices. The small-area exemption is the trap; and in pre-1978 housing the rule applies regardless of whether a young child lives there.

questions.q: Under EPA's RRP rule, interior work in pre-1978 housing qualifies as exempt minor repair and maintenance only if it disturbs no more than how much painted surface per room?
options: 2 square feet
10 square feet
6 square feet
20 square feet
questions.explanation: The minor repair and maintenance exception covers interior work disturbing 6 square feet or less per room. The 20 square foot figure is the exterior threshold, a common mix-up.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the federal lead disclosure rule from EPA's Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) rule?
options: Disclosure requires certified renovators; RRP requires sellers to share known inspection reports
Both rules require the seller to test for lead before a contract is signed
Disclosure governs information in sales and leases; RRP governs how paid work disturbing paint is done
RRP replaced the disclosure rule for all pre-1978 housing built after 1960
questions.explanation: The disclosure rule (Title X §1018) requires pamphlets, known-hazard disclosure and acknowledgments when target housing is sold or leased. The RRP rule separately requires certified firms and lead-safe practices for compensated renovation. Neither requires a seller to test.
questions.citation: 40 CFR Part 745, Subparts E and F

questions.q: Asbestos-containing material is described as 'friable' when it:
options: is hidden behind walls or under floors where it cannot be seen
can be crumbled or reduced to powder by hand pressure when dry
has been sealed with a coating that binds the fibers in place
is installed outdoors where it is exposed to rain and sun
questions.explanation: Friable asbestos material can be crumbled, pulverized or reduced to powder by hand pressure when dry, so fibers release easily. Being hidden does not make material friable, and a sealing coating describes encapsulation, which reduces fiber release.

questions.q: A buyer's inspector finds intact, undamaged vinyl floor tiles in a basement that likely contain asbestos. The buyer does not plan to renovate. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Undisturbed intact material poses little risk; disturbing it can release fibers
State law requires all asbestos tiles to be removed before title can be transferred
The tiles may be safely sanded smooth and then painted to seal in the fibers
The buyer may pull up the tiles and use a household vacuum to limit any dust
questions.explanation: EPA guidance is that asbestos material in good condition that will not be disturbed is often best left alone and monitored; sanding, scraping or improper removal releases fibers. There is no general rule that asbestos must be removed before a home can be sold.

questions.q: Radon gas found in homes comes primarily from:
options: incomplete combustion in oil- or gas-fired furnaces
off-gassing from urea-formaldehyde foam insulation
leaks from older electrical transformers and ballasts
the natural radioactive decay of uranium in soil and rock
questions.explanation: Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas produced by uranium decay in soil and rock; it enters through foundation cracks, sumps and other openings. Combustion produces carbon monoxide, UFFI releases formaldehyde, and old transformers are a PCB concern.
questions.citation: EPA, A Citizen's Guide to Radon

questions.q: A buyer orders a short-term radon test. Where should the test device generally be placed?
options: In the attic, where trapped gases collect at the highest point
