questions.explanation: Fixed expenses, such as property taxes and insurance, stay about the same regardless of occupancy. Variable expenses, such as repairs, utilities, and supplies, rise and fall with occupancy and use.
questions.citation: Income approach: fixed vs. variable operating expenses

questions.q: Two nearby rental houses sold recently: one for $312,000 renting at $2,400 per month, another for $286,000 renting at $2,200 per month. The similar subject house rents for $2,500 per month. Using a monthly gross rent multiplier, what is the subject's indicated value?
questions.explanation: GRM = price ÷ monthly rent: $312,000 ÷ $2,400 = 130 and $286,000 ÷ $2,200 = 130. Value = $2,500 × 130 = $325,000. Applying the monthly GRM to annual rent ($30,000 × 130 = $3,900,000) mixes time periods.
questions.citation: Gross rent multiplier: value = monthly rent × GRM

questions.q: A small commercial building produces annual gross income of $180,000. Comparable sales show a gross income multiplier of 7.5. What value does the GIM indicate?
questions.explanation: Value = annual gross income × GIM = $180,000 × 7.5 = $1,350,000. Dividing income by the multiplier ($24,000) reverses the formula, and using monthly income ($15,000 × 7.5 = $112,500) mismatches an annual multiplier.
questions.citation: Gross income multiplier: value = annual gross income × GIM

questions.q: What is the main weakness of valuing a property with a gross rent multiplier instead of capitalizing NOI?
options: It cannot be used for single-family rental homes
It requires a detailed estimate of land value
It ignores differences in vacancy and expenses
It depends on the buyer's mortgage interest rate
questions.explanation: A GRM works from gross rent, so two properties with the same rent but very different vacancy or operating costs receive the same value. It is actually the common shortcut for single-family rentals, and it uses no land value or financing inputs.

questions.q: A rental house sold for $360,000. It rents for $2,000 per month. What is its monthly gross rent multiplier?
questions.explanation: Monthly GRM = sale price ÷ monthly rent = $360,000 ÷ $2,000 = 180. Dividing by annual rent ($24,000) gives 15, an annual multiplier, which must not be paired with monthly rents.
questions.citation: Gross rent multiplier: GRM = price ÷ monthly rent

questions.q: An appraiser is valuing a fully leased 40-unit apartment building that investors buy for its rental income. Which approach should normally receive the most weight?
options: Income capitalization approach
Cost approach
Gross rent multiplier on one unit
Assessed value approach
questions.explanation: Buyers of income-producing property pay for the income stream, so the income approach best reflects their thinking. The cost approach gives little guidance for an established, income-producing building whose value depends on its rents.

questions.q: Why can the cost approach not be used by itself to value a vacant building lot?
options: Vacant land is exempt from property appraisal
Land must always be valued by income capitalization
Vacant land depreciates faster than the improvements do
There are no improvements to cost out or depreciate
questions.explanation: The cost approach estimates the cost of improvements less depreciation, then adds land value; with no improvements, it has nothing to measure. Land value itself is usually found by sales comparison, and land is not depreciated.

questions.q: For an owner-occupied single-family home in an active market with many recent sales, the approaches indicate: sales comparison $405,000, cost $440,000, income $390,000. Which conclusion best reflects proper reconciliation?
options: About $440,000, because cost new sets the ceiling on value
About $411,667, the simple average of the three indications
About $390,000, because the lowest figure is most conservative
About $405,000, giving the most weight to sales comparison
questions.explanation: Reconciliation weighs each indication by how reliable and relevant it is; for a home with abundant comparable sales, sales comparison deserves the most weight. A simple average ($1,235,000 ÷ 3 = $411,667) treats weak indications as equally valid, which reconciliation specifically avoids.

questions.q: An appraiser weights three indications: sales comparison $405,000 at 60%, cost $440,000 at 25%, and income $390,000 at 15%. What weighted value results?
questions.explanation: $405,000 × 0.60 = $243,000; $440,000 × 0.25 = $110,000; $390,000 × 0.15 = $58,500; total $411,500. Swapping the cost and income weights gives $406,500, and $411,667 is the unweighted average.

questions.q: A property's net operating income is $84,000 and its annual mortgage debt service is $54,000. The $30,000 left after paying the mortgage is called:
options: Before-tax cash flow
Effective gross income
Net operating income
Potential gross income
questions.explanation: $84,000 − $54,000 = $30,000 before-tax cash flow, the owner's return after financing. NOI is measured before debt service, which is why the income approach capitalizes NOI and not cash flow.
questions.citation: Income property analysis: NOI vs. before-tax cash flow

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act?
options: Familial status
Disability
Marital status
National origin
questions.explanation: The federal FHA protects seven classes: race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, and disability. Marital status is protected under NY Executive Law § 296, not the federal FHA — a classic federal-vs-state trap.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296

questions.q: The 1988 amendments to the federal Fair Housing Act added which protected classes?
options: Disability and familial status
Sex and sexual orientation
Age (55 and older) and marital status
Religion and national origin
questions.explanation: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 added disability (handicap) and familial status. Religion and national origin were in the original 1968 Act and sex was added in 1974; age, marital status, and sexual orientation are not listed classes in the federal statute.
questions.citation: Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988; 42 U.S.C. § 3604

questions.q: A homeowner selling her own single-family house without a broker and without advertising refuses to sell to a buyer because of the buyer's race, claiming the FHA single-family exemption. Which statement is correct?
options: The refusal is lawful because the owner used no broker and placed no advertising
The refusal is lawful only if the owner owns no more than three single-family homes
The refusal is lawful if the owner lived in the house at some point in the past 24 months
The refusal is unlawful because the Civil Rights Act of 1866 bars racial discrimination
questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 prohibits racial discrimination in property transactions with no exemptions, as confirmed by Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co. (1968). An FHA exemption never authorizes race discrimination.

questions.q: An Albany landlord rejects an applicant who meets all of the landlord's lawful income and credit criteria solely because part of the rent would be paid by a Housing Choice (Section 8) voucher. Under New York law, this is:
options: Lawful, because a voucher is not wage income
Unlawful lawful-source-of-income discrimination
Lawful if the building has fewer than six units
Unlawful only within New York City limits
questions.explanation: NY Executive Law § 296 protects lawful source of income statewide, including housing assistance vouchers. A landlord may apply neutral qualification criteria but may not reject an otherwise qualified applicant because assistance pays part of the rent; the trap is thinking this is NYC-only.

questions.q: A property manager learns that a rental applicant has an order of protection against a former partner and denies the application 'to avoid trouble in the building.' Under New York law, the denial is:
options: Lawful if the manager applies the policy to every such applicant
Lawful because domestic violence creates a safety risk
Unlawful discrimination based on status as a domestic violence victim
Unlawful only if the applicant also has minor children
questions.explanation: NY Executive Law § 296 protects status as a victim of domestic violence in housing. Applying the exclusion consistently does not cure it — a uniform policy of rejecting victims is still discrimination based on that status.

questions.q: Which protected category appears in the New York City Human Rights Law but not in the federal Fair Housing Act or NY Executive Law § 296?
options: Lawful occupation
Religion
Familial status
Disability
questions.explanation: The NYC Human Rights Law adds local categories such as lawful occupation and partnership status. Religion, familial status, and disability are already federal FHA classes, so local law layers on top of state and federal protections.
questions.citation: NYC Human Rights Law, NYC Admin. Code § 8-107

questions.q: Without being asked, a salesperson shows an Asian American buyer only listings in neighborhoods with large Asian populations, explaining that the buyer 'will feel more comfortable there.' This is:
options: Blockbusting
Redlining
Acceptable service because it is well intended
Steering
questions.explanation: Steering is guiding buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected characteristic. Good intentions do not excuse it; the licensee must offer the same available options and let the buyer choose.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296; DOS-2156 Fair Housing Disclosure

questions.q: To generate listings, a licensee mails flyers warning homeowners that 'families of a different religion are moving in — sell now before values fall.' This conduct is:
options: Steering (channeling buyers by area)
Blockbusting (panic peddling)
Redlining (area-based loan denial)
Lawful market advice to owners
questions.explanation: Blockbusting is inducing sales or listings by representing that protected-class members are entering a neighborhood and that harm (lower values, crime, worse schools) will follow. It is not market advice; it exploits fear tied to a protected status.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(e); NY Executive Law § 296; DOS-2156 Fair Housing Disclosure

questions.q: A lender refuses to make mortgage loans anywhere in certain neighborhoods because of the racial composition of those areas, regardless of individual applicants' qualifications. This practice is:
options: Redlining
Steering
Blockbusting
Puffing
questions.explanation: Redlining is denying or restricting loans, insurance, or services in an area based on discriminatory geographic classification rather than the individual applicant's or property's legitimate risk. Steering and blockbusting are licensee conduct aimed at buyers and sellers.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3605; NY Executive Law § 296

questions.q: Which advertisement wording is permissible for a New York rental listing?
options: Ideal for a single professional, no kids
Section 8 vouchers not accepted
Christian household strongly preferred
Two bedrooms, fenced yard, near train station
questions.explanation: Ads should describe the property, not the preferred occupant. The other choices express a preference based on familial status, lawful source of income, or religion, and adding an Equal Housing Opportunity logo would not cure them.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); NY Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: A tenant who uses a wheelchair asks to install grab bars and widen the bathroom doorway in her rental apartment. Under the federal Fair Housing Act, this request is best classified as a:
options: Reasonable accommodation, always paid by the landlord
Rent concession the landlord may decline
Reasonable modification, generally at the tenant's expense
Request the landlord may refuse in a pre-1991 building
questions.explanation: A physical change to the premises is a reasonable modification; in ordinary private housing it is generally at the tenant's expense, and the landlord may reasonably condition interior work on restoration. A reasonable accommodation is a change to a rule, policy, or service; federally assisted housing and NY law can shift costs in some cases.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(A); NY Executive Law § 296(18)

questions.q: A building has a strict no-pets policy. A tenant with a disability provides reliable documentation of a disability-related need for an emotional support animal. Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the landlord should generally:
options: Deny it, because the no-pets rule applies equally to everyone
Grant it as a reasonable accommodation without a pet deposit or fee
Grant it only if the tenant pays the standard pet deposit
Grant it only if the animal is a specially trained dog
questions.explanation: An assistance animal is not a pet; allowing it is a reasonable accommodation to the no-pets rule, and pet fees or deposits may not be charged (the tenant remains liable for actual damage). The 'trained dog' limit is the ADA service-animal definition, which does not narrow New York housing duties. Note: HUD withdrew its 2020 federal assistance-animal guidance (FHEO-2020-01) in September 2025, but the FHA statute and NY Executive Law § 296(18) still require reasonable accommodations.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law § 296(18)(2); Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B)

questions.q: Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the owner-occupied rental exemption applies only to a building with housing for no more than how many families, with the owner living in one unit?
options: Two
Three
Four
Six
questions.explanation: New York's owner-occupied exemption covers a building for no more than two families with the owner in residence. The federal 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption is broader (up to four units), so don't import the federal number into NY law.

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a four-family building in Buffalo and personally refuses to rent to a qualified applicant because of the applicant's religion. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It is lawful because owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units are always exempt
It is lawful under New York law but still violates the federal Fair Housing Act
A federal exemption may apply, but NY's two-family limit makes it unlawful
It violates only the Civil Rights Act of 1866, not the NY Human Rights Law
questions.explanation: The federal owner-occupied exemption covers up to four units, but New York's covers only two-family buildings, so the owner still violates NY Executive Law § 296. The 1866 Act covers race, not religion, and a federal exemption never removes state liability.

questions.q: An owner who lives in one unit of a two-family house hires a salesperson to rent the other unit and says, 'Advertise it as adults only — no children.' The salesperson should:
options: Comply, because the owner-occupied exemption covers the listing
Comply, but add the Equal Housing Opportunity logo to the ad
Advertise 'adults only' but still show the unit to families who ask
Decline; the owner's exemption doesn't cover the licensee or the ad
questions.explanation: Owner-occupancy exemptions belong to the owner, not the licensee, and the ban on discriminatory advertising survives them. A client's instruction never authorizes a licensee to discriminate, and a logo does not cure a 'no children' ad.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); NY Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: To qualify for the federal 55-and-older 'housing for older persons' exemption, at least what percentage of occupied units must have at least one occupant age 55 or older (along with published policies and age verification)?
questions.explanation: The 55+ category requires at least 80% of occupied units to have at least one person 55 or older, plus policies showing intent and age verification. The separate 62+ category requires all occupants to be 62 or older; either exemption excuses only familial-status exclusion, not race or disability discrimination.
questions.citation: Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995; 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b)

questions.q: When must a New York licensee provide the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form (DOS-2156) to a prospective buyer, seller, tenant, or landlord?
options: At the first substantive contact
When the purchase contract or lease is signed
Before the first showing, but only if the client asks
At closing, together with the deed
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR § 175.28 requires the DOS-2156 at first substantive contact, delivered in writing or electronically; an oral explanation alone does not satisfy it. The broker keeps the signed acknowledgment (or documented refusal) for three years.

questions.q: Under DOS fair housing regulations, where must the Fair Housing and Anti-Discrimination Notice be displayed?
options: Only inside the main office, posted next to the broker's license certificate
In each office/branch window, on licensee websites, and at open houses
Only on the brokerage's website home page and its social media profiles
Only on listing agreements and leases for one-to-four family residential homes
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR § 175.29 requires the notice in the window of every office and branch office, prominently on licensee-operated websites, and at each open house. Posting does not replace delivering the individual DOS-2156 disclosure.

questions.q: Under New York's standardized operating procedures law, a brokerage's written procedures for prospective homebuyers must state whether the brokerage requires buyers to:
options: Disclose their household size and religious affiliation
Show a credit score above a brokerage-set minimum
Pay a nonrefundable retainer before any showing
Show ID, sign an exclusive agreement, or get pre-approval
questions.explanation: RPL § 442-h requires brokers to adopt procedures stating whether ID, an exclusive buyer agreement, and pre-approval are required before services, apply them uniformly to every buyer, and post them on their websites/apps and make them available at the office. The law does not require the broker to demand these items — only to decide and apply the policy consistently.

questions.q: A renter believes a landlord violated the federal Fair Housing Act. Generally, how long does the renter have to file an administrative complaint with HUD?
options: 180 days
One year
Two years
Three years
questions.explanation: A HUD complaint is generally due within one year of the discriminatory act. A private federal FHA lawsuit generally has two years, and a complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights currently has three years — the periods are not interchangeable.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3610 (HUD complaint); 42 U.S.C. § 3613 (civil action); NY Executive Law § 297(5)

questions.q: A fair housing organization sends paired testers with similar qualifications but different races to inquire about the same apartment through a brokerage. Which statement is correct?
options: Testing is lawful, and unequal treatment of testers is evidence
Testing is illegal entrapment, so tester evidence is inadmissible
Licensees may refuse to deal with anyone they suspect is a tester
Testers lack standing to sue because they never intended to rent
questions.explanation: Paired testing is a recognized, lawful way to detect discrimination, and the Supreme Court held in Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982) that a tester falsely told a unit was unavailable has standing to sue. The safe practice is to treat every inquiry the same way.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604(d); Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman (1982)

questions.q: Which law most directly requires a real estate brokerage's public office to be accessible to customers with disabilities?
options: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (Regulation B)
The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)
Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act
Section 1982 of the Civil Rights Act of 1866
questions.explanation: ADA Title III covers places of public accommodation, which include a brokerage office open to the public. Disability issues in residential dwelling units are generally analyzed under the Fair Housing Act instead, so 'ADA' is not the answer to every housing-disability question.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 prohibits discrimination in property transactions on the basis of:
options: Race and religion, with owner-occupant exceptions
Race, with no exceptions for private owners
Race, but only in government-funded housing
All classes later listed in the Fair Housing Act
questions.explanation: The 1866 Act guarantees all citizens the same property rights 'as is enjoyed by white citizens,' so it reaches racial discrimination only, and it contains no exemptions. The trap is borrowing the FHA's owner-occupant exemptions, which do not exist under the 1866 Act.

questions.q: What was the significance of the Supreme Court's 1968 decision in Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co.?
options: It held racially restrictive covenants unenforceable in state courts
It applied the 1866 Act to private racial discrimination in property
It upheld the 1988 amendments adding familial status protection
It created HUD's administrative fair housing complaint process
questions.explanation: Jones held that the 1866 Act bars all racial discrimination, private as well as public, in the sale or rental of property. Making restrictive covenants unenforceable was Shelley v. Kraemer (1948), a different case.
questions.citation: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968); 42 U.S.C. § 1982

questions.q: In Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., the Supreme Court upheld Congress's power to ban private racial discrimination in property sales under which constitutional provision?
options: The Fourteenth Amendment
The Commerce Clause
The Thirteenth Amendment
The First Amendment
questions.explanation: The Court held that the Thirteenth Amendment lets Congress eliminate the 'badges and incidents of slavery,' including private racial barriers to buying property. The Fourteenth Amendment is the trap: it mainly restrains state action, not private sellers.
questions.citation: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968); U.S. Const. amend. XIII

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a three-family building, uses no broker, and runs no ads. He rejects one applicant because of religion and another because of race. Under federal law alone, which is correct?
options: Both refusals are lawful under the owner-occupant exemption
Both refusals violate the federal Fair Housing Act
Only the race-based refusal is unlawful
Only the religion-based refusal is unlawful
questions.explanation: The FHA owner-occupied exemption (four units or fewer) can shelter the religion-based refusal federally, but the Civil Rights Act of 1866 has no exemptions and bars the race-based refusal. New York law would separately reach the religion refusal because its owner-occupied exemption stops at two families.

questions.q: A buyer claims a seller refused to sell solely because of the buyer's race and relies on the Civil Rights Act of 1866. How is that right enforced?
options: By filing only a HUD administrative complaint
By petitioning the Department of State
By arbitration through a local Realtor board
By bringing a private civil lawsuit
questions.explanation: The 1866 Act has no administrative agency process; the victim enforces it by suing, and courts may award damages and injunctions. HUD's complaint process belongs to the Fair Housing Act, not the 1866 Act.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 1982; Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968)

questions.q: When first enacted as Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, the federal Fair Housing Act prohibited discrimination based on:
options: Race, color, religion, national origin, and sex
Race, color, national origin, and disability
Race, color, religion, and familial status
Race, color, religion, and national origin
questions.explanation: The original 1968 Act covered race, color, religion, and national origin. Sex was added in 1974, and disability and familial status in 1988, so the longer lists describe the later, amended law.
questions.citation: Civil Rights Act of 1968, Title VIII, 42 U.S.C. § 3604

questions.q: Sex was added as a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act by which law?
options: The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974
The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
The Civil Rights Act of 1866
The Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995
questions.explanation: The Housing and Community Development Act of 1974 added sex. The 1988 amendments are the common trap; they added disability and familial status and strengthened enforcement.
questions.citation: Housing and Community Development Act of 1974; 42 U.S.C. § 3604

questions.q: Which household is protected under the Fair Housing Act's familial status category?
options: A pregnant woman who has no other children yet
Two unrelated adult roommates sharing a lease
A married couple with no children under 18
A grandmother living with her 30-year-old son
questions.explanation: Familial status covers a person under 18 living with a parent, legal custodian, or designee, and expressly includes pregnant persons and those securing custody. Marriage alone is not familial status (marital status is protected in NY, not by the FHA), and an adult child does not count.

questions.q: A landlord assigns every household with children under 18 to first-floor apartments 'for their safety.' Under the Fair Housing Act, this policy is:
options: Unlawful familial-status discrimination
Lawful because it is motivated by child safety
Lawful if the units match in rent and size
Unlawful only if the building gets federal funds
questions.explanation: Assigning people to particular floors or sections of a building because of familial status is expressly prohibited, and a benign safety motive does not excuse it. The equal-rent distractor fails because segregating units by protected status is itself the violation.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act's definition of handicap (disability), which person is NOT protected?
options: A person in recovery who no longer uses illegal drugs
A person with a history of cancer now in remission
A person currently using illegal drugs
A person the landlord wrongly regards as mentally ill
questions.explanation: The FHA excludes current illegal use of or addiction to a controlled substance. A recovering person who no longer uses is protected, as are people with a record of an impairment or who are regarded as having one.

questions.q: A landlord rejects an applicant because he wrongly believes she is HIV-positive; she is not. Under the Fair Housing Act, the rejection is:
options: Lawful because the applicant has no actual disability
Lawful because HIV status is a health and safety issue
Unlawful because being regarded as disabled is protected
Unlawful only if the applicant later develops a disability
questions.explanation: The FHA disability definition includes being regarded as having an impairment, so acting on a mistaken belief is still discrimination. The 'no actual disability' distractor ignores that third prong of the definition.

questions.q: A salesperson tells a Black couple a listed house is already under contract, though it is not, and shows it to white buyers the next day. Which Fair Housing Act prohibition is most directly violated?
options: Falsely saying a dwelling is unavailable
Inducing owners to sell through panic
Denying credit in a particular area
Publishing a discriminatory advertisement
questions.explanation: The FHA specifically bars representing to any person, because of a protected class, that a dwelling is not available for inspection, sale, or rental when it is. Panic selling is blockbusting, and area-based credit denial is redlining.

questions.q: Unprompted, a salesperson tells a Hispanic buyer that a town's schools 'might not be a good fit for your family' while praising the same schools to other buyers. This is most likely:
options: Permissible sharing of school information
Blockbusting through fear of neighborhood change
Puffing that is protected as personal opinion
Steering through selective discouraging comments
questions.explanation: Steering includes discouraging a buyer from an area by comments that differ according to a protected class, not just refusing to show homes. It is not neutral school information because other buyers hear the opposite message.

questions.q: A licensee mails owners on one block urging them to sell soon because of the 'changing makeup' of the neighborhood's residents. No owner actually lists. Which statement is correct?
options: No violation occurs unless a property is sold
It is steering, since no buyers are involved
The solicitation itself can be unlawful blockbusting
It is lawful commentary on market trends
questions.explanation: The FHA prohibits inducing or attempting to induce, for profit, sales or rentals by representations about the entry of a protected class; the attempt is enough. Steering targets home seekers' choices, whereas blockbusting targets owners.

questions.q: An appraiser lowers valuations of homes because of the national origin of residents in the surrounding neighborhood. Which Fair Housing Act provision most directly covers this conduct?
options: Discriminatory advertising of dwellings for sale
Denial of access to multiple listing services
Discrimination in real estate-related transactions
Blockbusting by inducing owners to sell
questions.explanation: Section 3605 bars discrimination in residential real estate-related transactions, expressly including the appraising of residential property as well as lending. Blockbusting requires inducing owners to sell, which an appraisal does not do.

questions.q: A lender makes loans everywhere but, because a neighborhood is predominantly Black, requires larger down payments from qualified applicants buying there than from identical applicants buying elsewhere. This is best described as:
options: Steering, since it directs buyers' choices
Blockbusting, since it targets a neighborhood
Lawful risk pricing based on location
Redlining, a form of lending discrimination
questions.explanation: Redlining includes harsher credit terms, not only outright refusals, for areas defined by their residents' race. Steering is a trap because it describes how agents direct home seekers, not how lenders price credit by area.

questions.q: A landlord requires a $1,000 security deposit from applicants born outside the United States but $500 from U.S.-born applicants with the same credit. This is:
options: Lawful risk-based pricing of security deposits
Steering based on the applicants' national origin
Lawful if both deposits are within legal limits
Discrimination in terms based on national origin
questions.explanation: Charging different deposits, rents, or fees because of a protected class is discrimination in the terms and conditions of rental. Staying within a deposit cap does not cure unequal treatment.

questions.q: Which Fair Housing Act prohibition still applies to an owner who otherwise qualifies for the single-family or owner-occupied exemption?
options: Refusing to rent because of an applicant's religion
Refusing to sell to a family with young children
Making discriminatory notices or advertisements
Setting different lease terms based on sex
questions.explanation: The § 3603(b) exemptions cover § 3604 'other than subsection (c),' so even an exempt owner may not publish discriminatory notices, statements, or ads. The other choices describe conduct the federal exemption can shelter (though NY law may not).

questions.q: Which phrase in a rental advertisement is most likely to violate the Fair Housing Act?
options: Walk-in closets, fourth-floor walk-up
Quiet street near bus and park
No children, ideal for empty nesters
Non-smoking building, no pets allowed
questions.explanation: 'No children' states a familial-status limitation. Describing the property, its features, or the neighborhood is acceptable, and a no-pets rule is lawful (assistance animals are handled as accommodations, not as pets).

questions.q: For several years a developer's brochures for a large complex have shown only white models in every photo. Under the Fair Housing Act, this practice:
options: Can signal a racial preference and be unlawful
Is lawful because no discriminatory words appear
Violates the law only if it says 'whites only'
Is exempt because the models are paid actors
questions.explanation: The ban on ads that indicate a preference reaches images, not just words, and consistently using models of one race can communicate a racial preference. The 'no words' distractor ignores that the test is what the ad conveys to an ordinary reader.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c); 24 C.F.R. § 100.75(c)(1); Ragin v. New York Times Co., 923 F.2d 995 (2d Cir. 1991)

questions.q: After a tenant helps a neighbor file a fair housing complaint with HUD, the landlord refuses to renew the tenant's lease. This most likely violates the Fair Housing Act's ban on:
options: Interference and retaliation
Discriminatory advertising
Blockbusting for profit
Steering of tenants
questions.explanation: The FHA makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten, or interfere with anyone for aiding or encouraging another person in exercising fair housing rights. The tenant need not belong to a protected class; helping a complainant is enough.

questions.q: A multiple listing service denies membership to a broker because of the broker's religion. Under the Fair Housing Act, this is:
options: Lawful because the FHA protects only home seekers
Unlawful denial of access to a brokerage service
Lawful if the MLS is a private organization
Unlawful only if the broker is a NY resident
questions.explanation: The FHA bars denying access to or membership in any MLS or real estate brokers' organization because of a protected class. Its coverage is not limited to buyers and renters, and private status does not exempt the MLS.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act's single-family house exemption, a private individual owner may own no more than how many single-family houses at one time?
options: Two
Four
One
Three
questions.explanation: The exemption is limited to a private owner who owns no more than three single-family houses at any one time. Four is the trap: it is the unit limit for the separate owner-occupied ('Mrs. Murphy') exemption.

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a six-unit building and wants to rent the others without a broker or advertising. Can the federal owner-occupied exemption apply?
options: No; that exemption is limited to four units
Yes; any building the owner lives in qualifies
Yes; if he owns no more than three buildings
No; that exemption covers two units at most
questions.explanation: The federal 'Mrs. Murphy' exemption applies only to dwellings with living quarters for no more than four families living independently, with the owner living in one. Two units is New York's owner-occupied limit, not the federal one.

questions.q: An owner who neither lives in the house nor was its most recent occupant may use the federal single-family exemption for:
options: Up to three sales in any 12-month period
Only one such sale in any 24-month period
Unlimited sales if no broker is used
Only sales made to family members
questions.explanation: When the owner is not residing in the house or was not the most recent resident, the exemption applies to only one sale within any 24-month period. 'Three' refers to how many houses the owner may own, not how many sales are allowed.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act, an owner loses the single-family exemption by:
options: Using a licensee or a discriminatory advertisement
Selling to a buyer who obtains a mortgage
Owning a second single-family house
Having an attorney draft the contract
questions.explanation: The exemption requires the sale or rental to be made without a broker, agent, or salesperson and without discriminatory advertising, which is why licensees can never use it. Owning up to three houses is permitted, and an attorney preparing documents is allowed.

questions.q: A religious organization operating noncommercial housing may give preference to members of its own religion unless:
options: Its membership is restricted by race, color, or national origin
The housing contains more than four rental units
The organization lists the units with a broker
The units are offered below market rent
questions.explanation: The FHA lets religious organizations limit noncommercial housing to members of the same religion, but not if membership in the religion is restricted on account of race, color, or national origin. The four-unit limit belongs to the owner-occupied exemption.

questions.q: To qualify as housing for older persons under the 62-and-older category, generally:
options: 80% of units need one occupant 62+
Every occupant must be 62 or older
Half of all occupants must be 62+
Only the head of household must be 62+
questions.explanation: The 62+ category requires housing intended for and solely occupied by persons 62 or older (with narrow exceptions, such as certain employees). The 80% one-occupant test belongs to the separate 55+ category.

questions.q: A qualifying 55-and-older community lawfully excludes families with children. The Housing for Older Persons Act provides an exemption from the Fair Housing Act's ban on discrimination based on:
options: Age
Disability
Marital status
Familial status
questions.explanation: Housing for older persons is exempt from the familial status provisions only. Age is the trap: it is not a protected class under the federal FHA at all, and the community must still comply with disability rules.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b); Housing for Older Persons Act of 1995

questions.q: Which is NOT a requirement for a community to qualify for the 55-and-older housing exemption?
options: Every resident must be at least 55 years old
At least 80% of occupied units have a 55+ resident
It publishes policies showing intent to serve 55+
It reliably verifies the ages of its residents
questions.explanation: The 55+ exemption requires at least 80% of occupied units to have at least one resident 55 or older, published policies demonstrating that intent, and age verification. Requiring every resident to meet the age describes the 62+ category, not the 55+ one.

questions.q: A 55-and-older community has 150 occupied units, and 117 of them have at least one resident aged 55 or older. Does it meet the 80% occupancy test?
options: Yes; only 50% of units must qualify
No; every unit must have a 55+ resident
questions.explanation: 117 ÷ 150 = 0.78 = 78%, short of 80%; the community needs 150 × 0.80 = 120 qualifying units. The 82% distractor is an arithmetic slip, and the 'every unit' rule confuses this test with the 62+ category.

questions.q: A tenant with a mobility impairment asks for an assigned parking space near her door in a lot where parking is first-come, first-served. This is a request for:
options: A reasonable modification at her expense
A reasonable accommodation in a policy
A HOPA exemption from parking rules
ADA Title III barrier removal
questions.explanation: Changing a rule, policy, practice, or service, such as assigning a space, is a reasonable accommodation. A modification is a physical change to the premises, which is the trap here.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004)

questions.q: Which statement about reasonable modifications in privately owned rental housing is correct?
options: The landlord must pay for every physical modification
The landlord may raise the security deposit
Common areas must be restored at move-out
Interior restoration may be required if reasonable
questions.explanation: In private housing the tenant generally pays for a modification, and the landlord may, where reasonable, require the interior to be restored at move-out (normal wear and tear excepted). The landlord may not raise the security deposit for it and may not require restoration of common-use areas.

questions.q: In private housing, who generally bears the cost of a reasonable accommodation, such as an exception to a building policy?
options: The tenant, as with a physical modification
The housing provider, unless it is an undue burden
HUD, through a reimbursement program
The tenant, through a higher security deposit
questions.explanation: The provider bears accommodation costs unless they impose an undue financial and administrative burden. The trap is the modification rule: in private housing, tenants generally pay for physical changes, not for policy exceptions.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004)

questions.q: A housing provider may lawfully deny a requested reasonable accommodation when granting it would:
options: Require an exception to a written building rule
Impose an undue financial and administrative burden
Cost the provider any amount of money at all
Be requested orally rather than in writing
questions.explanation: An accommodation may be refused if it would impose an undue financial and administrative burden or fundamentally alter the provider's operations. Excusing a written rule is exactly what an accommodation is, so that cannot be a valid reason.
questions.citation: HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004); 24 C.F.R. § 100.204

questions.q: A tenant with a disability orally asks the manager for an exception to a building policy but never uses the words 'reasonable accommodation.' The manager:
options: May ignore it until a written form is filed
May deny it for failing to cite the FHA
Must treat it as an accommodation request
Must refer the tenant to HUD to decide it
questions.explanation: A request can be made orally and in plain language; no magic words or particular form are required. A provider may offer a form but cannot refuse to consider a request because it was not used.
questions.citation: HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004)

questions.q: A building bans dogs over 25 pounds. A tenant who is blind asks to keep her 60-pound trained guide dog. Under the Fair Housing Act and New York law, the landlord:
options: Generally must waive the pet weight limit
May enforce the weight limit as a neutral rule
May approve it only with an added pet deposit
May deny it unless every neighbor consents
questions.explanation: Refusing a reasonable accommodation in rules or policies that a person with a disability needs to use a dwelling is discrimination under the FHA, and HUD's regulation uses a blind tenant's guide dog under a no-pets rule as its example; a size limit is a pet rule to be waived the same way. New York Civil Rights Law §47-b separately bars any extra charge for a guide, hearing, or service dog in housing.

questions.q: A landlord may lawfully deny a request for a specific assistance animal when:
options: The building has a strict no-pets policy
The tenant's disability is not readily visible
Neighbors say they dislike having dogs nearby
This animal's own conduct shows a direct threat
questions.explanation: A provider may refuse an animal that, judged on its own actual conduct, poses a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage that another accommodation cannot reduce. A no-pets rule is exactly what an accommodation waives, and neighbors' dislike or a disability that is not visible is not a lawful reason to deny.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B), (f)(9); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004)

questions.q: Under the ADA Title III regulations, which animal does NOT meet the definition of a service animal?
options: A dog whose only role is emotional comfort
A dog trained to guide a person who is blind
A dog trained to alert its handler to seizures
A dog trained to interrupt a panic attack
questions.explanation: An ADA service animal is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, and providing emotional support or comfort does not count as a task. Psychiatric tasks such as interrupting a panic attack do qualify. Whether a housing provider must allow an untrained support animal is a separate reasonable-accommodation question under the FHA and New York law.

questions.q: A tenant whose disability is not obvious asks to keep an assistance animal despite a no-pets rule. Under the Fair Housing Act, the landlord may:
options: Demand her full medical records and diagnosis
Require details on how severe her impairment is
Deny the request since no disability is visible
Request reliable proof of the disability-related need
questions.explanation: When a disability or the need for an accommodation is not obvious, the provider may request reliable information verifying the disability and the disability-related need. It generally may not demand medical records, a diagnosis, or details about the nature or severity of the impairment, and an invisible disability is still a disability.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B); HUD/DOJ Joint Statement on Reasonable Accommodations (2004)

questions.q: In an apartment complex, which space is most likely covered by Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act?
options: Each tenant's individual apartment
A tenant's private storage locker
The owner's own residence unit
The rental office open to the public
questions.explanation: ADA Title III covers places of public accommodation, such as a leasing office that serves the public. The dwelling units themselves are covered by the Fair Housing Act's disability provisions rather than the ADA.

questions.q: Under ADA Title III, a brokerage operating in an existing building must remove architectural barriers in its public office when removal is:
options: Requested in writing
Required by its lease
Readily achievable
Paid by a federal grant
questions.explanation: In existing facilities, Title III requires removing barriers where removal is readily achievable, meaning easily accomplished without much difficulty or expense. The duty does not wait for a written request or depend on a lease clause.

questions.q: Which law primarily governs disability discrimination in renting the private apartment units themselves?
options: ADA Title III
Fair Housing Act
ADA Title I
Civil Rights Act of 1866
questions.explanation: The FHA covers dwellings, including disability discrimination in renting units. ADA Title III covers public accommodations such as leasing offices, Title I covers employment, and the 1866 Act reaches race only.

questions.q: A new 20-unit apartment building with no elevator was first occupied in 2024. Under the Fair Housing Act's design and construction rules, which units must meet the accessibility requirements?
options: Every unit in the building
Only the ground-floor units
Only units leased to tenants with disabilities
None, because the building has no elevator
questions.explanation: Covered multifamily dwellings first occupied after March 13, 1991 are all units in buildings of four or more units that have an elevator, plus the ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units. Without an elevator, only the ground-floor units need features such as an accessible route, wheelchair-width doors, usable kitchens and baths, and reinforced bathroom walls for grab bars.

questions.q: A lender refuses to count an applicant's reliable public assistance income when evaluating her mortgage application. Under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, this is:
options: Permitted because the income is not wages
Permitted if the lender treats everyone alike
Prohibited discrimination based on income source
Prohibited only if the applicant is over 62
questions.explanation: ECOA bars discriminating against an applicant because all or part of her income comes from a public assistance program. A lender may evaluate whether income is likely to continue, but it cannot discount it simply because of its source.

questions.q: A landlord rents a two-bedroom apartment to three unrelated adults but rejects a couple with one child for an identical unit, citing an occupancy limit. Under the Fair Housing Act, this most likely shows:
options: A reasonable occupancy limit applied lawfully
Pretext for familial-status discrimination
Lawful screening based on marital status
A permitted housing-for-older-persons preference
questions.explanation: The FHA allows reasonable occupancy limits, and HUD's occupancy policy treats two persons per bedroom as a general benchmark. Here three adults were accepted while a three-person family was refused, so the limit is not applied evenly and points to discrimination against a household with a child.
questions.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a); 42 U.S.C. § 3607(b)(1); HUD Occupancy Standards Statement of Policy, 63 Fed. Reg. 70256 (Dec. 18, 1998)

questions.q: An applicant was refused an apartment because of her religion 20 months ago and has never filed any complaint. Which remedy is still available under the Fair Housing Act?
options: A new HUD administrative complaint
A private FHA civil lawsuit
Nothing, since every FHA deadline is one year
Only a DOJ pattern-or-practice action
questions.explanation: A private FHA lawsuit may be filed within two years of the discriminatory act, so at 20 months it is timely. The HUD complaint window is one year, which has passed.

questions.q: The U.S. Attorney General may bring a Fair Housing Act suit directly when there is reasonable cause to believe a respondent engaged in:
options: Any single act reported to HUD
A dispute over one security deposit
A pattern or practice of discrimination
A licensing violation referred by a state
questions.explanation: The Department of Justice may sue on its own for a pattern or practice of discrimination or a denial of rights raising an issue of general public importance. An individual complaint usually proceeds through HUD or a private lawsuit instead.

questions.q: Which statement about Fair Housing Act enforcement is correct?
options: A victim must file with HUD before suing
A victim may sue without first filing with HUD
HUD complaints may be filed within 2 years
Only HUD may seek damages for the victim
questions.explanation: A private FHA suit does not require exhausting HUD's process; the person may go directly to court within two years. Two years is the lawsuit deadline, whereas a HUD complaint must be filed within one year.

questions.q: The New York State Human Rights Law protects religion in housing using which statutory term?
options: Faith tradition
Belief system
Creed
Spiritual preference
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5) lists "creed" where the federal Fair Housing Act says "religion." The other terms sound similar but are not the statute's wording.

questions.q: Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the housing protection for age does not apply to persons under what age?
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5)(f) says the age protections in housing do not apply to persons under 18; households with minors are covered under familial status instead. 55 and 62 are the senior-housing exemption ages, not the floor for age protection.

questions.q: A Rochester landlord turns down a qualified applicant because she is divorced, saying he prefers to rent to married tenants. Under New York law, this is:
options: Lawful, because marital status is not a federal class
Lawful, if the policy is applied to every applicant
Unlawful only if the applicant has minor children
Unlawful discrimination based on marital status
questions.explanation: Marital status (being single, married, divorced, separated, or widowed) is protected under Executive Law §296(5) even though the federal Fair Housing Act does not list it. Applying the preference to every applicant does not help, because the rule itself turns on a protected class. Note: NY courts have held that a married-couples-only rule for cohabiting partners is not marital status discrimination (Levin v. Yeshiva Univ.), which is why this stem uses an individual's own status.

questions.q: An applicant's income comes from Social Security disability benefits and court-ordered child support. The landlord says only wages from a job count toward qualifying. Under New York law, this policy is:
options: Lawful, because only housing vouchers are protected
Unlawful, because both are lawful sources of income
Lawful, because support payments can end at any time
Unlawful only if the landlord gets federal subsidies
questions.explanation: Executive Law §292(36) defines lawful source of income to include child support, alimony, Social Security, public assistance, housing vouchers, and any other lawful income. The protection is not limited to Section 8 vouchers.

questions.q: A Bronx apartment rents for $2,400 a month. The applicant's CityFHEPS voucher pays $1,800, and she pays the remaining $600. The landlord requires annual income of 40 times the monthly rent. Under NYC Commission on Human Rights guidance, what is the most annual income the landlord may require?
questions.explanation: An income test may be applied only to the tenant's share: $600 × 40 = $24,000. $96,000 wrongly uses the full rent ($2,400 × 40), $72,000 uses the voucher's share ($1,800 × 40), and $7,200 is just a year of her share ($600 × 12).
questions.citation: NYC Human Rights Law (lawful source of income); NYC Commission on Human Rights source-of-income guidance

questions.q: A Brooklyn applicant's housing subsidy covers 100% of the monthly rent. Under NYC source-of-income guidance, what minimum income requirement may the landlord impose?
options: 40 times the full monthly rent
40 times the amount the subsidy pays
Three times the monthly rent in wages
None, since the subsidy pays all of the rent
questions.explanation: When the program pays the entire rent, the applicant's own income has no bearing on whether rent gets paid, so any minimum income requirement acts as a voucher ban. Each distractor applies an ordinary market formula that screens out subsidy holders.
questions.citation: NYC Human Rights Law (lawful source of income); NYC Commission on Human Rights guidance

questions.q: A Buffalo landlord's online listing ends with "No programs, no Section 8." Under the New York State Human Rights Law, this statement is:
options: An unlawful ad expressing a source-of-income limit
Lawful, because it does not mention race or color
Lawful, as long as an Equal Housing logo appears
Unlawful only once a voucher holder is turned away
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5)(a)(3) prohibits any advertisement that expresses a limitation based on lawful source of income. The ad is a violation by itself, before anyone is refused, and a fair housing logo does not cure discriminatory text.

questions.q: A landlord tells his listing agent, "Tell anyone with a voucher the unit is already rented." A voucher holder calls about the available unit. The salesperson should:
options: Follow it, since only the owner can be held liable
Follow it only if the owner puts it in writing
Refuse the instruction; the licensee would be liable too
Refer the caller to a coworker to avoid conflict
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5)(c) independently bars brokers and salespersons from refusing to negotiate based on lawful source of income, or from falsely saying a unit is unavailable. Following a client's discriminatory order is not a defense, and handing the caller to a coworker does not change that.

questions.q: A landlord in Albany advertises an apartment for "U.S. citizens only." Under New York law, the ad is:
options: Lawful, because the federal Fair Housing Act omits it
Lawful, if the same rule applies to every applicant
Unlawful; citizenship or immigration status is protected
Unlawful only inside the five boroughs of New York City
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5) protects citizenship or immigration status statewide, not just in NYC. A narrower federal list is no defense to violating state law.

questions.q: A property manager in Westchester withdraws a lease offer after learning that the applicant is transgender. Under New York law, this is:
options: Unlawful gender identity or expression discrimination
Lawful, because only sex assigned at birth is covered
Lawful, unless the building receives public funds
Unlawful only under the NYC Human Rights Law
questions.explanation: Gender identity or expression is a protected class statewide under Executive Law §296(5), added in 2019. The protection applies to private housing, not just publicly assisted housing or NYC.

questions.q: A rental application in Utica asks, "Are you a member of the New York National Guard or other organized militia?" Under New York law, this question is:
options: Lawful, because deployments can affect lease terms
Lawful, if the question is asked of every applicant
Unlawful only for publicly assisted housing
Unlawful, though an applicant may volunteer membership
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5)(g) bars written or oral inquiries about membership in the state organized militia in housing, but lets a member disclose it voluntarily. Military status is also a protected class under §296(5).

questions.q: A Syracuse rental application asks, "Have you ever been arrested?" An applicant was arrested once, and the charge was dismissed. Under Executive Law §296(16), which statement is correct?
options: She must disclose it, because arrest records are public information
She may answer as if the arrest never happened
She must disclose it but may attach a copy of the dismissal order
She must disclose it only if the landlord runs a background check
questions.explanation: Section 296(16) makes it unlawful in housing to ask about or act on a non-pending arrest that ended in the person's favor, and says a person asked for that information may respond as if the arrest did not occur. A dismissal is a favorable termination, so she need not disclose it under any of the distractors' conditions.

questions.q: Executive Law §296(16) does NOT bar a housing provider from asking about which of the following?
options: An adjournment in contemplation of dismissal
An unsealed criminal conviction
A youthful offender adjudication
A conviction sealed under the Clean Slate Act
questions.explanation: Section 296(16) protects favorable terminations, ACDs, youthful offender adjudications, and sealed convictions (including Clean Slate sealing). An unsealed conviction is outside §296(16), although other rules such as NYC's Fair Chance Housing Law and disparate-impact principles can still limit how it is used.

questions.q: Under New York City's Fair Chance Housing Law, when may a covered landlord who chooses to run a criminal background check do so?
options: Before accepting the application, so unqualified applicants pay no fee
At any point, if the applicant signs a written consent to the check
Only after the tenant moves in and the lease term has begun
After reviewing general eligibility and making a conditional offer
questions.explanation: Since January 1, 2025, covered NYC providers must first review all non-criminal qualifications (income, credit, references) and extend a conditional offer before running any criminal background check. The applicant's consent does not allow an earlier check.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §8-107 (Fair Chance Housing Law, Local Law 24 of 2024)

questions.q: Under New York City's Fair Chance Housing Law, a covered landlord may review a misdemeanor conviction only if the applicant's release date (or sentencing date, if there was no incarceration) falls within the last:
options: 3 years
5 years
7 years
10 years
questions.explanation: Reviewable history is limited to misdemeanors within 3 years and felonies within 5 years of release or sentencing, plus convictions requiring current sex-offense registration. 5 years is the felony window.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §8-107 (Fair Chance Housing Law)

questions.q: Which line in a Manhattan rental ad would violate New York City's Fair Chance Housing Law?
options: Income verification required of all
Two-year lease available at signing
Criminal background check required
Pets considered on a case-by-case basis
questions.explanation: The NYC Commission on Human Rights treats statements about criminal background checks in ads or applications, such as "background check required" or "no felons," as expressing an unlawful limitation, unless federal or state law requires or authorizes the check (and the ad cites that law). The other lines describe neutral lease terms.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §8-107 (Fair Chance Housing Law); NYC Commission on Human Rights guidance

questions.q: An owner lives in one unit of a two-family house in Albany and posts an online ad for the other unit stating a preference against families with children. Under Executive Law §296(5)(a)(4), what is the result?
options: The ad is lawful, because the exemption covers advertising too
The ad is unlawful, but refusals to rent remain exempt
The ad is unlawful, and the owner also loses the two-family exemption
Nothing, because the exemption applies only to licensees
questions.explanation: The two-family owner-occupied exemption covers only refusals and terms (subparagraphs 1 and 2), not discriminatory ads (subparagraph 3). The statute also says the property is no longer exempt if the owner engages in prohibited advertising.

questions.q: A Syracuse homeowner who lives in her house advertises a spare bedroom in it for "female renters only." Under the New York State Human Rights Law, this ad is:
options: Permitted under the owner-occupied room-rental exemption
Prohibited, because advertising is never exempt
Permitted only if a licensed broker places the ad
Prohibited unless the house contains two units
questions.explanation: Section 296(5)(a)(4)(ii) exempts renting a room in a housing accommodation by an owner who lives there from the refusal, terms, and advertising provisions alike. That is different from the two-family exemption, which does not cover ads.

questions.q: A landlord in Binghamton offers a rent discount to tenants who are 65 or older. Under the New York State Human Rights Law, this is:
options: Prohibited age discrimination
Permitted only in 55-and-older housing
Permitted only with DHR approval
Expressly permitted by the statute
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(17) says nothing in §296 prohibits offering and accepting a housing discount for persons 65 or older. No senior-community status or agency approval is required.

questions.q: A landlord adopts a facially neutral screening rule with no intent to discriminate, but the rule predictably excludes a protected group at a much higher rate. Under New York's Human Rights Law, the rule:
options: Is lawful, because no discriminatory intent was shown
Can be unlawful unless a legally sufficient justification exists
Is lawful if it is applied the same way to all applicants
Is unlawful only if a court finds intentional bias later
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5-a) lets a housing claim be proved by discriminatory effect. The practice survives only if it is necessary to a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest that a less discriminatory practice could not serve.

questions.q: An appraiser lowers a home's value because many nearby residents share a particular national origin. Under the New York State Human Rights Law, this is:
options: A permissible use of neighborhood data
An unlawful discriminatory practice
Allowed if disclosed in the report
Only a professional-ethics concern
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5)(h) prohibits basing an appraisal or opinion of value on the protected characteristics of owners or occupants of the property or of properties nearby. Disclosing the factor does not make it lawful.

questions.q: A broker refuses to show a vacant storefront to a business owner because of the owner's national origin, reasoning that fair housing law covers only homes. Under New York law, the broker is:
options: Correct, because only dwellings are covered
Correct, unless the space includes an apartment
Wrong only if the space is publicly assisted
Wrong; the state law covers commercial space too
questions.explanation: Executive Law §296(5)(c) bars brokers and salespersons from discriminating in housing, land, or commercial space. The federal Fair Housing Act focuses mainly on dwellings, but New York's broker provision is broader.

questions.q: A salesperson representing a landlord is leasing a commercial office suite. Must she give a prospective tenant the Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure (DOS-2156)?
options: Yes, at first substantive contact; the rule covers all real property
No, because the form applies only to one- to four-family homes
No, because the form is required only for residential dwellings
Only if the prospective tenant specifically asks to receive it
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR §175.28(c) applies the disclosure to all real property, including condos, co-ops, vacant land, and commercial property. The one- to four-family limit is a trap borrowed from the agency disclosure rule.

questions.q: Each of the following satisfies the DOS-2156 delivery rule EXCEPT:
options: Emailing a link with text saying it explains the NYS Human Rights Law
Handing over a hard copy and getting a signed acknowledgment
Explaining fair housing rights orally during a showing
Texting the prospective buyer the form as an attachment
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR §175.28(b) allows email, text, electronic messaging, fax, or hard copy, and allows a link if accompanying text says it contains Human Rights Law information. It expressly states that oral disclosure does not satisfy the rule.

questions.q: A prospective seller receives a hard copy of the DOS-2156 but refuses to sign the acknowledgment. What must the salesperson do?
options: Stop working with the seller until the acknowledgment is signed
Note the refusal on the agency disclosure form and keep it 1 year
Prepare a sworn written declaration of when it was given and keep it at least 3 years
Ask the seller's attorney to sign the acknowledgment on the seller's behalf
questions.explanation: Under 19 NYCRR §175.28(d), if the consumer declines to sign, the licensee sets out under oath or affirmation a written declaration of when the notice was provided and keeps it at least 3 years. Refusing to sign does not end the relationship.

questions.q: Which statement does the DOS-2156 Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure NOT make to consumers?
options: A fee is charged to file a complaint
Steering is a violation of the law
Retaliation for complaining is unlawful
Complaints may be filed with DHR or DOS
questions.explanation: The form says complaints may go to the Division of Human Rights or the Department of State, lists steering among violations, and states that retaliation is unlawful. It also says there is no fee for these services.
questions.citation: DOS-2156 Housing and Anti-Discrimination Disclosure Form; 19 NYCRR §175.28

questions.q: A prospective tenant signs the acknowledgment on the DOS-2156. By signing, the tenant is:
options: Agreeing to be represented by the brokerage
Waiving the right to file a DHR complaint
Certifying eligibility under fair housing law
Confirming only that the form was received
questions.explanation: The signature acknowledges receipt of the disclosure and nothing more. It creates no agency relationship and cannot waive Human Rights Law rights.

questions.q: A broker's branch office is on the 12th floor of an office tower and cannot be reached from the sidewalk. Where must the Fair Housing and Anti-Discrimination Notice be displayed?
options: On the tower's ground-floor lobby directory
Where the office's business license is posted
Nowhere, because there is no street window
On the outside door of the elevator bank
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR §175.29(b) generally requires the notice in an office window visible from the sidewalk. If the office is not accessible from the sidewalk, the notice must be posted where the business license is posted under RPL §441-a.

questions.q: A salesperson runs a personal website showing her listings. What does 19 NYCRR §175.29 require of the site?
options: Nothing, because the broker's website already has one
A prominent homepage link to the DOS fair housing notice
The notice only on pages that show rental listings
A copy of the broker's operating procedures only
questions.explanation: Section 175.29(c) requires every website created and maintained by brokers, associate brokers, salespersons, and teams to display prominently on the homepage a link to the Department's notice. The broker's own posting does not cover the agent's separate site.

questions.q: A broker tells his agents that because the Fair Housing Notice is posted in the office window, they no longer need to hand out the DOS-2156 form. The broker is:
options: Correct, because the posted notice has the same content
Correct for walk-in customers but not for online leads
Wrong only for transactions involving rental property
Wrong; posting and individual disclosure are separate duties
questions.explanation: The posting requirement (19 NYCRR §175.29) and the individual disclosure at first substantive contact (§175.28) are independent obligations. Meeting one does not satisfy the other.

questions.q: A brokerage's written standardized operating procedures say buyers do not need mortgage pre-approval before receiving services. One of its agents demands pre-approval letters only from some buyers. Which statement is correct?
options: The agent is violating the SOPs and faces RPL §441-c discipline
The agent may impose stricter terms on a case-by-case basis
There is no violation, because pre-approval is a common practice
Only the broker is accountable, because the SOPs are the broker's
questions.explanation: RPL §442-h(4) requires brokers to set uniform prerequisites for prospective homebuyers. Any broker or salesperson who does not follow them is subject to penalties under RPL §441-c. Applying requirements selectively is the unequal treatment the law targets.

questions.q: Under RPL §442-h, what must a broker do with the brokerage's standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers?
options: File them with the Division of Human Rights for approval before use
Have every buyer sign them before the first property showing
Date stamp, notarize, and post them on the broker's website and apps
Publish them once a year in a newspaper serving each office area
questions.explanation: Section 442-h(4)(b) requires brokers to date stamp, notarize, and post the procedures on any public website and mobile app they maintain, and to provide copies on request at their offices. There is no DHR filing or buyer-signature requirement.

questions.q: A broker changes the brokerage's standardized operating procedures for prospective homebuyers. Within how many days must the revised procedures be date stamped, notarized, and posted?
options: 10 days
60 days
30 days
90 days
questions.explanation: RPL §442-h(4)(b) requires changed procedures to be date stamped, notarized, and posted within 30 days, and the changes must be archived.

questions.q: A real estate team operates its own website separate from its broker's site. Regarding the broker's standardized operating procedures, the team's site should:
options: Post the broker's procedures or link directly to them
Post the team's own separate procedures instead
Omit them, since only the broker's site is covered
Post them only on pages that feature listings
questions.explanation: RPL §442-h(4)(b) provides that a website or mobile app maintained by a team or salesperson should post the broker's policies or link directly to them on the broker's site or app. Teams do not write their own separate procedures.

questions.q: A salesperson suspects that a caller asking about a listing is a fair housing tester. The best response is to:
options: Ask the caller directly whether they are working as a tester
Refer the call to the broker and give no listing information
Provide only information the caller asks for in writing
Give the same information and service required by the firm's procedures
questions.explanation: Testers check whether similar people receive similar treatment, so the safe course is to treat every prospect the same way under the brokerage's uniform procedures. Screening or deflecting suspected testers produces the very unequal treatment they are designed to detect.

questions.q: A renter in Yonkers believes a landlord discriminated against her on May 1, 2026. Under current Executive Law §297(5), she generally has how long to file a complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights?
options: 1 year
3 years
2 years
180 days
questions.explanation: For conduct on or after February 15, 2024, §297(5) allows 3 years to file with DHR. One year is the HUD complaint period under the federal Fair Housing Act, and 2 years is the federal private lawsuit period.

questions.q: An applicant files a housing discrimination complaint with the NYS Division of Human Rights. Later, while the complaint is pending, she wants to sue in state court on the same claim. Generally:
options: She may pursue both forums at the same time on the same claim
Filing with DHR elected that forum and bars a court suit on the same claim
She must first sue in court before DHR can investigate the claim
She may sue in court only after DHR issues a probable-cause finding
questions.explanation: Under the election-of-remedies rule in Executive Law §297(9), filing with DHR generally bars a later court action on the same claim, with narrow exceptions such as a dismissal for administrative convenience. Choosing a forum at the start is important.

questions.q: A buyer believes a salesperson steered her away from certain neighborhoods. Besides filing with the Division of Human Rights, the DOS-2156 tells her she may also complain to:
options: The county clerk's office where the deed is recorded
The local board of assessment review
The Department of Financial Services
The Department of State, Division of Licensing Services
questions.explanation: The DOS-2156 lists both DHR and the Department of State, Division of Licensing Services, which can discipline the licensee under RPL §441-c. The other agencies have no role in licensee fair housing complaints.

questions.q: Of the 22.5 continuing education hours a New York salesperson needs each two-year term, at least how many must cover fair housing and/or discrimination?
options: 3 hours
2 hours
2.5 hours
1 hour
questions.explanation: The fair housing requirement is 3 hours. 2 hours is the requirement for cultural competency and implicit bias, 2.5 is ethical business practices, and 1 hour is recent legal matters (and agency after the first term).

questions.q: A salesperson is renewing for a second (or later) two-year term. After the required components (fair housing 3, agency 1, ethical business practices 2.5, recent legal matters 1, cultural competency 2, implicit bias 2), how many of the 22.5 hours are left for other approved courses?
options: 10 hours
13 hours
11 hours
9 hours
questions.explanation: Required hours: 3 + 1 + 2.5 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 11.5, so 22.5 − 11.5 = 11. 10 uses the first-term agency requirement of 2 hours (22.5 − 12.5 = 10). 13 leaves out the 2 implicit bias hours (22.5 − 9.5 = 13).

questions.q: The implicit bias training now required in New York real estate continuing education addresses which concept?
options: Conscious, openly stated hostility toward a protected class
Statistical redlining by lenders in specific neighborhoods
Attitudes or stereotypes that affect decisions unconsciously
Rules on reasonable accommodations for disabled tenants
questions.explanation: Implicit bias refers to attitudes or stereotypes that shape a person's understanding, actions, and decisions without conscious awareness. That is why the state requires 2 dedicated CE hours even for licensees who would never knowingly discriminate.

questions.q: Which pair of New York CE components each requires 2 hours per license term?
options: Cultural competency and implicit bias
Fair housing and ethical business practices
Recent legal matters and fair housing
Ethical business practices and recent legal matters
questions.explanation: Cultural competency and implicit bias are 2 hours each. Fair housing is 3, ethical business practices 2.5, and recent legal matters 1.

questions.q: Under 19 NYCRR §177.9, an entity approved to teach fair housing courses must:
options: Have every student sign a fair housing pledge to DOS
Submit each student's exam answers to DHR within 30 days
Limit each fair housing class to 25 students in person
Record each course in video and audio and keep it one year
questions.explanation: Section 177.9, added with the 2020 fair housing regulations, requires a full audio and video recording of each fair housing course, kept for one year.

questions.q: The Secretary of State finds that owners in a defined area are being repeatedly solicited by agents and fear that values will fall because people of a different background are moving in. A nonsolicitation order may stay in effect for no more than:
options: 1 year
5 years
3 years
10 years
questions.explanation: RPL §442-h(2)(a) limits a nonsolicitation order to 5 years, though it may be re-adopted or amended through the same procedure. The order targets blockbusting-style solicitation.

questions.q: A cease-and-desist zone is in effect. A salesperson mails a listing solicitation postcard to an owner whose name appears on the zone's current cease-and-desist list. This is:
options: Permitted, because only phone calls and door knocks are barred
A violation, because direct solicitation of listed owners is barred
Permitted, if the postcard includes a fair housing statement
A violation only if the owner already has the home listed
questions.explanation: Under RPL §442-h(3), licensees may not solicit a listing from an owner on the current cease-and-desist list, and the ban covers direct forms such as mail, phone, and personal contact. A fair housing statement does not create an exception.

questions.q: A Queens landlord rejects an otherwise qualified applicant because of her body weight. Which statement is most accurate?
options: No law applies, because weight is not a protected class
It is lawful if the landlord cites building safety concerns
Only the federal Fair Housing Act covers this situation
The NYC Human Rights Law expressly protects height and weight
questions.explanation: New York City added height and weight to its Human Rights Law in 2023, covering housing. Those classes are not on the state or federal lists, which is why local law matters for NYC transactions.

questions.q: Under Executive Law §170-d and DHR's regulation, when must a real estate licensee give a prospective tenant the notice of rights to reasonable accommodations and modifications for persons with disabilities?
options: At first substantive contact with the prospective tenant
Within 30 days after the tenant's lease begins
Only when the tenant requests an accommodation
