questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (umbrella policies)

questions.q: A landlord insures a rental two-family house under a landlord's (dwelling) policy. A tenant's laptop is stolen from her unit. Which statement is correct?
options: The landlord's policy covers the laptop because the theft occurred inside the landlord's insured building
The landlord's policy generally does not cover tenants' belongings; she needs her own renter's (HO-4) policy
NY law requires the landlord to reimburse tenants for any theft that occurs inside a rental unit
The landlord's owner's title insurance policy covers theft losses suffered by tenants
questions.explanation: A landlord's policy insures the building, the landlord's own property, and typically liability and loss of rents, not the tenants' personal property. Tenants protect their contents and liability with an HO-4.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-4; commercial/landlord policies)

questions.q: A buyer's insurance agent warns that the home's CLUE report shows two prior water-damage claims. What is a CLUE report?
options: A municipal record of open building permits and code violations filed against the property
A credit bureau report on the buyer's mortgage payment history and outstanding debts
A FEMA map showing the flood zone boundaries and base flood elevations for the property
An insurance-industry report of a property's claims history, typically for up to seven years
questions.explanation: The Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (CLUE) report lists past insurance claims on a property, typically for up to seven years. Prior claims can raise premiums or affect insurability, so sellers can order a report on their own property before listing.
questions.citation: Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (LexisNexis); Fair Credit Reporting Act

questions.q: Which comparison of the HO-1 and HO-2 forms is correct?
options: Both are named-peril forms, but HO-2 (broad) covers more listed perils than HO-1 (basic)
HO-1 is an open-peril form covering all losses not excluded, while HO-2 is named-peril
HO-2 is designed only for renters, and HO-1 is designed only for condominium unit owners
HO-1 covers flood damage from rising water, while HO-2 excludes flood entirely
questions.explanation: HO-1 (basic) covers a limited list of named perils, and HO-2 (broad) covers those plus additional named perils. Neither is open-peril, and neither covers flood.
questions.citation: NYS DOS 77-hr Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 12: Property Insurance (HO-1 Basic, HO-2 Broad)

questions.q: In a standard homeowner's policy, which lettered coverage protects the house itself, including attached structures such as an attached garage?
options: Coverage A (dwelling)
Coverage B (other structures)
Coverage C (personal property)
Coverage D (loss of use)
questions.explanation: Coverage A insures the dwelling and structures attached to it, such as an attached garage or deck. Coverage B is the trap: it applies to structures set apart from the dwelling, like a detached garage or fence.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy (ISO HO form) Section I coverages

questions.q: A windstorm knocks over a homeowner's backyard fence and crushes a detached tool shed. The house is undamaged. Which part of the homeowner's policy responds?
options: Coverage A (dwelling)
Coverage C (personal property)
Coverage B (other structures)
Coverage E (personal liability)
questions.explanation: Fences and detached sheds are structures separated from the dwelling, so they fall under Coverage B. Coverage A is limited to the house and attached structures, and Coverage C covers movable belongings rather than buildings.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy (ISO HO form) Section I, Coverage B

questions.q: After a covered fire makes their house unlivable, a family stays in a hotel for six weeks and spends more than usual on meals. Which coverage helps pay these increased costs?
options: Coverage F (medical payments to others)
Coverage D (loss of use)
Coverage B (other structures)
Coverage C (personal property)
questions.explanation: Coverage D, loss of use, pays additional living expense (the increase over normal living costs) while a covered loss keeps the insured out of the home. Medical payments is unrelated; it pays guests' injury bills.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy (ISO HO form) Section I, Coverage D

questions.q: A neighbor's child cuts his hand on a homeowner's broken gate. No lawsuit is filed, and the homeowner wants the policy to pay the child's $600 urgent-care bill whether or not the homeowner was at fault. Which coverage is designed for this?
options: Coverage E (personal liability)
Coverage D (loss of use)
Coverage A (dwelling)
Coverage F (medical payments)
questions.explanation: Coverage F pays reasonable medical expenses of guests injured on the premises without requiring proof that the insured was legally liable. Coverage E is the trap: it responds when the insured is legally liable or sued, and it pays defense costs.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy (ISO HO form) Section II, Coverage F

questions.q: Which claim would a homeowner's personal liability coverage (Coverage E) generally NOT pay?
options: A guest's broken wrist from a fall on loose stairs
An injury the insured intentionally caused in a fight
Legal defense costs for a covered injury lawsuit
A neighbor's window the insured's child broke by accident
questions.explanation: Liability coverage excludes bodily injury or property damage the insured expected or intended. Accidental injuries to guests, accidental damage to others' property by household members, and defense of covered suits are what Coverage E is for.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy (ISO HO form) Section II exclusions

questions.q: Under an open-peril (special form) dwelling coverage, how is a loss treated compared with a named-peril policy?
options: It is covered unless the policy specifically excludes its cause
It is covered only when its cause appears on a list of perils
It is covered only for fire, lightning, and windstorm losses
It is covered for every cause, with no exclusions of any kind
questions.explanation: Open-peril ("all risk") coverage pays for direct physical loss unless an exclusion applies; named-peril coverage pays only if the cause is listed. The trap is believing "all risk" means no exclusions: flood, earth movement, and wear and tear are still excluded.
questions.citation: Homeowner's policy forms: named-peril vs open-peril coverage (NYS 77-hr syllabus, property insurance)

questions.q: A homeowner files a claim, and the insurer disputes coverage. Under an open-peril policy, which party generally must show that an exclusion applies?
options: The homeowner, by proving a listed peril caused the loss
The mortgage lender named on the declarations page
The insurer, by proving the cause falls in an exclusion
The state insurance department, after an inspection
questions.explanation: Under open-peril coverage the insured shows a direct physical loss, and the insurer must prove an exclusion applies to deny it. Under a named-peril policy the burden runs the other way: the insured must show a listed peril caused the loss.
questions.citation: General insurance law: burden of proof under named-peril vs open-peril policies

questions.q: An HO-3 policyholder accidentally spills a can of paint on an expensive area rug, ruining it. Accidental spills are not on the HO-3 personal property peril list. What is the likely result?
options: Covered, since HO-3 covers all contents on an open-peril basis
Covered under Coverage A, since the rug was inside the dwelling
Covered under Coverage F, since it was an accident in the home
Not covered, though an HO-5 form would generally cover it
questions.explanation: An HO-3 gives open-peril coverage to the dwelling but only named-peril coverage to personal property, so an unlisted cause is not covered. An HO-5 (or an HO-3 with a special personal property endorsement) extends open-peril coverage to contents.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy forms HO-3 and HO-5 (NYS 77-hr syllabus, types of homeowner's policies)

questions.q: Which peril is typically covered by the HO-2 broad form but NOT by the HO-1 basic form?
options: Fire or lightning
Weight of ice, snow, or sleet
Windstorm, hail, or explosion
Vandalism or malicious mischief
questions.explanation: HO-2 adds perils to the HO-1 list, such as falling objects, weight of ice, snow, or sleet, and accidental discharge of water from plumbing or heating systems. Fire, lightning, windstorm, hail, explosion, and vandalism are already on the basic HO-1 list.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy forms HO-1 and HO-2 (NYS 77-hr syllabus, types of homeowner's policies)

questions.q: A 30-year-old roof slowly deteriorates and finally leaks, staining the ceiling. The owner has an HO-3 policy. How will the insurer most likely treat the roof itself?
options: Excluded as wear, tear, and deterioration
Covered in full as an open-peril dwelling loss
Covered as a windstorm loss to the dwelling
Covered at replacement cost after a deductible
questions.explanation: Homeowner's policies insure sudden, accidental physical loss; gradual wear, tear, and deterioration is excluded even under open-peril coverage. Calling it a windstorm loss is the trap, because no storm caused the damage.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy (ISO HO form) Section I exclusions

questions.q: During heavy rain, water backs up through a basement floor drain and ruins carpeting and furniture. The owner's standard HO-3 has no added endorsements. What is the likely outcome?
options: Covered as an accidental discharge from plumbing
Covered under the NFIP because rain was involved
Not covered without a water backup endorsement
Covered under Coverage D as a loss of use claim
questions.explanation: Standard homeowner's forms exclude water that backs up through sewers or drains; a water backup and sump overflow endorsement adds that coverage for an extra premium. Accidental discharge from plumbing is a different, covered event and is the trap here.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy water exclusion; water backup endorsement

questions.q: In insurance terms, what is an endorsement?
options: A sworn statement the insured files to support a claim
The summary page listing the insured, limits, and premium
A temporary contract of coverage issued before the policy
A written attachment that adds to or changes the policy
questions.explanation: An endorsement (also called a rider) amends the policy by adding, removing, or changing coverage. The other choices describe a proof of loss, the declarations page, and a binder.
questions.citation: General insurance terminology; NYS 77-hr syllabus, adding to the basic policy

questions.q: A buyer's $18,000 engagement ring would be paid only up to a low special theft limit under her homeowner's personal property coverage. What is the usual way to insure it for its full value?
options: Raise the Coverage A dwelling limit
Add a scheduled personal property endorsement
Add a loss assessment endorsement
Raise the Coverage F medical payments limit
questions.explanation: Homeowner's forms cap theft of jewelry and similar valuables at a special sublimit; scheduling the item (a floater or scheduled personal property endorsement) insures it for an agreed value. Raising Coverage A does not lift a Coverage C sublimit.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy special limits; scheduled personal property endorsement

questions.q: A homeowner worries that construction costs will rise faster than the dwelling limit over the next few years. Which endorsement automatically raises the Coverage A limit over the policy term?
options: Inflation guard endorsement
Ordinance or law endorsement
Loss assessment endorsement
Scheduled property endorsement
questions.explanation: An inflation guard endorsement increases the dwelling limit by a set percentage over time to keep pace with rebuilding costs. Ordinance or law coverage is the trap: it pays the extra cost of meeting current building codes, not general inflation.

questions.q: After a fire, the local building department requires an older home's rebuilt wiring and stairs to meet the current code, which raises the repair cost. Which coverage addresses that added expense?
options: Additional living expense coverage
Inflation guard coverage
Ordinance or law coverage
Medical payments coverage
questions.explanation: Ordinance or law coverage pays the increased cost to repair or rebuild in compliance with current building codes, which standard dwelling coverage limits or excludes. Inflation guard only adjusts the limit for general cost increases.
questions.citation: Homeowner's policy ordinance or law coverage

questions.q: A condominium association's master policy carries a $25,000 deductible, and after a covered roof loss the board assesses each unit owner a share. Which coverage in a unit owner's HO-6 policy can pay that assessment?
options: Coverage B (other structures)
Coverage D (loss of use)
Coverage F (medical payments)
Loss assessment coverage
questions.explanation: Loss assessment coverage pays the unit owner's share of an association assessment arising from a covered loss to common property, often including a master-policy deductible. The master policy itself does not pay its own deductible.
questions.citation: HO-6 condominium unit owner's policy, loss assessment coverage

questions.q: A roof with a 20-year useful life is 15 years old when a covered storm destroys it. Replacing it costs $24,000. The policy pays actual cash value using straight-line depreciation, with a $1,000 deductible. How much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: Depreciation = $24,000 × 15/20 = $18,000, so ACV = $24,000 − $18,000 = $6,000; payment = $6,000 − $1,000 = $5,000. $17,000 wrongly pays the depreciation amount less the deductible, $6,000 forgets the deductible, and $23,000 is replacement cost less the deductible.
questions.citation: Actual cash value = replacement cost − depreciation (NYS 77-hr syllabus, amount of insurance needed)

questions.q: A replacement cost policy pays actual cash value first and releases the withheld depreciation once repairs are finished. Kitchen cabinets cost $12,000 to replace, and depreciation is $4,000. Ignoring the deductible, how much is the second payment, released after the owner completes the replacement?
questions.explanation: Initial ACV payment = $12,000 − $4,000 = $8,000; the $4,000 holdback (recoverable depreciation) is released when replacement is complete. $8,000 is the first payment, and $12,000 is the total of both payments, not the second payment.
questions.citation: Replacement cost loss settlement with depreciation holdback

questions.q: A home's replacement cost is $500,000. The owner carries $300,000 of dwelling coverage under an 80% coinsurance clause. A fire causes $60,000 of covered damage. Ignoring the deductible, how much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: Required = 80% × $500,000 = $400,000. Payment = $300,000 ÷ $400,000 × $60,000 = $45,000. $36,000 divides by the full $500,000 instead of the required $400,000; $48,000 just takes 80% of the loss.
questions.citation: 80% coinsurance formula: (insurance carried ÷ insurance required) × loss

questions.q: A home with a $400,000 replacement cost is insured for $240,000 under an 80% coinsurance clause. A fire totally destroys it, a $400,000 covered loss. Ignoring the deductible, what is the most the insurer will pay?
questions.explanation: The coinsurance formula gives $240,000 ÷ $320,000 × $400,000 = $300,000, but an insurer never pays more than the policy limit, so payment is capped at $240,000. Forgetting the face-amount cap produces the $300,000 trap.
questions.citation: Coinsurance formula limited by policy face amount

questions.q: A home's replacement cost rises from $350,000 to $425,000 after a large addition. The owner carries $300,000 under an 80% coinsurance clause. How much more coverage is needed to avoid a coinsurance penalty?
questions.explanation: New requirement = 80% × $425,000 = $340,000; $340,000 − $300,000 = $40,000. $0 relies on the old $280,000 requirement, $60,000 is 80% of only the $75,000 increase, and $125,000 insures to full replacement cost.
questions.citation: 80% coinsurance requirement based on current replacement cost

questions.q: A home's replacement cost is $400,000, and it is insured for $300,000 under a policy with a 90% coinsurance clause. A covered loss totals $36,000. Ignoring the deductible, how much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: Required = 90% × $400,000 = $360,000. Payment = $300,000 ÷ $360,000 × $36,000 = $30,000. $33,750 wrongly assumes an 80% clause ($320,000 required), and $27,000 divides by the full $400,000.
questions.citation: Coinsurance formula: (insurance carried ÷ insurance required) × loss

questions.q: A Long Island home has a $450,000 dwelling limit and a 2% windstorm deductible. A hurricane causes $28,000 of covered damage. Assuming no other limits, how much will the insurer pay?
questions.explanation: A percentage deductible is applied to the dwelling limit, not the loss: 2% × $450,000 = $9,000; $28,000 − $9,000 = $19,000. $27,440 wrongly takes 2% of the $28,000 loss, and $9,000 is only the deductible.
questions.citation: Percentage (windstorm/hurricane) deductible based on Coverage A limit

questions.q: A policy sets Coverage B at 10% of the $380,000 dwelling limit. A covered fire causes $45,000 of damage to a detached garage. Ignoring the deductible, how much will Coverage B pay?
questions.explanation: Coverage B limit = 10% × $380,000 = $38,000, so payment is capped at $38,000 even though damage was $45,000. $7,000 is the uncovered shortfall, and $36,000 wrongly takes 80% of the loss.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy Coverage B limit as a percentage of Coverage A

questions.q: A pipe bursts and the homeowner discovers it promptly. Under the policy's duties after a loss, what should the homeowner do right away besides notifying the insurer?
options: Hire a contractor to finish full repairs before an inspection
Make reasonable temporary repairs to prevent further damage
Discard the damaged items so the home is safe to occupy
Wait for the adjuster's visit before touching anything at all
questions.explanation: Policies require the insured to give prompt notice and protect the property from further damage, such as shutting off water and making reasonable temporary repairs. Completing full repairs or throwing out damaged items before the adjuster sees them can undermine the claim.
questions.citation: Standard homeowner's policy Section I conditions, duties after loss

questions.q: A contractor's careless welding starts a fire in a client's home. The homeowner's insurer pays the claim and then sues the contractor to recover what it paid. This right is called:
options: subrogation
coinsurance
indemnification
contribution
questions.explanation: Subrogation lets the insurer, after paying a loss, step into the insured's rights against the party who caused it. Indemnification is the broader principle of restoring the insured to the pre-loss position, not the insurer's right to sue.

questions.q: A seller keeps her homeowner's policy in force after the closing. Two weeks later, the house burns. Why can she generally NOT collect on the dwelling coverage?
options: Because property policies never cover fires after a sale
Because the buyer's lender holds the only valid claim
Because she no longer had an insurable interest at the time of loss
Because the policy limits were too low under the coinsurance clause
questions.explanation: Property insurance indemnifies only a party with an insurable interest at the time of the loss; after the deed passed, the seller suffered no financial loss. The buyer, who now owns the home, needs a policy of the buyer's own in force from closing.
questions.citation: Insurable interest requirement for property insurance (NY Insurance Law §3401)

questions.q: A buyer's mortgage lender requires proof of hazard insurance at closing, but the insurer has not yet issued the formal policy. What document typically satisfies the lender until the policy arrives?
options: A title insurance commitment
A CLUE claims-history report
A certificate of occupancy
An insurance binder
questions.explanation: An insurance binder is temporary written evidence that coverage is in effect until the policy is issued; the lender wants it to show coverage starting at closing with the lender named in the mortgagee clause. A title commitment concerns title defects, not physical loss.
questions.citation: Lender hazard insurance requirement at closing; insurance binder

questions.q: A mortgaged home suffers a $40,000 covered fire loss. Because the policy contains a standard mortgagee clause, how is the claim check most likely issued?
options: Payable to the homeowner alone
Payable jointly to the homeowner and the lender
Payable to the lender alone, which keeps the funds
Payable to the contractor selected by the insurer
questions.explanation: A mortgagee clause protects the lender's insurable interest, so dwelling loss payments are typically made jointly to the owner and lender, which then supervises release of repair funds. The lender does not simply keep the money as a windfall.
questions.citation: Standard mortgage clause in homeowner's policies

questions.q: A FEMA map shows a house inside the "100-year floodplain." What does that designation actually mean?
options: The area is expected to flood exactly once every 100 years
The area has about a 1% chance of flooding in any given year
The area has not flooded at any time in the past 100 years
The area will remain flood-free for the next 100 years
questions.explanation: A "100-year" or base flood is one with a 1% chance of being equaled or exceeded in any year, so it can strike in back-to-back years. Reading it as "once per century" is the classic trap; over a 30-year mortgage the cumulative odds are substantial.
questions.citation: 44 CFR §59.1 (base flood definition); National Flood Insurance Program

questions.q: On a Flood Insurance Rate Map, a beachfront lot is labeled Zone VE. What does the V designation indicate?
options: A coastal high-hazard area subject to storm-driven wave action
A moderate-risk area outside the Special Flood Hazard Area
An area where the flood risk has not yet been studied
A riverine area protected by a certified levee system
questions.explanation: V zones are coastal high-hazard Special Flood Hazard Areas where waves (velocity) add to flood depth. Moderate- and low-risk areas are mapped as Zone X (or older B/C), and undetermined risk is Zone D.
questions.citation: FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map zone designations; 44 CFR §64.3

questions.q: A buyer's home is in Zone X on the flood map, and her lender does not require flood insurance. Which advice is accurate?
options: FEMA disaster aid will fully reimburse any flood loss, so coverage is unnecessary
Flood coverage cannot be purchased because the home sits outside the high-risk zone
Her HO-3 policy will cover flood damage because the zone is rated low risk
Flood coverage is optional there, but the home can still flood and a policy is available
questions.explanation: Zone X is outside the Special Flood Hazard Area, so the federal purchase mandate does not apply, but NFIP coverage is still sold there and many claims come from outside high-risk zones. Standard homeowner's forms exclude flood regardless of zone.
questions.citation: National Flood Insurance Act of 1968; Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973

questions.q: A buyer is taking a $320,000 federally backed mortgage on a single-family home in a Special Flood Hazard Area. The building's insurable value is $400,000, and the NFIP maximum building coverage for a residence is $250,000. What is the minimum flood coverage the lender must require?
questions.explanation: The mandate is the lesser of the outstanding loan balance or the maximum NFIP coverage available: min($320,000, $250,000) = $250,000 (and never more than insurable value). $320,000 ignores the program cap; $256,000 wrongly applies 80% of the loan ($320,000 × 0.80).

questions.q: A homeowner buys her NFIP flood policy from a well-known private insurance company rather than directly from FEMA. Under the Write Your Own program, which statement is correct?
options: The private company sets its own flood rates and keeps the underwriting risk itself
The private company sells and services it, while the federal program bears the risk
The policy is a private flood policy that federally backed lenders cannot accept
The policy covers less than a direct NFIP policy because a private carrier issued it
questions.explanation: Write Your Own carriers issue and service NFIP policies under their own names, but coverage terms and rates are the federal program's and the government carries the risk. That differs from a separately underwritten private flood policy, which is a distinct product.

questions.q: A buyer applies and pays the premium for an NFIP flood policy on May 1 as a condition of the mortgage, and the loan closes on May 10. A flood hits on May 12. What is the likely result?
options: Covered, because coverage tied to a loan closing takes effect at closing without the 30-day wait
Not covered, because every NFIP policy carries a 30-day waiting period from purchase
Not covered, because coverage starts only 30 days after the loan closing date
Covered only for contents, because building coverage always waits 30 days
questions.explanation: NFIP policies normally take effect 30 days after the application and premium are completed, but the wait does not apply to an initial purchase made in connection with making, increasing, extending, or renewing a loan; that coverage can be effective at closing. Applying the 30-day rule to every purchase is the trap.

questions.q: A borrower with a federally backed mortgage on a house in a Special Flood Hazard Area lets his required flood policy lapse. What does federal law require the lender or servicer to do?
options: Report the lapse to FEMA, which then buys a policy at public expense
Call the loan due immediately without giving the borrower any notice
Do nothing, because the purchase requirement applies only at loan closing
Notify him, then force-place coverage at his cost if he doesn't act within 45 days
questions.explanation: Flood insurance must be maintained for the life of the loan. If it lapses, the lender or servicer must notify the borrower, and if he does not obtain coverage within 45 days of the notice, it must purchase (force-place) the coverage and may charge him the premiums and fees.

questions.q: Why might an owner in a mapped flood-hazard area be unable to buy an NFIP policy at all?
options: Her mortgage lender is a private bank rather than a federal government agency
Her home is worth more than the maximum NFIP building coverage limit
Her municipality does not participate in the NFIP's floodplain management program
Her home was built before the area's first flood insurance rate map was issued
questions.explanation: NFIP coverage is sold only in communities that join the program and adopt and enforce floodplain management ordinances. A high home value just means coverage is capped, and older (pre-map) buildings remain eligible.
questions.citation: National Flood Insurance Act of 1968, 42 U.S.C. §4012(c); 44 CFR Part 60

questions.q: A tenant in a ground-floor apartment in a flood zone asks how to protect her belongings from flood damage. Which answer is correct?
options: She cannot buy flood coverage, because only owners of the building may purchase NFIP policies
She can buy an NFIP contents-only policy, because building and contents coverage are separate
Her landlord's NFIP building policy automatically covers each tenant's belongings
Her HO-4 policy covers flood as long as the water enters through a window
questions.explanation: NFIP building and contents coverage are bought separately, and renters may purchase contents coverage on their own. A landlord's building policy does not protect tenants' property, and renter's (HO-4) policies exclude flood.
questions.citation: NFIP Standard Flood Insurance Policy, Dwelling Form (44 CFR Part 61, App. A(1))

questions.q: A condominium's master policy is written on a "bare walls" basis. A fire guts one unit's kitchen. Who should have insured the cabinets, countertops, and flooring?
options: The unit owner, under an HO-6 policy covering interior improvements
The association, because its master policy covers everything in the building
The unit owner's mortgage lender, under its lender's title policy
No one, because fixtures are excluded from every property policy
questions.explanation: A bare-walls master policy covers the structure and common elements but not unit interiors, so fixtures, cabinets, and finishes fall to the owner's HO-6. Assuming the master policy covers everything inside each unit is the common mistake.
questions.citation: Condominium declaration and bylaws; ISO HO 00 06 (unit-owners form)

questions.q: A storm damages a condominium's roof, and the repair cost exceeds the master policy limit, so the board levies a $6,000 special assessment on each unit owner. Which coverage may reimburse an owner?
options: The owner's title insurance policy on the unit
Fair rental value coverage under a dwelling policy
The building's workers' compensation policy
Loss assessment coverage under the owner's HO-6
questions.explanation: Loss assessment coverage on an HO-6 can pay a unit owner's share of an association assessment resulting from a covered loss, subject to its limit. Title insurance addresses ownership defects, not physical damage or assessments.
questions.citation: ISO HO 00 06, Additional Coverages (loss assessment); condominium bylaws

questions.q: A cooperative shareholder spent $60,000 renovating her apartment's kitchen and bathroom. Which statement about insurance is most accurate?
options: Her stock certificate and proprietary lease make her improvements uninsurable by any carrier
The building policy covers her improvements because the corporation owns the entire building
The co-op's building policy may not cover her improvements, so she needs her own coverage
She needs no coverage, because shareholders are not liable for anything inside their units
questions.explanation: The cooperative corporation owns and insures the building, but shareholder improvements, personal property, and personal liability usually fall to the shareholder's own policy. Check the proprietary lease and building policy rather than assuming the corporation covers interior upgrades.
questions.citation: Proprietary lease and co-op bylaws; NYS DFS homeowner's insurance guidance

questions.q: A dinner guest trips over a rug inside a condo unit and sues the unit owner. Which policy is primarily designed to respond?
options: The association's master policy for common areas
The unit owner's HO-6 personal liability coverage
The association's directors and officers policy
The unit owner's title insurance policy
questions.explanation: Injuries occurring inside an individual unit are generally the unit owner's liability exposure, covered by the HO-6's personal liability section. The master policy's liability coverage is aimed at common areas such as lobbies and walkways.
questions.citation: ISO HO 00 06 (Section II liability); condominium bylaws

questions.q: A kitchen fire in a neighbor's unit makes a tenant's apartment uninhabitable for six weeks, and she must stay in a hotel. Which part of her HO-4 policy helps with the hotel bills?
options: Loss of use (additional living expense) coverage
Personal liability coverage for claims by others
Medical payments to others coverage for guests
Dwelling coverage for the apartment building
questions.explanation: Loss of use pays the increase in living costs, such as a hotel, while a covered loss makes the residence unfit to live in. HO-4 forms provide no dwelling coverage, because the landlord insures the building.
questions.citation: ISO HO 00 04, Coverage D (loss of use)

questions.q: A tenant leaves a candle burning, and the fire damages the landlord's hallway and a neighboring apartment. The landlord's insurer pays and then sues the tenant. Which coverage is most likely to respond for the tenant?
options: Her NFIP contents policy, because water was used to fight the fire
Personal property coverage under her HO-4
The landlord's dwelling coverage, because it is the building's policy
Personal liability coverage under her HO-4
questions.explanation: Negligently damaging other people's property is a liability exposure, and the HO-4's personal liability section can defend and pay such claims. Her personal property coverage protects only her own belongings, and the landlord's insurer can pursue her through subrogation.

questions.q: Which owner is most likely to need a dwelling (DP) policy rather than a homeowner's policy?
options: A couple living full time in their owner-occupied single-family house
An owner who lives in one unit of her two-family home and rents the other
An investor who rents out a single-family house he does not live in
A condo owner who lives in his unit year-round
questions.explanation: Homeowner's forms are built for owner-occupied residences, including an owner-occupied two-family home. A non-owner-occupied rental is generally insured under a dwelling (DP) policy.
questions.citation: ISO Dwelling Property program (DP 00 01/02/03); ISO homeowner's eligibility

questions.q: How does a DP-3 (special form) dwelling policy generally differ from a DP-1 (basic form)?
options: DP-3 adds personal liability automatically; DP-1 excludes all liability coverage
DP-3 insures the dwelling against open perils; DP-1 covers only named perils
DP-3 is for condo units; DP-1 is for single-family rental houses
DP-3 covers flood damage; DP-1 excludes flood and earthquake
questions.explanation: Like the HO-3, the DP-3 insures the building against all risks not excluded, while the DP-1 is a basic named-peril form often settled at actual cash value. Neither dwelling form includes liability automatically, and both exclude flood.
questions.citation: ISO Dwelling Property forms DP 00 01 and DP 00 03

questions.q: A fire forces the tenants out of a landlord's rental house for four months, and no rent is collected. Which dwelling policy coverage addresses that lost income?
options: Fair rental value coverage
Additional living expense coverage
Loss assessment coverage
Medical payments coverage
questions.explanation: Fair rental value pays the rent a landlord loses while a covered loss makes the rental unfit to occupy. Additional living expense is for the insured's own extra costs of living elsewhere, which does not fit a landlord who doesn't live there.
questions.citation: ISO Dwelling Property forms, Coverage D (fair rental value)

questions.q: A landlord insures his rental house under a standard DP-3 policy with no endorsements. A tenant's visitor falls on a broken step and sues the landlord. What is the likely problem?
options: The DP-3 pays the claim, but only at actual cash value after depreciation
The DP-3 covers the injury only if the step was damaged by a named peril
The visitor must sue the tenant, because a landlord is never liable for injuries
Dwelling forms exclude liability unless an endorsement or separate policy adds it
questions.explanation: Unlike homeowner's packages, dwelling policies are property-only; landlords add premises liability through an endorsement or a separate liability policy. Without it, the landlord may face the suit uninsured.
questions.citation: ISO Dwelling Property program (personal liability supplement)

questions.q: An owner has $300,000 of liability coverage on his homeowner's policy and a $1,000,000 umbrella policy. A court awards $1,100,000 to a guest injured on his property, a covered claim. How much does the umbrella insurer pay?
questions.explanation: The umbrella pays only after the underlying policy is exhausted: $1,100,000 − $300,000 = $800,000, which is within its $1,000,000 limit. $1,000,000 wrongly assumes the umbrella pays its full limit first; $700,000 is $1,000,000 − $300,000.

questions.q: A homeowner with a $2,000,000 umbrella policy assumes it will pay for flood damage to his house. Which statement is correct?
options: The umbrella pays for flood damage once his HO-3 limit is exhausted
An umbrella is excess liability coverage and does not pay for damage to the insured's own property
The umbrella replaces the need for an NFIP policy if its limit exceeds the home's value
The umbrella covers flood only if the home is outside a Special Flood Hazard Area
questions.explanation: Umbrella policies sit above underlying liability policies and respond to claims by others, not first-party property losses. Flood damage to his own home requires flood insurance, and insurers typically require specified underlying liability limits before issuing an umbrella.

questions.q: How do premium payments for an owner's title insurance policy and a homeowner's (hazard) policy typically differ?
options: Title is a one-time premium paid at closing; hazard is paid periodically and renewed
Both are paid annually and escrowed by the lender with the property taxes
Title is paid monthly with the mortgage; hazard is a one-time charge at closing
Title premiums end when the mortgage is paid off; hazard premiums continue for life
questions.explanation: An owner's title policy is bought once at closing and protects the owner (and heirs) for as long as they hold title. Hazard insurance protects against future physical losses and must be renewed, often through the lender's escrow account.
questions.citation: General insurance principles; NY Insurance Law Article 64 (title insurance)

questions.q: A homeowner has been turned down by several insurers because of the property's high risk. Which New York entity serves as the FAIR plan insurer of last resort?
options: The Federal Housing Administration (FHA)
The National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)
The NYS Department of State, Division of Licensing Services
The New York Property Insurance Underwriting Association (NYPIUA)
questions.explanation: NYPIUA is a pool of the insurers writing property coverage in New York, offering limited property coverage to owners unable to get it in the voluntary market, generally at higher premiums. The NFIP handles only flood, and the Department of State licenses real estate agents.
questions.citation: NY Insurance Law Article 54; NYS DFS insurance availability programs

questions.q: An owner obtains a NYPIUA policy on her house after being declined in the voluntary market. Which gap should she expect?
options: The policy covers only flood, so she must buy fire coverage elsewhere
The policy covers everything a standard HO-5 covers, but at a higher premium
It excludes liability, theft, and flood, which she must insure elsewhere
The policy covers the house only after a 30-day waiting period
questions.explanation: DFS describes NYPIUA policies as limited property coverage that excludes liability, flood, and theft, so they are not a complete homeowner's package. Assuming the last-resort policy matches a full HO form is the trap.
questions.citation: NYS DFS insurance availability guidance; NY Insurance Law Article 54

questions.q: A seller wants to show buyers that the house has a clean insurance claims history. Which statement about a CLUE report is accurate?
options: Only the buyer's insurer may order it, and neither the seller nor the buyer may see it
The owner can get a free copy each year, and it lists claims tied to the property and the owner
It is a public record kept by the county clerk alongside the deed
It reports only claims the insurer actually paid, not other reported losses
questions.explanation: The Comprehensive Loss Underwriting Exchange (CLUE) is an insurance-industry claims database; a consumer can request a free annual disclosure under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. It is not a recorded public document, and it can show reported losses that were not paid.

questions.q: The superintendent of a cooperative apartment building injures his back while moving trash cans. Which statement best describes how workers' compensation applies?
options: The co-op must carry it, and it pays medical costs and lost wages regardless of fault
Coverage applies only if the super proves the board was negligent
Building employees are exempt, so he must claim against his own health insurance
He must sue the shareholders individually, because the co-op cannot be an employer
questions.explanation: New York requires employers, including co-op and condo boards or their managing agents who employ building staff, to carry workers' compensation. It is no-fault and is generally the employee's exclusive remedy against the employer.

questions.q: A building owner hires a roofing contractor to replace the roof. Before work starts, what is the prudent step regarding insurance?
options: Rely on the owner's title insurance to cover any injuries on the roof
Add the roofers to the owner's homeowner's policy as named insureds
Ask the contractor to sign a waiver promising his workers will never sue
Get proof of the contractor's workers' compensation and liability coverage
questions.explanation: Requiring proof of the contractor's workers' compensation and liability insurance helps keep a worker's injury from becoming a claim against the owner. New York also requires proof of workers' compensation coverage before a building permit is issued.
questions.citation: NY Workers' Compensation Law §57 (proof of coverage for permits)

questions.q: A salesperson's listing advertises a home as 2,400 square feet when it is actually 1,900, and the buyer sues for the overpayment. Which insurance is designed to cover this claim?
options: The buyer's owner's title insurance policy, because the square footage was wrong
The seller's homeowner's policy, under its personal property coverage
The firm's errors and omissions policy, if the error was negligent, not intentional
The firm's workers' compensation policy, because an employee made the error
questions.explanation: E&O is professional liability coverage that defends and pays claims arising from a licensee's negligent errors, subject to policy limits and deductibles. It typically excludes intentional fraud, so it is not immunity for knowingly false statements.

questions.q: During an open house, a visitor slips on the listing agent's spilled coffee in the hallway and breaks her wrist. Which statement about the agent's errors and omissions policy is most accurate?
options: E&O will pay, because the injury occurred while the agent was performing licensed services
E&O likely won't respond, since bodily injury is a general liability exposure
E&O will pay only if the seller's homeowner's policy denies the claim first
E&O will pay because any claim against a licensee counts as a professional claim
questions.explanation: E&O policies cover economic harm from professional mistakes and generally exclude bodily injury and property damage. Injuries on premises fall under general liability coverage, such as the seller's homeowner's policy or the firm's commercial general liability policy.
questions.citation: General insurance principles (E&O vs. general liability)

questions.q: A real property tax described as "ad valorem" is one that is:
options: Based on the value of the property
Charged at a flat amount per parcel
Based on the owner's annual income
Imposed only when the property is sold
questions.explanation: Ad valorem means "according to value": the tax is the taxable assessed value times the tax rate. A flat per-parcel fee or a tax triggered by a sale (transfer tax) is a different kind of charge.

questions.q: A home has a taxable assessed value of $180,000 and the tax rate is 32 mills. What is the annual property tax?
questions.explanation: One mill is $1 per $1,000 (0.001). $180,000 × 32 ÷ 1,000 = $5,760. The trap is misplacing the decimal ($576 or $57,600).

questions.q: A school district needs a tax levy of $4,500,000. The total taxable assessed value in the district is $150,000,000. What is the tax rate?
options: $3 per $1,000 of assessed value (3 mills)
$30 per $1,000 of assessed value (30 mills)
$300 per $1,000 of assessed value
$0.30 per $1,000 of assessed value
questions.explanation: Tax rate = levy ÷ taxable assessed value: $4,500,000 ÷ $150,000,000 = 0.03, which is $30 per $1,000, or 30 mills.

questions.q: In the municipal budget process, the property tax levy is best described as:
options: The total approved budget, before state aid and fees are counted
The total assessed value of all taxable parcels in the municipality
The tax rate multiplied by a single parcel's full market value
The approved budget minus revenue from non-property-tax sources
questions.explanation: The levy is what must be raised by real property taxes: total appropriations minus non-property-tax revenue (state aid, fees, etc.). The levy is then divided by the total taxable assessed value to set the rate.

questions.q: A town's equalization rate is 45%. A house in that town is assessed at $90,000. What is its estimated full market value?
questions.explanation: Full market value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate: $90,000 ÷ 0.45 = $200,000. Multiplying ($90,000 × 0.45 = $40,500) is the common trap.

questions.q: Why does New York State calculate equalization rates for municipalities?
options: To set each homeowner's individual tax bill directly from the state level
To fairly apportion taxes among towns that assess at different percentages of value
To determine the minimum opening bid for property sold at a county tax auction
To convert a property's market value into its replacement cost for insurance
questions.explanation: New York municipalities may assess at a uniform percentage of value that differs from place to place. When a county or school district spans several municipalities, equalization rates put their assessments on a common full-value basis so the levy is apportioned fairly.

questions.q: A property has an assessed value of $200,000 and qualifies for a $30,000 exemption. The tax rate is 25 mills. What is the tax?
questions.explanation: Exemptions reduce the taxable assessed value: $200,000 − $30,000 = $170,000. Then $170,000 × 25 ÷ 1,000 = $4,250. Taxing the full $200,000 ($5,000) ignores the exemption.
questions.citation: NY RPTL (exemptions and taxable assessed value)

questions.q: A village installs new sidewalks and charges only the owners whose lots front the new sidewalk. This charge is a:
options: Special assessment
General ad valorem tax
Real estate transfer tax
Mortgage recording tax
questions.explanation: A special assessment is levied only against the specific properties that benefit from a local improvement, and it becomes a specific lien on those parcels. A general ad valorem tax is spread over all taxable property.
questions.citation: NY RPTL (special ad valorem levies and special assessments)

questions.q: A homeowner has a first mortgage recorded in 2019 and stops paying property taxes in 2026. Regarding lien priority, the unpaid real property tax lien generally:
options: Takes priority over the mortgage even though the mortgage was recorded first
Is junior to the mortgage because the mortgage was recorded seven years earlier
Has equal priority with the mortgage, and the two share any sale proceeds pro rata
Does not become a lien on the property until the owner sells or refinances
questions.explanation: Real property tax liens are given priority over private liens such as mortgages regardless of recording date. That is why lenders often escrow taxes. "First in time, first in right" does not apply to property tax liens.

questions.q: Which statement about the STAR program is correct?
options: Basic STAR is available only to owner-occupants age 65 or older
STAR reduces county and town property taxes but never school taxes
Enhanced STAR is for seniors 65+ with income under a lower limit than Basic STAR
STAR is available for any rental or investment property the owner holds
questions.explanation: STAR (School Tax Relief) reduces school taxes on an owner-occupied primary residence. Basic STAR has no age requirement. Enhanced STAR gives a larger benefit to income-qualified seniors age 65 and over.

questions.q: A couple buys their first home in New York in 2026 and wants STAR school tax relief. How do new STAR applicants generally receive the benefit?
options: As a seller credit against the purchase price applied at closing
As a STAR credit check from NYS after registering with Tax and Finance
As an itemized deduction claimed on their federal income tax return only
As an automatic exemption the assessor applies with no registration needed
questions.explanation: Since 2016, new STAR applicants register with NYS Tax and Finance and receive a STAR credit check rather than a new exemption on the assessment roll. Existing exemption holders could keep the exemption.
questions.citation: NY RPTL § 425; NY Tax Law § 606(eee) (STAR credit)

questions.q: An owner who is 70, lives in the home, and has limited income may qualify for a partial real property tax exemption of up to 50% under which program?
options: The alternative veterans exemption
The agricultural assessment
The Basic STAR credit
The senior citizens exemption
questions.explanation: The senior citizens exemption lets localities give owners 65 and over with limited income a partial exemption, up to 50% of assessed value. The veterans and agricultural programs have different eligibility rules.

questions.q: A farmer's land in an agricultural district is valued for tax purposes on its farming value instead of its development value. This is called:
options: A special assessment
An equalization adjustment
A tax certiorari
An agricultural assessment
questions.explanation: The agricultural assessment program taxes qualifying farmland on its agricultural value. Land converted to non-farm use can owe payments for the taxes it was spared.

questions.q: A homeowner thinks her assessment is too high. What is generally her FIRST formal step to challenge it?
options: File a Small Claims Assessment Review petition before the tentative roll is filed
File a grievance (complaint) with the Board of Assessment Review by Grievance Day
Start a tax certiorari proceeding in State Supreme Court
Stop paying taxes until the assessor reduces the value
questions.explanation: Administrative review comes first: a written complaint to the Board of Assessment Review (BAR) by Grievance Day. SCAR or tax certiorari follow only after the BAR decides. Withholding taxes creates a tax lien and penalties.

questions.q: In most New York towns, Grievance Day, when the Board of Assessment Review hears complaints, falls on:
options: The first Monday in January
March 1, the taxable status date
The fourth Tuesday in May
The last business day of December
questions.explanation: In towns, the BAR generally meets on the fourth Tuesday in May. March 1 is the usual taxable status date, not Grievance Day. Dates can differ in cities, villages, and some counties, so owners should check locally.

questions.q: Which owner may use Small Claims Assessment Review (SCAR)?
options: An owner-occupant of a one- to three-family home who first filed a BAR grievance
The owner of a 40-unit apartment building who skipped the BAR grievance
Any commercial owner whose assessment exceeds $1 million after BAR review
A rent-stabilized tenant who disputes the annual increase set by the RGB
questions.explanation: SCAR is an informal, low-cost review mainly for owner-occupied 1–3 family residential property, and it requires a prior BAR complaint. Commercial and larger properties challenge assessments through tax certiorari in Supreme Court.

questions.q: A county takes title to a home through tax foreclosure for $12,000 in unpaid taxes and later sells it for $250,000. Under the U.S. Supreme Court's 2023 ruling, the former owner:
options: Is entitled to the surplus value above the tax debt and allowed costs
Loses all equity because the taxes were unpaid
Receives only the original $12,000 back
Must pay the county the difference between the tax and the sale price
questions.explanation: In Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023), the Court held that a government keeping surplus equity beyond the tax debt is an unconstitutional taking. New York amended its tax foreclosure law afterward to provide for surplus claims.
questions.citation: Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023); NY RPTL Article 11

questions.q: A homeowner who itemizes on her federal return may generally deduct which pair of items for her main home?
options: Mortgage principal payments and homeowners insurance premiums on the home
Depreciation on the home and the cost of routine repairs and painting
Qualified mortgage interest and real property taxes, subject to the SALT cap
Real property taxes with no dollar cap, plus monthly HOA or condo dues
questions.explanation: Itemizers can deduct qualified home mortgage interest and state and local taxes (including property taxes), but state and local taxes together are subject to an annual cap. Principal, insurance, repairs, and depreciation on a personal residence are not deductible.

questions.q: A married couple filing jointly bought their home for $400,000, added $50,000 of capital improvements, lived there 6 years, and sold it for $1,050,000 with $50,000 of selling costs. How much gain is taxable after the home-sale exclusion?
questions.explanation: Amount realized = $1,050,000 − $50,000 = $1,000,000. Adjusted basis = $400,000 + $50,000 = $450,000. Gain = $550,000. Minus the $500,000 joint exclusion = $50,000 taxable.

questions.q: A single seller wants to exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of her home. Which test must she generally meet?
options: She owned the home for at least 5 consecutive years before the sale
She reinvests the proceeds in a more expensive home within 2 years
She is at least 55 years old and has never claimed the exclusion
She owned and lived in it as her main home 2 of the 5 years before sale
questions.explanation: The § 121 exclusion ($250,000 single / $500,000 joint) requires ownership and use as a main home for 2 of the 5 years before sale. The old age-55 rule and "roll-over into a pricier home" rule were repealed in 1997.

questions.q: An investor sells a rental building and wants to defer gain with a Section 1031 exchange. Which statement is correct?
options: She may exchange into a new personal residence she plans to live in
She may receive the cash proceeds directly and still defer all gain
The exchange permanently eliminates federal tax on the deferred gain
She must identify a replacement within 45 days and close within 180 days
questions.explanation: A 1031 exchange applies to real property held for investment or business use and defers (does not eliminate) gain. Replacement property must be identified within 45 days and acquired within 180 days, and a qualified intermediary should hold the funds. Cash received (boot) is taxable.

questions.q: An investor buys a residential rental for $350,000, of which $75,000 is land. Using simple straight-line depreciation over 27.5 years, the annual depreciation is:
questions.explanation: Land is not depreciable, so the basis is $350,000 − $75,000 = $275,000. $275,000 ÷ 27.5 = $10,000 per year. Using the full $350,000 gives $12,727, which is the trap. A personal residence cannot be depreciated at all.

questions.q: A town's tax rate is 28.5 mills. Expressed per $100 of taxable assessed value, the rate is:
questions.explanation: A mill is $1 per $1,000 (0.001), so 28.5 mills = $28.50 per $1,000 = $28.50 ÷ 10 = $2.85 per $100. $28.50 is the per-$1,000 figure mislabeled as per $100.
questions.citation: Real Property Tax Law (tax rate computation); NYS ORPTS tax rate terminology

questions.q: A school district adopts a $12,500,000 budget and expects $4,100,000 from state aid and other non-property-tax revenue. The district's total assessed value is $300,000,000, of which $20,000,000 is wholly exempt. What tax rate is needed?
questions.citation: Real Property Tax Law; levy ÷ total taxable assessed value

questions.q: A house has a taxable assessed value of $85,000. The village tax rate is $4.20 per $100 of assessed value. What is the annual village tax?
questions.explanation: $85,000 ÷ 100 = 850 hundreds; 850 × $4.20 = $3,570. $357 comes from dividing by 1,000 instead of 100, treating the per-$100 rate as a per-$1,000 rate.
questions.citation: Real Property Tax Law; ad valorem tax computation

questions.q: A town assesses all property at a uniform 55% of market value. A home's market value is $320,000 and the town tax rate is $36 per $1,000 of assessed value, with no exemptions. What is the town tax?
questions.explanation: Assessed value = $320,000 × 0.55 = $176,000; tax = $176,000 ÷ 1,000 × $36 = $6,336. $11,520 applies the rate to market value instead of assessed value; $5,184 wrongly uses 45% (100% − 55%).
questions.citation: RPTL §305 (uniform percentage of value); tax computation

questions.q: Market values in a town have fallen since its last reassessment, and the state equalization rate for the town is now 125%. A home there is assessed at $250,000. What is its indicated full market value?
questions.explanation: Full value = assessed value ÷ equalization rate = $250,000 ÷ 1.25 = $200,000. An equalization rate above 100% means assessments exceed market value, so multiplying ($312,500) moves in the wrong direction.
questions.citation: RPTL Article 12 (state equalization rates); NYS ORPTS

questions.q: A school district lies in two towns. Town A has $45,000,000 of taxable assessed value and an equalization rate of 50%; Town B has $120,000,000 and an equalization rate of 80%. The district must raise $6,000,000. How much of the levy is apportioned to Town A?
questions.citation: RPTL Article 12 (equalization); apportionment of school district levies

questions.q: A town assesses uniformly at 60% of market value. An owner's home is assessed at $189,000, but a credible appraisal and recent comparable sales show its market value is $270,000. What assessment should the owner request at grievance?
questions.explanation: The fair assessment is market value × the town's level: $270,000 × 0.60 = $162,000 (the current $189,000 implies $189,000 ÷ 0.60 = $315,000). $270,000 ignores fractional assessment, and $144,000 subtracts the full $45,000 market-value difference from the assessment instead of 60% of it.
questions.citation: RPTL §305 (uniform percentage); RPTL Article 5, Title 1-A (assessment review)

questions.q: A veteran who served in a combat zone during wartime owns and lives in a home assessed at $240,000. The town offers the alternative veterans exemption, and its maximum caps are not reached. How much is the exemption from the town assessment?
questions.explanation: The alternative veterans exemption gives 15% for wartime service plus an additional 10% for combat-zone service: 25% × $240,000 = $60,000. $36,000 applies only the 15% wartime portion and misses the combat-zone add-on.

questions.q: A 72-year-old owner qualifies for a 50% senior citizens exemption that her town has adopted. Her home is assessed at $160,000 and the town tax rate is 22 mills. What is her town tax?
questions.explanation: Taxable assessed value = $160,000 × 50% = $80,000; tax = $80,000 × 0.022 = $1,760. $3,520 ignores the exemption ($160,000 × 0.022); $176 misplaces the decimal by dividing by 10,000 instead of 1,000.

questions.q: A village installs sidewalks along one street at a cost of $180,000, charged to the benefited lots by front footage. The street has 2,400 total front feet. A lot measures 90 feet of frontage by 150 feet deep. What is that lot's special assessment?
questions.explanation: Cost per front foot = $180,000 ÷ 2,400 = $75; 90 front feet × $75 = $6,750. $11,250 multiplies by the 150-foot depth ($75 × 150) instead of the frontage that faces the sidewalk.
questions.citation: Village Law and Town Law (local improvements / special assessments)

questions.q: A town keeps its levy at $5,000,000 and completes a full-value reassessment, raising its total taxable assessed value from $100,000,000 to $250,000,000. An owner's assessment rises from $40,000 to $100,000. What happens?
options: The rate falls from $50 to $20 per $1,000, and her tax stays $2,000
The rate stays $50 per $1,000, and her tax rises to $5,000
The rate falls to $20 per $1,000, and her tax falls to $800
The rate rises to $125 per $1,000, and her tax rises to $12,500
questions.explanation: Old rate = $5,000,000 ÷ $100,000,000 = $50/1,000, tax $40,000 × 0.05 = $2,000; new rate = $5,000,000 ÷ $250,000,000 = $20/1,000, tax $100,000 × 0.02 = $2,000. Her assessment rose 2.5x, the same as the town total, so her share of the unchanged levy (and her tax) stays the same; keeping the old rate is the trap.

questions.q: A Queens two-family house in NYC tax class 1 had last year's assessed value of $30,000. This year the Department of Finance's market value rises sharply with no physical changes, and the five-year cap is not a limiting factor. What is the most its assessed value can be this year?
questions.explanation: Class 1 assessment increases are capped at 6% a year (and 20% over five years) absent physical changes: $30,000 × 1.06 = $31,800. $32,400 applies the 8% cap for small class 2 buildings; $36,000 applies the five-year 20% cap in a single year.

questions.q: Four towns quote their tax rates differently. Which rate is the highest?
options: 31 mills
2.9% of assessed value
questions.explanation: Convert all to dollars per $1,000: 31 mills = $31.00; $3.05 per $100 = $30.50; 2.9% = $29.00; $30.80 stays $30.80. 31 mills is highest; $3.05 per $100 looks larger only if you forget to multiply by 10.
questions.citation: Tax rate units (mills, per $100, per $1,000, percent)

questions.q: A fire district levies a tax on every taxable parcel inside its boundaries in proportion to each parcel's assessed value. This charge is best described as a:
options: Special assessment based on front footage
Special district ad valorem levy
Countywide general municipal tax
Real estate transfer tax on the parcel
questions.explanation: A special district (fire, water, sewer, lighting) serves a defined area and may levy by assessed value, making it an ad valorem levy confined to the district. A special assessment instead allocates a specific improvement's cost by benefit or frontage, not by value.
questions.citation: RPTL §102 (special ad valorem levy, special assessment definitions)

questions.q: Outside New York City and Nassau County, which statement about assessment levels is correct?
options: Every town must assess at 100% of market value each year
Homes may be assessed at a lower percentage than stores
A town may use any percentage if it is uniform for all parcels
The county sets one assessment percentage for every town
questions.explanation: New York lets an assessing unit assess at full value or at any uniform fraction of it, as long as every parcel shares the same percentage. Different percentages by property class are allowed only in the statutory class systems of NYC and Nassau County.

questions.q: After a buyer closes on a home for $600,000, the assessor raises only that parcel to reflect the sale price while similar unsold homes on the street keep their old assessments. The buyer's strongest grievance claim is that the assessment is:
options: Unequal, because it is at a higher level than comparable parcels
Unlawful, because a sale price can never be used as evidence
Misclassified, because a sale changes the property's class
Excessive, because the levy exceeds the 2% tax cap
questions.explanation: Reassessing only recently sold parcels ("welcome stranger" assessing) puts the buyer at a higher percentage of value than similar homes, which is an unequal assessment. Sale prices are valid evidence of value, so the claim is not that sales can never be used.
questions.citation: RPTL §522 and §524 (grounds for complaint: unequal assessment); RPTL §305

questions.q: Which agency establishes the state equalization rates used to apportion county and school levies among New York municipalities?
options: Each town's Board of Assessment Review
The NYS Office of Real Property Tax Services
The county real property tax service agency
The local assessor of each assessing unit
questions.explanation: Equalization rates are set at the state level by the Office of Real Property Tax Services in the Department of Taxation and Finance (via the State Board of Real Property Tax Services). The BAR hears individual grievances; it does not measure a municipality's overall level of assessment.
questions.citation: RPTL Article 12; NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, ORPTS

questions.q: A town's equalization rate drops from 80% to 70% with no change to any assessment. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Every homeowner's tax bill in the town will fall by 10%
Market values rose while the town's assessments stayed the same
The assessor illegally lowered assessments on the town roll
Owners in the town automatically win their pending grievances
questions.explanation: The equalization rate is total assessed value ÷ total market value; if assessments are unchanged and the rate falls, market values rose. It measures the town as a whole and neither changes an individual bill directly nor decides any owner's grievance.

questions.q: A homeowner preparing a grievance wants a state-certified figure showing the overall ratio of residential assessments to residential market value in her town. Which figure should she use?
options: The residential assessment ratio (RAR)
The town's tax rate per $1,000 of value
The school district's levy limit
The STAR credit savings amount
questions.explanation: The residential assessment ratio measures residential assessed value against residential market value and may be used as evidence at the BAR and in SCAR. The tax rate converts value into tax and says nothing about the level of assessment.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a recognized ground for an assessment grievance?
options: The parcel is assessed above its full market value
The parcel is assessed at a higher level than similar parcels
The parcel is wholly exempt but was assessed as taxable
The school board adopted a budget the owner thinks is wasteful
questions.explanation: Grievances may claim an excessive, unequal, unlawful, or (where classes apply) misclassified assessment. Disagreeing with spending is a budget issue for the budget vote, not proof the parcel's assessment is wrong.

questions.q: An owner in a typical town plans to file a formal assessment complaint (Form RP-524). When must it reach the assessor or Board of Assessment Review?
options: Within 30 days after the final roll is filed in July
On or before Grievance Day, when the board meets
Any time before the first tax bill becomes due
Within 4 months after the owner's tax bill is paid
questions.explanation: The RP-524 must be filed with the assessor before, or with the BAR on, Grievance Day (usually the fourth Tuesday in May in towns); a form mailed in time but arriving late is not enough. The 30-day window after the final roll is the later SCAR/Article 7 deadline.
questions.citation: RPTL §524 (time and manner of filing complaint)

questions.q: Place these events of a typical New York town's assessment calendar in order: (1) final assessment roll filed, (2) taxable status date, (3) Grievance Day, (4) tentative assessment roll filed.
questions.explanation: In most towns: taxable status date March 1, tentative roll May 1, Grievance Day the fourth Tuesday in May, final roll July 1. Grievance must follow the tentative roll because owners can only contest a published assessment.

questions.q: A farmer in a typical town wants a new partial exemption to appear on this year's assessment roll. By when must the application generally be filed with the assessor?
options: The Grievance Day in late May
The final roll date of July 1
The taxable status date, March 1
The first day of the school tax year
questions.explanation: Exemption applications (including agricultural assessment applications) are generally due by the taxable status date, March 1 in most towns. Grievance Day is for contesting the tentative roll, not the normal deadline for new exemption applications.
questions.citation: RPTL §302 (taxable status date); exemption application rules

questions.q: An eligible homeowner lost her BAR grievance and wants Small Claims Assessment Review. Which statement about the petition is correct?
options: It must be filed within 30 days after the final roll is filed
It may be filed any time within one year of the BAR decision
It must be filed before Grievance Day with the town clerk
It requires a licensed attorney and a $500 index fee
questions.explanation: A SCAR petition must be filed within 30 days after the final assessment roll is filed (or notice of filing, if later), with a $30 fee, and an attorney is not required. Missing the 30-day window ends the SCAR option for that roll.

questions.q: The owner of a shopping center grieved her assessment and the Board of Assessment Review denied relief. What is her ordinary next step for judicial review?
options: A SCAR petition before a hearing officer
A second complaint to the same Board of Assessment Review
An appeal to the county clerk who records deeds
An Article 7 tax certiorari proceeding in Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Commercial owners use a tax certiorari proceeding under RPTL Article 7 in NY Supreme Court, generally commenced within 30 days after the final roll is filed. SCAR is limited to eligible owner-occupied one- to three-family homes and certain small vacant parcels.

questions.q: A Brooklyn homeowner believes the NYC Department of Finance overvalued her house. Where does she file her administrative assessment appeal?
options: The NYC Tax Commission
The county Board of Assessment Review
The Kings County clerk
The NYS Division of Licensing Services
questions.explanation: New York City has no town-style BAR or Grievance Day; administrative assessment appeals go to the NYC Tax Commission. Nassau likewise uses its own Assessment Review Commission, so the upstate BAR model does not apply.
questions.citation: NYC Charter and Administrative Code (NYC Tax Commission); RPTL Article 5

questions.q: In New York City, a 20-unit rental apartment building is in which property tax class?
options: Class 1
Class 3
Class 4
Class 2
questions.explanation: Class 2 covers primarily residential property not in class 1, including rental buildings of four or more units, co-ops, and larger condos. Class 1 is mostly one- to three-family homes; class 3 is utility property; class 4 is commercial and industrial property such as offices and hotels.

questions.q: Which NYC property would be placed in tax class 4?
options: A three-family house in the Bronx
A 50-unit co-op building in Manhattan
An office building in Long Island City
Equipment owned by an electric utility
questions.explanation: Class 4 holds commercial and industrial property such as office buildings, stores, hotels, and factories. Utility equipment is class 3, co-ops are class 2, and a three-family house is class 1.

questions.q: A couple lives in a Westchester home and buys a lake cottage upstate as a weekend getaway. Regarding STAR, which is correct?
options: They may receive STAR on both homes if each is owner-occupied
STAR can apply only to their primary residence, not the cottage
STAR reduces town and county taxes on any home they own
The cottage gets STAR if its seller had already received it
questions.explanation: STAR relieves school taxes on an owner's primary residence only, so a vacation home does not qualify. STAR does not reduce town or county taxes, and a seller's STAR benefit never transfers with the property.
questions.citation: RPTL §425; Tax Law §606(eee) (STAR exemption and credit)

questions.q: A longtime homeowner still receiving the STAR exemption on her school tax bill is considering switching to the STAR credit. What should she know?
options: The switch is temporary and reverses automatically next year
The credit replaces only her town tax, not her school tax
Once she switches to the credit, she cannot return to the exemption
The exemption may grow 2% a year, while the credit is frozen
questions.explanation: Switching from the STAR exemption to the STAR credit is irreversible. The trap reverses the growth rules: the exemption savings are frozen, while the credit can increase up to 2% a year.
questions.citation: RPTL §425; Tax Law §606(eee); NYS Tax Department STAR guidance

questions.q: A married couple owns and lives in their home. One spouse turns 65 in November of this year; the other is 60. For this year's Enhanced STAR age requirement, the couple:
options: Fails, because both owners must be 65 by January 1
Fails, because the younger spouse is under 62
Qualifies only after both spouses reach age 65
Meets it, if one owner is 65 by December 31 of the year
questions.explanation: Enhanced STAR requires that at least one resident owner (or a spouse who resides there) be 65 by December 31 of the benefit year, and their combined qualifying income must be within the limit. Requiring both spouses to be 65 is the common trap.

questions.q: A listing shows annual taxes of $4,100 because the 78-year-old seller receives Enhanced STAR and a senior citizens exemption. A 35-year-old buyer asks what she will pay. The licensee should explain that:
options: The seller's exemptions end with her ownership, so the buyer's taxes may be higher
The seller's exemptions pass to the buyer at closing for five more years
Taxes are fixed at the sale price, so the $4,100 figure will not change
The buyer keeps the exemptions if she files a grievance by Grievance Day
questions.explanation: Exemptions such as Enhanced STAR and the senior exemption depend on the owner's personal eligibility, so they do not transfer to a buyer who does not qualify. Advertising the seller's reduced bill as the buyer's future bill can mislead.

questions.q: How does the senior citizens exemption differ from Enhanced STAR?
options: The senior exemption is state-mandated; Enhanced STAR is optional
An owner may receive only one of the two in any given year
The senior exemption is local and can cover town and county taxes
Enhanced STAR can cut up to 50% of every tax on the bill
questions.explanation: The senior citizens exemption is adopted locally by each county, city, town, village, or school district and can reduce up to 50% of the assessment for those taxes; Enhanced STAR applies only to school taxes. Eligible owners may receive both, so "only one" is the trap.

questions.q: A church owns a building and uses the first floor for worship. It leases the second floor to a for-profit accounting firm. How is the building generally treated for property tax purposes?
options: Fully exempt, because a religious organization owns it
Fully taxable, because any rental income ends the exemption
Exempt only if the tenant firm agrees to pay the tax
Exempt for the worship space; the leased floor is taxable
questions.explanation: The religious/charitable exemption requires both qualifying ownership and qualifying use, so the portion used for worship stays exempt while the portion leased for a nonexempt purpose is taxable. Ownership alone is the trap.

questions.q: Land inside an agricultural district received an agricultural assessment last year. This year the owner sells it to a builder who starts constructing a subdivision. What is the likely property tax consequence?
options: A conversion payment recapturing part of the taxes saved
No consequence, because the owner changed but not the soil
A permanent exemption, because land in an ag district stays farmland
A transfer of the agricultural assessment to the builder's homes
questions.explanation: Converting land to a nonagricultural use within five years after it last received an agricultural assessment (eight years outside an ag district) triggers a conversion payment. Merely letting farmland sit idle is not a conversion; building a subdivision is.
questions.citation: Agriculture and Markets Law §305 and §306 (agricultural assessment; conversion payments)

questions.q: A county starts a tax foreclosure proceeding under RPTL Article 11 against a parcel with years of unpaid taxes. Calling this an in rem proceeding means that it:
options: Seeks a personal money judgment against the owner's wages
Is directed against the property itself rather than the owner
Can be brought only after the owner files for bankruptcy
Applies only to commercial property and not to homes
questions.explanation: In rem means against the thing: the action enforces the tax lien against the parcel, not a personal judgment against the owner. Article 11 in rem proceedings can reach residential as well as commercial parcels.
questions.citation: RPTL Article 11 (§1120 et seq., in rem tax foreclosure)

questions.q: Where a municipality sells its delinquent tax liens to an investor, what does the investor acquire at the sale?
options: Immediate title and the right to evict the owner
The owner's mortgage and the duty to pay the lender
The right to collect the debt, while the owner keeps title
A deed that cuts off the owner's right to pay the taxes
questions.explanation: A tax lien sale transfers the right to collect the delinquent taxes with interest and charges; the owner keeps title and can still pay off the lien. Title passes only if the lien is later foreclosed through the required legal process.
questions.citation: RPTL Article 11; NYC Admin. Code §11-319 et seq. (tax lien sales)

questions.q: Under New York's property tax cap, a school district that proposes a tax levy above its calculated levy limit must:
options: Obtain written consent from every property owner
Obtain at least 60% voter approval of the budget
Lower all assessments by the amount of the excess
Get approval from the State Board of Real Property
questions.explanation: The cap limits annual levy growth to the lesser of 2% or inflation (with adjustments and exclusions); a school budget exceeding the levy limit needs at least 60% voter approval. The cap governs the total levy, so an individual bill can still rise more than 2%.
questions.citation: Education Law §2023-a; General Municipal Law §3-c (property tax cap)

questions.q: A city adopts the homestead tax option after a reassessment. What is the main effect of this option?
options: Residential owners pay no school taxes for five years
Every parcel is assessed at a different percentage of value
All exemptions are replaced by one flat credit per household
Separate tax rates apply to homestead and non-homestead property
questions.explanation: The locally adopted homestead option creates two tax rates, one for homestead (mostly 1–3 family residential) property and one for non-homestead property, to keep residential owners from absorbing an outsized share after a reassessment. Assessments themselves stay at a uniform percentage of value.
questions.citation: RPTL Article 19 (§1901 et seq., homestead tax option)

questions.q: Under current federal law, interest on a home equity loan counts as deductible qualified residence interest only when the borrowed money is used to:
options: Pay off high-interest credit card balances the owner carries
