Buy, build, or substantially improve the home that secures it
Pay college tuition for the owner's dependent child
Purchase a vehicle the owner drives to work each day
questions.explanation: Home equity debt is deductible only if it is acquisition debt, meaning the proceeds buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing the loan (within the $750,000 acquisition-debt limit, made permanent by the 2025 tax law). Paying off credit cards or tuition with a home equity loan is personal use, so the interest is not deductible even though the loan is secured by the home.

questions.q: A New York homeowner itemizes deductions. Under the federal SALT limitation, which items share one capped deduction?
options: Real property taxes and state and local income (or sales) taxes combined
Real property taxes only, while state income taxes remain uncapped
Mortgage interest and real property taxes paid on the main home
State income taxes and federal income taxes withheld from wages
questions.explanation: The SALT cap limits the combined itemized deduction for state and local taxes: property taxes plus state and local income (or sales) taxes. The 2025 tax law raised the cap from $10,000 to $40,000 ($40,400 for 2026, phased down for high incomes, reverting to $10,000 in 2030). Mortgage interest is a separate deduction outside the SALT cap, and federal income tax is never deductible.

questions.q: A first-time buyer pays $9,000 of mortgage interest and property taxes this year, but she takes the standard deduction because it is larger than her total itemized deductions. How much additional federal tax benefit does the $9,000 give her?
options: A deduction of the full $9,000
A deduction of the interest portion only
No additional benefit at all
A deduction of half, or $4,500
questions.explanation: Mortgage interest and property taxes are itemized deductions. A taxpayer who takes the standard deduction cannot also deduct them, so the $9,000 produces no extra federal benefit; the trap is assuming homeowners always deduct these costs.

questions.q: At a July 1 closing, the seller had already paid the full calendar-year property tax, and the buyer reimbursed the seller for July through December as a proration credit. For federal income tax purposes, who deducts the July–December taxes?
options: The seller, because the seller wrote the check to the tax collector
Neither party, because proration credits are not deductible taxes
Each party deducts half of the full-year tax regardless of dates
The buyer, because those taxes cover the period the buyer owns it
questions.explanation: When real property is sold, the property tax for the year is divided by days of ownership: the seller deducts the part up to the sale date and the buyer deducts the rest. The buyer is treated as paying the July–December taxes through the proration, even though the seller paid the town.

questions.q: A married couple used the home-sale exclusion on their previous home 14 months ago. They now sell their current main home, and no job change, health issue, or unforeseen circumstance is involved. The full exclusion on this sale is generally:
options: Available, because married couples may use it every year
Unavailable, because it is a once-in-a-lifetime benefit
Unavailable, because it may be used only once in 2 years
Available, but only if both spouses are age 55 or older
questions.explanation: The §121 exclusion can be claimed repeatedly, but generally not more than once in any 2-year period. The once-in-a-lifetime, age-55 rule is the old pre-1997 exclusion and no longer applies.

questions.q: For the home-sale exclusion's use test, the 2 years the seller lived in the home during the 5 years before the sale:
options: Must be one unbroken 24-month stretch of residence
May be added up from separate periods within those 5 years
Must be the final 24 months immediately before the sale
Must be the first 24 months after the owner bought it
questions.explanation: The ownership and use tests require 24 months (730 days) within the 5-year period ending on the date of sale, and the months need not be consecutive. Requiring the last 2 years or an unbroken stretch is a common misstatement of the rule.

questions.q: To exclude up to $500,000 of gain on a joint return, a married couple selling their home must generally show that:
options: Either spouse meets the ownership test and both meet the use test
Both spouses are on title, though only one must have lived there
Only one spouse meets both the ownership and the use tests
Both spouses owned and lived in it for 5 of the last 8 years
questions.explanation: For the $500,000 joint exclusion, only one spouse needs to meet the 2-year ownership test, but both must meet the 2-year use test, and neither may have used the exclusion in the prior 2 years. If only one spouse qualifies, the couple is generally limited to that spouse's $250,000.

questions.q: A single owner bought a condo, lived in it for exactly 12 months, and then sold it because her employer transferred her across the country. Her gain is $140,000. Assuming the job move qualifies for a reduced exclusion, how much gain is taxable?
questions.explanation: A qualifying job move allows a reduced maximum exclusion prorated by months: 12 ÷ 24 × $250,000 = $125,000. Taxable gain = $140,000 − $125,000 = $15,000. Answering $0 wrongly applies the full $250,000, and $140,000 ignores the partial exclusion.

questions.q: A homeowner sells her main home for $60,000 less than her adjusted basis. For federal income tax purposes, the loss is:
options: Deductible against ordinary income at $3,000 per year
Not deductible, because the home is personal-use property
Fully deductible as a capital loss in the year of sale
Added to the basis of the next home the seller buys
questions.explanation: A loss on the sale of a personal residence is a nondeductible personal loss. The $3,000-per-year capital loss rule applies only to deductible capital losses, such as losses on investment property, so it is a trap here.

questions.q: A seller qualifies for the home-sale exclusion but earlier claimed $8,000 of depreciation for a home office inside the house. How is gain equal to that $8,000 generally treated?
options: It is excluded along with the rest of the qualifying gain
It is subtracted from the price as an ordinary closing cost
It is taxable even though the remaining gain is excluded
It raises the seller's exclusion limit by the same $8,000
questions.explanation: The §121 exclusion does not cover gain equal to depreciation claimed after May 6, 1997, so that portion is taxed while the remaining qualifying gain can still be excluded. Depreciation never increases the exclusion limit.

questions.q: A buyer paid $320,000 for a home plus $6,000 of title insurance, recording, and attorney fees. Later she added a $15,000 new roof and a $30,000 family room, and spent $4,000 repainting several rooms. What is her adjusted basis?
questions.explanation: Basis = $320,000 price + $6,000 capitalized closing costs + $15,000 roof + $30,000 addition = $371,000. Repainting is a repair, not a capital improvement, so including it ($375,000) is the trap; leaving out closing costs gives $365,000.

questions.q: An owner with an adjusted basis of $371,000 sells for $610,000, pays $36,000 in commission and other selling costs, and uses $250,000 of the proceeds to pay off her mortgage. What is her realized gain?
questions.explanation: Amount realized = $610,000 − $36,000 = $574,000; gain = $574,000 − $371,000 = $203,000. The mortgage payoff reduces cash at closing but not the gain; $324,000 is net cash after payoff ($610,000 − $36,000 − $250,000), and $239,000 ignores the selling costs.

questions.q: Which expenditure on a personal residence is a capital improvement that is added to the owner's basis?
options: Installing a new central air-conditioning system
Repainting the living room and the front hallway
Fixing a leaking faucet in the kitchen sink
Replacing one cracked pane in a bedroom window
questions.explanation: A capital improvement adds value, prolongs useful life, or adapts the home to new uses, as a new central air system does. Painting, fixing leaks, and replacing a broken pane only keep the home in ordinary repair, so they do not increase basis.

questions.q: Each of the following generally increases a homeowner's basis EXCEPT:
options: Owner's title insurance premium paid at the purchase closing
The cost of building a new detached two-car garage
Annual homeowner's insurance premiums paid each year
A special assessment for new sidewalks in front of the lot
questions.explanation: Hazard insurance premiums are ongoing personal living costs and are never added to basis. Owner's title insurance is a capitalized acquisition cost, a garage is a capital improvement, and assessments for local improvements such as sidewalks increase basis.

questions.q: An investor buys an office building for $1,560,000, of which $390,000 is allocated to the land. Using straight-line depreciation over the nonresidential recovery period, what is the annual depreciation deduction (ignoring partial-year conventions)?
questions.explanation: Depreciable building = $1,560,000 − $390,000 = $1,170,000; $1,170,000 ÷ 39 years = $30,000. $40,000 wrongly depreciates the land ($1,560,000 ÷ 39), and $42,545 uses the 27.5-year residential period ($1,170,000 ÷ 27.5).

questions.q: An investor bought a rental house for $500,000, with $87,500 allocated to land, and claimed $15,000 of depreciation each year for 6 years. She now sells for $650,000 (ignore selling costs). What is her gain?
questions.explanation: Depreciation reduces basis: $15,000 × 6 = $90,000; adjusted basis = $500,000 − $90,000 = $410,000; gain = $650,000 − $410,000 = $240,000. Ignoring depreciation gives $150,000, and subtracting the land from basis gives $327,500 ($650,000 − $322,500).

questions.q: An investor owns several properties. Which one may she depreciate for federal income tax purposes?
options: The land underneath her rental duplex
The duplex building that she rents out
The house she lives in as her main home
A vacant lot she holds for appreciation
questions.explanation: Only property used in a trade or business or held to produce income, with a limited useful life, can be depreciated: the rental building qualifies. Land never wears out, and a personal residence is not income-producing, so neither is depreciable.

questions.q: A mixed-use building earns 85% of its gross rents from apartments and 15% from a ground-floor store. For depreciation, the building is generally recovered over:
options: 39 years, because any commercial use makes it nonresidential
27.5 years for the apartments and 39 years for the store
27.5 years, because at least 80% of rents come from dwellings
15 years, because it is classified as a mixed-use property
questions.explanation: A building is residential rental property, depreciated over 27.5 years, if at least 80% of its gross rental income comes from dwelling units. At 85% residential rents, the whole building uses 27.5 years; the split-recovery option is the trap.

questions.q: In a delayed §1031 exchange, the investor's relinquished property closes on March 1, 2026. Which deadlines generally apply?
options: Identify by April 15, 2026; acquire by August 28, 2026
Identify by April 15, 2026; acquire by October 12, 2026
Identify by March 31, 2026; acquire by August 28, 2026
Identify by April 15, 2026; acquire by March 1, 2027
questions.explanation: Both periods run from the relinquished closing: March 1 + 45 days = April 15 to identify, and March 1 + 180 days = August 28 to acquire (or the tax-return due date, if earlier). The 180 days are not added after the 45 days, which is how October 12 is reached.

questions.q: An investor has a $300,000 realized gain in a §1031 exchange. The replacement property costs less, and she receives $60,000 in cash at the closing. How much gain is recognized (taxable) now?
questions.explanation: Cash received is boot, and recognized gain is the lesser of boot received or realized gain: $60,000 vs. $300,000, so $60,000 is taxed now and $240,000 is deferred. $240,000 is the deferred amount, not the taxable amount.

questions.q: An investor exchanges a building subject to a $400,000 mortgage for a replacement building with a $300,000 mortgage. No cash is paid or received. Which statement is correct?
options: The exchange is fully deferred because no cash changed hands
The $100,000 debt relief is boot that can produce taxable gain
The exchange fails because the two mortgages must be equal
The $100,000 debt reduction is deductible as a capital loss
questions.explanation: Net relief from debt is treated like cash received, so $400,000 − $300,000 = $100,000 of mortgage boot can be taxed up to the realized gain. The trap is thinking only cash counts as boot; the investor could have avoided it by adding cash or taking on more debt.

questions.q: Why does an investor doing a delayed §1031 exchange use a qualified intermediary?
options: To appraise both properties and confirm they are like-kind
To obtain advance IRS approval of the exchange before closing
To hold the sale proceeds so the investor never receives them
To act as the buyer's agent in locating the replacement property
questions.explanation: If the investor actually or constructively receives the sale proceeds, the exchange fails and the gain is taxable. The qualified intermediary holds the funds and uses them to buy the replacement; no advance IRS approval exists.

questions.q: Which exchange can qualify as like-kind under §1031?
options: A rental house traded for vacant land held for investment
A personal residence traded for a rental condominium
A rental building traded for a fleet of delivery trucks
A builder's unsold new homes traded for an apartment building
questions.explanation: Any real property held for investment or business use is like-kind to other such real property, so improved rental property for raw investment land qualifies. A personal home is not investment property, trucks are personal property (excluded since 2018), and a builder's inventory is held for sale.

questions.q: An investor's relinquished property had an adjusted basis of $400,000 and sold for $650,000. She buys a $900,000 replacement, adds $250,000 of her own cash, and receives no boot. What is her basis in the replacement property?
questions.explanation: Deferred gain = $650,000 − $400,000 = $250,000. Replacement basis = $900,000 cost − $250,000 deferred gain = $650,000 (equivalently, $400,000 carried-over basis + $250,000 cash added). Using full cost of $900,000 would erase the deferred gain.

questions.q: A seller sells land for $400,000 with an adjusted basis of $240,000 and takes back a purchase-money note. No mortgage is assumed. In the year of sale she receives an $80,000 down payment. Using the installment method, how much gain does she report that year?
questions.explanation: Gross profit = $400,000 − $240,000 = $160,000; gross profit ratio = $160,000 ÷ $400,000 = 40%. Gain reported = 40% × $80,000 = $32,000. $48,000 wrongly applies the 60% basis share, and $160,000 reports all gain up front.

questions.q: A father bought a house for $90,000. It was worth $410,000 when he died and left it to his daughter, who sold it a few months later for $425,000. What is her taxable gain (ignore selling costs)?
questions.explanation: Inherited property generally takes a stepped-up basis equal to fair market value at death: $410,000. Gain = $425,000 − $410,000 = $15,000. Using the father's $90,000 cost gives $335,000, which is the trap.

questions.q: A father bought a house for $90,000 and, while still alive, gives it to his daughter when it is worth $410,000. Her basis for figuring gain on a later sale is generally:
options: $90,000, carried over from the father
$410,000, the value on the gift date
$0, because she paid nothing for it
$250,000, the gift's excluded amount
questions.explanation: A lifetime gift generally carries over the donor's basis ($90,000), so the built-in gain follows the property. Only property received at death gets a stepped-up basis to fair market value; confusing the two is a common trap.

questions.q: To qualify for long-term capital gain treatment, investment real estate must generally be held for:
options: At least 6 months before the sale
More than 1 year before the sale
At least 2 of the 5 years before the sale
More than 3 years before the sale
questions.explanation: Gain on a capital asset held more than one year is long-term and qualifies for lower capital gain rates. The 2-of-5-year test belongs to the home-sale exclusion, not the holding period.

questions.q: A house in Monroe County sells for $437,250. What is the New York State real estate transfer tax?
questions.explanation: The rate is $2 for each $500 or fractional part: $437,250 ÷ $500 = 874.5, rounded up to 875 units × $2 = $1,750. Rounding down gives $1,748, and multiplying without rounding units gives $1,749.

questions.q: A seller closes and records the deed but fails to pay the NYS real estate transfer tax. Under the Tax Law, the unpaid tax:
options: Is waived once the deed has been recorded
Is deducted from the listing broker's commission
Becomes a lien only on the seller's other property
Becomes the obligation of the buyer (grantee)
questions.explanation: The grantor (seller) is primarily liable for the NYS transfer tax, but if the grantor fails to pay, the grantee (buyer) becomes liable for it. The tax is not waived by recording, and brokers are not liable for it.

questions.q: A single-family home in Westchester County sells for $1,250,000. How much is the additional 1% "mansion tax," and who pays it?
options: $12,500, paid by the buyer
$12,500, paid by the seller
$2,500, paid by the buyer
$5,000, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: The mansion tax is 1% of the entire consideration once residential price reaches $1,000,000: 1% × $1,250,000 = $12,500, paid by the buyer. $2,500 taxes only the excess over $1 million, and $5,000 is the seller's basic transfer tax ($1,250,000 ÷ $500 × $2).

questions.q: A Manhattan condominium unit sells for $750,000. Considering only the NYC Real Property Transfer Tax (not state tax), what is the tax?
questions.explanation: For residential property over $500,000, the NYC RPTT is 1.425% of the full price, not a tiered rate: 1.425% × $750,000 = $10,687.50. $8,562.50 wrongly applies 1% to the first $500,000 and 1.425% to the rest.

questions.q: A Brooklyn house sells for $600,000. What is the seller's combined NYS transfer tax and NYC Real Property Transfer Tax?
questions.explanation: NYS: $600,000 ÷ $500 × $2 = $2,400. NYC residential over $500,000: 1.425% × $600,000 = $8,550. Total = $10,950. $8,550 omits the state tax, $8,400 uses NYC 1%, and $8,825 wrongly tiers the NYC rate ($5,000 + $1,425 + $2,400).
questions.citation: NY Tax Law §1402; NYC Admin. Code §11-2102

questions.q: A buyer purchases a home for $480,000 with a $384,000 mortgage. Assuming a combined mortgage recording tax rate of 1.05% in that county, what is the mortgage recording tax?
questions.explanation: Mortgage recording tax is based on the secured debt, not the price: 1.05% × $384,000 = $4,032. Using the price gives $5,040, and taxing the $96,000 down payment gives $1,008.

questions.q: A homeowner owes $280,000 on her mortgage and refinances into a $350,000 loan using a consolidation, extension, and modification agreement (CEMA) with the existing mortgage assigned. Mortgage recording tax is generally due on:
options: The full $350,000 new loan amount
The $280,000 existing unpaid balance
Only the $70,000 of new money borrowed
The combined $630,000 of both mortgages
questions.explanation: With a CEMA, the existing mortgage is assigned and modified rather than paid off, so recording tax was already paid on the $280,000 balance; only the new money ($350,000 − $280,000 = $70,000) is taxed. This is why CEMAs save money on New York refinances.

questions.q: A foreign individual sells a $900,000 investment building to a U.S. buyer who will not live there. Under FIRPTA, the buyer must generally withhold:
options: $90,000, which is 10% of the sales price
$45,000, which is 15% of the seller's gain
$135,000, which is 15% of the sales price
Nothing, because the seller owes the tax
questions.explanation: FIRPTA requires the buyer, as withholding agent, to withhold 15% of the amount realized (gross price): 15% × $900,000 = $135,000. Withholding is on the gross price, not the gain, which is the $45,000 trap.

questions.q: An individual buyer pays a foreign seller $280,000 for a condo and has definite plans to live in it as a residence. Under FIRPTA, the buyer generally must withhold:
options: Nothing, under the residence exception for $300,000 or less
$42,000, which is the standard 15% of the purchase price
$28,000, which is the reduced 10% rate for residences
Nothing, because condominiums are exempt from FIRPTA
questions.explanation: No FIRPTA withholding is required when an individual buyer acquires the property as a residence and the amount realized is $300,000 or less. The reduced 10% rate applies to residences priced above $300,000 up to $1,000,000.

questions.q: A Florida resident with no New York residency sells her vacation home in the Catskills at a gain. At closing, New York generally requires her to:
options: Have the buyer withhold 15% of the price for the state
Pay estimated NYS income tax on the gain before recording
Pay nothing, because only NYS residents owe state income tax
Pay the state tax only after filing her federal return
questions.explanation: A nonresident individual selling NY real property must pay estimated NYS personal income tax on the gain (Form IT-2663) at closing; the county clerk will not record the deed without it. The 15% buyer withholding is the federal FIRPTA rule for foreign sellers, not a NY rule.

questions.q: For federal income tax purposes, how are real estate transfer taxes generally treated by the seller or buyer who pays them at closing?
options: Both parties deduct them as property taxes in the year of sale
The seller deducts them as SALT; the buyer adds them to basis
Neither party's taxes are affected by any transfer tax paid
They reduce the seller's amount realized and add to the buyer's basis
questions.explanation: Transfer taxes are not deductible as real property taxes. A seller treats them as a selling expense that reduces the amount realized (lowering gain), and a buyer who pays them adds them to basis.

questions.q: A buyer closes on the purchase of an apartment in a New York cooperative. What does the buyer actually acquire?
options: A deed to the apartment plus an undivided interest in the common elements
Shares in the cooperative corporation plus a proprietary lease for the apartment
A recorded leasehold estate in the apartment plus a deed to a share of the land
Fee title to the apartment, with the corporation owning only the lobby and grounds
questions.explanation: A co-op corporation owns the building (or its ground lease); the purchaser receives stock in the corporation and a proprietary lease giving occupancy rights. No deed to the unit is delivered; a deed plus an undivided common interest describes a condominium.
questions.citation: NY cooperative ownership (corporate shares and proprietary lease); contrast NY RPL Article 9-B

questions.q: Which best describes what a condominium unit owner owns in New York?
options: Stock in a corporation that owns the building, plus a lease for the unit
Fee title to the unit only, while the association separately owns all land and common areas
Fee title to the unit plus an appurtenant undivided percentage interest in the common elements
A long-term leasehold in the unit from the sponsor, renewable by the board of managers
questions.explanation: A condo owner holds the unit as real property (commonly in fee simple) plus an undivided interest in the common elements, which can include the land. The common interest travels with the unit. An association owning all common areas describes a typical HOA, not a condo.

questions.q: For legal purposes, how are the shares a co-op shareholder holds in the cooperative corporation classified?
options: Real property, because they are tied to a specific apartment
A fixture, because the apartment is attached to the building
A real property interest conveyed by deed and recorded
Personal property
questions.explanation: Co-op shares are personal property, even though they carry the right to occupy a specific apartment under the proprietary lease. That is why co-op sales use stock transfers and share loans rather than deeds and real-property mortgages.
questions.citation: NY cooperative ownership; NY UCC Article 9 (shares as personal property collateral)

questions.q: How are real estate taxes handled for an individual condominium unit in New York?
options: Each unit is separately assessed and taxed, and the owner receives the unit's own tax bill
The whole building is taxed as a single parcel, and the board pays the bill out of common charges
Taxes are paid by the sponsor until every unit in the building is sold
The unit owner pays a share of taxes through monthly maintenance to the corporation
questions.explanation: Under the Condominium Act each unit, with its common interest, is a separate tax parcel billed to its owner. A single building tax paid through monthly maintenance describes a co-op, where the corporation owns the building.

questions.q: A co-op shareholder asks what the monthly maintenance payment covers. Which answer is most accurate?
options: Only the shareholder's personal share-loan payment to the bank
A proportionate share of building operating costs, real estate taxes, and the underlying mortgage debt service
Only cleaning, staff, and utilities for the common areas, since each shareholder receives a separate tax bill
Installments of the flip tax owed to the city on each apartment
questions.explanation: Maintenance funds the corporation's operations plus the shareholder's allocated share of the building's real estate taxes and any underlying (blanket) mortgage. A personal share loan is paid separately to the shareholder's own lender.
questions.citation: NY cooperative ownership (proprietary lease maintenance obligations)

questions.q: A condo seller accepts a buyer's offer. The condominium's declaration and bylaws give the board of managers a right of first refusal. What must happen before closing?
options: The board must interview the buyer and may then reject the purchase without stating any reason
The buyer must purchase shares in the condominium and sign a proprietary lease with the board of managers
The board must be offered the chance to buy on the same terms, or must waive that right in writing
Nothing, because New York condominiums cannot restrict a unit owner's resale
questions.explanation: Where the governing documents create a right of first refusal, the board may elect to acquire the unit on the same terms or waive the right; a waiver is commonly delivered before closing. A co-op-style admission interview and shares belong to cooperatives, not condos.
questions.citation: Condominium declaration and bylaws; NY RPL Article 9-B

questions.q: A co-op board reviewing a purchase application may NOT lawfully reject an applicant on which of these grounds?
options: Liquid assets below the board's written post-closing reserve standard
An incomplete board package after repeated requests for documents
A debt-to-income ratio above the board's financial policy
The applicant's household includes two young children
questions.explanation: Co-op boards have broad business-judgment discretion over financial qualifications and often need not state reasons, but they may not reject on a protected basis. Familial status (children under 18) is protected under both federal and New York fair housing law.
questions.citation: NY Executive Law § 296; Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604

questions.q: Which government office reviews and accepts for filing the offering plans for new condominiums and co-op conversions in New York?
options: The New York Attorney General's Real Estate Finance Bureau
The Department of State's Division of Licensing Services
New York State Homes and Community Renewal
The local building department that issues the certificate of occupancy
questions.explanation: Under the Martin Act, sponsors offering condo or co-op interests to the public must file an offering plan with the Attorney General, whose Real Estate Finance Bureau reviews it. DOS licenses brokers and salespersons; it does not accept offering plans.

questions.q: In a New York condo or co-op offering, what is the 'red herring'?
options: The final offering plan as printed and distributed after the Attorney General accepts it for filing
A preliminary version of the offering plan that has not yet been accepted for filing
A notice the sponsor sends to purchasers when it abandons the offering plan before closing
A tenant's formal objection to a conversion plan
questions.explanation: The red herring is the preliminary offering plan, named for the red legend stating it is not final and not yet accepted. Once accepted for filing, the plan is commonly called the black book.
questions.citation: NY GBL § 352-e (Martin Act); NY AG offering-plan regulations

questions.q: A sponsor's salesperson tells a prospect: 'The Attorney General accepted our offering plan, so the state has confirmed these prices are a good investment.' Why is this statement wrong?
options: The Attorney General accepts offering plans only for buildings outside New York City; NYC plans go to HPD
Offering plans are reviewed and accepted by the Department of State's Division of Licensing Services instead
Acceptance for filing reflects disclosure review only; it does not endorse the price or investment value
The Attorney General's acceptance certifies only that construction is free of defects, not that prices are fair
questions.explanation: Acceptance for filing is a disclosure review under the Martin Act, not a government guarantee of fair price, value, profit, or construction quality. Representing it as an endorsement is misleading.

questions.q: A sponsor has an accepted CPS-1 application to test the market for a new condo, but the offering plan has not yet been accepted. A prospect offers a $2,000 fully refundable payment to hold a unit. What may the sponsor do?
options: Accept it, because a fully refundable payment is permitted during an accepted CPS-1 market-testing period
Accept it, as long as the money is held in a segregated escrow account by the sponsor's attorney
Take a nonbinding reservation without collecting money, then collect the deposit once the plan is accepted
Accept no deposit or reservation; it may only note the prospect's nonbinding indication of interest
questions.explanation: Under CPS-1, no deposits and no reservations, binding or nonbinding, may be accepted until the offering plan is accepted for filing. Refundability or escrow does not cure the violation; only a nonbinding indication of interest is allowed.
questions.citation: NY AG Cooperative Policy Statement No. 1 (CPS-1)

questions.q: A co-op contract says the seller will pay the 'flip tax.' What is a flip tax?
options: A transfer fee imposed by the co-op corporation under its documents, usually paid by the seller
The New York State real estate transfer tax as it applies to transfers of co-op shares
A New York City surcharge imposed on investors who resell an apartment within one year of buying
A penalty the Attorney General imposes on sponsors who sell units too quickly
questions.explanation: Despite its name, a flip tax is not a government tax; it is a charge the co-op corporation levies on transfers under its proprietary lease or bylaws, commonly paid by the seller and often credited to the building's reserves. Government transfer taxes are a separate item.

questions.q: In co-op financing, what is a recognition agreement?
options: An agreement in which the buyer and seller formally recognize which broker was the procuring cause and earned the commission
An agreement among the share lender, the co-op corporation, and the shareholder acknowledging the lender's security interest
A letter from the Attorney General recognizing the offering plan as effective so the sponsor can begin closings
The board's written approval recognizing the purchaser as a shareholder after the admissions interview
questions.explanation: The recognition agreement is signed by the share lender, the cooperative corporation, and the borrowing shareholder. It acknowledges the lender's security interest and sets duties such as notifying the lender of a maintenance default.
questions.citation: Co-op share financing; NY UCC Article 9

questions.q: A co-op buyer financing the purchase asks whether the bank will record a mortgage against the apartment with the county clerk. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; a co-op loan is recorded with the county clerk against the unit exactly like a house mortgage
No; the bank instead takes and holds a deed to the apartment until the loan is fully paid off
No; the loan is secured by the shares and proprietary lease, perfected by a UCC financing statement
No; the co-op corporation itself becomes the borrower and adds the loan to its underlying mortgage
questions.explanation: Because co-op shares are personal property, the purchaser's financing is a share loan secured by the stock and proprietary lease, perfected through UCC filing. It is not a recorded real-property mortgage on an individual unit.

questions.q: Which document submits a property to New York's Condominium Act and describes the units, common elements, and each unit's common interest?
options: The proprietary lease
The preliminary offering plan
The house rules
The declaration
questions.explanation: The recorded declaration creates the condominium regime and defines units, common elements, and percentage interests. Bylaws govern administration; a proprietary lease is a co-op document.

questions.q: A condo unit owner stops paying common charges for six months. What remedy does the board of managers generally have?
options: A lien on the unit for the unpaid common charges, which can be foreclosed
Cancellation of the owner's proprietary lease and forfeiture of the owner's shares
No remedy, because common charges are voluntary contributions
A complaint asking the Attorney General to fine the owner under the offering plan
questions.explanation: Unpaid condo common charges become a lien on the unit that the board can enforce, including by foreclosure. Cancelling a proprietary lease is a co-op remedy because only co-ops use proprietary leases.

questions.q: A rental building is being converted to a co-op under a non-eviction plan. A tenant in occupancy decides not to buy. What is the tenant's status?
options: The tenant must vacate when the plan is declared effective
The tenant may remain as a tenant and cannot be evicted for failing to buy
The tenant must buy within 90 days or lose the apartment
The tenant may be evicted one year after the plan is declared effective
questions.explanation: A non-eviction plan does not permit eviction of non-purchasing tenants merely because they decline to buy; they remain tenants, subject to ordinary lawful grounds such as nonpayment. Eviction plans are a different, now heavily restricted category.

questions.q: What is a 'condop'?
options: A co-op whose bylaws permit unlimited subletting and no board interview, so it operates like a condo
A condo whose board interviews and approves every buyer the way a co-op does, although buyers still receive deeds
A condominium in which the residential portion is one unit owned by a co-op corporation, whose buyers receive shares
A townhouse community where owners hold their own lots and belong to a homeowners' association
questions.explanation: In a true condop, the building is a condominium in which one unit (the residential part) is owned by a cooperative corporation, often with separately owned commercial units. Residential buyers get shares and a proprietary lease, not condo deeds; flexible rules alone do not make a co-op a condop.
questions.citation: NY RPL Article 9-B; cooperative ownership structure

questions.q: In a typical homeowners' association (HOA) subdivision, what does each homeowner own?
options: Shares in the association plus a proprietary lease for the home, as in a co-op building
An undivided percentage interest in all land in the community, including the clubhouse and roads
Nothing; the association owns the homes and leases them to residents
Fee title to the home and lot; the association owns the common areas, funded by assessments
questions.explanation: HOA homeowners own their own lots and homes in fee; the association holds title to the common areas and charges assessments to maintain them. An undivided interest in common elements is the condo model.
questions.citation: Homeowners' association declaration; NY GBL § 352-e (HOA offerings)

questions.q: Which homeowners insurance form is designed for a condominium unit owner to cover the unit's interior improvements, personal property, and liability?
options: HO-6
HO-3
HO-4
HO-2
questions.explanation: HO-6 is the unit-owner form used for condos (and commonly co-ops), complementing the association's master policy on the building. HO-4 is a renter's policy; HO-2 and HO-3 are for owners of whole houses.

questions.q: An owner who bought a co-op apartment ten years ago is now reselling it. Must the owner file an offering plan with the Attorney General?
options: Yes; every resale requires the seller to file an amendment to the building's offering plan
No; offering-plan filing applies to sponsor public offerings, not an ordinary owner's resale
Yes, but only if the price exceeds $1 million and the mansion tax applies
Only if the buyer is financing the purchase with a share loan
questions.explanation: The Martin Act filing requirement covers public offerings by sponsors (and holders of unsold shares under the plan). An ordinary shareholder's resale of an apartment is not automatically a new public offering.

questions.q: For federal income tax purposes, what may a tenant-stockholder in a qualifying cooperative generally deduct?
options: Nothing, because co-op shares are personal property
The entire monthly maintenance payment, including the building's operating and staff costs
Their proportionate share of the corporation's real estate taxes and mortgage interest
Only the flip tax paid when they bought the apartment
questions.explanation: IRC § 216 lets tenant-stockholders of a qualifying cooperative deduct their proportionate share of the corporation's real estate taxes and mortgage interest. Operating costs in maintenance are not deductible, and the corporation must meet § 216's tests.

questions.q: Under New York's Condominium Act, which method may the declaration use to set each unit's percentage of common interest?
options: The unit's approximate share of total fair value or floor area, or equal shares
A yearly board vote based on how often the owner uses the amenities
The county assessor's current market value shown on each unit's tax bill
The number of people occupying each unit on the day of closing
questions.explanation: RPL §339-i(1) lets the declaration fix the common interest by approximate relative fair value or floor area at the time of the declaration, by equal percentages, or by floor space adjusted for location and similar factors. It is fixed in the declaration, not reset by usage, occupancy, or each year's tax assessment.

questions.q: A condo owner plans to sell her apartment to one buyer and separately sell her 1.8% interest in the common elements to an investor. What is the legal result?
options: She may, if the board of managers approves the split in writing
She may, but the investor must then pay the unit's common charges
She cannot; the common interest may not be separated from the unit
She may only if the declaration calls the interest a limited common element
questions.explanation: The common interest is appurtenant to the unit and, under RPL §339-i(2), shall not be separated from the unit to which it belongs. Board approval cannot authorize a split that the statute forbids.

questions.q: An owner in a 40-unit condominium sues to partition the building's parking garage so she can own her proportionate share of it outright. How should the court rule?
options: Grant it if a majority of the unit owners consent to the partition
Deny it; common elements stay undivided and are not subject to partition
Grant it once she has owned her unit for at least ten years
Grant it for parking areas but not for structural common elements
questions.explanation: RPL §339-i(3) provides that common elements remain undivided and no right to partition exists while the property is a condominium; any contrary provision is void. Majority consent, length of ownership, and the type of common element do not create a partition right.

questions.q: Which action is required to change the percentage of common interest assigned to a condominium unit in the declaration?
options: A resolution adopted by the board of managers at its annual meeting
A majority vote of all unit owners at a duly called special meeting
An amended declaration with consent of all unit owners affected
A new appraisal of the unit ordered by the owner's mortgage lender
questions.explanation: Under RPL §339-i(2) the common interest has a permanent character and may not be altered without the consent of all affected unit owners, expressed in an amended declaration. A board resolution or simple majority vote cannot reallocate someone's interest.

questions.q: A condominium's annual operating budget is $612,000. Unit 4C's common interest is 1.75%. What are Unit 4C's monthly common charges?
questions.explanation: Common expenses are charged by common interest: $612,000 × 0.0175 = $10,710 per year; $10,710 ÷ 12 = $892.50 per month. $10,710 is the annual figure mistaken for monthly; $1,071 and $8,925 are decimal-point slips.

questions.q: A 100-unit condominium levies a $1,250,000 special assessment for façade repairs, allocated by common interest. Unit 9F holds a 0.8% common interest. What is 9F's share?
questions.explanation: Allocation by common interest: $1,250,000 × 0.008 = $10,000. $12,500 is the equal-share trap ($1,250,000 ÷ 100 units), which ignores the declaration's percentages; $1,000 and $100,000 are decimal errors.

questions.q: A declaration sets common interests strictly by floor area. Unit 3A has 1,400 sq ft, and all units together total 56,000 sq ft. What is Unit 3A's common interest?
questions.explanation: 1,400 ÷ 56,000 = 0.025 = 2.50%. Dividing 56,000 by 1,400 gives 40, which leads to the 4% mistake; 0.25% and 25% misplace the decimal.

questions.q: In a typical New York condominium, which of these is NOT a common element?
options: The land beneath and around the building itself
The building's foundation, exterior walls, and roof
The lobby, hallways, elevators, and stairwells
The interior space inside an owner's unit boundaries
questions.explanation: RPL §339-e(3) lists the common elements, unless the declaration provides otherwise: the land, structural parts such as foundations, main walls, and roofs, and shared areas like lobbies, halls, stairs, and elevators. The space inside the unit's boundaries is the unit itself, owned exclusively by its owner. Saying that condo owners own no land is a known trap; the land is a common element they own in undivided shares.

questions.q: The declaration describes a balcony reachable only from Unit 12B as a common element reserved for 12B's exclusive use. Who owns the balcony?
options: All unit owners in common, with use reserved to 12B
The owner of Unit 12B, in fee, as part of the unit
The board of managers, as property of the association
The sponsor, until every unit in the building has sold
questions.explanation: A limited common element remains part of the common elements owned by all unit owners in undivided shares, but the declaration reserves its use to one or more units. RPL §339-i(4) recognizes such substantially exclusive advantages. The board administers common elements; it does not own them.

questions.q: A condo's declaration and bylaws authorize allocating costs by exclusive use. The board charges roof-deck upkeep only to the three penthouses that alone can reach the deck. Is this proper?
options: No; every expense must be split strictly by common interest
Yes; the documents authorize allocation based on exclusive use
Yes; a board may shift any cost to the owners it chooses
No; such costs bind penthouse owners only if agreed at closing
questions.explanation: RPL §339-m normally spreads common expenses by common interest, but it permits special allocation based on exclusive use or control of particular common areas when the declaration and bylaws authorize it. Without that authorization the board could not do this, and the power is not unlimited.

questions.q: Which condominium document, attached to the declaration, governs administration such as electing the board, holding meetings, and collecting common charges?
options: The offering plan
The bylaws
The unit deed
The house rules
questions.explanation: Under RPL §339-u the operation of the property is governed by the bylaws, a true copy of which is annexed to the declaration, and §339-v(1) requires them to cover the election of the board, calling of owners' meetings, and collection of common charges. The offering plan is a sponsor's disclosure document, and house rules are detailed rules adopted under the bylaws.

questions.q: A condo board adopts a house rule that conflicts with a provision of the recorded declaration. Which controls?
options: The declaration, which ranks above board-adopted rules
The house rule, because it was adopted most recently
Whichever provision is more restrictive on owners
The house rule, once posted in the building lobby
questions.explanation: The governing documents form a hierarchy: the Condominium Act, then the declaration, then the bylaws, then rules the board adopts under them. A rule cannot override the declaration, regardless of when it was adopted or how strict it is.

questions.q: A buyer's attorney reviews the deed to a condominium unit before closing. Which would the deed ordinarily include?
options: A metes-and-bounds survey of only the unit's interior walls
The stock certificate number and the shares allocated
The unit designation, declaration reference, and common interest
The proprietary lease term and the monthly maintenance due
questions.explanation: RPL §339-o requires a unit deed to include a description of the land with the recording data of the declaration, the unit designation from the declaration, the use for which the unit is intended, and the unit's common interest. Shares and a proprietary lease belong to a co-op, not a condo.

questions.q: A condo owner wants to borrow against her unit. May she give a mortgage on it?
options: Yes; the unit and its common interest are real property
No; only the board may mortgage the building as a whole
Only with written consent from every other unit owner
Only through a share loan perfected by a UCC filing
questions.explanation: Under RPL §339-g each unit with its common interest is real property for all purposes, so the owner may convey or mortgage it like a house. A share loan with a UCC filing is co-op financing.

questions.q: A married couple is buying a condominium unit in New York. How may they take title?
options: Only in one spouse's name, as condo units allow a sole owner
Only as joint tenants, because the common elements are shared
Only as tenants in common, unless the board approves otherwise
As tenants by the entirety, like any other real property
questions.explanation: A condo unit is real property, and RPL §339-i(3) confirms that the no-partition rule for common elements does not prevent ownership of a unit by the entirety, jointly, or in common. Married couples commonly take title as tenants by the entirety.

questions.q: The owner of one unit in a 60-unit condominium fails to pay the unit's real estate taxes. Against what may the taxing authority enforce the tax?
options: The entire building, including every other owner's unit
All units, by adding the shortfall to everyone's common charges
Other units only if the board guaranteed the owner's taxes
Only that unit and its common interest, a separate tax parcel
questions.explanation: RPL §339-y treats each unit and its common interest as a separate parcel for assessment and taxation; the building and common elements are not a parcel. The unpaid tax is a lien on that unit only, not on neighbors' units.

questions.q: A condo unit has a first mortgage and a home equity loan, both recorded before the board files its lien for unpaid common charges. How does the common-charge lien rank?
options: Behind every mortgage that was recorded before the lien was filed
Ahead of all other liens, including the unit's real estate taxes
Behind taxes and the first mortgage but ahead of the home equity loan
Equal in rank with the home equity loan, sharing any proceeds
questions.explanation: RPL §339-z makes the common-charge lien prior to all other liens except tax liens, sums unpaid on a first mortgage of record, and certain government-agency mortgages. A second mortgage or HELOC is junior even if recorded earlier, which is the trap in the first-in-time distractor.

questions.q: A condo board files a notice of lien for unpaid common charges. If the charges are not paid, how long does the lien remain in effect?
options: One year from the date the notice of lien is filed
Ten years from the date of the first missed payment
Six years from the date the notice of lien is filed
Indefinitely, until the unit is next sold or refinanced
questions.explanation: Under RPL §339-aa the lien continues until paid or until six years from filing, whichever is sooner, and may be foreclosed like a mortgage. One year is the typical mechanic's-lien duration, which is a different lien.

questions.q: Before closing, a condo buyer gets a written statement from the board showing $1,200 in unpaid common charges. After closing, the board finds $3,000 was actually owed. Who owes the extra $1,800?
options: The buyer, because the lien for charges runs with the unit
No one; neither party is liable beyond the $1,200 stated
The seller, and the unit stays subject to a lien meanwhile
The buyer and seller jointly, each owing half the shortfall
questions.explanation: RPL §339-z entitles a grantor or grantee to a statement of unpaid common charges, and neither is liable for, nor is the unit subject to a lien for, pre-conveyance charges beyond the amount stated. That is why buyers' attorneys order the statement.

questions.q: A condo owner who never uses the pool or gym tells the board she will stop paying the part of her common charges that funds them. What is her legal position?
options: She still owes the full charges despite not using the amenities
She may deduct the amenity share after notifying the board
She owes only the share for structural and safety items
She is exempt once she signs a written waiver of use
questions.explanation: RPL §339-x provides that no unit owner may escape liability for common charges by waiving use or enjoyment of any common elements. Charges follow the common interest, not personal usage.

questions.q: If the bylaws permit it, which act ends a condo owner's liability for common charges accruing afterward?
options: Moving out and returning the keys to the managing agent
Sending the board written notice that she abandons the unit
Ceasing all use of the common elements and amenities
Conveying the unit and its common interest to the board
questions.explanation: RPL §339-x says abandonment of a unit or waiver of use does not exempt an owner, but, subject to the bylaws, conveying the unit and common interest to the board of managers on behalf of the other owners exempts the owner from charges accruing afterward.

questions.q: The owner of Unit 7C hires a contractor to renovate her kitchen and does not pay. Against what may the contractor file a mechanic's lien?
options: The entire condominium property
The common elements of the building
Only Unit 7C and its common interest
Unit 7C and any units the crew passed through
questions.explanation: Once the declaration is recorded, RPL §339-l bars new liens against the common elements (absent unanimous owner consent), and work on a unit supports a lien only against the unit of an owner who requested or consented to it.

questions.q: The board of managers hires a contractor to modernize the building's elevators and fails to pay. What does the Condominium Act provide for this contractor?
options: A mechanic's lien on the common elements for the bill
Common charges collected are trust funds for paying the work
A mechanic's lien on every unit in equal dollar shares
A lien on the units owned by each board member
questions.explanation: RPL §339-l states that labor or materials furnished to the common elements are not the basis of a lien on them; instead, common charges received by the board are trust funds that must first pay for work the board authorized.

questions.q: A ground-floor condo owner wants to excavate a new basement beneath her unit. What does the Condominium Act require before she starts?
options: Consent of all unit owners affected
A building permit and nothing more
Approval by a majority of the board
Written notice to the managing agent
questions.explanation: RPL §339-k forbids a unit owner from adding a material structure, excavating an additional basement or cellar, or doing work that jeopardizes soundness or safety without first obtaining the consent of all affected unit owners. A permit addresses building codes, not owners' consent.

questions.q: Water is pouring from Unit 9A into Unit 8A, and 9A's owner is traveling. May the board's managing agent enter 9A to stop the leak?
options: Only after obtaining a court order to enter the unit
Yes; the board may access units to make emergency repairs
Only with the absent owner's prior written consent
Only after giving thirty days' written notice of entry
questions.explanation: RPL §339-i(5) gives unit owners an irrevocable right, exercised by the board, to access each unit as needed to operate the property or make emergency repairs that prevent damage to the common elements or other units.

questions.q: A condo unit owner asks to examine the condominium's books of receipts and expenditures. What does the Condominium Act provide?
options: Only board members and auditors may inspect the records
The records must be available for unit owners to examine
Records open only after a majority vote of the owners
Owners may see the records only under a court order
questions.explanation: RPL §339-w requires the board or manager to keep detailed books of receipts and expenditures and make them available for examination by unit owners at convenient hours.

questions.q: Once the sponsor's period of control ends, how is a condominium's board of managers chosen?
options: The Attorney General appoints its members
The managing agent appoints its members
Unit owners elect it as the bylaws provide
The sponsor appoints it until all units sell
questions.explanation: The sponsor typically names the first board, but its control is limited by the offering plan and applicable rules; afterward unit owners elect the board under the bylaws, which RPL §339-v requires to address election of the board. The managing agent works for the board.

questions.q: After collecting three bids, a condo board hires a window contractor that is not the cheapest. An owner sues, arguing a lower bid existed. How will a New York court generally review the decision?
options: It decides which contractor it would have chosen instead
It defers if the board acted in good faith within its authority
It voids any contract not awarded to the lowest bidder
It upholds the choice only if most owners ratify it
questions.explanation: Under the business judgment rule (Levandusky), courts defer to board decisions made in good faith, within the board's authority, and for legitimate building purposes. Courts do not substitute their own judgment, and no lowest-bid rule applies.
questions.citation: Business judgment rule, Levandusky v. One Fifth Ave. Apt. Corp., 75 N.Y.2d 530 (1990)

questions.q: A condo board with a right of first refusal dislikes a seller's contract buyer. Which response is available to the board?
options: Reject the buyer for any lawful reason, as a co-op board may
Demand a higher price from the buyer before it will waive
Buy the unit on the contract's terms or waive the right
Delay the closing until a buyer it prefers comes forward
questions.explanation: A right of first refusal lets the board match the bona fide offer and acquire the unit itself; otherwise it waives and the sale proceeds. It is not an approval power like a co-op board's, so the board cannot simply reject a buyer.
questions.citation: Condominium declaration/bylaws; general contract law of rights of first refusal

questions.q: A condo's bylaws give the board 30 days after notice to exercise its right of first refusal, after which the right expires. The board takes no action within 30 days. What generally follows?
options: The sale is void until the board holds a formal vote
The board may still exercise its right up to closing
The owner must re-offer the unit to the board at a higher price
The right lapses for this sale, and the owner may close on those terms
questions.explanation: When the right is not exercised in the stated period, it expires for that transaction, and the seller may sell to the buyer on the noticed terms. Title companies typically want a written waiver or proof of lapse at closing; materially changing the terms could trigger a new offer to the board.
questions.citation: Condominium declaration/bylaws; general contract law of rights of first refusal

questions.q: Who usually obtains a condominium's master insurance policy, and how is it paid for?
options: Each owner separately, with a copy filed with the managing agent
The sponsor permanently, using funds from the original unit sales
The board of managers, with premiums paid as a common expense
The first mortgage lender, by adding the premium to every escrow
questions.explanation: RPL §339-bb requires the board to insure the building against fire and other hazards when the declaration, the bylaws, or a majority of unit owners require it, and makes the premiums a common expense funded by common charges. Each owner may still insure the unit for its own benefit, typically with an HO-6 policy for interior improvements, contents, and liability.

questions.q: A storm damages the roof. The master policy's $100,000 deductible is passed to owners as a special assessment, and one owner's share is $2,000. Which part of the owner's HO-6 policy may respond?
options: Additional living expense coverage
Loss assessment coverage
Personal liability coverage
Personal property coverage
questions.explanation: Loss assessment coverage in an HO-6 pays an owner's share of an association assessment for a covered loss, such as a master-policy deductible, up to the coverage limit (often low unless increased by endorsement). Living expense, liability, and personal property coverages address other losses.

questions.q: Why are a condo's monthly common charges often lower than co-op maintenance for a comparable apartment?
options: Common charges exclude unit real estate taxes and building mortgage debt
Condo boards are prohibited by law from keeping any reserve funds
Condo building staff wages are paid by the original sponsor forever
Condo master insurance premiums are paid by the local municipality
questions.explanation: Condo owners pay their unit's real estate taxes on a separate bill and carry their own mortgages, so common charges cover mainly operations, insurance, and reserves. Co-op maintenance usually also covers the building's taxes and underlying mortgage.

questions.q: A homeowner in a planned community installs a fence that the recorded declaration of covenants prohibits. Who ordinarily enforces the restriction?
options: Only the town zoning board, as a land-use matter
The homeowners' association, under the covenants
Only the developer that recorded the covenants
No one, because she owns her lot in fee simple
questions.explanation: Recorded covenants run with the land and bind each lot owner; the HOA enforces them through its declaration and bylaws. Fee ownership of the lot does not free the owner from recorded restrictions, and private covenants are separate from zoning.
questions.citation: Recorded covenants and restrictions; general law of covenants running with the land

questions.q: A townhouse community is organized as an HOA, not a condominium. An owner stops paying assessments. Where do the association's lien and collection rights come from?
options: The Condominium Act's statutory common-charge lien
The Lien Law's mechanic's lien for services furnished
The recorded declaration of covenants and the HOA's bylaws
The owner's proprietary lease with the association
questions.explanation: An HOA's assessment and lien rights arise from the recorded declaration of covenants and its governing documents. The RPL §339-z common-charge lien applies to property submitted to the Condominium Act, and a proprietary lease is a co-op document.
questions.citation: Recorded covenants and restrictions; RPL Art. 9-B applies only to condominiums

questions.q: In Community X, buyers get a deed to the house and its lot, and an association owns the green. In Community Y, buyers get a unit plus a percentage interest in all land, including the green. How are they classified?
options: X is a condominium, and Y is an HOA community
Both are condominiums because they share a green
Both are cooperatives because an entity governs them
X is an HOA community, and Y is a condominium
questions.explanation: An HOA owner holds fee title to a lot while the association owns the common areas. A condo owner holds a unit plus an undivided interest in the common elements, which can include land. Appearance and shared amenities do not decide the legal form.
questions.citation: RPL Art. 9-B; general law of planned communities and HOAs

questions.q: A rent-stabilized tenant does not buy when her building's non-eviction condominium conversion plan is declared effective. What is her status?
options: She keeps rent-stabilization rights, including lease renewals
She must vacate when her current lease term finally expires
She becomes a market-rate tenant on a month-to-month basis
She must buy her unit within 90 days or forfeit her lease
questions.explanation: Under a non-eviction plan, non-purchasing tenants cannot be evicted for failing to buy, and rent-regulated tenants keep their protections, including renewal rights. The new unit owner or sponsor takes subject to that tenancy.

questions.q: In a condominium conversion of an occupied rental building, what is the 'insider price'?
options: The price the sponsor charges its own employees
The price the Attorney General approves as fair
The price investors pay for the vacant units
A discount price offered to tenants in occupancy
questions.explanation: Conversion sponsors commonly offer tenants in occupancy an insider price below the price offered to outsiders, encouraging tenant purchases. The Attorney General's acceptance of an offering plan for filing concerns disclosure; it does not set prices or approve them as fair.
questions.citation: GBL Art. 23-A (Martin Act); AG offering-plan practice

questions.q: A sponsor's construction loan is a blanket mortgage covering the entire condominium. When the sponsor sells an individual unit, what must happen?
options: The buyer assumes a pro rata share of the blanket construction loan
The blanket lender automatically becomes the buyer's first mortgagee
The blanket mortgage stays in place until every unit has sold
The unit must be released from the blanket mortgage at closing
questions.explanation: RPL §339-r: at the first conveyance of each unit, every blanket mortgage or other lien covering that unit and other units must be paid and satisfied of record, or the unit and its common interest must be released by a recorded partial release (typically on payment of a release price), so the buyer takes title free of the sponsor's loan.

questions.q: Who holds title to the land and building in a typical New York housing cooperative?
options: Each shareholder, as a tenant in common with the other owners
The board of directors, personally and in their own names
The cooperative corporation, either in fee or under a ground lease
The managing agent, as trustee for all of the shareholders
questions.explanation: The corporation is the property owner (in fee simple or as ground lessee); shareholders own stock and occupy under proprietary leases. Tenancy in common describes co-owners of real property, which co-op shareholders are not.
questions.citation: NY Business Corporation Law (cooperative housing corporations)

questions.q: Which document gives a co-op shareholder the right to occupy a specific apartment and sets rules on maintenance, alterations, and subletting?
options: The proprietary lease issued by the corporation
The stock certificate issued to the shareholder
The certificate of incorporation of the co-op
The recognition agreement signed with the lender
questions.explanation: The proprietary lease is the occupancy agreement between the corporation (as landlord) and the shareholder. The stock certificate only evidences how many shares the shareholder owns.

questions.q: Shares in a New York co-op are allocated to each apartment. What does the number of shares allocated to an apartment primarily determine?
options: The apartment's separate real estate tax assessment by the city
The minimum price at which the apartment may be resold
The maximum number of occupants allowed to live in the unit
The apartment's proportionate share of maintenance and tax deductions
questions.explanation: Maintenance and the shareholder's pass-through share of the corporation's taxes and mortgage interest are allocated by shares. Co-op apartments are not separately assessed; the building receives one tax bill.
questions.citation: Cooperative offering plan share allocation; IRC §216

questions.q: A co-op building has 50,000 total shares and an annual budget of $2,400,000 covering operations, real estate taxes, and the underlying mortgage. An apartment is allocated 625 shares. What is its monthly maintenance?
questions.explanation: $2,400,000 ÷ 50,000 shares = $48 per share per year; 625 × $48 = $30,000 per year; $30,000 ÷ 12 = $2,500 per month. $30,000 is the annual figure, the trap of forgetting to divide by 12.
questions.citation: Cooperative maintenance allocation by shares (general co-op practice)

questions.q: A co-op pays $1,200,000 a year in real estate taxes on the building, which has 60,000 shares outstanding. An apartment holds 750 shares. How much of the shareholder's monthly maintenance represents real estate taxes?
questions.explanation: $1,200,000 ÷ 60,000 = $20 per share; 750 × $20 = $15,000 per year; $15,000 ÷ 12 = $1,250 per month. $15,000 is the annual tax share, not the monthly amount.
questions.citation: Cooperative tax allocation by shares (general co-op practice)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT part of a co-op shareholder's monthly maintenance payment to the corporation?
options: The shareholder's share of building real estate taxes
Debt service on the corporation's underlying mortgage
Building staff wages and common-area utilities
Payments on the shareholder's own share loan
questions.explanation: A share loan is the buyer's personal debt, paid directly to the share lender. Maintenance covers corporate costs: operations, building taxes, and debt service on the underlying (building) mortgage.

questions.q: A co-op corporation defaults on its underlying blanket mortgage. Why is this a concern even for shareholders who have paid maintenance on time?
options: The lender can foreclose on the whole building, endangering every shareholder
The lender can collect the full debt from any single shareholder personally
The shareholders' share loans automatically become due in full that day
The city will reassess each apartment and bill shareholders individually
questions.explanation: The underlying mortgage is a lien on the corporation's entire property, so a corporate default puts every shareholder's occupancy at risk. Shareholders are not personally liable for the corporation's mortgage debt.
questions.citation: Cooperative underlying mortgage risk (general co-op law)

questions.q: A co-op sits on land the corporation leases rather than owns. What should a buyer's attorney review most closely for this building?
options: Whether the shareholder will receive a deed to the land at closing
Whether the ground lease lets each shareholder record a mortgage
The remaining ground lease term, rent increases, and end-of-term rights
Whether the land is separately taxed to each individual shareholder
questions.explanation: In a leasehold co-op, the corporation's rights end when the ground lease ends, and rent resets can sharply raise maintenance. Shareholders never receive a deed under either fee or leasehold structures.

questions.q: Which item would NOT typically be included in a co-op board package?
options: Copies of the applicant's recent federal tax returns
A fully executed contract of sale for the shares
Personal and professional reference letters
An owner's title insurance policy for the apartment
questions.explanation: Board packages contain the application, signed contract, financial statement, tax returns, employment verification, and references. Title insurance is not something the board reviews; a co-op buyer acquires shares (personal property) and normally relies on a lien search rather than a deed-based title examination.
questions.citation: Cooperative board package practice (general co-op law)

questions.q: A co-op board rejects a purchase applicant and gives no reason. Under New York case law, how will a court generally review the board's decision?
options: De novo, substituting the judge's own view of the applicant's fitness
As void, because every rejection must be explained to the applicant in writing
With deference under the business judgment rule, absent bad faith or discrimination
Under a strict scrutiny standard that requires the least restrictive option
questions.explanation: Levandusky v. One Fifth Ave. Apt. Corp. applies the business judgment rule: courts defer to good-faith board decisions within its authority. That deference does not protect discrimination prohibited by fair housing laws.
questions.citation: Levandusky v. One Fifth Ave. Apt. Corp., 75 N.Y.2d 530 (1990)

questions.q: Which reason for rejecting a co-op purchase applicant is most likely lawful?
options: The applicant's household income comes largely from lawful Social Security disability benefits
The applicant's post-closing liquid assets fall below the building's uniformly applied standard
The applicant served in the armed forces and remains an active member of the military reserves
The applicant was born abroad and speaks English as a second language at home and at work
questions.explanation: Applying a consistent financial requirement is a legitimate business judgment. The NY Human Rights Law protects lawful source of income, military status, and national origin, so the other rejections are discriminatory.

questions.q: A co-op buyer obtains a share-loan commitment with a 30-day rate lock, but the board has not yet scheduled an interview. The buyer asks the salesperson whether bank approval means closing can happen next week. What is the best response?
options: No; board approval is a separate requirement, so coordinate the package and lock timing
Yes; the lender's commitment letter is binding on the co-op board as well
Yes; the board must approve any buyer whose lender has issued a commitment
No; the buyer must first record the share loan with the county clerk's office
questions.explanation: Lender approval and board approval are independent, and the board does not have to accept a financed buyer. The agent should coordinate a complete package and the interview date with the rate lock and contract dates.

questions.q: A standard New York co-op contract makes the sale contingent on board approval. The board rejects the buyer. What is the usual result?
options: Either party may cancel, and the buyer's down payment is returned
The buyer forfeits the down payment because approval was the buyer's risk
The seller may sue the board for specific performance of the sale
The buyer may close anyway and appeal the decision to the Attorney General
questions.explanation: Co-op contracts customarily condition the sale on board consent; if consent is refused, the contract may be canceled and the down payment refunded. The Attorney General does not hear appeals of resale board decisions.
questions.citation: Standard NY co-op contract of sale (board approval contingency)

questions.q: At a co-op closing financed with a share loan, what collateral does the lender typically hold?
options: A recorded mortgage and the deed to the apartment
The stock certificate and the assignment of the proprietary lease
A recorded lien on the building's land and common areas
The corporation's blanket mortgage note and its title policy
questions.explanation: Share loans are secured by the borrower's shares and proprietary lease; the lender keeps the original stock certificate, a stock power, and the lease assignment. There is no deed or recorded mortgage on a co-op apartment.

questions.q: A co-op buyer finances with a share loan. Which closing cost applies to a typical NYC condo purchase with a mortgage but NOT to this co-op purchase?
options: Lender's attorney fees
Lien search fees
Mortgage recording tax
Loan appraisal fees
questions.explanation: Mortgage recording tax is imposed when a real property mortgage is recorded. A share loan is secured by personal property and perfected with a UCC filing, so no mortgage is recorded and the tax is not charged.
questions.citation: NY Tax Law Article 11 (mortgage recording tax)

questions.q: A co-op shareholder with a share loan stops paying maintenance. Under the recognition agreement, what is the corporation typically obligated to do?
options: Pay the shareholder's loan installments until the default is resolved
Release its own lien on the shares in favor of the share lender
Begin judicial foreclosure against the shareholder in Supreme Court
Notify the share lender and allow it an opportunity to cure the default
questions.explanation: In the recognition agreement the co-op acknowledges the lender's interest and agrees to give notice of shareholder defaults and a chance to cure before canceling the lease. The co-op does not pay the loan or waive its own lien.
questions.citation: Cooperative recognition agreement (general co-op lending practice)

questions.q: What is the purpose of a co-op lien search before closing?
options: To confirm the boundaries of the apartment against a recorded survey
To find mechanic's liens filed against the building's common elements
To find UCC filings, judgments, or tax liens against the seller or the shares
To verify the deed chain to the apartment for an owner's title policy
questions.explanation: Because co-op shares are personal property, buyers search for UCC financing statements, judgments, and liens affecting the seller or the shares. Deed chains and unit surveys apply to real property such as condos.
questions.citation: NY UCC Article 9; cooperative closing practice

questions.q: A co-op shareholder defaults on a share loan. How does the lender ordinarily enforce its security interest?
options: By judicial foreclosure of a mortgage in New York Supreme Court
By a strict foreclosure that transfers the deed to the lender
By an eviction proceeding brought in the lender's own name
By a nonjudicial UCC sale of the shares and proprietary lease
questions.explanation: A share loan is secured by personal property, so the lender may sell the collateral under UCC Article 9 after proper notice. Judicial foreclosure is the procedure for real property mortgages, not co-op shares.
questions.citation: NY UCC §9-610 (disposition of collateral after default)

questions.q: A shareholder falls several months behind on maintenance. Which remedy is generally available to the co-op corporation but NOT to a condominium board of managers?
options: Filing a lien for unpaid charges against the owner's interest
A summary nonpayment proceeding as landlord under the proprietary lease
Suing the owner in court to collect the past-due amounts
Charging late fees permitted by the governing documents
questions.explanation: The co-op is the shareholder's landlord, so it can bring a landlord-tenant proceeding and terminate the proprietary lease. A condo board relies on a lien against a fee-owned unit, not a landlord relationship.
questions.citation: RPAPL Article 7 (summary proceedings); cooperative proprietary lease

questions.q: A co-op seller's contract price is $1,150,000, and the co-op imposes a flip tax of 2% of the gross sale price. What is the flip tax?
questions.explanation: $1,150,000 × 0.02 = $23,000. $11,500 results from using 1%, and $2,300 or $230,000 come from misplacing the decimal.
questions.citation: Cooperative flip tax under governing documents (BCL §501(c))

questions.q: A co-op's flip tax is 15% of the seller's profit. The seller bought for $600,000 and now sells for $900,000. What flip tax is due?
questions.explanation: Profit = $900,000 − $600,000 = $300,000; $300,000 × 0.15 = $45,000. $135,000 applies 15% to the sale price and $90,000 applies it to the purchase price.
questions.citation: Cooperative flip tax under governing documents (BCL §501(c))

questions.q: Which statement about a co-op flip tax is accurate?
options: It is a charge the corporation collects under its own documents, often for reserves
It is a state tax collected by the county clerk when the shares are transferred
It is a federal tax on gains from selling shares within one year of purchase
It is a city fee that replaces the NYS transfer tax on co-op apartment sales
questions.explanation: Despite its name, a flip tax is a private transfer fee payable to the co-op as authorized by its proprietary lease or bylaws, usually funding reserves. It is separate from and does not replace government transfer taxes.
questions.citation: NY Business Corporation Law §501(c) (cooperative transfer fees)

questions.q: A seller transfers co-op shares for $850,000. How much NYS real estate transfer tax applies, and who customarily pays it?
options: $3,400, paid by the buyer
$1,700, paid by the seller
$3,400, paid by the seller
$8,500, paid by the buyer
questions.explanation: NYS transfer tax applies to transfers of co-op shares: $850,000 ÷ $500 = 1,700 units × $2 = $3,400, paid by the seller. $8,500 confuses it with the 1% mansion tax, which does not apply below $1,000,000.

questions.q: A buyer agrees to pay $750,000 for a co-op apartment. The board requires at least 25% down. What is the largest share loan the buyer may use?
questions.explanation: Minimum down payment = $750,000 × 0.25 = $187,500; maximum loan = $750,000 − $187,500 = $562,500. $187,500 is the down payment itself, not the loan.
