questions.q: A co-op requires buyers to hold, after closing, liquid assets equal to 24 months of combined maintenance and share-loan payments. Maintenance is $2,100 a month and the loan payment is $3,400 a month. What liquidity is required?
questions.explanation: ($2,100 + $3,400) × 24 = $5,500 × 24 = $132,000. $81,600 counts only the loan payment, and $66,000 uses 12 months instead of 24.

questions.q: A tenant-stockholder holds 400 of a qualifying co-op's 40,000 shares. This year the corporation paid $900,000 in real estate taxes, $600,000 in mortgage interest, $500,000 in mortgage principal, and $1,000,000 in operating costs. How much may the shareholder generally deduct under IRC §216?
questions.explanation: Shareholder's share = 400 ÷ 40,000 = 1%; deductible items are taxes and interest: 1% × ($900,000 + $600,000) = $15,000. $20,000 wrongly adds principal, and $9,000 counts taxes only.

questions.q: Under the current version of IRC §216, which is one way a cooperative housing corporation can qualify so its tenant-stockholders may take the §216 deduction?
options: At least 80% of its square footage is used or available for tenant-stockholders' residential use
At least 51% of its shareholders occupy their apartments as primary residences
At least half of its income comes from leasing commercial space to outsiders
It holds an accepted offering plan filed with the New York Attorney General
questions.explanation: §216(b)(1)(D) allows an 80% gross-income test, an 80% square-footage test, or a 90% expenditure test. An accepted offering plan is a state disclosure filing, not a federal tax qualification.

questions.q: Why does Real Property Law §226-b, which lets many residential tenants request permission to sublet, NOT give a co-op shareholder a statutory sublet right?
options: The statute applies only to buildings with fewer than four apartment units
The statute was repealed in 2019 and replaced by the Good Cause Eviction Law
The statute requires the shareholder first to obtain approval from the Attorney General
The statute expressly excludes proprietary leases, so the lease and rules control
questions.explanation: RPL §226-b expressly does not apply to proprietary leases held by co-op shareholders, so sublet rights depend on the proprietary lease, bylaws, and house rules. The statute's sublet right applies to buildings with four or more units.

questions.q: A co-op board approves a shareholder's two-year sublet. During the sublet, the subtenant damages the hallway and the shareholder stops paying maintenance. Who remains responsible to the corporation?
options: The shareholder, who stays bound by the proprietary lease
The subtenant alone, as the current occupant of the apartment
The board, because it approved the sublet arrangement
The managing agent, who screened the subtenant's application
questions.explanation: Subletting transfers occupancy but not the shareholder's obligations; the shareholder remains liable for maintenance and lease compliance. Board approval of a sublet does not shift that liability to the board.

questions.q: Under a typical conversion offering plan, which party may usually sublet its apartments or sell its shares without co-op board approval?
options: Any shareholder who has owned the apartment for at least two years
Any investor who buys an apartment from an existing shareholder
Any shareholder who pays the flip tax to the corporation in advance
A holder of unsold shares as defined in the offering plan
questions.explanation: Offering plans commonly let the sponsor and qualified holders of unsold shares sublet and sell without board consent. An investor buying on resale from a shareholder does not automatically become a holder of unsold shares.
questions.citation: Martin Act offering plan; cooperative proprietary lease

questions.q: A buyer is reviewing a co-op in which the sponsor still holds 40% of the shares. Why is this a significant financial concern?
options: The sponsor's unsold shares are exempt from the corporation's real estate taxes
If the sponsor stops paying maintenance on those shares, the building's budget suffers
The sponsor can force every other shareholder to sell back their shares at cost
The Attorney General will revoke the offering plan once sponsor control passes 25%
questions.explanation: A sponsor with a large block of unsold shares owes maintenance on all of them; a sponsor default can strain operations and the underlying mortgage. The sponsor's shares bear the same allocated costs as anyone else's.
questions.citation: Martin Act offering plan disclosure (sponsor holdings)

questions.q: Under the Martin Act, what must a sponsor do before offering co-op shares to the public in a building it is converting?
options: Obtain a final certificate of occupancy from the Department of State
Have the plan's prices approved as fair market value by an appraiser
File an offering plan and receive the Attorney General's acceptance for filing
Register the building with the county clerk as a cooperative corporation
questions.explanation: The Martin Act bars public offerings of co-op interests until the Attorney General accepts the offering plan for filing. The AG reviews disclosure; it does not set or approve prices.

questions.q: Place these steps of a New York co-op conversion in their usual order: (1) black book distributed, (2) red herring submitted to the AG and given to tenants, (3) plan declared effective, (4) closings on the apartments.
questions.explanation: The preliminary red herring comes first; after AG acceptance, the black book (accepted plan) is distributed; the sponsor declares the plan effective once the purchase requirement is met; closings follow. Declaring effectiveness before the black book is the common mistake.

questions.q: A sponsor submits a plan to convert an occupied New York City rental building with 80 apartments, all occupied by bona fide tenants, into a co-op. Under current law, how many tenants in occupancy must sign purchase agreements before the plan can be declared effective?
questions.explanation: Since the 2019 HSTPA amendments, an NYC non-eviction plan needs purchase agreements from at least 51% of bona fide tenants in occupancy: 80 × 0.51 = 40.8, rounded up to 41. Twelve reflects the repealed 15% standard; 40 falls short of 51%.

questions.q: Under NYC's conversion statute as amended in 2019, which purchases count toward the percentage needed to declare a non-eviction plan effective?
options: Purchases of vacant apartments by outside buyers who intend to live there
Purchases of any apartments by investors buying them for rental income
Purchases of apartments by the sponsor's affiliates and their relatives
Purchases by bona fide tenants in occupancy when the plan was accepted
questions.explanation: The amended §352-eeee counts only bona fide tenants in occupancy on the date the AG accepted the plan for filing. Before 2019, outside purchasers of vacant units could help reach the old 15% threshold.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the NYC conversion statute (GBL §352-eeee) with the statute for opting-in municipalities in Nassau, Westchester, and Rockland (GBL §352-eee)?
options: Eviction plans are no longer available in NYC but remain possible under §352-eee
Eviction plans remain available in NYC but are prohibited under §352-eee
Both statutes allow eviction plans if 15% of the tenants agree to buy
Neither statute protects tenants who decline to buy under any plan
questions.explanation: The 2019 HSTPA eliminated eviction plans in NYC for new submissions, while §352-eee still permits them in municipalities that adopted it. Both statutes protect non-purchasing tenants.

questions.q: A Westchester village has adopted GBL §352-eee, and a sponsor's eviction plan has been declared effective. A 70-year-old tenant who qualifies as an eligible senior citizen declines to buy. What is the tenant's status?
options: The tenant must vacate when the current lease expires, just like the other nonpurchasing tenants
The tenant cannot be evicted for not buying and is protected against unconscionable rent increases
The tenant may stay only if the board later approves the tenant as a shareholder of the corporation
The tenant may stay for one more year and then must either buy the apartment or move out
questions.explanation: Under §352-eee, eligible senior citizens (62 or older) and eligible disabled persons cannot be evicted under an eviction plan for declining to buy. Other nonpurchasers can eventually be displaced under an eviction plan.

questions.q: A sponsor's CPS-1 application to test the market has been accepted. Which activity is permitted?
options: Advertising the project with the required disclaimers to collect nonbinding interest
Signing purchase agreements that become binding when the plan is accepted
Telling prospects the Attorney General has approved the offering plan
Collecting refundable deposits to hold units for interested buyers
questions.explanation: CPS-1 acceptance lets a sponsor gauge demand through approved advertising and nonbinding indications of interest only. It is not acceptance of the offering plan, so no contracts or deposits are allowed.
questions.citation: NY Attorney General Cooperative Policy Statement No. 1 (CPS-1)

questions.q: A buyer purchases an apartment in the residential section of a Manhattan condop. Which statement best describes the purchase?
options: The buyer receives a deed to the apartment plus a percentage of the common elements
The buyer receives a deed to the commercial condominium unit on the ground floor
The buyer receives co-op shares and a proprietary lease, usually subject to board approval
The buyer receives a long-term ground lease directly from the land's fee owner
questions.explanation: In a condop, the residential portion is a condo unit owned by a co-op corporation, so residential buyers get shares and a proprietary lease. The commercial unit is a separate condo that can be owned and sold independently.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Law Article 9-B; cooperative ownership structure

questions.q: Under a typical gross lease, which statement is correct?
options: The tenant pays base rent plus its share of property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs
The tenant pays fixed rent; the landlord pays operating costs like taxes, insurance, and maintenance
The tenant's rent is calculated solely as a percentage of the tenant's gross sales revenue
The tenant leases only the land and constructs and maintains its own building improvements
questions.explanation: In a gross lease the landlord pays the operating expenses out of the rent; it is common for residential and many office leases. Shifting taxes, insurance, and maintenance to the tenant describes a net lease; always read the actual clause for exceptions such as utilities.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A drugstore chain signs a triple net (NNN) lease. Conventionally, this means the tenant pays:
options: Base rent plus property taxes, insurance, and maintenance/repairs
Base rent plus the property taxes only, with the landlord paying the rest
Base rent plus property taxes and insurance only
Only base rent, with the landlord paying all taxes, insurance, and maintenance
questions.explanation: Conventional shorthand: single net = taxes; double net = taxes + insurance; triple net = taxes + insurance + maintenance. The lease language still controls items like roof replacement or capital repairs.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A tenant's lease is described as a double net (net-net) lease. In addition to base rent, the tenant conventionally pays:
options: Property taxes only
Utilities only
Property taxes and insurance
Property taxes, insurance, and maintenance
questions.explanation: Double net conventionally adds taxes and insurance; taxes alone is single net, and adding maintenance makes it triple net. Labels are shorthand only; the clause controls.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A retail lease requires base rent of $3,000 per month plus 4% of annual gross sales over $600,000. The tenant's gross sales this year were $850,000. What is the total annual rent?
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A percentage lease has annual base rent of $60,000 and percentage rent of 6% of gross sales. Assuming a natural breakpoint, at what level of annual gross sales does percentage rent begin?
questions.explanation: Natural breakpoint = annual base rent ÷ percentage rate = $60,000 ÷ 0.06 = $1,000,000. Above that, 6% of sales exceeds the base rent. A lease may instead set a negotiated (artificial) breakpoint.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A boutique's percentage lease requires 5% of gross sales over a breakpoint. Sales exceeded the breakpoint, but the owner tells the landlord no percentage rent is owed because the store lost money this year. Is the owner correct?
options: No, percentage rent is based on gross sales, not on profit
Yes, percentage rent is owed only when the tenant shows a net profit
Yes, a loss year automatically suspends percentage rent
No, percentage rent is based on the landlord's operating expenses
questions.explanation: Percentage rent is computed on defined gross sales above the breakpoint, regardless of whether the tenant's business is profitable. These leases are most common for retail tenants in shopping centers.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — percentage lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An index lease sets annual rent at $80,000 when the Consumer Price Index is 250. The rent adjusts by the full percentage change in the CPI, with no cap. If the CPI rises to 260, what is the new annual rent?
questions.explanation: CPI change = (260 − 250) ÷ 250 = 10 ÷ 250 = 4%. New rent = $80,000 × 1.04 = $83,200. Treating the 10-point rise as 10 percent or adding points to the rent are the traps.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — index lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An office lease sets rent at $30 per square foot in year 1, $32 in year 2, and $34 in year 3, as written in the lease from the start. This is a:
options: Index lease
Percentage lease
Net lease
Graduated lease
questions.explanation: A graduated (step-up) lease raises rent by fixed, pre-set amounts on a schedule. An index lease instead moves rent with an outside measure such as the CPI, so the future amounts are not known in advance.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — graduated lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A fast-food chain leases a vacant parcel for 49 years and constructs its own restaurant on it. This arrangement is best described as a:
options: Ground lease
Gross lease
Percentage lease
Graduated lease
questions.explanation: A ground lease is a long-term lease of land only, with the tenant building and usually paying expenses on the improvements. Unless the lease provides otherwise, the improvements commonly pass to the landowner when the lease ends.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — ground lease; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: In an office building, how does rentable square footage differ from usable square footage?
options: Rentable area excludes the lobbies and corridors that are included in usable area
Rentable area adds the tenant's pro-rata share of common areas like lobbies and restrooms
Rentable and usable area are always identical; the terms are interchangeable in office leases
Rentable area counts only the finished space with carpeting and ceilings installed
questions.explanation: Usable area is the space the tenant actually occupies; rentable area adds its share of building common areas. Rent is usually quoted per rentable square foot, so rentable is the larger number.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — area measurement; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A suite has 10,000 rentable square feet and 8,500 usable square feet. What is the loss factor?
questions.explanation: Loss factor = (rentable − usable) ÷ rentable = 1,500 ÷ 10,000 = 15%. Dividing by usable (1,500 ÷ 8,500 ≈ 17.6%) gives the add-on/load percentage instead, and 85% is the efficiency (usable ÷ rentable).
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — loss factor; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A tenant needs 4,000 usable square feet. The building has a 20% add-on (load) factor applied to usable area, and rent is $45 per rentable square foot per year. What is the monthly rent?
questions.explanation: Rentable = 4,000 × 1.20 = 4,800 sq ft. Annual rent = 4,800 × $45 = $216,000; monthly = $216,000 ÷ 12 = $18,000. Using usable area (4,000 × $45 ÷ 12 = $15,000) ignores the load.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — load factor; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A tenant occupies 3,000 square feet in a 60,000-square-foot shopping center. Annual common area maintenance (CAM) costs are $240,000, shared pro rata by square footage. What is the tenant's annual CAM charge?
questions.explanation: Pro-rata share = 3,000 ÷ 60,000 = 5%. CAM = $240,000 × 0.05 = $12,000 per year ($1,000 per month). CAM is a cost-sharing charge for common areas such as parking lots and landscaping, not a measurement of space.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — CAM charges; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A lease provides a tenant improvement (TI) allowance of $40 per rentable square foot on 5,000 rentable square feet. The tenant's build-out costs $260,000, and the lease says the tenant pays any excess. How much does the tenant pay toward the build-out?
questions.explanation: TI allowance = $40 × 5,000 = $200,000 paid by the landlord. Tenant pays the excess: $260,000 − $200,000 = $60,000. TI allowances are a negotiated landlord concession to customize space.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles — tenant improvements; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An investor buys a building with $350,000 cash invested. NOI is $120,000 and annual debt service is $85,000. What is the investor's cash-on-cash return?
questions.explanation: Before-tax cash flow = NOI − debt service = $120,000 − $85,000 = $35,000. Cash-on-cash = $35,000 ÷ $350,000 = 10%. Dividing NOI by cash invested (34.3%) skips debt service.
questions.citation: Real estate investment analysis; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: An investor finances a purchase mostly with borrowed money. Positive leverage occurs when:
options: The loan's interest rate is higher than the property's rate of return
The investor pays all cash so no debt service is owed
The property's NOI is less than the annual debt service
The property's rate of return exceeds the cost of the borrowed funds
questions.explanation: Leverage uses borrowed money to increase the return on the investor's own cash. It is positive when the property earns more than the debt costs; if the debt costs more, leverage is negative and magnifies losses.
questions.citation: Real estate investment analysis; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: A building listed at $1,100,000 has gross scheduled income of $96,000, operating expenses of $30,000, and annual mortgage payments of $40,000. What is the capitalization rate at the list price?
questions.explanation: NOI = $96,000 − $30,000 = $66,000 (mortgage payments are not operating expenses). Cap rate = NOI ÷ price = $66,000 ÷ $1,100,000 = 6%. Using gross income (8.7%) or deducting debt service (2.4%) are traps.
questions.citation: Real estate investment analysis — capitalization rate; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property)

questions.q: In an ordinary deferred Section 1031 exchange, after the relinquished property is transferred, the investor must identify replacement property and then receive it within what time limits?
options: Identify within 45 days; receive within 180 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
Identify within 30 days; receive within 90 days or by the tax-return due date, if earlier
Identify within 60 days; receive within 120 days of closing on the relinquished property
Identify within 45 days; receive within one year
questions.explanation: Replacement property must be identified in writing within 45 days and received by the earlier of 180 days after the transfer or the tax-return due date (with extensions). A qualified intermediary should hold the proceeds so the investor never receives them.

questions.q: An investor exchanges a rental building for a larger warehouse under Section 1031 and also receives $40,000 in cash. The $40,000 is:
options: Like-kind property, so it is fully tax-deferred
A qualified intermediary fee deductible as an expense
Boot, generally taxable up to the amount of realized gain
Excluded from tax because the exchange was between real properties
questions.explanation: Cash or other non-like-kind property received is boot and can trigger taxable gain up to the realized gain. A rental building for a warehouse is like-kind because both are investment/business real property; a personal home does not qualify.

questions.q: A salesperson represents a buyer of a 20,000-square-foot warehouse in New York. Which statement about required disclosure forms is correct?
options: Both the RPL § 443 agency disclosure form and the fair housing and discrimination notice are required
Neither form is required because commercial transactions are exempt from all DOS notices
Only the RPL § 443 agency disclosure form is required
The RPL § 443 agency disclosure form is not required, but the fair housing and discrimination notice is
questions.explanation: The RPL § 443 agency disclosure form covers residential (1-4 family, condo, co-op) transactions, so it does not apply to a warehouse. The DOS Fair Housing and Discrimination notice under 19 NYCRR § 175.28 applies to all real property, including commercial and vacant land.

questions.q: A restaurant tenant wants to lease space in a zoning district where restaurants are allowed only if the zoning board finds that specified conditions in the ordinance (parking, hours, traffic) are met. The tenant should apply for a:
options: Use variance
Special use permit
Nonconforming use designation
Spot zoning amendment
questions.explanation: A special use permit (special exception) allows a use the ordinance already permits subject to stated conditions. A use variance is needed for a use the ordinance prohibits and requires proof of unnecessary hardship.
questions.citation: NY Town Law § 274-b; NY Village Law § 7-725-b

questions.q: A retail tenant's lease says the tenant is solely responsible for ADA compliance. A customer who uses a wheelchair cannot enter the store because of steps at the entrance. Under ADA Title III, who may be responsible to the public?
options: Only the tenant, because the lease validly shifted all ADA compliance responsibility to it
Only the landlord, because it owns the building and controls the common entrance and steps
Both the landlord and the tenant; the lease allocates the burden but does not erase either's duty
Neither, because ADA Title III applies only to residential housing
questions.explanation: Title III covers public accommodations such as stores, and both the landlord and the tenant can be liable; a lease can allocate the burden between them but cannot waive duties owed to the public. Existing facilities must remove barriers where readily achievable.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12181 et seq.; 28 CFR § 36.201(b)

questions.q: An office tenant pays a fixed base rent plus its own electricity and in-suite janitorial service, while the landlord pays the property taxes, insurance, and building maintenance. This lease is best described as a:
options: Triple net lease
Percentage lease
Ground lease
Modified gross lease
questions.explanation: A modified gross lease is a middle ground: the landlord carries the major operating costs (taxes, insurance, maintenance) while the tenant pays specified items such as its own utilities or janitorial. A triple net lease would shift taxes, insurance, and maintenance to the tenant.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — modified gross lease

questions.q: An office lease includes an expense stop of $8.00 per square foot. The tenant leases 5,000 square feet, and this year's operating expenses are $9.50 per square foot. How much does the tenant owe for operating expenses this year in addition to base rent?
questions.explanation: With an expense stop the landlord pays expenses up to the stop and the tenant pays the excess: ($9.50 − $8.00) × 5,000 = $1.50 × 5,000 = $7,500. Billing the full $9.50 × 5,000 = $47,500 ignores the stop; $40,000 is the landlord's portion; $625 is the monthly amount ($7,500 ÷ 12).
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — expense stop

questions.q: A tenant compares two 3,000-square-foot spaces. Space A is $40 per square foot per year on a gross lease. Space B is $28 per square foot per year on a triple net lease, with taxes, insurance, and maintenance estimated at $10 per square foot per year. Based on these figures, which is true?
options: Space A costs about $6,000 less per year
Space B costs about $36,000 less per year
The two spaces cost exactly the same per year
Space B costs about $6,000 less per year
questions.explanation: Space A: $40 × 3,000 = $120,000. Space B: ($28 + $10) × 3,000 = $38 × 3,000 = $114,000. Difference = $6,000 in B's favor. Comparing base rents alone (($40 − $28) × 3,000 = $36,000) ignores the net charges the NNN tenant pays on top of rent.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — gross vs. net lease comparison

questions.q: A retail tenant signed a lease that its broker described as "triple net." The building's roof now needs a full replacement. What decides whether the tenant must pay for it?
options: The triple net label, which always makes the tenant pay
A general rule that landlords pay for every roof repair
The specific repair and capital-cost terms of the lease
The broker's oral description of the lease at signing
questions.explanation: "Triple net" is conventional shorthand for taxes, insurance, and maintenance; it does not by itself settle who pays capital items such as a roof replacement. The actual lease clauses control, so the label alone cannot answer the question.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — net lease cost allocation

questions.q: A store's lease calls for $72,000 annual base rent plus 6% of gross sales above the natural breakpoint. Annual gross sales are $1,500,000. What is the total annual rent (base plus percentage rent)?
questions.explanation: Natural breakpoint = $72,000 ÷ 0.06 = $1,200,000. Percentage rent = ($1,500,000 − $1,200,000) × 0.06 = $18,000. Total = $72,000 + $18,000 = $90,000 (which equals 6% of all sales once the natural breakpoint is passed). Adding 6% of all sales to base ($72,000 + $90,000 = $162,000) double-counts.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — percentage lease, natural breakpoint

questions.q: A lease sets $60,000 annual base rent plus 5% of gross sales over a negotiated breakpoint of $900,000. This year's gross sales are $1,100,000. How much percentage rent is owed for the year?
questions.explanation: The lease's artificial breakpoint controls: ($1,100,000 − $900,000) × 0.05 = $200,000 × 0.05 = $10,000. Answering $0 wrongly uses the natural breakpoint ($60,000 ÷ 0.05 = $1,200,000); $55,000 applies 5% to all sales; $70,000 is total rent, not percentage rent.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — percentage lease, artificial breakpoint

questions.q: In a percentage lease, an artificial breakpoint is:
options: The sales level found by dividing annual base rent by the percentage rate
A negotiated sales threshold other than base rent divided by the rate
The point at which the tenant's business first becomes profitable
The maximum percentage rent the landlord may collect in one year
questions.explanation: An artificial (negotiated) breakpoint is any sales threshold the parties agree to that differs from the natural breakpoint. Annual base rent ÷ percentage rate is the natural breakpoint, and breakpoints are tied to sales, not profitability.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — percentage lease breakpoints

questions.q: A tenant pays $48,000 annual base rent plus 4% of gross sales above the natural breakpoint. Total rent for the year (base plus percentage rent) was $60,000. What were the tenant's gross sales?
questions.explanation: Natural breakpoint = $48,000 ÷ 0.04 = $1,200,000. Percentage rent = $60,000 − $48,000 = $12,000, so sales above the breakpoint = $12,000 ÷ 0.04 = $300,000. Gross sales = $1,200,000 + $300,000 = $1,500,000. $300,000 is only the excess; $2,700,000 adds the breakpoint to $60,000 ÷ 0.04.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — percentage lease

questions.q: A lease adjusts its $60,000 annual rent each year by the change in the Consumer Price Index, capped at 3% per year. The CPI rises from 240 to 252. What is the new annual rent?
questions.explanation: CPI change = (252 − 240) ÷ 240 = 12 ÷ 240 = 5%, but the cap limits the increase to 3%: $60,000 × 1.03 = $61,800. $63,000 ignores the cap; $67,200 treats the 12-point rise as 12%; $64,800 stacks the 3% cap on top of the 5% change.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — index lease with cap

questions.q: A lease raises its $90,000 annual rent by 50% of the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index. The CPI moves from 300 to 318. What is the new annual rent?
questions.explanation: CPI change = (318 − 300) ÷ 300 = 18 ÷ 300 = 6%; 50% of 6% = 3%; $90,000 × 1.03 = $92,700. $95,400 passes through the full 6%; $98,100 treats the 18-point rise as 18% and halves it (9%); $91,350 halves the change twice (1.5%).
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — index lease, partial CPI pass-through

questions.q: A 2,000-square-foot lease starts at $25.00 per square foot per year and increases 3% each year, compounded. What is the annual rent in year 3?
questions.explanation: Year 3 reflects two increases: $25 × 1.03 × 1.03 = $26.5225 per sq ft; × 2,000 = $53,045. $53,000 uses a simple 6% ($25 × 1.06 × 2,000); $54,636 applies three increases (year 4); $51,500 applies only one.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — graduated lease

questions.q: A five-year lease sets monthly rent at $4,000 in year 1 and raises it by $200 per month at the start of each later year. What total rent will the tenant pay over the full term?
questions.explanation: Monthly rents by year: $4,000 + $4,200 + $4,400 + $4,600 + $4,800 = $22,000; × 12 months = $264,000. $288,000 charges the year-5 rate for all 60 months; $240,000 charges the year-1 rate throughout; $206,400 counts only four years.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — graduated lease

questions.q: Why are ground leases typically written for long terms, such as 49 or 99 years?
options: The tenant needs time to recover the cost of the building it constructs
State law requires every ground lease to run at least 49 years
A long term lets the landowner avoid paying any property taxes
The tenant receives fee title to the land once the term ends
questions.explanation: In a ground lease the tenant leases only the land and builds its own improvements, so it needs a term long enough to recoup and finance that investment. No statute sets a minimum term, and the land normally reverts to the owner, not the tenant, at the end.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — ground lease

questions.q: A shopping center's annual CAM costs are $180,000. The lease adds a 15% administrative fee to CAM costs, and the tenant's pro rata share is 4%. What is the tenant's annual CAM charge?
questions.explanation: CAM with fee = $180,000 × 1.15 = $207,000; tenant share = $207,000 × 0.04 = $8,280. $7,200 omits the fee ($180,000 × 0.04); $1,080 is only the tenant's share of the fee; $34,200 adds the whole fee without prorating it.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — CAM charges

questions.q: A tenant leases 2,500 square feet in a center with 50,000 square feet of gross leasable area, of which 10,000 square feet are vacant. Annual CAM costs are $300,000, and the lease allocates CAM by the tenant's area divided by total gross leasable area. What is the tenant's annual CAM charge?
questions.explanation: Share = 2,500 ÷ 50,000 = 5%; $300,000 × 0.05 = $15,000 per year. Dividing by the 40,000 occupied square feet ($18,750) would shift vacant-space costs to tenants, which this lease does not do; $1,250 is the monthly figure, and $1,562.50 is the monthly figure on the wrong occupied-area basis.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — CAM allocation

questions.q: A tenant pays estimated CAM of $1,200 per month. At the year-end reconciliation, the tenant's actual share of CAM costs is $15,600. Under a typical reconciliation clause, what happens?
options: The landlord refunds $1,200 to the tenant
The tenant owes the landlord $15,600 more
Nothing, because monthly estimates are final
The tenant owes the landlord an additional $1,200
questions.explanation: Estimates paid = $1,200 × 12 = $14,400. Actual share $15,600 − $14,400 = $1,200 underpaid, so the tenant pays the shortfall. Reconciliation true-ups run both ways; a refund would apply only if estimates exceeded the actual share.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — CAM reconciliation

questions.q: A tenant needs 6,000 usable square feet in a building with a 20% loss factor (measured against rentable area). Rent is $40 per rentable square foot per year. What is the annual base rent?
questions.explanation: Loss factor is a share of rentable area, so rentable = 6,000 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = 7,500 sq ft; 7,500 × $40 = $300,000. Multiplying usable by 1.20 (7,200 × $40 = $288,000) treats the loss factor as an add-on factor; $240,000 prices usable area; $192,000 shrinks the area by 20%.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — loss factor

questions.q: Two spaces each give a tenant 5,000 usable square feet. Space A rents for $50 per rentable square foot per year with a load factor of 1.15. Space B rents for $48 per rentable square foot per year with a load factor of 1.22. Which statement about annual base rent is correct?
options: Space B costs $10,000 less per year
Space B costs $5,300 more per year
Space A costs $5,300 more per year
Both spaces cost the same per year
questions.explanation: A: 5,000 × 1.15 = 5,750 rentable × $50 = $287,500. B: 5,000 × 1.22 = 6,100 rentable × $48 = $292,800. B costs $292,800 − $287,500 = $5,300 more. Comparing only the quoted rates on usable area ($2 × 5,000 = $10,000) ignores B's higher load.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — rentable vs. usable area

questions.q: An office is quoted at $45 per rentable square foot per year, and the building's load (rentable-to-usable) factor is 1.20. What is the tenant's effective cost per usable square foot per year?
questions.explanation: Each usable square foot carries 1.20 rentable square feet of rent: $45 × 1.20 = $54.00 per usable sq ft. Dividing ($45 ÷ 1.20 = $37.50) or multiplying by 0.80 ($36.00) moves the number the wrong way; $45 is the rentable rate, not the usable cost.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — load factor

questions.q: A lease grants a tenant improvement (TI) allowance of $50 per rentable square foot. The suite has 8,000 rentable and 6,800 usable square feet. What is the total allowance?
questions.explanation: The allowance is quoted per rentable square foot: $50 × 8,000 = $400,000. Using usable area ($50 × 6,800 = $340,000) misapplies the stated basis; $60,000 is only the difference between the two; $460,000 adds that difference on top.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — tenant improvement allowance

questions.q: A five-year lease has a face rent of $6,000 per month, with the first 6 months free. What is the effective (average) monthly rent over the full term?
questions.explanation: Rent paid = (60 − 6) × $6,000 = 54 × $6,000 = $324,000; $324,000 ÷ 60 months = $5,400. $6,000 is the face rent; $5,000 spreads the $36,000 concession over 36 months instead of 60; $3,000 deducts it all within one year.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — free rent concessions

questions.q: A triple net lease grants the tenant four months of "base rent abatement." During those four months, the tenant ordinarily still owes:
options: Its share of taxes, insurance, and CAM as additional rent
Nothing at all, because every lease charge is abated
Only the base rent, with all additional rent abated
Half of the base rent plus half of the CAM charges
questions.explanation: A base rent abatement waives only fixed base rent; net charges such as taxes, insurance, and CAM are additional rent and remain payable unless the lease also abates them. Reading "base rent" as "all charges" is the common mistake.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — free rent / rent abatement

questions.q: A commercial lease states that it is subordinate to any present or future mortgage on the property. This means:
options: The tenant's lease has priority over any later mortgage
The mortgage has priority over the tenant's leasehold interest
The tenant must pay the landlord's mortgage directly
The lender becomes the landlord as soon as the loan closes
questions.explanation: Subordination places the lease below the mortgage in priority, so a foreclosure could cut off the lease unless the tenant also has nondisturbance protection. It does not make the tenant pay the debt or make the lender the landlord.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — SNDA (subordination)

questions.q: A tenant's lease is subordinate to the landlord's mortgage. Which agreement protects the tenant's right to stay in possession if the lender later forecloses, as long as the tenant is not in default?
options: An estoppel certificate
An attornment agreement
A nondisturbance agreement
A personal guaranty
questions.explanation: Nondisturbance is the lender's promise not to disturb a non-defaulting tenant's possession after foreclosure. Attornment is the tenant's reciprocal promise to recognize the new owner; an estoppel certificate only confirms lease facts.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — SNDA (nondisturbance)

questions.q: After a foreclosure sale, a commercial tenant agrees to recognize the purchaser as its new landlord and pay rent to it. This tenant obligation is called:
options: Nondisturbance
Subordination
Assignment
Attornment
questions.explanation: Attornment is the tenant's agreement to accept a successor (such as a foreclosure purchaser) as landlord. Nondisturbance runs the other way, protecting the tenant's possession; subordination concerns lien priority.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — SNDA (attornment)

questions.q: A buyer of an office building and the buyer's lender ask each tenant to sign a statement confirming its rent, lease dates, security deposit, prepaid rent, and any claimed landlord defaults. This document is:
options: A subordination agreement
A letter of intent
A rent roll
An estoppel certificate
questions.explanation: An estoppel certificate is a tenant-signed confirmation of lease facts that a buyer or lender can rely on. A rent roll is the landlord's own summary of tenants and rents, so it does not give the tenant's confirmation.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — estoppel certificate

questions.q: A tenant signed an estoppel certificate stating that no rent was prepaid and the landlord was not in default. After the sale, the tenant claims it prepaid three months' rent to the prior owner. Generally:
options: The buyer must credit the prepaid rent because certificates are not binding
The tenant may be barred from asserting the prepayment against the buyer
The certificate binds only the seller, so the buyer has no protection
The tenant may void the lease because the building has been sold
questions.explanation: The purpose of an estoppel certificate is reliance: a buyer who relied on the tenant's statements can generally hold the tenant to them, so the tenant is estopped from asserting contrary facts such as an undisclosed prepayment. A sale of the building does not let the tenant void the lease.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — estoppel certificate

questions.q: Tenant 1, with four years remaining on its lease, transfers the premises for the entire remaining term and keeps no interest. Tenant 2 transfers its space for all but the last month of its term. Which is correct?
options: Tenant 1 made a sublease; Tenant 2 made an assignment
Both made assignments because each transferred possession
Tenant 1 made an assignment; Tenant 2 made a sublease
Both made subleases because each signed the original lease
questions.explanation: An assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest; a sublease transfers less than the whole, with the tenant keeping a reversion (here, the last month). Whether the lease permits either transfer is a separate question under its consent clause.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — assignment vs. sublease

questions.q: A tenant assigns its lease to a new operator with the landlord's consent, but the landlord signs no release. The assignee later stops paying rent. Generally, the original tenant:
options: Is automatically released once the landlord consents
Is liable only if it shared in the assignee's profits
Remains liable on its lease promise to pay rent
Is liable only for rent due before the assignment
questions.explanation: The original tenant's contractual promise to pay rent survives an assignment; consent alone is not a release. Only an express release or a novation substituting the assignee would end the original tenant's liability.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — assignment; privity of contract

questions.q: A tenant sublets half of its space to a subtenant for two years. The subtenant stops paying. Who is generally responsible to the landlord for the full rent under the main lease?
options: The subtenant, who steps into all of the tenant's lease duties
The original tenant, who remains bound by the main lease
The tenant and subtenant, each for half of the total rent
No one, because subletting suspends the main lease
questions.explanation: In a sublease the original tenant remains the landlord's tenant and stays liable for all rent; the subtenant's obligations run to the original tenant under the sublease, not directly to the landlord. The tenant's remedy is against the subtenant.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — sublease

questions.q: A newly formed LLC with no operating history wants to lease retail space. The landlord asks the LLC's owner to sign a personal guaranty. The main purpose of the guaranty is to:
options: Convert the lease from a net lease into a gross lease
Make the owner personally liable if the LLC fails to perform
Give the owner a recorded ownership interest in the building
Replace the need for the LLC to sign the lease itself
questions.explanation: A personal guaranty adds an individual's credit behind an entity tenant whose limited liability and thin history give the landlord little recourse. The LLC remains the tenant and must still sign; the guaranty does not change the lease type or create ownership.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — personal guaranty

questions.q: A New York City office lease includes a "good guy" guaranty. The guarantor's personal liability generally ends when the tenant:
options: First misses a rent payment and receives a notice of default
Gives the required notice, pays rent through surrender, and vacates
Obtains landlord consent to refinance its business loans
Reaches the halfway point of the term, whether or not it stays
questions.explanation: A good guy guaranty limits the guarantor's exposure: if the tenant gives the required advance notice, pays rent through the surrender date, and turns over vacant possession, the guarantor is released from rent accruing after surrender. A default triggers liability rather than ending it.
questions.citation: Commercial lease guaranty practice (NYC); the guaranty's specific terms control

questions.q: A commercial tenant's three-year lease expires, the tenant stays, and the landlord accepts a rent payment for the following month. With no other agreement, New York law treats the tenancy as:
options: A renewal for another three-year term
A month-to-month tenancy
A renewal for a one-year term
A tenancy at will ending without notice
questions.explanation: When a tenant whose term exceeded one month holds over and the landlord accepts rent for a later period, a month-to-month tenancy results unless the parties agreed otherwise. New York rejects the common-law rule letting a landlord bind the holdover tenant to a new term.

questions.q: A commercial lease sets monthly rent at $10,000 and requires holdover rent of 150% of the last monthly rent. The tenant holds over for two months. Under the lease clause, how much does the tenant owe for those two months?
questions.explanation: Holdover rent = $10,000 × 1.50 = $15,000 per month; × 2 months = $30,000. $20,000 ignores the holdover premium; $40,000 assumes double rent; $15,000 counts only one month.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing principles; NYS DOS Salesperson Syllabus (Commercial and Investment Property) — holdover

questions.q: An investor compares office buildings in the same market. Which description best fits a Class A office building?
options: A newer, high-quality building in a prime location that commands top-of-market rents
An older but well-kept building with rents somewhat below the best space in the market
A dated building needing major upgrades whose rents are among the lowest in the market
A building used mainly for light manufacturing with some office space near the docks
questions.explanation: Class A space is the newest, best-located, best-finished space and earns the highest rents in its market. Class B is a step down (older but well maintained, lower rents); the trap is treating any well-kept building as Class A.
questions.citation: General commercial real estate practice (BOMA office building classes)

questions.q: A value-add investor wants an older office building with rents among the lowest in the market and systems needing major upgrades, which she can renovate and reposition. Which class of building is she most likely targeting?
options: Class A
Class C
Class B
Trophy class
questions.explanation: Class C buildings are older, often need significant upgrades, and rent at the low end of the market, which gives a renovating buyer room to raise rents. Class B buildings are older but still well maintained and desirable, so they offer less repositioning upside.
questions.citation: General commercial real estate practice (office building classes)

questions.q: A developer is planning a shopping center and first tries to sign a large supermarket chain before leasing the smaller stores. Why does the supermarket matter so much to the project?
options: As the anchor tenant, it is legally required to guarantee the rent owed by the smaller stores
As the ground lessee, it takes title to the land under the center when its lease term expires
As the anchor tenant, it draws customer traffic that helps the smaller satellite stores succeed
As the managing agent, it controls the leasing and the common-area budget for the whole center
questions.explanation: An anchor tenant is the major store whose customer draw supports the smaller (satellite) tenants, so lenders and other tenants care whether it is signed. An anchor does not guarantee other tenants' rent; any such obligation would have to be in a contract.
questions.citation: General commercial real estate practice (retail property, anchor tenants)

questions.q: How does a strip center generally differ from a regional mall?
options: A strip center draws shoppers from a much wider trade area; a regional mall serves only the immediate neighborhood
A strip center always has a department store anchor; a regional mall usually has no anchor tenant at all
A strip center is zoned industrial; a regional mall is zoned commercial and may be built only in cities
A strip center is a small row of stores serving the immediate area; a regional mall draws shoppers from a much wider trade area
questions.explanation: Strip centers are small, convenience-oriented rows of stores serving nearby residents, while regional malls are large enclosed or open centers with major anchors and a broad trade area. Reversing the trade areas is the common mix-up.
questions.citation: General commercial real estate practice (retail center types)

questions.q: A distribution company asks a salesperson to find warehouse space. Which set of building features is most important to verify for this type of user?
options: Ceiling clear height, floor load capacity, loading docks, and truck access
Lobby finishes, elevator count, window lines, and the building's office class
Foot traffic, storefront visibility, co-tenancy, and nearby anchor stores
Unit mix, rent-stabilization status, laundry income, and tenant turnover
questions.explanation: Industrial and warehouse users need stacking height, floor strength, loading facilities, and truck circulation. Foot traffic and storefront visibility are retail concerns, and lobby finishes matter for office tenants.
questions.citation: General commercial real estate practice (industrial and warehouse property)

questions.q: A client buys a 24-unit apartment building as an investment. In lending and brokerage practice, how is this property generally treated?
options: As a one-to-four family home financed mainly on the buyer's personal salary
As income-producing multifamily property financed mainly on the building's income
As industrial property because it holds more than twenty dwelling units
As retail property because the owner collects rent from many separate tenants
questions.explanation: Apartment buildings with five or more units are generally treated as commercial (income) multifamily property, and lenders underwrite them largely on NOI and debt coverage. One-to-four family dwellings are the residential category financed mainly on the borrower's personal income.
questions.citation: General real estate finance practice (multifamily 5+ units)

questions.q: Two otherwise similar buildings each produce $100,000 of NOI. Investors apply a 6% cap rate to one and a 9% cap rate to the other. What does the difference most likely reflect?
options: Investors see more risk in the building valued at the 6% cap rate
The building valued at the 9% cap rate is worth more than the other
Investors see more risk in the building valued at the 9% cap rate
The 9% building must have larger mortgage payments than the other
questions.explanation: A higher cap rate means investors demand a higher return for the same income, which signals greater perceived risk and produces a lower value ($100,000 ÷ 0.09 = $1,111,111 versus $100,000 ÷ 0.06 = $1,666,667). Financing does not determine the cap rate, because NOI is measured before debt service.
questions.citation: Income capitalization approach (Value = NOI ÷ cap rate)

questions.q: An 18-unit building rents each unit for $2,200 per month. Vacancy and collection loss is 6%, laundry income is $9,600 a year, operating expenses are $168,000, annual debt service is $140,000, and the owner claims $30,000 of depreciation. What is the annual net operating income?
questions.explanation: Potential gross = 18 × $2,200 × 12 = $475,200; minus 6% vacancy ($28,512) = $446,688; plus $9,600 other income = $456,288; minus $168,000 expenses = $288,288. Debt service ($148,288 trap) and depreciation ($258,288 trap) are not operating expenses, and skipping vacancy gives $316,800.

questions.q: A retail building has effective gross income of $210,000 and operating expenses of $84,000. Comparable sales indicate a 7% capitalization rate. What is the indicated value?
questions.explanation: NOI = $210,000 − $84,000 = $126,000; value = $126,000 ÷ 0.07 = $1,800,000. Capitalizing gross income instead of NOI gives $3,000,000, and using an 8% rate gives $1,575,000.
questions.citation: Income capitalization approach (IRV: Value = Income ÷ Rate)

questions.q: A seller prices a building with $150,000 of NOI at a 7.5% cap rate. The buyer insists on an 8% cap rate. By how much does the buyer's indicated value fall below the seller's?
questions.explanation: Seller: $150,000 ÷ 0.075 = $2,000,000. Buyer: $150,000 ÷ 0.08 = $1,875,000. Difference = $125,000. Multiplying the 0.5% rate change by the price ($10,000 or $9,375) understates how sensitive value is to the cap rate.
questions.citation: Income capitalization approach (Value = NOI ÷ cap rate)

questions.q: A small office building has effective gross income of $260,000, operating expenses of $95,000, and annual debt service of $112,000. The owner also claims $28,000 of depreciation. What is the before-tax cash flow?
questions.explanation: NOI = $260,000 − $95,000 = $165,000; before-tax cash flow = $165,000 − $112,000 = $53,000. Depreciation is a non-cash tax deduction, so subtracting it ($25,000) is the trap; $165,000 is NOI, not cash flow.
questions.citation: Investment analysis (NOI − debt service = before-tax cash flow)

questions.q: An investor buys a building for $2,400,000 with a 70% loan, paying the rest in cash plus $30,000 of closing costs. NOI is $180,000 and annual debt service is $115,500. What is the cash-on-cash return?
questions.citation: Investment analysis (cash-on-cash = before-tax cash flow ÷ cash invested)

questions.q: A $1,000,000 building earns $60,000 of NOI. A buyer finances $750,000 with annual debt service of $56,250 and invests $250,000 in cash. What is the buyer's cash-on-cash return?
options: 1.5%, showing negative leverage
6%, the same as an all-cash purchase
24%, showing positive leverage
22.5%, showing positive leverage
questions.explanation: Cash flow = $60,000 − $56,250 = $3,750; $3,750 ÷ $250,000 = 1.5%. All cash would earn $60,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 6%, so borrowing at a 7.5% annual loan constant ($56,250 ÷ $750,000) costs more than the property earns and lowers the equity return. Dividing NOI by the equity ($60,000 ÷ $250,000 = 24%) ignores debt service.

questions.q: A lender requires a debt service coverage ratio of at least 1.25 on an apartment building with NOI of $210,000. What is the maximum annual debt service the lender will allow?
questions.explanation: DSCR = NOI ÷ debt service, so maximum debt service = $210,000 ÷ 1.25 = $168,000. Multiplying by 1.25 ($262,500) reverses the formula, and taking 75% of NOI ($157,500) is not the same as dividing by 1.25.
questions.citation: Commercial lending practice (DSCR = NOI ÷ annual debt service)

questions.q: A building's NOI is $140,000. Annual debt service is $85,000, of which $70,000 is interest and $15,000 is principal, and the owner may deduct $40,000 of depreciation. Ignoring other items, what is the taxable income from operations?
questions.explanation: Taxable income = NOI − mortgage interest − depreciation = $140,000 − $70,000 − $40,000 = $30,000. Principal repayment is not deductible, so subtracting the full $85,000 debt service gives $15,000; $55,000 is the before-tax cash flow, not taxable income.
questions.citation: Federal income tax treatment of investment property (interest and depreciation deductions)

questions.q: An investor owns a 40-unit apartment building and a medical office building. Ignoring land, over what straight-line recovery periods are the two buildings generally depreciated?
options: 39 years for the apartment building and 27.5 years for the medical office building
39 years for both, because each building is commercial investment property
27.5 years for both, because each building is leased to multiple tenants
27.5 years for the apartment building and 39 years for the medical office building
questions.explanation: Residential rental buildings (including large apartment buildings) use 27.5 years, while nonresidential real property such as offices, stores, and warehouses uses 39 years. Treating a large apartment building as nonresidential just because it is a commercial investment is the trap.
questions.citation: IRC §168(c) (27.5-year residential rental; 39-year nonresidential real property)

questions.q: A restaurant owner sells his building along with the kitchen equipment and furniture, and wants to defer all gain under §1031. Which part of the sale can qualify for like-kind exchange treatment?
options: Only the building and land, because §1031 now covers real property only
The building, land, equipment, and furniture, because all are business assets
Only the equipment and furniture, because they are used directly in the business
None of it, because property used in a business can never qualify under §1031
questions.explanation: Since 2018, §1031 applies only to real property held for business or investment use; equipment and other personal property no longer qualify. Business-use real property still qualifies, so 'none of it' is wrong.
questions.citation: IRC §1031(a), as amended by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017

questions.q: In a delayed §1031 exchange, an investor wants to list several possible replacement properties in case some deals fall through. Under the three-property rule, she may identify:
options: Up to three properties worth no more than her sale price
Up to three properties of any value
Any number of properties of any total value
Only one property, plus one backup
questions.explanation: The three-property rule lets the investor identify up to three replacement properties regardless of their value. Identifying more than three generally requires meeting the separate 200% rule (total value of identified properties no more than twice the relinquished property's value).

questions.q: Which property is NOT eligible for a §1031 like-kind exchange?
options: A warehouse leased to a distribution company
Vacant land held long-term for investment
Houses a builder renovates and holds for quick resale
An office building used in the owner's own business
questions.explanation: Property held primarily for sale (dealer or fix-and-flip inventory) does not qualify, because §1031 requires property held for productive use in a business or for investment. A warehouse, investment land, and an owner-used office building all qualify.

questions.q: A buyer's lender orders a Phase I environmental site assessment on a former gas station. Which activity is NOT normally part of a Phase I assessment?
options: Reviewing historical records of the site's prior uses
Walking the site to look for signs of contamination
Interviewing owners and occupants about past operations
Drilling and sending soil samples to a laboratory
questions.explanation: A Phase I is investigative: records review, site reconnaissance, and interviews to identify recognized environmental conditions. Collecting and testing soil or groundwater samples is Phase II work, ordered when a Phase I finds a concern.
questions.citation: ASTM E1527-21 Phase I ESA standard; CERCLA all appropriate inquiries (40 CFR Part 312)

questions.q: A buyer wants to purchase a building occupied by an auto repair shop that was legal when built but no longer conforms to the current zoning. The buyer plans to double the shop's size. What should the buyer expect?
options: The use may generally continue, but expanding it usually needs zoning relief
The use must stop immediately once the title passes to the new owner
The use may expand freely because the legal status runs with the land
The use becomes conforming automatically after ten years of operation
questions.explanation: A legal nonconforming use may generally continue and pass to a new owner, but local ordinances typically bar enlarging it and may end it if it is discontinued. Assuming the right to continue includes a right to expand is the trap; check the local ordinance.
questions.citation: NY Town Law, Village Law, and General City Law zoning; local zoning ordinance

questions.q: A buyer acquires an older retail building that predates the ADA and has a step at the entrance. Under ADA Title III, what is the owner generally required to do?
options: Nothing, because buildings constructed before the ADA are exempt from it
Remove architectural barriers where readily achievable, such as adding a ramp
Rebuild the store to meet all new-construction standards within one year
Post a sign directing customers who use wheelchairs to another store
questions.explanation: Title III requires places of public accommodation in existing buildings to remove barriers when doing so is readily achievable (easily accomplishable without much difficulty or expense). Older buildings are not exempt, but full new-construction standards apply to new construction and alterations.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, 42 U.S.C. §12182(b)(2)(A)(iv)

questions.q: A salesperson leases space in a large apartment complex. Which part of the complex is covered by ADA Title III?
options: The individual apartment units leased to tenants
Every area of the complex, including each apartment
The rental leasing office that is open to the public
No part, because housing is fully exempt from the ADA
questions.explanation: Title III covers places of public accommodation, such as a leasing office open to the public, but not the private dwelling units themselves. Accessibility in the apartments is governed by the Fair Housing Act and state and local law instead.
questions.citation: ADA Title III, 42 U.S.C. §12181(7); Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. §3604(f)

questions.q: A salesperson lists a 12-unit apartment building for sale in New York. Which disclosure requirement applies when she meets a prospective buyer?
options: The RPL §443 agency disclosure form is required; the fair housing notice is not
Both the RPL §443 agency form and the fair housing notice are required
Neither form is required, because the building is commercial property
The fair housing notice is required; the RPL §443 agency disclosure form is not
questions.explanation: The RPL §443 agency disclosure covers sales of one-to-four family residential property, so a 12-unit building is outside it. The fair housing notice under 19 NYCRR §175.28 applies to all real property, including multifamily and commercial.

questions.q: A commercial broker represents the landlord of an office building and is asked to represent a prospective tenant for the same space. The §443 agency form does not apply. What must the broker do before acting for both sides?
options: Obtain the informed consent of both parties after full disclosure
Nothing, because agency duties do not apply to commercial deals
Obtain the consent of the tenant only, since it is the new client
Get permission from the Department of State for each dual agency
questions.explanation: Common-law fiduciary duties apply in commercial transactions too, so dual agency requires full disclosure and the informed consent of both principals. The §443 form not applying removes only the prescribed form, not the duties behind it.
questions.citation: New York common law of agency; RPL §443 (form scope)

questions.q: The owner of a warehouse tells a broker, 'Sell it, and you keep anything over $3 million as your fee.' How should the broker treat this proposal in New York?
options: Accept it, because the net listing ban applies only to residential sales
Decline it, because net listings are prohibited even for commercial property
Accept it, as long as the arrangement is signed by the owner in writing
Accept it, as long as the final fee stays under the customary 6 percent
questions.explanation: New York prohibits net listings, and the rule does not exempt commercial property. Putting the arrangement in writing or capping the fee does not cure it; the broker should negotiate a stated commission instead.

questions.q: A landlord's broker earns 5% of the aggregate base rent on a 5-year lease of 4,000 square feet. Rent is $36 per square foot in year 1, rising by $1 per square foot each year. What is the total commission?
questions.explanation: Annual rates: $36 + $37 + $38 + $39 + $40 = $190 per sq ft over the term; × 4,000 sq ft = $760,000 aggregate rent; × 5% = $38,000. Using $36 for all five years gives $36,000, and using only year 1 rent gives $7,200.
questions.citation: Commercial leasing commission practice (percentage of aggregate rent)

questions.q: A salesperson finds a tenant for a retail space. The landlord offers to pay the salesperson's share directly to save time. What is the correct response?
options: Accept, because commercial deals are exempt from the license law's fee rules
Accept, as long as the salesperson reports the payment to the broker later
Accept, as long as the tenant signs a statement consenting to the payment
Decline, because the salesperson may be paid only through the sponsoring broker
questions.explanation: A salesperson acts on behalf of the sponsoring broker and may receive compensation only from that broker, not directly from a principal. Telling the broker afterward or getting the tenant's consent does not cure the violation.

questions.q: A building superintendent tips off a broker about a tenant looking for space, and the deal closes. The super holds no real estate license. May the broker pay him part of the commission?
options: No, a broker may not share a commission with an unlicensed person
Yes, because he did not negotiate any of the lease's terms
Yes, if the payment is under the broker's $500 referral limit
Yes, if the landlord agrees in writing to the fee being shared
questions.explanation: New York prohibits a broker from paying any part of a commission to a person who is not licensed for the services rendered. There is no small-referral exception, and the landlord's consent does not change the rule.

questions.q: Three commercial brokerage firms in a county agree that none of them will take an office listing for less than a 6% commission. This agreement is:
options: Legal, because commercial commissions are not regulated
Illegal price fixing under the antitrust laws
Legal, as long as the rate is published to every client
Illegal only if a firm's commission rate exceeds 6%
questions.explanation: Commission rates are negotiable between each broker and client; competing firms agreeing on a rate or a floor is price fixing. Publishing the rate or limiting it to commercial deals does not make a conspiracy lawful.
questions.citation: Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. §1; NY Donnelly Act, GBL §340

questions.q: A buyer purchases a bakery: the building it occupies, the ovens and display cases, the inventory, and the business name. Which documents typically transfer ownership?
options: A deed for everything, because all of it is located inside the same building
A bill of sale for everything, because the property is being sold as a business
A deed for the land and building, and a bill of sale for the equipment and inventory
A lease for the building, and a deed for the ovens and the remaining inventory
questions.explanation: Real property is conveyed by deed; personal property such as equipment, inventory, and goodwill is transferred by bill of sale or assignment. Selling a going business does not turn its building into personal property or its equipment into real property.
questions.citation: New York real property law (deeds) and UCC Article 2 (sale of goods)

questions.q: A deli tenant installed refrigerated display cases for its business. The landlord now sells the building. Unless the lease says otherwise, the display cases are generally:
options: Fixtures that became part of the building and now pass to the landlord's buyer
Fixtures that the deli must leave behind but may bill the new owner for at closing
Fixtures that belong to whichever party is first to claim them after the closing
Trade fixtures that remain the tenant's property and may be removed before the lease ends
questions.explanation: Equipment a tenant installs for its trade or business is a trade fixture: it remains the tenant's personal property and may be removed by the end of the lease, with any damage repaired. A listing broker should not describe such items as included in the building sale.
questions.citation: New York common law of trade fixtures

questions.q: A buyer is purchasing a retail business's assets, including its inventory and equipment, in New York. What must the buyer do to avoid becoming liable for the seller's unpaid sales tax?
options: Notify the Tax Department at least 10 days before paying or taking possession
Notify the Tax Department within 10 days after the sale has fully closed
Obtain the seller's written promise that all of its sales taxes were paid
Record the bill of sale with the county clerk at least 30 days before closing
questions.explanation: In a bulk sale of business assets, the purchaser must file Form AU-196.10 with the Tax Department at least 10 days before taking possession or paying, whichever comes first. A seller's assurance does not protect the buyer, and filing after closing is too late.

questions.q: A building and the business operating in it sell together for $1,500,000, with $300,000 of the price properly allocated to equipment and goodwill. The NYS real estate transfer tax is $2 per $500 of consideration for the real property. What is the transfer tax?
questions.explanation: The transfer tax applies to the consideration for the real property only: $1,500,000 − $300,000 = $1,200,000; $1,200,000 ÷ $500 = 2,400 units × $2 = $4,800. Taxing the full $1,500,000 gives $6,000, taxing only the $300,000 personal-property portion gives $1,200, and 2,400 is the number of units, not the tax.

questions.q: A property manager handles leasing, rent collection, and repairs for an owner's apartment building under an ongoing management agreement. The manager is best described as a:
options: Universal agent
Special agent
General agent
Dual agent
questions.explanation: A manager with ongoing authority over a range of tasks for one business is a general agent. A universal agent can act on all of the principal's affairs (e.g., broad power of attorney), and a special agent is limited to one transaction, like a typical listing.
questions.citation: NY agency law; NY RPL Article 12-A

questions.q: An unlicensed company offers, for a fee, to negotiate leases and collect rents for several building owners. Under New York law, the company:
options: Needs no license because management is not a sale
Needs a real estate broker license, since this is brokerage activity
Needs only an assumed-name certificate from the county clerk
Needs a license only if it manages more than ten units
questions.explanation: RPL § 440 defines brokerage to include negotiating rentals and collecting rent for another for compensation, so the company needs a broker license and its salespersons work under that broker. An owner managing his own property or a maintenance-only contractor is a different case.

questions.q: Which document creates the property manager's authority and should spell out the manager's fees, spending limits, reporting duties, and termination terms?
options: Management proposal
Rent roll
Operating budget
Management agreement
questions.explanation: The written management agreement creates the agency relationship and defines authority, compensation, budgets, spending limits, reporting, and termination. A management proposal only recommends a plan; the rent roll and budget are reports/tools used under the agreement.
questions.citation: NY RPL Article 12-A; property management agency principles

questions.q: A management agreement lets the manager approve repairs up to $1,500 without owner consent, except in emergencies. A contractor quotes $14,000 to replace the building's aging but working boiler next spring. The manager should:
options: Get the owner's approval before authorizing the replacement
Authorize it, since a general agent decides all building matters
Split the job into ten $1,400 invoices to stay under the limit
Pay from tenant security deposits and bill the owner later
questions.explanation: A planned capital replacement above the agreed limit, with no emergency, needs the owner's approval; general-agent status does not override the agreement's spending terms. Splitting invoices evades the limit, and security deposits are tenant trust money, never operating cash.
questions.citation: Management agreement / agency law; NY GOL § 7-103

questions.q: A plumbing contractor offers a property manager a $200 personal 'thank-you' rebate on each job billed to the owner. Under DOS rules, the manager may:
options: Keep it, since it does not raise the owner's cost
Keep it if it is reported as personal income
Accept it only with the owner's full knowledge and consent
Accept it whenever the contractor is the lowest bidder
questions.explanation: A broker managing property may not accept a commission, rebate, or profit on expenditures made for the owner without the owner's full knowledge and consent. Secretly pocketing it breaches the fiduciary duties of loyalty and disclosure even if the price is fair.

questions.q: An owner wants to set money aside each year for a roof replacement expected in six years. That planned set-aside belongs in the:
options: Operating budget as a routine repair
Capital reserve budget
Rent roll as a tenant charge
Security deposit escrow account
questions.explanation: A capital reserve budget plans for large, infrequent replacements and improvements like a roof. The operating budget covers recurring income and expenses; patching a small leak is operating, replacing the roof is capital.
questions.citation: Property management budgeting (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A report listing each unit, the tenant, lease start and end dates, the monthly rent, and any balance owed is called a:
options: Operating statement
Management proposal
Capital reserve schedule
Rent roll
questions.explanation: A rent roll lists units, tenants, lease terms, scheduled rents, and arrears. It shows what is scheduled and owed — it is not proof that every scheduled dollar was actually collected.
questions.citation: Property management reporting (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A building has potential gross rent of $180,000, a 5% vacancy and collection loss, $2,000 of laundry income, $70,000 of operating expenses, and $40,000 of annual mortgage payments. What is the net operating income?
questions.explanation: EGI = $180,000 × 0.95 + $2,000 = $171,000 + $2,000 = $173,000; NOI = $173,000 − $70,000 = $103,000. Mortgage debt service is not an operating expense, so subtracting it ($63,000) is the trap.
questions.citation: Income property analysis: NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses

questions.q: Replacing furnace and air-conditioner filters on a fixed quarterly schedule, before any problem appears, is an example of:
options: Corrective maintenance
Construction
Preventive maintenance
Cosmetic maintenance
questions.explanation: Preventive maintenance is periodic servicing that prevents wear and failure, such as scheduled filter changes. Corrective maintenance fixes something already broken, like a leaky faucet a tenant reports.
questions.citation: Property management maintenance categories (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: Remodeling a vacant office suite to a new commercial tenant's specifications (tenant improvements) is classified as:
options: Preventive maintenance
Corrective maintenance
Routine maintenance
Construction
questions.explanation: Construction covers budgeted remodeling, tenant build-outs, and new capital improvements. Routine maintenance is day-to-day upkeep like cleaning common areas; corrective maintenance repairs a reported defect.
questions.citation: Property management maintenance categories (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A property manager advises the owner to buy a general liability policy covering injuries in the building's common areas. Which risk management technique is this?
options: Avoiding the risk
Transferring the risk
Retaining the risk
Controlling the risk
questions.explanation: Buying insurance shifts the financial risk to the insurer, which is risk transfer. Insurance does not excuse leaving a known hazard unrepaired — control (inspections, repairs) still applies.
questions.citation: Property management risk management (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: Rather than face drowning liability, an owner decides to close and fill in the building's swimming pool. This risk management technique is:
