options: Avoiding the risk
Transferring the risk
Retaining the risk
Controlling the risk
questions.explanation: Eliminating the activity that creates the risk is avoidance. Adding fencing or lifeguards would be control, buying insurance would be transfer, and self-insuring or carrying a large deductible would be retention.
questions.citation: Property management risk management (NYS 77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A non-rent-regulated apartment in Rochester rents for $1,950 per month. At lease signing, what is the most the landlord may collect for the first month's rent plus security?
options: $5,850 for first month, last month, and security
$1,950 for first month only, with no deposit
$3,900 for first month plus one month's security
$4,875 for first month plus 1.5 months' security
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 caps any security deposit or advance at one month's rent: $1,950 first month + $1,950 security = $3,900. Demanding last month's rent on top of security is an extra advance and exceeds the cap.

questions.q: A tenant in a non-regulated apartment moves out on June 1. To keep any part of the security deposit for damage, the landlord must give an itemized statement and return the balance within:
options: 30 days after the tenant vacates
7 days after the tenant vacates
45 days after the scheduled lease end
14 days after the tenant vacates
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires an itemized statement of deductions and return of the balance within 14 days after the tenant vacates; missing the deadline forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit. Deductions are limited to items like unpaid rent and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear.

questions.q: A landlord of a building with six or more apartments must keep tenants' security deposits in an interest-bearing New York bank account. How much of the interest may the landlord keep?
options: An administrative fee of 1% per year of the deposit
All interest, because the landlord holds the account
Half of the interest, split with the tenant
None; all interest must be paid to the city
questions.explanation: Under GOL § 7-103 the landlord may retain 1% per year of the deposit for administrative expenses; the rest of the interest belongs to the tenant (paid annually, applied to rent, or paid at lease end). The tenant must be told in writing the bank's name and address and the deposit amount.

questions.q: A property manager deposits tenants' security deposits into the management company's operating account to cover payroll until rent comes in. This is:
options: Permitted if repaid within 30 days
Unlawful commingling of trust funds
Permitted if the owner verbally approves
Permitted in buildings with fewer than six units
questions.explanation: Security deposits remain the tenant's money held in trust and may not be commingled with the landlord's or manager's funds, regardless of building size or owner approval. Broker rules separately require client funds to be kept in a separate special account.

questions.q: An owner tells the property manager, 'Don't rent the third-floor walk-up to families with kids — the stairs are too dangerous for children.' The manager should:
options: Follow it, because the instruction protects children's safety on the stairs
Follow it only if the owner puts the instruction in writing and signs it
Refuse; a safety-based ban on children is familial status discrimination
Rent to families only if the parents sign a stair-injury liability waiver
questions.explanation: Limiting units for families with children based on paternalistic safety concerns is familial status discrimination. A principal's instruction never authorizes a manager to discriminate; screening must use the same lawful criteria for everyone.
questions.citation: Federal Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 3604; NY Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: A property manager oversees an existing shopping center. Under Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act, the manager must generally:
options: Rebuild the whole center to new-construction standards at once
Wait until a customer with a disability files a complaint
Comply only if the center receives federal funding
Remove barriers where readily achievable, such as adding ramps
questions.explanation: Existing places of public accommodation must remove architectural barriers where it is readily achievable (easily accomplished without much difficulty or expense). The duty is ongoing, applies without federal funding, and does not require an immediate full rebuild.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III, 42 U.S.C. § 12182

questions.q: A tenant is two months behind on rent. The property manager changes the locks while the tenant is at work and puts the tenant's belongings on the curb. Under New York law this is:
options: A lawful self-help remedy after 30 days of nonpayment
An unlawful eviction; a court summary proceeding is required
Lawful if the lease contains a lockout clause
Lawful if a 14-day rent demand was served first
questions.explanation: Residential self-help (lockouts, utility shutoffs, removing belongings) is prohibited; possession must be recovered through a summary proceeding and a warrant executed by a marshal or sheriff. The 2019 HSTPA made unlawful eviction a crime, and a lease clause cannot waive these protections.

questions.q: Before starting a nonpayment summary proceeding against a residential tenant, the landlord must generally serve a written rent demand giving the tenant at least:
options: 14 days to pay
3 days to pay
5 days to pay
30 days to pay
questions.explanation: The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act lengthened the rent demand from 3 days to 14 days. The 5-day figure is the separate late-rent notice/late-fee trigger, a common mix-up.

questions.q: A tenant in a non-regulated New York apartment pays $1,800 per month and pays rent more than five days late. What is the maximum late fee the landlord may charge?
questions.explanation: The late fee may not exceed the lesser of $50 or 5% of monthly rent: 5% × $1,800 = $90, so the cap is $50. A fee may be charged only when rent is more than five days late.

questions.q: In New York City, the maximum allowable rent increases for rent-stabilized lease renewals are set by the:
options: NYC Rent Guidelines Board
NYS Department of State
Landlord, up to the Good Cause 5% + CPI cap
U.S. Department of HUD
questions.explanation: The NYC Rent Guidelines Board votes annual renewal increases for stabilized apartments, and stabilized tenants have renewal rights. The Good Cause Eviction rent test applies to covered unregulated units, and the 2019 HSTPA ended high-rent/high-income deregulation.
questions.citation: NYC Rent Stabilization Law (NYC Admin. Code § 26-501 et seq.); HSTPA 2019

questions.q: After an owner says she 'likes' a manager's written management proposal, but before any contract is signed, the manager starts signing tenant leases in the owner's name. The manager's position is best described as:
options: Lacking authority, since a proposal does not create the agency
Authorized, because the owner approved the proposal orally
Authorized, because praising a proposal makes it binding
Lacking authority only for leases longer than one year
questions.explanation: A management proposal only recommends a plan; the manager's agency and authority come from the signed management agreement. Verbal approval of a proposal does not grant authority to bind the owner to leases, whatever their length.
questions.citation: Agency law; management agreement creates the agency (77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: A management agreement gives a manager broad authority to lease, collect rent, hire staff, and contract for repairs at a 40-unit building. A buyer offers to purchase the building. The manager may:
options: Sign the contract of sale, since general agents handle all owner affairs
Accept the offer if the price exceeds the building's appraised value
Present the offer to the owner, but not sell without specific authority
Reject the offer, since managers may not pass along purchase offers
questions.explanation: A property manager is a general agent only for the management business the agreement defines. Selling the building is outside that scope, so the manager passes the offer to the owner; 'general agent' does not mean unlimited power over the owner's property.
questions.citation: Agency law; scope of authority defined by the management agreement

questions.q: An owner instructs his property manager to tell apartment applicants that the building has never had bedbugs, although the manager knows of two treated infestations last year. The manager should:
options: Follow the instruction, since a manager owes the owner obedience
Refuse, since the duty of obedience covers only lawful, honest orders
Follow it only if applicants do not ask directly about pests
Refuse only if the infestations occurred within the past six months
questions.explanation: The fiduciary duty of obedience extends only to lawful instructions. Telling applicants a false fact is misrepresentation, and the manager is liable for it regardless of the owner's order or the timing of the infestations.
questions.citation: Fiduciary duties; misrepresentation (RPL §441-c grounds for discipline)

questions.q: A prospective commercial tenant asks the building manager, 'What's the lowest rent the owner will really accept for this suite?' The manager knows the owner would take $500 a month less than the asking rent. The manager should:
options: Disclose the figure to keep the negotiation honest and efficient
Disclose it only if the tenant signs a confidentiality agreement
Disclose it, because tenants are owed the same loyalty as owners
Keep it confidential, since it is the owner's bargaining information
questions.explanation: The manager is the owner's agent and owes the owner confidentiality and loyalty. The tenant is a customer owed honesty, not the owner's private negotiating position; revealing the owner's floor would breach the fiduciary duty.
questions.citation: Fiduciary duties of loyalty and confidentiality

questions.q: Under DOS regulations, a broker who collects rents while managing property for a client must:
options: Hold all collections until the management agreement ends, then remit
Remit only the net income left after the broker's fiscal year closes
Account to the client only if the client asks for it in writing
Account to the client and remit unspent funds within a reasonable time
questions.explanation: 19 NYCRR §175.2 requires a broker to render an account to the client and remit collected, unexpended money within a reasonable time. Holding funds until the agreement ends or the broker's year closes, or accounting only on written request, falls short of that duty.

questions.q: A management company receives a tenant's rent check on a Friday. Under 19 NYCRR §175.1, the owner's money must be deposited into a separate, special bank account:
options: Within three business days, safeguarded securely until deposited
Within ten business days, along with that month's other receipts
By month's end, when the owner's statement is being prepared
Within thirty days, unless the owner asks for faster deposit
questions.explanation: Section 175.1 bars commingling and requires client money to be deposited in a separate, special, federally insured account within three business days, kept in a secure location until then. Batching receipts until month-end or a 10- or 30-day window violates the rule.

questions.q: A management agreement pays the manager 5% of rents actually collected. This month the building's scheduled rents total $40,000, but $2,500 went uncollected. What is the manager's fee for the month?
questions.explanation: Collections = $40,000 − $2,500 = $37,500; fee = $37,500 × 0.05 = $1,875. Applying 5% to scheduled rent ($2,000) ignores the 'actually collected' basis; $125 is 5% of the uncollected amount.

questions.q: A manager's agreement provides a base fee of $600 per month plus 4% of collected rents. Collections this month are $28,750. What is the manager's total fee?
questions.explanation: Percentage portion = $28,750 × 0.04 = $1,150; total = $600 + $1,150 = $1,750. Stopping at $1,150 omits the base fee; $1,174 takes 4% of collections plus the base fee ($29,350 × 0.04) instead of adding the base fee; $715 uses 0.4% instead of 4%.

questions.q: A manager earns 5% of monthly collections plus a leasing fee of one-half month's rent for each new lease signed. In March the manager collects $30,000 and signs three new leases at $2,400 per month. What is the manager's total March compensation?
questions.explanation: Management fee = $30,000 × 0.05 = $1,500. Leasing fees = 3 × ($2,400 × 0.5) = $3,600. Total = $1,500 + $3,600 = $5,100. $2,700 counts only one lease; $3,600 omits the management fee; $8,700 pays a full month's rent per lease.

questions.q: At a trade association dinner, managers from three competing management firms agree that none will charge less than 6% of collections. This agreement is:
options: Lawful, because management fees are not sales commissions
Lawful if the 6% minimum is disclosed in every agreement
A permissible industry standard set by a trade group
Illegal price fixing under federal and state antitrust law
questions.explanation: Competitors must set their fees independently; agreeing on a minimum fee is price fixing. Antitrust law reaches management fees as well as sales commissions, and disclosing the fixed rate does not make the agreement legal.
questions.citation: Sherman Antitrust Act §1; NY Donnelly Act (GBL §340)

questions.q: A manager's budget for a newly purchased building strips out the one-time costs of the current lease-up and a temporary tax abatement to show income and expenses under normal, ongoing operation. This is a:
options: Stabilized budget
Capital reserve budget
Construction budget
Cash-basis budget
questions.explanation: A stabilized budget projects income and expenses under expected normal operation, excluding temporary conditions such as a lease-up period or a temporary abatement. A capital reserve budget funds large future replacements, not ordinary operations.
questions.citation: Property management budgeting (77-hr syllabus, Property Management)

questions.q: In a property's operating budget, which expense is generally classified as VARIABLE rather than fixed?
options: Real estate taxes
Annual property insurance premium
Common-area cleaning supplies
Fixed-price elevator service contract
questions.explanation: Variable expenses rise and fall with use or occupancy, as cleaning supplies do. Property taxes, an insurance premium, and a fixed-price service contract are set amounts for the period regardless of how heavily the building is used.
questions.citation: Property management budgeting: fixed vs. variable expenses

questions.q: The roof on a 20-unit building is expected to need a $96,000 replacement in 8 years. If the manager funds a capital reserve in equal monthly amounts, ignoring interest, how much should be set aside per unit per month?
questions.explanation: $96,000 ÷ 8 years = $12,000 per year; ÷ 12 = $1,000 per month; ÷ 20 units = $50 per unit per month. $1,000 is the whole building's monthly amount; $600 is per unit per year; $400 ($96,000 ÷ 20 ÷ 12) ignores the 8-year horizon.

questions.q: Scheduled rent is $54,000 and the manager collects $52,300. Operating expenses paid are $18,450, the agreement sets a 6% fee on collections, and the owner directs a $2,000 transfer to the capital reserve. How much is remitted to the owner?
questions.explanation: Fee = $52,300 × 0.06 = $3,138. Remittance = $52,300 − $18,450 − $3,138 − $2,000 = $28,712. $28,610 takes the fee on scheduled rent ($3,240); $30,712 skips the reserve transfer; $31,850 skips the management fee.
questions.citation: Owner reporting and trust accounting; 19 NYCRR §175.2

questions.q: The periodic statement a manager sends the owner showing rents received, expenses paid, disbursements, and the ending account balance is the:
options: Management proposal
Stabilized budget
Rent roll
Property management report
questions.explanation: The property management report tells the owner what came in, what went out, and what remains for the period. A rent roll lists units, tenants, lease terms, rents, and arrears but does not account for expenses and disbursements.
questions.citation: Owner reporting (77-hr syllabus key term: property management report)

questions.q: A manager handles buildings for two different owners. Owner A's funds are $3,000 short for an emergency boiler repair, so the manager pays the contractor from Owner B's funds, planning to repay when A's rents arrive next week. This is:
options: Improper, because each client's money may be used only for that client
Proper, because the repair was a genuine emergency
Proper if the manager repays Owner B within 30 days
Improper only if Owner B ends up suffering an actual loss
questions.explanation: Each client's money is held in trust for that client alone; using one owner's funds to cover another's shortfall is conversion, even briefly and even with intent to repay. The proper step is to ask Owner A for funds.

questions.q: A tenant's rent, due on the 1st, still has not arrived by the 6th. Under RPL §235-e, the landlord or its agent must:
options: Immediately serve a notice of petition for nonpayment
Charge the maximum late fee before taking any other step
Wait 30 days before contacting the tenant about the rent
Send the tenant written notice of the late rent by certified mail
questions.explanation: RPL §235-e requires written notice by certified mail when rent is not received within five days of the due date; failing to send it is an affirmative defense in a later nonpayment case. This reminder is separate from, and does not replace, the 14-day rent demand.

questions.q: A residential tenant pays the month's rent with a money order. Under New York law, the landlord must:
options: Refuse it, since only checks are lawful payment
Provide the tenant with a written receipt
Charge a processing fee of up to $20
Give a receipt only if requested in writing
questions.explanation: RPL §235-e requires a written receipt whenever rent is paid in cash or any form other than the tenant's personal check, and money orders fall into that category. The 'only on request' rule applies to personal checks.

questions.q: A manager requires one applicant who speaks with a foreign accent to supply two extra landlord references, while other applicants with similar credit supply none. This practice:
options: Violates fair housing law by applying screening criteria unequally
Is lawful, because references are a legitimate screening tool
Is lawful as long as the applicant is eventually approved
Violates fair housing law only if the owner ordered it
questions.explanation: Imposing tougher terms on an applicant because of national origin is discrimination even if the applicant is later approved. A legitimate screening tool becomes unlawful when applied selectively, and the manager is liable for the manager's own conduct.
questions.citation: Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. §3604(b); Executive Law §296(5)

questions.q: An owner tells the manager to turn away any applicant who would pay part of the rent with a Housing Choice (Section 8) voucher. Under the New York State Human Rights Law, the manager should:
options: Comply, since federal law does not protect voucher holders
Comply only if the building has fewer than six units
Refuse, because lawful source of income is a protected class
Comply if the owner applies the policy to every applicant
questions.explanation: New York's Human Rights Law prohibits housing discrimination based on lawful source of income, which includes vouchers. That federal law lacks this protection does not matter, and applying a discriminatory policy to everyone does not cure it.

questions.q: An applicant has steady income and good credit, but a screening report shows she was a party to a summary proceeding against a prior landlord three years ago. Under New York law, the manager:
options: May not deny her because of that past landlord-tenant case
May deny her automatically for any prior housing court case
May deny her only if the court ruled against her
May deny her if the case is less than five years old
questions.explanation: RPL §227-f bars refusing to rent because an applicant was a party to a prior or pending landlord-tenant proceeding; denial after checking court records raises a presumption of a violation. No outcome or age-of-case exception exists.

questions.q: A month-to-month tenant in a non-rent-regulated apartment moved in seven months ago. The owner decides to end the tenancy. Under RPL §226-c, the manager must give written notice at least:
options: 30 days before the tenancy ends
90 days before the tenancy ends
14 days before the tenancy ends
60 days before the tenancy ends
questions.explanation: RPL §226-c ties the notice to occupancy or lease term, whichever is longer: under 1 year = 30 days, at least 1 but under 2 years = 60 days, 2 years or more = 90 days. Seven months of occupancy with no lease of a year or more falls in the 30-day tier.

questions.q: A manager plans to offer a renewal at a 6% rent increase to a tenant who has occupied a non-regulated apartment for 15 months under one-year leases. What notice does New York law require?
options: At least 60 days' written notice of the increase
At least 30 days' written notice of the increase
At least 90 days' written notice of the increase
None, since increases under 10% need no notice
questions.explanation: RPL §226-c requires advance written notice of an increase of 5% or more, using the same 30/60/90-day tiers as non-renewal. With at least 1 but under 2 years of occupancy, 60 days applies; if notice is late, the tenancy continues at the existing rent until the period runs.

questions.q: After depositing a new tenant's security in a New York bank, the landlord must notify the tenant in writing of:
options: The account number and the bank's current interest rate
The bank's name and address and the amount deposited
The date the deposit will be released to the landlord
The name of the bank officer who oversees the account
questions.explanation: GOL §7-103(2) requires written notice to each tenant of the name and address of the banking organization holding the security and the amount deposited. The deposit stays the tenant's money; it is never 'released' to the landlord as income.

questions.q: A tenant's $2,000 security deposit is held in an interest-bearing account for a 12-unit building. The account earns 3.2% this year. How much of the year's interest belongs to the tenant?
questions.explanation: Interest = $2,000 × 0.032 = $64. Landlord's administrative fee = 1% of the deposit = $2,000 × 0.01 = $20. Tenant's share = $64 − $20 = $44. $63.36 wrongly takes 1% of the interest instead of 1% of the deposit.

questions.q: A landlord of a 30-unit building in Albany wants to keep tenants' security deposits in an interest-bearing account at an online bank with no place of business in New York. Under GOL §7-103, this is:
options: Allowed, as long as the account is federally insured
Allowed if each lease contains the tenant's written consent
Not allowed; the bank must have a place of business in New York
Allowed only if the bank pays above the local prevailing rate
questions.explanation: GOL §7-103 requires security deposits placed in a bank to be held in a banking organization with a place of business within the state, and for buildings of six or more units the account must earn the prevailing local rate. Federal insurance or a higher rate does not satisfy the in-state rule, and a lease clause waiving the statute is void.

questions.q: The owner of a non-rent-regulated four-unit building collects a security deposit from each tenant. Under GOL §7-103, the owner:
options: May treat the deposits as rent income once each lease begins
Must use an interest-bearing account, just like larger buildings
May commingle them because the building has under six units
Must hold the deposits in trust, unmixed, but need not earn interest
questions.explanation: Every security deposit remains the tenant's money, held in trust and not commingled with the owner's funds. The interest-bearing requirement applies only to buildings with six or more family dwelling units, so a four-unit owner need not earn interest.

questions.q: A lease drafted by the manager states that the tenant 'waives all rights under General Obligations Law §7-103 regarding the security deposit.' This clause is:
options: Valid if the tenant initials the clause separately
Valid for leases with terms longer than one year
Void, because the statute's protections cannot be waived
Valid only in buildings with fewer than six units
questions.explanation: GOL §7-103 declares any lease provision waiving its security-deposit protections void. Separate initials, a longer lease term, or building size do not make such a waiver enforceable.

questions.q: After a landlord wins a judgment of possession and a warrant of eviction issues, who may physically remove the residential tenant?
options: The property manager, once the judgment has been entered
The landlord, with a police officer standing by to observe
A sheriff, city marshal, or constable acting under the warrant
A locksmith hired by the owner's attorney to change locks
questions.explanation: Only an enforcement officer (sheriff, marshal, or constable) executes a warrant of eviction. A judgment does not authorize the owner, manager, or a hired locksmith to remove the tenant, and doing so is an unlawful eviction.

questions.q: Before executing a warrant of eviction against a residential tenant, the enforcement officer must serve written notice at least:
options: 72 hours before the eviction
14 days before the eviction
30 days before the eviction
5 business days before the eviction
questions.explanation: Since the 2019 HSTPA, RPAPL §749 requires at least 14 days' written notice before a warrant is executed, and execution must occur on a business day between sunrise and sunset. The 72-hour notice was the pre-2019 rule.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly reflects a typical New York residential nonpayment eviction?
options: Rent demand, petition, judgment, warrant, officer's notice, removal
Petition, rent demand, warrant, judgment, officer's notice, removal
Rent demand, warrant, petition, judgment, officer's notice, removal
Officer's notice, rent demand, petition, judgment, warrant, removal
questions.explanation: A nonpayment case starts with the written 14-day rent demand, then the court petition and hearing, a judgment of possession, a warrant, the officer's 14-day notice, and only then removal. A warrant cannot precede the judgment, and the officer's notice follows the warrant.

questions.q: Which person does NOT need a New York real estate license for the activity described?
options: A management firm employee who negotiates leases for the firm's clients
A person who collects rents for unrelated owners for a percentage fee
A leasing agent paid per lease by an owner she does not work for
An owner's building superintendent who only does repairs and upkeep
questions.explanation: Building superintendents and maintenance workers doing only maintenance are not performing brokerage. Negotiating leases or collecting rent for another for a fee falls within the RPL §440 definition of a broker and requires a license.

questions.q: An investor who owns three apartment buildings in her own name personally screens tenants, signs leases, and collects rent. She:
options: Needs a broker's license once she owns more than two buildings
Needs a salesperson license to sign leases with tenants
Needs a license only if she charges application fees
Needs no license, because she acts for herself, not for another
questions.explanation: The RPL §440 broker definition covers acting 'for another and for a fee,' so an owner managing her own property needs no license regardless of how many buildings she owns.

questions.q: A licensed salesperson wants to manage rental buildings for several owners and collect a management fee directly from each owner. Under New York law, the salesperson:
options: Must work through her supervising broker, not in her own name
May contract directly, since salespersons may collect rent
May contract directly if each owner signs a written agreement
May contract directly for buildings of fewer than six units
questions.explanation: A salesperson acts only under a supervising broker and may be paid only through that broker. Managing for owners in her own name would be unlicensed brokerage, whatever the paperwork or building size.

questions.q: A tenant reports a dripping kitchen faucet, and the super replaces the worn cartridge that afternoon. This work is best classified as:
options: preventive maintenance
corrective maintenance
deferred maintenance
construction maintenance
questions.explanation: Corrective maintenance repairs an existing defect after it appears, as here. Preventive maintenance is scheduled servicing done before anything fails, so it is the tempting but wrong label for a same-day fix of a reported leak.
questions.citation: NYS Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 19 (corrective vs. preventive maintenance)

questions.q: Mopping the lobby daily, emptying common-area trash, and sweeping the sidewalk each morning are examples of:
options: routine (custodial) maintenance
construction maintenance
corrective maintenance
capital improvement work
questions.explanation: Routine or custodial maintenance is the recurring housekeeping that keeps a building clean and orderly day to day. Nothing is broken, so it is not corrective, and nothing new is built or replaced, so it is neither construction work nor a capital improvement.
questions.citation: General property management principles (types of maintenance)

questions.q: To show higher net operating income before a planned sale, an owner tells the manager to postpone repointing a deteriorating brick facade for several years. The postponed work is:
options: construction maintenance for a future buyer
preventive maintenance that has been rescheduled
routine maintenance shifted to the next budget
deferred maintenance that tends to cost more later
questions.explanation: Deferred maintenance is needed work that is put off; the deterioration keeps progressing, so the eventual repair usually costs more and the property's value suffers. Calling it 'rescheduled preventive maintenance' is the trap: preventive work is done before failure, while this facade is already deteriorating.

questions.q: After several slip-and-fall complaints, a manager installs anti-slip stair treads, brighter lighting, and new handrails in the stairwells. This risk management technique is:
options: risk retention
risk transfer
risk control
risk avoidance
questions.explanation: Risk control (reduction) keeps the activity but lowers the chance or severity of loss, here through safer stairs and better lighting. It is not avoidance, because the stairwells stay in use; avoidance would mean eliminating the activity entirely.
questions.citation: NYS Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 19 (insurance and risk management)

questions.q: An owner chooses a property policy with a $25,000 deductible and plans to pay smaller losses out of building reserves. As to those smaller losses, the owner is using:
options: risk transfer
risk retention
risk avoidance
risk control
questions.explanation: Keeping a layer of loss on the owner's own books, through a deductible or self-insurance, is risk retention. Only the portion of a loss above the deductible is transferred to the insurer, so 'transfer' describes the policy as a whole, not the small losses the owner absorbs.
questions.citation: NYS Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 19 (insurance and risk management)

questions.q: A management agreement requires every contractor to carry liability insurance, name the owner and managing agent as additional insureds, and sign a hold-harmless (indemnification) clause. These requirements primarily:
options: transfer the risk to the contractor and its insurer
avoid the risk by eliminating the activity
retain the risk within the owner's reserves
control the risk by supervising the contractor's work
questions.explanation: Insurance requirements, additional-insured status, and indemnification clauses shift the financial consequences of a contractor's mistakes to the contractor and its insurer, which is risk transfer. The work still happens and nobody is supervising it more closely, so this is neither avoidance nor control.
questions.citation: NYS Salesperson Syllabus, Subject 19 (insurance and risk management)

questions.q: A building's property policy has a $5,000 per-occurrence deductible. This year there were two covered water losses, one of $3,200 and one of $14,500. How much of the losses did the owner retain in total?
questions.explanation: The $3,200 loss is below the deductible, so the owner pays all $3,200. On the $14,500 loss the owner pays the $5,000 deductible and the insurer pays $14,500 − $5,000 = $9,500. Total retained = $3,200 + $5,000 = $8,200. The $10,000 trap charges a full deductible on a loss smaller than the deductible.
questions.citation: General insurance principles (per-occurrence deductible as risk retention)

questions.q: A fire makes 6 of a building's 20 apartments uninhabitable for 5 months. Each of the 6 units rents for $2,250 per month, and the owner carries rent loss (loss of rents) coverage. Ignoring any waiting period, what is the covered rent loss?
questions.explanation: Rent loss coverage replaces rent lost from the damaged units during restoration: 6 units × $2,250 × 5 months = $67,500. Multiplying by all 20 units ($225,000) counts apartments that were never vacated, and using 12 months ($162,000) ignores the actual 5-month restoration period.
questions.citation: General insurance principles (rent loss / business income coverage)

questions.q: The managing agent's staff collect rents and handle tenants' security deposits. Which coverage protects the owner if an employee steals those funds?
options: Rent loss coverage on the building property policy
A fidelity bond or employee dishonesty (crime) policy
Commercial general liability coverage
An umbrella (excess liability) policy
questions.explanation: A fidelity bond or crime policy covers theft by employees who handle money. Rent loss coverage pays only when a covered physical loss, like a fire, interrupts rent; general liability and umbrella policies cover injury and damage claims by third parties, not employee embezzlement.
questions.citation: General insurance principles (fidelity bonds / commercial crime coverage)

questions.q: The standard property policy on an apartment building excludes mechanical breakdown. To cover a sudden boiler failure or the burnout of electrical switchgear, the manager should recommend:
options: equipment breakdown coverage
flood insurance through the NFIP
umbrella excess liability coverage
a fidelity bond on employees
questions.explanation: Equipment breakdown (boiler and machinery) coverage insures sudden mechanical and electrical failure of building equipment that standard property forms exclude. An umbrella policy only adds liability limits for injury claims; it does not pay to repair the owner's own boiler.
questions.citation: General insurance principles (equipment breakdown / boiler and machinery coverage)

questions.q: A management company runs a leasing office open to the public at a large apartment complex. Which law makes the leasing office itself subject to accessibility rules for places of public accommodation?
options: No law, since it is privately owned
Only the Fair Housing Act
Only the local zoning code
The ADA's Title III
questions.explanation: A rental or sales office open to the public is a place of public accommodation under ADA Title III, even though the apartments themselves are dwellings governed by the Fair Housing Act. Private ownership does not exempt a public-facing business from Title III.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, 42 U.S.C. §12181–12182; 28 CFR §36.104

questions.q: Under the ADA, a new commercial building designed and built for first occupancy after January 26, 1993 must generally be:
options: altered only where barrier removal is readily achievable
made accessible only when a disabled tenant asks for it
readily accessible to and usable by people with disabilities
exempt if it is privately financed and privately owned
questions.explanation: ADA Title III requires new construction for first occupancy after January 26, 1993 to be readily accessible to and usable by people with disabilities. The 'readily achievable' barrier-removal standard is the trap: it is the lower standard for existing facilities, not for new buildings.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III; 28 CFR §36.401 (new construction)

questions.q: A landlord leases a storefront to a restaurant. Under ADA Title III, responsibility for making the space accessible:
options: rests only with the tenant, because it operates the business
rests with both landlord and tenant, who may allocate it by lease
rests only with the landlord, because it owns the building
does not arise until a customer files a DOJ complaint
questions.explanation: DOJ rules make both the landlord who owns the place of public accommodation and the tenant who operates it responsible for compliance; the lease may allocate the duty between them, but neither escapes it as to the public. Placing the duty on the tenant alone is the common misconception.
questions.citation: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III; 28 CFR §36.201(b) (landlord and tenant responsibilities)

questions.q: In New York City, a building taller than six stories must have its exterior walls (facade) inspected by a qualified professional:
options: every five years under FISP (Local Law 11)
once a year before the heat season begins
only when the building is sold or refinanced
only after facade debris has actually fallen
questions.explanation: NYC's Facade Inspection Safety Program (Local Law 11 of 1998) requires a periodic facade inspection every five years for buildings taller than six stories. It does not wait for a sale or an accident; the point is to catch unsafe conditions before anything falls.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §28-302; 1 RCNY §103-04 (Facade Inspection Safety Program)

questions.q: A tenant calls the management office to report a strong smell of gas in a hallway. The manager's best first step is to:
options: tell the tenant to open a window and wait it out
have the super locate the leak before calling anyone
enter it as a work order for the next business day
have people leave and call 911 and the gas utility
questions.explanation: A suspected gas leak is an emergency: get people out and call 911 and the utility from a safe place, without operating switches or flames. Having the super hunt for the leak first delays the professional response a manager should recognize is required.
questions.citation: General building systems oversight; NYC HPD and utility gas-leak safety guidance

questions.q: Which New York City property must be registered annually with HPD?
options: A one-family house occupied only by the owner's family
A two-family house whose owner lives in one of the units
A rented two-family house whose owner lives out of state
An office building with no residential units at all
questions.explanation: HPD registration is required for every multiple dwelling (3+ units) and for one- or two-family homes where neither the owner nor the owner's immediate family lives. An owner-occupied two-family house is exempt, and a purely commercial building is not residential property.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2097 (Housing Maintenance Code registration)

questions.q: A NYC owner of a 12-unit building has not filed the required HPD property registration, and a tenant falls behind on rent. The owner:
options: may proceed but owes HPD a late fee before the trial
cannot recover possession for nonpayment until it registers
must register with DHCR instead, since HPD has no role
faces no court effect, since registration is voluntary
questions.explanation: An owner that fails to file a required HPD registration is denied the right to recover possession for nonpayment of rent during the period of noncompliance, and may also face civil penalties. DHCR registration of stabilized units is a separate obligation that does not replace HPD registration.

questions.q: On a November afternoon in New York City, the outdoor temperature is 48°F. Under the Housing Maintenance Code, the indoor temperature in each apartment must be at least:
questions.explanation: During the heat season, between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m., when it is below 55°F outside, the inside temperature must be at least 68°F. The 62°F figure is the overnight (10 p.m.–6 a.m.) minimum, which is the most common mix-up.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2029 (heat); HPD heat and hot water rules

questions.q: At 2 a.m. on a mild April night in New York City, it is 60°F outdoors and a tenant's apartment reads 59°F. Is the owner in compliance?
options: No; 68°F is required at all hours during the heat season
Yes; overnight rules apply only when it is below 40°F outside
Yes; NYC's heat season ended on March 31
No; 62°F is required overnight regardless of outdoor temperature
questions.explanation: The heat season runs October 1 through May 31, and from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. the inside temperature must be at least 62°F no matter how warm it is outside. The 55°F outdoor trigger applies only to the daytime 68°F rule, so a mild night does not excuse 59°F.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2029 (heat); HPD heat and hot water rules

questions.q: In New York City, an owner must supply hot water at a constant minimum temperature of 120°F:
options: only from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.
only during the October–May heat season
year-round, every day
only in buildings with nine or more units
questions.explanation: The 120°F hot water requirement applies 365 days a year, not just during heat season. The heat season (October 1–May 31) and the 6 a.m.–10 p.m. window are rules for heat, not hot water.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2031 (hot water); HPD heat and hot water rules

questions.q: In a NYC building with three or more apartments, the owner must install approved window guards in an apartment when:
options: a child under age 6 lives there and the tenant also asks for them
a child age 10 or younger lives there, or the tenant asks for them
the apartment is located above the sixth floor of the building
a child under 18 lives there and the lease includes a guard rider
questions.explanation: Window guards are required in any apartment where a child 10 or younger resides, and an owner must also install them whenever any tenant asks in writing, for any reason (windows giving access to a fire escape are excepted). 'Under 6' is the trap: that age threshold belongs to the lead paint law, not window guards.
questions.citation: NYC Health Code §131.15; NYC Admin. Code §27-2043.1 (window guards)

questions.q: A NYC owner delivers the combined annual lead paint and window guard notice in January. One tenant never returns it by February 15. The owner must:
options: inspect the unit to find out whether a child lives there
assume no young children live there and close the file
charge the tenant a fee for failing to return the form
start a holdover proceeding for breach of the lease
questions.explanation: If the annual notice is not returned by February 15, the owner may not assume no child lives there; the owner must try to inspect the apartment to find out, and report to the Health Department if access cannot be obtained. Treating silence as a 'no' is the violation.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2056.4; NYC Health Code §131.15 (annual notice)

questions.q: Under NYC's Local Law 1 of 2004, paint in a multiple dwelling is presumed to be lead-based, triggering duties for units where a child under 6 lives, when the building was built:
options: before 1986
before 1978
before 1940
before 1960
questions.explanation: NYC's lead law presumes lead-based paint in buildings built before 1960 (and in 1960–1978 buildings only if the owner knows lead paint is present). 1978 is the federal lead-disclosure cutoff for sales and leases, a separate rule and the most common trap.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2056.1 et seq. (Local Law 1 of 2004)

questions.q: When an apartment in a pre-1960 NYC multiple dwelling becomes vacant, Local Law 1 requires the owner, before the next tenant moves in, to:
options: give the new tenant a pamphlet only, with no work required
do no work unless the incoming tenant has a child under age 6
fix lead hazards and make floors and sills smooth and cleanable
test only the common hallways, never the vacant unit itself
questions.explanation: Turnover rules require the owner to correct lead hazards (including friction surfaces on doors and windows) and make floors, sills, and window wells smooth and cleanable before re-occupancy, whether or not the next tenant has a child. The duty does not wait for a young child to move in.

questions.q: When signing a vacancy lease for a NYC apartment, the owner must give the tenant a disclosure of the building's bedbug infestation history for the prior:
options: two years
one year
five years
six months
questions.explanation: NYC requires a bedbug history disclosure (HCR form DBB-N) at a vacancy lease covering the apartment and building for the preceding one year. Longer look-back periods appear in other disclosure rules but not this one.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §27-2018.1; HCR Form DBB-N

questions.q: Under Local Law 69 of 2017, an owner of a NYC multiple dwelling must each year:
options: file a bedbug report with HPD, even if there were no infestations
file a bedbug report only if an infestation was confirmed
send each unit's pest records to the Health Department
hire a licensed exterminator to treat every unit
questions.explanation: Local Law 69 requires an annual bedbug filing with HPD for every multiple dwelling, including a report of zero infestations, and the owner must then share the filing with tenants. Believing the duty arises only after an infestation is the common error.

questions.q: In a NYC apartment, who is generally responsible for replacing the battery in a battery-powered smoke or carbon monoxide detector after move-in?
options: The Fire Department, during an annual inspection
The owner, who must replace batteries every six months
The super, under the janitorial services rules
The tenant, who must maintain the device during occupancy
questions.explanation: The owner must install approved smoke and CO detectors and replace any missing or inoperable device before a new occupancy begins, but during the tenancy the occupant must keep them in good repair, which includes changing batteries. The owner's only mid-tenancy duty is to replace a device that fails within one year of installation because of a manufacturing defect.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §§27-2045, 27-2046.1; HPD smoke and CO detector rules

questions.q: Under New York law, a stand-alone smoke alarm sold in the state that runs solely on battery power must:
options: be hardwired into the building's electrical system
use a replaceable 9-volt battery changed each spring and fall
use a sealed, non-removable battery designed to last 10 years
be monitored by a licensed central-station company
questions.explanation: Since April 1, 2019, battery-only smoke alarms sold in New York must have a sealed, non-removable battery with at least a 10-year life, so occupants cannot pull the battery to silence the alarm. Hardwired and panel-connected systems are exempt rather than required.

questions.q: Owners of rent-stabilized apartments must register each unit's legal rent and tenancy with:
options: NYC HPD, but only when a unit becomes vacant
NYS Homes and Community Renewal (DHCR) every year
the NYC Rent Guidelines Board, every two years
the Department of State, with the broker's license
questions.explanation: Rent-stabilized units are registered annually with the state's Division of Housing and Community Renewal (part of HCR), reporting the rent as of April 1, and the tenant gets a copy. The Rent Guidelines Board sets renewal increases but does not take registrations, and HPD registration is a separate city building filing.
questions.citation: NYC Rent Stabilization Law, Admin. Code §26-517; Rent Stabilization Code, 9 NYCRR Part 2528

questions.q: An owner fails to file the annual DHCR registration for a rent-stabilized unit. Until a proper registration is filed, the owner generally:
options: cannot collect rent increases above the last registered rent
loses the right to collect any rent from the tenant
may raise the rent freely because the unit is deregulated
must refund all rent paid since the last registration
questions.explanation: Failure to register freezes the rent at the last registered legal rent: the owner cannot collect increases until it files, and the cure is prospective only. The tenant still owes the lawful frozen rent, so 'no rent at all' overstates the penalty.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §26-517(e); Rent Stabilization Code, 9 NYCRR §2528.4

questions.q: New York City's Local Law 97 primarily:
options: requires solar panels on all new one-family homes
requires owners to post an energy-efficiency letter grade
bans gas stoves in every existing apartment building
caps carbon emissions for most buildings over 25,000 sq ft
questions.explanation: Local Law 97 (Climate Mobilization Act of 2019) sets annual greenhouse gas emission limits, which tighten over time, for most buildings over 25,000 gross square feet, with penalties for exceeding them. The posted letter grade comes from a different law (Local Law 33).
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code Title 28, Article 320 (Local Law 97 of 2019)

questions.q: A NYC manager must enter a large building's annual energy and water use into EPA's ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager and then post the resulting efficiency grade near the public entrance. These duties come from:
options: Local Law 1 of 2004 on lead-based paint hazards
the Housing Maintenance Code heat and hot water rules
the benchmarking and energy-grade laws (LL84 and LL33)
the Facade Inspection Safety Program (Local Law 11)
questions.explanation: Local Law 84 requires annual energy and water benchmarking for large buildings, and Local Law 33 (as amended by Local Law 95) turns that score into a letter grade posted near each public entrance. Local Law 97 caps emissions; it is not the benchmarking and posting rule.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code §28-309 (Local Law 84 of 2009; Local Law 33 of 2018)

questions.q: A NYC owner who does not live in a 20-unit multiple dwelling and does not use an approved 24-hour janitorial service must provide a janitor who lives:
options: anywhere in the same borough, as long as reachable by phone
in it or within the greater of one block or 200 feet
within one mile of the building, with a 24-hour phone line
in the building itself, never in a nearby or adjoining one
questions.explanation: For multiple dwellings of nine or more units, the janitor must live in the building or within one block or 200 feet, whichever is greater, unless the owner lives there or an approved 24-hour service is used. A janitor may live in an adjoining building, so 'never nearby' is wrong.

questions.q: Under NYC's Housing Maintenance Code, 'janitorial services' include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: collecting rent and signing renewal leases
making minor repairs to building equipment
removing garbage from the premises
clearing snow from the sidewalk
questions.explanation: The code defines janitorial services as cleaning and maintenance, minor repairs, furnishing heat and hot water from a central source, garbage removal, and removing snow and ice from the sidewalk. Collecting rent and negotiating leases are management tasks, and doing them for others for a fee is licensed brokerage activity.

questions.q: A landlord in Albany charges rental applicants a $50 application fee. The actual cost of the credit and background check is $35. What is the most the landlord may lawfully charge?
questions.explanation: RPL § 238-a caps the combined background/credit check charge at the actual cost or $20, whichever is less. The lesser of $35 and $20 is $20; no separate application or processing fee is allowed.

questions.q: A rental applicant gives the landlord a credit and background check report obtained three weeks ago. What must the landlord do about the background-check fee?
options: Waive the fee, because the applicant supplied a report from within the past 30 days
Charge the $20 fee anyway, since the landlord may always require and bill for its own report
Charge half the usual fee for verifying the applicant's report
Charge actual cost up to $50 for a fresh report
questions.explanation: Under RPL § 238-a, the landlord must waive the fee when the applicant provides a background or credit check conducted within the past 30 days. Three weeks falls inside that window.

questions.q: A landlord of an ordinary (non-regulated) apartment renting for $2,600 per month asks the new tenant for first month's rent, last month's rent, and a two-month security deposit at lease signing. What is the most the landlord may collect at signing?
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 caps any deposit or advance at one month's rent, and a 'last month's rent' advance counts toward that cap. The landlord may collect first month's rent ($2,600) plus a deposit/advance of $2,600, for $5,200 total.

questions.q: After a tenant of an ordinary residential rental moves out, how long does the landlord have to return the security deposit with an itemized statement of any deductions?
options: 30 days
10 business days
14 days
60 days
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires the landlord to provide an itemized statement and return any remaining deposit within 14 days after the tenant vacates. Missing the deadline forfeits the landlord's right to retain any portion.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a New York tenant's pre-move-out inspection right for an ordinary residential rental?
options: The landlord inspects only after the tenant returns the keys, and no advance notice to the tenant is required
The landlord must inspect monthly during the final 90 days of the lease, on 24 hours' oral notice to the tenant each time
Inspection is required only at move-in; any later damage is settled from the deposit after the tenant leaves
On the tenant's request, inspect 1 to 2 weeks before move-out on 48 hours' written notice so the tenant can cure issues
questions.explanation: GOL § 7-108 requires the landlord to tell the tenant of the right to request an inspection no earlier than two weeks and no later than one week before the tenancy ends, on at least 48 hours' written notice. The tenant may then cure the noted conditions before vacating.

questions.q: A tenant's monthly rent is $1,400. Rent due on the 1st is paid on the 9th. What is the maximum late fee the landlord may charge?
questions.explanation: RPL § 238-a limits late fees to $50 or 5% of monthly rent, whichever is less. 5% × $1,400 = $70, so the $50 cap controls. Payment more than five days late allows a fee.

questions.q: A tenant's $900 rent is due on the 1st and is paid on the 4th. The lease provides a late fee. What may the landlord charge?
options: $45, which is 5% of the monthly rent and less than the $50 statutory cap
No late fee, because the rent was paid within five days of the due date
$50, the statutory maximum, because the lease expressly provides a late fee
$9 per day for each day late, as long as the total stays under $50
questions.explanation: Under RPL § 238-a, no late fee may be charged unless rent remains unpaid more than five days after it was due. Paid on the 4th, the rent is within the grace period, so no fee is allowed even though the lease provides one.

questions.q: A landlord of an ordinary rental tells an approved applicant to pay a $300 non-refundable 'move-in processing fee' in addition to first month's rent and a one-month security deposit. Is this lawful?
options: Yes, as long as the fee is disclosed in writing in the lease and on the rental application
Yes, because a processing fee under 15% of one month's rent is allowed for approved applicants
No; aside from the capped background/credit check fee, no fee may be charged before or at lease start
No, but only because the fee is non-refundable; a refundable processing fee of that amount would be allowed
questions.explanation: RPL § 238-a bars landlords from demanding any payment, fee, or charge for processing an application or before or at the beginning of a tenancy, other than the capped background/credit check fee. Labeling it refundable would not make an extra deposit lawful, because GOL § 7-108 caps deposits at one month.

questions.q: A New York City landlord hires a broker to list and fill a vacant apartment. Under the FARE Act, who pays that broker's fee?
options: The tenant, as long as the fee is clearly disclosed in the listing
The tenant and landlord split it equally
The tenant, unless the monthly rent exceeds a set luxury threshold
The landlord; the tenant cannot be charged for the landlord's agent
questions.explanation: The NYC FARE Act (effective June 11, 2025) bars charging a tenant the fee of a broker who represents or was engaged by the landlord. Disclosure does not shift the fee to the tenant.
questions.citation: NYC FARE Act (Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses Act), eff. June 11, 2025

questions.q: In New York City, a tenant voluntarily signs an agreement hiring her own broker to find an apartment, agreeing to a fee of 12% of the first year's rent. She leases a unit at $3,000 per month. What is the result?
options: She may pay her own broker $4,320
The fee is prohibited by the FARE Act, so she owes nothing
She owes $360, since fees are based on one month's rent
The landlord must pay her broker $4,320
questions.explanation: The FARE Act stops tenants from paying the landlord's agent, but a tenant may still hire and pay her own broker. $3,000 × 12 = $36,000 annual rent; $36,000 × 12% = $4,320.

questions.q: A salesperson is showing an apartment in a three-family house to a prospective tenant on behalf of the landlord. Which agency disclosure form must the salesperson provide?
options: DOS-1736, the New York State Disclosure Form for Buyer and Seller
DOS-1735, the New York State Disclosure Form for Landlord and Tenant
The Property Condition Disclosure Statement
The FARE Act fee disclosure, which replaces the agency form
questions.explanation: For rentals of 1-4 family residential property (and condo/co-op units), RPL § 443 requires the Landlord and Tenant disclosure form, DOS-1735. DOS-1736 is the buyer/seller version used for sales.

questions.q: What is the key difference between an assignment of a lease and a sublease?
options: A sublease transfers the entire remaining term; an assignment transfers only part
An assignment requires no landlord involvement; a sublease always requires a new lease
In an assignment the tenant transfers the entire remaining interest; in a sublease the tenant transfers less and keeps an interest
An assignment ends the original tenant's liability automatically; a sublease creates a new landlord-tenant relationship with the owner
questions.explanation: An assignment transfers the tenant's whole remaining leasehold, while a sublease transfers part of it and the original tenant keeps an interest. Neither one automatically releases the original tenant from contractual liability to the landlord.

questions.q: A tenant in a 12-unit privately owned building (not rent-regulated) asks the landlord in writing for consent to sublet for six months. Under RPL § 226-b, how may the landlord respond?
options: Refuse for any reason or no reason, since the lease bars subletting
Ignore the request, since only rent-stabilized tenants may sublet
Charge a sublet fee equal to one month's rent before considering it
Withhold consent only on reasonable grounds
questions.explanation: In buildings with four or more residential units, RPL § 226-b lets a tenant sublet with the landlord's written consent, which may not be unreasonably withheld. The tenant must follow the statute's written request procedure.

questions.q: A lease clause says the tenant waives all warranty of habitability claims in exchange for a $100-per-month rent reduction. What is the effect of the clause?
options: It is void; the warranty of habitability cannot be waived
It is enforceable because the tenant received consideration
It is enforceable only for leases longer than one year
It is valid unless the landlord fails to make repairs within 30 days
questions.explanation: RPL § 235-b implies a warranty of habitability in every residential lease, and any agreement waiving it is void as against public policy. Consideration does not save the waiver.

questions.q: A tenant is two months behind on rent. While the tenant is at work, the landlord changes the locks and puts the tenant's belongings in storage. What is the best description of the landlord's action?
options: Lawful, because two months of unpaid rent allows a residential landlord to retake possession of the apartment
An unlawful eviction; the landlord must go to court, and only a marshal or sheriff may execute a warrant
Lawful, as long as the landlord first served a 14-day written rent demand and waited it out
Lawful, because the tenant's belongings were safely stored rather than thrown away
questions.explanation: New York prohibits residential self-help eviction. Removing a tenant by changing locks or removing possessions without a court order is unlawful eviction under RPAPL § 768; only a court-issued warrant executed by a marshal or sheriff can remove the tenant.

questions.q: In a New York City multiple dwelling, a landlord must install window guards in an apartment where a child of what age lives (or where the tenant requests them)?
options: Under 6
Under 18
10 years old or younger
12 years old or younger
questions.explanation: The NYC Health Code requires window guards in apartments where a child 10 or younger resides, and in any apartment whose tenant requests them. 'Under 6' is the threshold for the separate NYC lead paint rule.

questions.q: Under New York City's lead paint law, the landlord's annual notice asks tenants in older buildings whether a child of what age lives in the apartment?
options: 10 years old or younger
Under 18
Under 12
Under 6
questions.explanation: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 targets children under 6, who are most vulnerable to lead poisoning; landlords must ask annually and perform required inspections and work where such a child resides. The 10-or-younger age belongs to the window guard rule.
questions.citation: NYC Local Law 1 of 2004 (Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Act)

questions.q: For a rent-stabilized apartment in New York City, who sets the maximum allowable rent increase for a renewal lease?
options: The NYC Rent Guidelines Board
The building owner, based on market rents
The NYS Department of State
The New York Attorney General
questions.explanation: The Rent Guidelines Board votes each year on the maximum increases for one- and two-year renewal leases of rent-stabilized units, and the tenant chooses the term. NYS Homes and Community Renewal administers the program; DOS and the AG do not set rents.
questions.citation: NYC Rent Stabilization Law (NYC Admin Code Title 26, Chapter 4)

questions.q: A buyer's offer on a house has just been accepted, and the office manager asks the salesperson for the deal sheet. Which set of information is essential to include?
options: The MLS photos, listing remarks, number of showings, and feedback from every buyer who toured the home
The buyer's age, marital status, number of children, and place of employment for the seller's review
Price, deposit, mortgage amount, contingencies, closing date, broker compensation split, and both attorneys' contacts
Only the accepted price and the parties' names, since the attorneys will gather and negotiate every other term themselves
questions.explanation: The deal sheet (memorandum of sale) summarizes the accepted terms so the attorneys can draft the contract: price, earnest money, financing, contingencies, closing date, listing/cooperating broker compensation, and contact details for both attorneys. Protected-class details are irrelevant and should not be recorded.
questions.citation: NY brokerage practice (memorandum of sale / deal sheet)

questions.q: A deal sheet shows an accepted price of $640,000, a mortgage of 80% of the price, and a 10% contract deposit. Excluding closing costs, what are the mortgage amount and the remaining down payment due at closing?
options: Mortgage $576,000; $64,000 due at closing
Mortgage $512,000; $128,000 due at closing
Mortgage $448,000; $64,000 due at closing
Mortgage $512,000; $64,000 due at closing
questions.explanation: Mortgage = $640,000 × 0.80 = $512,000, so the down payment is $640,000 - $512,000 = $128,000. The deposit of $640,000 × 0.10 = $64,000 counts toward the down payment, leaving $128,000 - $64,000 = $64,000 due at closing.
questions.citation: Real estate math (loan amount and down payment)

questions.q: On a $640,000 sale, the listing agreement provides a 5% commission, split 60% to the listing broker and 40% to the cooperating (selling) broker. How much does the cooperating broker receive?
questions.explanation: Total commission = $640,000 × 0.05 = $32,000. Cooperating broker's share = $32,000 × 0.40 = $12,800; the listing broker receives $32,000 × 0.60 = $19,200.

questions.q: After an accepted offer, the buyer asks whether the signed deal sheet means the seller can no longer accept another buyer. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; the deal sheet becomes the binding contract of sale as soon as the office manager signs it
No; it summarizes terms for the attorneys, and the parties generally are not bound until both sign a contract
Yes, but only after the buyer's earnest money has been deposited in the listing broker's escrow account
No, because real estate offers in New York become binding only when they are made and accepted orally
questions.explanation: In New York practice, the deal sheet is not the contract; the attorneys draft a contract of sale, and the deal is generally not binding until both parties sign it (the statute of frauds requires a signed writing for real property sales). Until then, the seller may still entertain other offers.

questions.q: A tenant of an ordinary market-rate apartment in Buffalo moved out on March 1. The landlord, who wants to deduct for a window the tenant broke, does not send an itemized statement until March 25. What is the result under the security-deposit law?
options: The landlord forfeits the right to keep any part of the deposit
The landlord may still deduct, since the tenant caused the damage
The landlord must add a late charge of 5% to the refund owed
The landlord may keep the deposit but must pay the tenant interest
questions.explanation: The landlord must return the deposit with an itemized statement of deductions within 14 days after the tenant vacates; missing that deadline forfeits the right to retain any portion. Tenant-caused damage is normally deductible, but only if it is itemized on time.

questions.q: After a three-year tenancy, a landlord lists several charges against the tenant's security deposit. Which one is a proper deduction?
options: Repainting walls that faded from normal living
Replacing carpet worn thin along the hallway path
Replacing a door the tenant's dog chewed through
Fixing damage left by the previous tenant
questions.explanation: Deductions are limited to items such as unpaid rent or utilities and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear. Faded paint and carpet worn by normal use are ordinary wear, and a prior occupant's damage cannot be charged to this tenant.

questions.q: A landlord of a 20-unit building holds a tenant's $3,000 security deposit in an interest-bearing New York bank account that earned 2% this year. If the landlord takes the maximum administrative fee allowed, how much of the year's interest belongs to the tenant?
questions.explanation: Buildings with six or more units must hold deposits in interest-bearing accounts; the landlord may keep 1% per year of the deposit as an administrative fee. Interest: $3,000 × 2% = $60; fee: $3,000 × 1% = $30; tenant: $60 − $30 = $30. The $59.40 trap takes 1% of the interest instead of 1% of the deposit.

questions.q: A tenant's $850 monthly rent is due on the 1st and is paid on the 10th. The lease provides for a late fee. What is the most the landlord may charge?
questions.explanation: Rent paid more than five days late may draw a late fee capped at the lesser of $50 or 5% of monthly rent: $850 × 5% = $42.50, which is less than $50. The $50 figure is the ceiling only when 5% of the rent exceeds $50 (rent above $1,000).

questions.q: Rent due on the 1st still has not arrived on the 7th. What written step does New York law require the landlord to take at this point?
options: Serve a three-day notice to pay the rent or move out
Post a notice of default on the door of the apartment
Mail the tenant a notice of nonpayment by certified mail
Wait 30 days before contacting the tenant about rent
questions.explanation: If rent is not received within five days of the due date, the landlord must send a written notice of nonpayment by certified mail; failing to do so is an affirmative defense in a nonpayment case. The three-day demand is the pre-2019 rule, now replaced by a 14-day rent demand.

questions.q: A landlord's screening policy rejects any applicant who appears in a housing-court database as a party to a past landlord-tenant case, even a case the tenant won. Is the policy lawful in New York?
options: No; refusing to rent because of a past landlord-tenant case is prohibited
Yes, provided the policy is applied equally to every applicant
Yes, because housing-court records are public information
Yes, but only for prior cases that ended in a money judgment
questions.explanation: Since 2019, New York bars landlords from refusing to rent to an applicant because of the applicant's involvement in a prior landlord-tenant action or summary proceeding (the so-called tenant blacklist ban). Applying an unlawful policy uniformly does not make it lawful.

questions.q: A Rochester landlord does not plan to renew the lease of a tenant who has lived in the apartment for 18 months. How much advance written notice must the landlord give?
options: 30 days
90 days
14 days
60 days
questions.explanation: Notice of nonrenewal (or of a rent increase of 5% or more) depends on the longer of occupancy or lease term: under 1 year, 30 days; at least 1 but under 2 years, 60 days; 2 years or more, 90 days. Eighteen months falls in the 60-day tier.

questions.q: A tenant has occupied an apartment for three years. At renewal the landlord wants to raise the rent by 7%. What notice is required?
options: At least 60 days' written notice of the increase
At least 90 days' written notice of the increase
At least 30 days' written notice of the increase
No notice, because the increase is under 10%
questions.explanation: An increase of 5% or more triggers advance written notice, and a tenancy of two years or longer requires 90 days. The 10% distractor confuses this rule with the Good Cause presumptive-unreasonableness cap.

questions.q: A landlord plans to renew a two-year tenant's lease with a 4% rent increase. The unit is not rent-regulated and not covered by Good Cause Eviction. Does the advance-notice statute require notice of this increase?
options: No; for a renewal increase, notice applies only at 5% or more
Yes; 90 days' notice applies to any rent increase at all
Yes; 30 days' notice applies to any rent increase at all
No; the notice rule applies only to lease non-renewals
questions.explanation: Section 226-c requires advance notice only for nonrenewal or a rent increase of 5% or more; a 4% increase falls below the trigger. The trap that the rule covers only non-renewals ignores the 5%-increase trigger.

questions.q: A landlord gives a tenant of four years only 40 days' written notice of a 10% rent increase before the lease ends. What is the result?
options: The increase takes effect on the lease end date anyway
The notice is void and the tenant gets a new two-year lease
Old terms continue until 90 days after the notice was given
The tenant may stay rent-free until proper notice arrives
questions.explanation: When the landlord gives late notice, the tenancy continues on the existing terms from the date actual notice was given until the full notice period (here 90 days for a tenancy of two years or more) runs. The law does not void the increase forever or excuse rent.

questions.q: A tenant moved in under a one-year lease. The landlord decides not to renew when the lease ends. What is the minimum advance notice the landlord must give?
options: 30 days, because occupancy is still under one year
60 days, because the lease term is at least one year
90 days, because the lease runs a full year
None, because the lease simply expires on its own
questions.explanation: The notice tier uses occupancy or lease term, whichever qualifies for the longer period; a lease of at least one year but under two requires 60 days even though the tenant has lived there less than a year. The 30-day tier applies only when both occupancy and lease term are under a year.

questions.q: In February a tenant in a 20-unit apartment building files a good-faith complaint with the city code-enforcement office about a broken boiler. In September of the same year the landlord notifies the tenant that the lease will not be renewed. How is the nonrenewal treated?
options: It is lawful, because more than six months passed since the complaint
It is automatically void, and no landlord evidence can rebut it
It is lawful, because a nonrenewal is never treated as retaliation
It is presumed retaliatory, and the landlord must rebut that presumption
questions.explanation: Since 2019, a landlord's notice to quit, eviction filing, or substantial change in tenancy terms within one year after a tenant's good-faith complaint is presumed retaliatory; the presumption is rebuttable. The six-month window was the pre-2019 rule.

questions.q: Which tenant activity is protected from landlord retaliation?
options: Subletting without asking for the landlord's consent
Keeping a pet that the lease expressly prohibits
Organizing a tenants' association in the building
Refusing the landlord access for a scheduled repair
questions.explanation: The retaliation statute protects good-faith complaints to government agencies, good-faith efforts to enforce lease or habitability rights, and participation in a tenants' organization. Breaking lease terms or blocking repairs is not protected activity.

questions.q: A tenant falls asleep with the bathtub running, and the overflow ruins the bathroom floor. The tenant then withholds rent, claiming breach of the warranty of habitability. What is the best analysis?
options: The warranty does not cover a condition the tenant's own conduct caused
The landlord is strictly liable for every condition in the unit
The claim succeeds because the warranty can never be limited
The claim succeeds only if the lease expressly mentions the warranty
questions.explanation: The warranty of habitability is implied and cannot be waived, but the landlord is not liable for conditions caused by the misconduct of the tenant or persons under the tenant's control. 'Non-waivable' does not mean the landlord insures against the tenant's own acts.

questions.q: Which statement accurately describes New York's warranty of habitability?
options: It applies only to written leases that expressly recite it
It covers the apartment itself but never lobbies or hallways
It applies only in buildings containing three or more units
It is implied in every residential lease and covers common areas
questions.explanation: The warranty is implied in every residential lease, written or oral, and covers the premises and areas used in connection with them; the landlord warrants they are fit for habitation and free of conditions dangerous to life, health, or safety.

questions.q: A tenant in a 30-unit building mails a complete sublet request to the landlord by certified mail. The landlord never responds. What is the effect after 30 days?
options: The request is deemed denied and the tenant may not sublet
The landlord's silence is deemed consent to the sublet
The tenant is released from the lease on 30 days' notice
The tenant must refile the request before any sublet
questions.explanation: The landlord must respond within 30 days after the request (or any requested additional information) is mailed; failure to respond is deemed consent. Release on 30 days' notice is the remedy for an unreasonably refused assignment, not for a sublet request.

questions.q: A tenant in a privately owned three-unit building wants to sublet for the summer, but the lease prohibits subletting. Does the statutory sublet right let the tenant sublet over the landlord's objection?
options: No; the sublet right covers buildings with four or more units
Yes; consent can never be unreasonably withheld in any building
Yes; any lease clause barring sublets is void as a matter of law
No; the sublet right covers only rent-stabilized apartments
questions.explanation: The statutory right to sublet with consent that may not be unreasonably withheld applies to tenants in dwellings with four or more residential units; in a three-unit building the lease terms control. The right is not limited to rent-stabilized units.

questions.q: A tenant asks the landlord to consent to assigning the lease to a creditworthy friend. The landlord refuses without giving any reason. If the refusal is unreasonable, what is the tenant's remedy?
options: An automatic right to complete the assignment
A rent abatement for the rest of the lease term
Release from the lease on 30 days' notice
Release from the lease on 90 days' notice
questions.explanation: A landlord may withhold consent to an assignment, but if consent is unreasonably withheld, the tenant's sole remedy is release from the lease on request with 30 days' notice. The tenant does not gain a right to force the assignment through.

questions.q: A rent-stabilized tenant whose legal regulated rent is $1,800 per month lawfully sublets the apartment fully furnished. What is the most the tenant may charge the subtenant?
questions.explanation: A stabilized prime tenant may charge a subtenant the legal regulated rent plus a surcharge of up to 10% if the unit is sublet fully furnished: $1,800 × 1.10 = $1,980. The $2,160 trap applies 20%, and $1,800 ignores the furnished surcharge.

questions.q: A lease names only one tenant. Without the landlord's consent, whom may that tenant share the apartment with?
options: Immediate family only, unless the landlord later consents in writing
Immediate family and up to two unrelated adults and their children
One other adult occupant, but none of that occupant's children
Immediate family, one other occupant, and that occupant's dependent children
