questions.explanation: Under the roommate law, a sole named tenant may share with immediate family, one additional occupant, and the occupant's dependent children, provided the tenant or spouse occupies the unit as a primary residence. A lease clause restricting occupancy further is unenforceable to that extent.

questions.q: A tenant who lived with a lawful roommate under the roommate law moves out when the lease ends. What right does the roommate have to remain?
options: The roommate automatically becomes the tenant of record
The roommate may stay one more year at the same rent
None, unless the landlord expressly consents in writing
The roommate may stay if they paid half of the rent
questions.explanation: An occupant added under the roommate law gains no right to continued occupancy if the tenant leaves, unless the landlord gives express written consent. Paying part of the rent does not convert the occupant into a tenant.

questions.q: Before starting a nonpayment proceeding against a residential tenant, what written rent demand must the landlord serve?
options: A demand giving the tenant at least 14 days to pay
A demand giving the tenant at least 3 days to pay
A demand giving the tenant at least 30 days to pay
A demand giving the tenant at least 5 days to pay
questions.explanation: Since the 2019 HSTPA, a nonpayment proceeding requires a written demand giving the tenant at least 14 days to pay (formerly 3 days). The 5-day figure is the separate certified-mail late-rent notice trigger, not the rent demand.

questions.q: A homeowner lets a friend stay in a spare room with no lease and no rent. After seven weeks the homeowner wants the friend out and changes the locks while the friend is away. What is the best analysis?
options: Lawful, because the friend never signed a lease or paid any rent
Lawful, because self-help is allowed in an owner-occupied home
Unlawful only if the homeowner also removed the friend's belongings
Unlawful; an occupant of 30+ days can be removed only by court process
questions.explanation: It is unlawful to evict, without a court-issued warrant executed by a marshal, sheriff, or constable, anyone who has lawfully occupied a dwelling for 30 consecutive days or longer, even without a lease. Changing the locks alone is a prohibited lockout.

questions.q: To pressure a tenant who is behind on rent to leave, a landlord shuts off the apartment's heat and hot water. How does New York law treat this?
options: As a permitted step once a 14-day rent demand goes unpaid
As an unlawful eviction, punishable as a class A misdemeanor
As lawful if the lease lets the landlord suspend services
As a building-code violation with no eviction consequences
questions.explanation: Interrupting or discontinuing essential services to force out an occupant is an unlawful eviction: a class A misdemeanor, plus civil penalties of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation. A rent demand starts court process; it never authorizes self-help.

questions.q: A New York City apartment covered by the Good Cause Eviction Law rents for $2,400 per month. Assume the applicable annual CPI change is 3%. Above what monthly renewal rent is an increase presumptively unreasonable?
questions.explanation: The threshold is the lower of 5% plus CPI or 10%. Here 5% + 3% = 8%, which is lower than 10%: $2,400 × 1.08 = $2,592. The $2,640 trap applies 10% without comparing; $2,520 uses 5% alone.

questions.q: Under the Good Cause Eviction Law, which reason, standing alone, is NOT good cause for a covered landlord to refuse to renew a tenant?
options: The tenant has failed to pay the rent owed
The tenant is using the unit for an illegal purpose
The lease term has simply come to its end
The tenant unreasonably refused access for repairs
questions.explanation: For covered units, expiration of the lease alone is not grounds to refuse renewal. Nonpayment, illegal use, and unreasonable refusal of access for required repairs are among the listed good-cause grounds.

questions.q: Four New York City apartments each rent for well below any high-rent exemption level. Which one is exempt from the Good Cause Eviction Law?
options: A market-rate unit in a 40-unit building built in 1965
A rent-stabilized unit in a 1960s elevator building
A market-rate unit owned by a landlord with 60 units
A market-rate unit in a prewar walk-up with 12 units
questions.explanation: Good Cause exempts units already governed by rent regulation, such as rent stabilization, which has its own renewal and rent rules. Older market-rate units owned by landlords above the small-landlord threshold are covered.

questions.q: A New York City rental building received its first certificate of occupancy in 2015. Its market-rate units are owned by a large landlord. How does the Good Cause Eviction Law apply to them?
options: They are covered, because the landlord owns more than ten units
They are covered once each tenant's first lease is renewed
They are exempt only if the building has fewer than six units
They are exempt for 30 years from the date that certificate issued
questions.explanation: Housing whose first certificate of occupancy issued on or after January 1, 2009 is exempt from Good Cause for 30 years from issuance. Portfolio size matters only for the separate small-landlord exemption.

questions.q: A tenant in a village outside New York City asks whether the Good Cause Eviction Law protects her apartment. What determines coverage?
options: Nothing; the law applies automatically to every rental statewide
Only whether her current lease was signed after April 2024
Whether her locality opted in, and whether the unit is exempt
Only whether her building contains six or more apartments
questions.explanation: Good Cause applies automatically in New York City but elsewhere only in localities that opt in, and even then exemptions (small landlords, regulated units, newer buildings, high-rent units, and others) can apply. The six-unit test belongs to rent stabilization under ETPA.

questions.q: A rent-stabilized tenant in New York City believes she is being charged more than the legal regulated rent. Which body handles her overcharge complaint?
options: NYS Division of Housing and Community Renewal
NYC Rent Guidelines Board
NYS Department of State, Licensing Services
NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
questions.explanation: DHCR (part of NYS Homes and Community Renewal) administers rent stabilization, including rent registrations and overcharge complaints. The Rent Guidelines Board only sets the annual renewal-increase percentages; it does not decide individual complaints.
questions.citation: Rent Stabilization Law; Rent Stabilization Code (9 NYCRR Parts 2520–2531)

questions.q: Which change did the Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 make to rent stabilization?
options: It created a 20% vacancy bonus on each apartment turnover
It required the Legislature to renew the law every year
It exempted all buildings with fewer than 50 apartments
It ended high-rent vacancy deregulation of stabilized units
questions.explanation: The HSTPA ended high-rent vacancy and high-income deregulation, eliminated the vacancy bonus, and made the rent laws permanent rather than subject to periodic renewal. The 20% vacancy bonus is the opposite of what the law did.
questions.citation: Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019

questions.q: A New York City rent-stabilized tenant's lease expires on August 31. When must the owner offer a renewal lease, and what term may the tenant choose?
options: 30 to 60 days before expiration; a 1- or 2-year term at the owner's option
90 to 150 days before expiration; a 1- or 2-year term at the tenant's option
90 to 150 days before expiration; a 2-year term only, set by the owner
60 to 90 days before expiration; a 1-year term only, set by the owner
questions.explanation: The owner must offer renewal on the DHCR form no more than 150 and no fewer than 90 days before the lease expires, and the tenant chooses a one- or two-year term at the Rent Guidelines Board rate for that term. The tenant then has 60 days to accept.

questions.q: In New York City, a broker posts a rental listing online with the landlord's permission. A prospective tenant contacts the broker and rents the unit. May the broker collect a fee from the tenant?
options: No; an agent listing with permission may not charge the tenant
Yes, if the tenant signs a separate fee agreement at the showing
Yes, if the fee is capped at one month's rent for the unit
No, unless the landlord refuses to pay the broker any fee
questions.explanation: Under the FARE Act, an agent who publishes a listing with the landlord's permission may not impose or collect any fee from the tenant, and an agent who publishes a listing is rebuttably presumed to have that permission. Signing a fee agreement at the showing does not change that.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21(a)(2), (e) (FARE Act, effective June 11, 2025)

questions.q: A New York City listing agent tells applicants they may apply for an apartment only if they first sign an agreement making the agent a dual agent and paying a fee. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, because the dual agency arrangement is disclosed in writing
Yes, if the fee amount was stated in the listing beforehand
No; a rental cannot be conditioned on hiring any agent, dual or not
No, unless the agent holds a broker's rather than salesperson's license
questions.explanation: The FARE Act prohibits conditioning the rental of an apartment on the tenant engaging any agent, including a dual agent. Written disclosure of dual agency does not cure the prohibited condition.

questions.q: Compared with the sale of the same 1965-built house, what does the federal lead-based paint rule NOT require when the house is leased for one year?
options: Disclosing any known lead-based paint or lead hazards
Giving the tenant a 10-day opportunity to test for lead
Providing the EPA lead hazard information pamphlet
Including a lead warning statement in the lease
questions.explanation: For pre-1978 housing, lessors must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, give the EPA pamphlet, and include a lead warning statement, just as sellers do. The 10-day risk-assessment or inspection opportunity applies only to purchasers.

questions.q: NYC's lead law (Local Law 1 of 2004) presumes that paint contains lead in which apartments?
options: Any apartment in a residential building built before 1978
Units with a child under 6 in buildings of 6+ units built before 1974
Any apartment in any building where a child under 6 resides
Units with a child under 6 in buildings of 3+ units built before 1960
questions.explanation: Local Law 1 presumes that paint is lead-based in any dwelling unit where a child under 6 resides (and in common areas) in a multiple dwelling (three or more units) built before January 1, 1960; the owner may rebut the presumption with certified testing. The 1978 date is the federal disclosure cutoff, and the six-unit/1974 test belongs to rent stabilization.

questions.q: A New York City landlord of a six-unit building must install window guards in an apartment where a child age 10 or under lives. Which window is excluded?
options: A window in the apartment's bathroom
A window in the apartment's kitchen
A window that opens onto a fire escape
A window that faces an interior courtyard
questions.explanation: Window guards must go on every window in the apartment, including bathroom and kitchen windows, except a window that gives access to a fire escape, which must stay clear for emergency exit.
questions.citation: NYC Health Code § 131.15; NYC Admin. Code § 27-2043.1

questions.q: In a New York City apartment building, who is responsible for replacing the removable battery in a working smoke detector that the owner installed?
options: The tenant, who must keep the device maintained
The owner, within 30 days of the tenant's request
The superintendent, at least once each year
The fire department, during annual inspections
questions.explanation: In NYC the owner must install smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, but the occupant must keep them in good repair, including replacing batteries. The owner replaces devices at the end of their useful life.

questions.q: What does New York's Amanda's Law require?
options: Smoke alarms with sealed 10-year batteries in every rental unit
Annual radon testing in every rental that has a basement
CO alarms only in buildings that contain three or more units
CO alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage
questions.explanation: Amanda's Law (2010) extended carbon monoxide alarm requirements to one- and two-family homes and other residences that have fuel-burning appliances or systems or an attached garage, not only to larger buildings.

questions.q: A salesperson represents a landlord who is renting out a two-family house. When must the salesperson give a prospective tenant the DOS-1735 agency disclosure?
options: At the first substantive contact with the prospective tenant
When the tenant submits a completed rental application
At lease signing, together with the lease and riders
Only if the tenant asks whom the salesperson represents
questions.explanation: The agency disclosure is due at the first substantive contact, before the tenant shares information or negotiates. Waiting until the application or the lease signing defeats its purpose, which is to let the tenant know whose interests the agent represents before anything is said.
questions.citation: RPL § 443; DOS-1735 (New York State Disclosure Form for Landlord and Tenant)

questions.q: After a showing, a prospective tenant signs the DOS-1735 the landlord's salesperson gives her. She then asks whether she is now committed to renting through that firm. What is the best answer?
options: Yes; it commits her to rent through the firm for 30 days
No; her signature only acknowledges that she received the form
Yes; signing it creates a tenant's-agency relationship by law
No; it binds her only once the landlord also signs the form
questions.explanation: The form is headed "THIS IS NOT A CONTRACT." Signing only acknowledges receipt of the agency disclosure. It does not create an agency relationship or a duty to rent, and adding the landlord's signature would not change that.

questions.q: A prospective tenant reads the DOS-1735 the landlord's salesperson presents but refuses to sign the acknowledgment. What should the salesperson do?
options: Refuse to keep working with the tenant until the form is signed
Write 'refused' on the form and discard it after the showing
Prepare a sworn written declaration of the facts and keep it
Have the landlord sign the form in the tenant's place instead
questions.explanation: When a consumer refuses to sign, the licensee makes a written declaration of the facts of the refusal under oath or affirmation and keeps it for at least three years. A refusal does not cancel the duty to disclose, and it does not require the agent to stop working with the tenant.

questions.q: A listing broker at Firm A asks a salesperson at Firm B to help find a tenant for Firm A's landlord client. The Firm B salesperson does not represent any tenant. Which relationship should the Firm B salesperson check on DOS-1735?
options: Tenant's agent for the prospective tenant
Dual agent for both the landlord and tenant
Landlord's agent engaged directly by the landlord
Broker's agent acting in the landlord's interest
questions.explanation: A broker's agent is engaged by the listing agent, works at a different firm, and has no direct relationship with the landlord. The listing agent directs that work and answers for it, and the landlord has no vicarious liability for the broker's agent. That lack of a direct engagement is what separates it from a landlord's agent.

questions.q: Under New York City's FARE Act, what must every residential rental listing or advertisement disclose clearly and conspicuously?
options: The listing broker's commission split with cooperating firms
The landlord's minimum income requirement for applicants
Every fee a tenant must pay to rent the unit
The unit's complete rent history for the past four years
questions.explanation: The FARE Act requires listings to disclose clearly and conspicuously every fee a tenant must pay to rent the unit, so tenants are not surprised at signing. It does not require a listing to show broker splits, income criteria, or rent history.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.22(a) (FARE Act, Local Law 119 of 2024)

questions.q: Before a New York City tenant signs a lease, which FARE Act document must the tenant receive and sign?
options: A sworn statement that the tenant chose not to hire a broker
A DOS-1736 buyer and seller agency acknowledgment form
A landlord certificate that the unit is not rent stabilized
An itemized written disclosure of all fees the tenant must pay
questions.explanation: Before the lease is signed, the tenant must receive and sign an itemized written disclosure of every fee owed to the landlord or to a third party at the landlord's direction. The tenant gets a copy, and the landlord or agent keeps the signed disclosure for 3 years. DOS-1736 is the sales agency form; rentals use DOS-1735.

questions.q: A salesperson posts a New York City apartment on a rental website. When an applicant calls, she says the tenant must pay her broker fee because she never signed a written listing agreement with the landlord. Which statement is correct?
options: She is presumed to list with the landlord's OK; the fee is barred
The fee is allowed since no written listing agreement exists
The fee is allowed if it is disclosed clearly in the listing
The fee is allowed if the tenant acknowledges DOS-1735
questions.explanation: Under the FARE Act, an agent who publishes a rental listing is rebuttably presumed to do so with the landlord's permission, and an agent who lists with the landlord's permission may not charge the tenant any fee. Permission does not require a written listing agreement, so its absence alone does not rebut the presumption. Disclosing an unlawful fee in the listing does not make it lawful, and DOS-1735 is only an agency disclosure.

questions.q: A Buffalo landlord's rental broker asks whether the FARE Act decides who pays her fee on Buffalo apartments. What is the correct answer?
options: Yes; the FARE Act governs every rental in the state
No; the FARE Act is a New York City local law
Yes; it covers any city with 100,000+ residents
No; it covers only rent-stabilized units in NYC
questions.explanation: The FARE Act is a New York City local law (Local Law 119 of 2024), so it does not reach a Buffalo rental. Statewide rules such as RPL § 238-a's fee limits still apply there. The FARE Act is not a statewide ban on broker fees, and within NYC it is not limited to stabilized units.
questions.citation: NYC Local Law 119 of 2024 (FARE Act); RPL § 238-a

questions.q: A New York City listing agent tells applicants they may tour her landlord's apartment only if they first sign a tenant-representation agreement with her firm and pay her a fee. Under the FARE Act, this practice is:
options: Prohibited; access can't be conditioned on hiring a broker
Permitted, because the tenant signs the agreement voluntarily
Permitted if the fee is capped at one month's rent
Permitted if the fee is shown in the advertisement
questions.explanation: No person may condition the rental of an NYC apartment on the tenant engaging any agent, including a dual agent; DCWP applies this even when the broker demands to be hired before the tenant can see the unit. A listing agent is also a landlord's agent, who may not collect any fee from the tenant. A tenant may still choose to hire her own broker, but a forced agreement is not voluntary, and neither a fee cap nor ad disclosure fixes it.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21(a), (c) (FARE Act); DCWP FARE Act FAQ

questions.q: A New York City landlord screens applicants with the common '40 times the rent' income standard. The apartment rents for $3,250 per month. What annual income must an applicant show?
questions.explanation: $3,250 × 40 = $130,000 of annual income. $39,000 is just one year's rent ($3,250 × 12), $97,500 uses 30×, and $156,000 uses 48×.
questions.citation: Landlord screening practice (40× monthly rent); no statute sets this multiplier

questions.q: An applicant earns $112,000 a year and is looking at buildings that use the 40-times-the-rent income standard. What is the highest monthly rent she qualifies for?
questions.explanation: $112,000 ÷ 40 = $2,800 per month. $3,733 divides by 30, $9,333 divides by 12 (her monthly income, not a rent ceiling), and $2,333 divides by 48.

questions.q: An applicant earns too little to qualify, so the building's policy calls for a guarantor earning 80 times the monthly rent. The rent is $2,900. What is the minimum annual income the guarantor needs?
questions.explanation: $2,900 × 80 = $232,000. Landlords commonly set the guarantor multiple higher than the tenant's 40× ($116,000) because the guarantor also carries their own housing costs. $34,800 is one year's rent, and $290,000 uses 100×.
questions.citation: Landlord screening practice (guarantor multiple set by building policy)

questions.q: A tenant asks why so many New York City landlords demand annual income of 40 times the monthly rent. Which description of this standard is accurate?
options: A state law limiting the rent any tenant may be charged
A requirement of RPL § 238-a for every rental application
A federal HUD rule that applies to all market-rate rentals
A common landlord screening policy, not a statutory rule
questions.explanation: 40× is a business practice landlords choose, not a legal requirement, and it is subject to fair housing limits. RPL § 238-a governs application and screening fees, not income ratios, and no HUD rule sets the 40× figure.

questions.q: An NYC apartment rents for $2,800 a month. An applicant's housing voucher pays $2,100 of it, and she pays the rest. The landlord uses a 40-times-the-rent income test. What is the most income the landlord may lawfully require of her?
options: $0, because no income test is allowed
questions.explanation: Under source-of-income guidance, an income test may apply only to the tenant's own share of the rent: $2,800 − $2,100 = $700, and $700 × 40 = $28,000. Applying 40× to the full rent ($112,000) discriminates against voucher holders. A ban on any income test applies only when the voucher covers 100% of the rent.
questions.citation: NYC Admin. Code § 8-107(5); NYC Commission on Human Rights source-of-income guidance; Executive Law § 296(5)

questions.q: A graduate student's father signs a lease guaranty for her apartment. What is the father's role?
options: A co-tenant who gains the right to occupy the apartment
A third party who promises to pay if the tenant defaults
A broker who vouches for the tenant's credit to the landlord
An escrow agent who holds the tenant's security deposit
questions.explanation: A guarantor promises to cover the tenant's lease obligations if the tenant fails to perform. A guarantor is liable but has no right to possession. That separates a guarantor from a co-tenant, who both owes the rent and may live in the unit.
questions.citation: General Obligations Law § 5-701 (guaranty must be in a signed writing); general contract law

questions.q: A landlord turns down an applicant solely because a screening report shows she was named in a nonpayment case that was dismissed two years ago. This rejection is:
options: Unlawful under RPL § 227-f's ban on tenant blacklisting
Lawful, because the case appears in a public court record
Lawful, as long as the landlord refunds the screening fee
Unlawful only if the tenant prevailed in the earlier case
questions.explanation: RPL § 227-f bars refusing to rent because an applicant was involved in a past or pending landlord-tenant proceeding, whatever the outcome. If a landlord checks court or screening-bureau records and then rejects the applicant, the rejection is presumed to rest on that record. A record being public does not make relying on it lawful.

questions.q: In New York City, a landlord hires a broker to rent an apartment at $3,400 per month. The credit and background check actually costs $30. Under current law, what is the most the tenant can be required to pay up to and including lease signing?
questions.explanation: $3,400 first month + $3,400 security (one-month cap) + $20 screening fee (the lesser of actual cost and $20) = $6,820. The landlord's broker fee cannot be charged to the tenant under FARE, so $12,940 (adding a 15% annual fee) is wrong. $10,220 adds a last-month advance, which the one-month deposit cap does not allow, and $6,800 leaves out the lawful $20 fee.
questions.citation: GOL § 7-108; RPL § 238-a; NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21 (FARE Act)

questions.q: In New York City, a tenant voluntarily hires her own broker for a fee of one month's rent. She leases a $2,750-per-month apartment with a one-month security deposit and a $20 screening fee. What is her total due at signing, including her broker's fee?
questions.explanation: $2,750 rent + $2,750 security + $20 screening + $2,750 broker fee = $8,270. FARE allows a tenant to pay a broker she hired herself. $5,520 leaves out her broker's fee, $11,020 adds an extra month's rent, and $10,470 uses a 15%-of-annual-rent fee ($4,950) the stem doesn't give.
questions.citation: GOL § 7-108; RPL § 238-a; NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21 (tenant-hired broker allowed)

questions.q: A Rochester landlord rents a non-regulated apartment for $1,600 a month. The applicant's background and credit check actually cost $15. What is the most the landlord may collect from the tenant up to and including lease signing?
questions.explanation: $1,600 first month + $1,600 security (one-month cap) + $15 screening fee = $3,215. The fee is the lesser of actual cost and $20, so $3,220 overcharges. $4,815 adds a third month, and $3,250 treats the $50 late-fee cap as an upfront fee.

questions.q: A landlord pays the listing brokerage a fee of one month's rent on a $4,200-per-month apartment. The listing salesperson's split with her broker is 60/40 in her favor. What does the salesperson earn?
questions.explanation: The fee is $4,200, and the salesperson gets 60%: $4,200 × 0.60 = $2,520. $1,680 is the brokerage's 40%, $2,100 assumes a 50/50 split, and $4,536 applies 60% to a 15% annual-rent fee the stem doesn't give.
questions.citation: Commission arithmetic; RPL § 442-a (salesperson paid through the broker)

questions.q: A New York City tenant hiring her own broker is choosing between two fee offers on a $3,100-per-month apartment: (1) one month's rent, or (2) 15% of the first year's rent. Which fee is larger, and by how much?
options: The one-month fee, by $2,635
The 15% fee, by $5,580
The two fees are exactly equal
The 15% fee, by $2,480
questions.explanation: 15% fee: $3,100 × 12 × 0.15 = $5,580. One-month fee: $3,100. Difference: $5,580 − $3,100 = $2,480. Taking 15% of a single month ($465) gives the $2,635 error, and $5,580 is the larger fee itself, not the difference.
questions.citation: Commission arithmetic; NYC Admin. Code § 20-699.21 (tenant-hired broker)

questions.q: A salesperson places an online rental ad that shows only her name, her cell number, and the apartment details. What is wrong with the ad?
options: Her license number and expiration date must appear
The name of her associated brokerage must appear
Nothing; a salesperson may advertise in her own name
The landlord's name and phone number must appear
questions.explanation: An ad that names a salesperson must also include the name of the broker or brokerage she is associated with; an ad lacking it is a blind ad. (The rule also requires the broker's address or phone number and an accurate statement of her license type.) License numbers, expiration dates and the landlord's contact information are not required.

questions.q: A brokerage keeps advertising a $2,100 one-bedroom that was rented a month ago because the ad draws calls. Callers are then steered to $2,700 units. How is this practice best described?
options: Acceptable if the ad says rents start 'from $2,100'
Allowed for up to 60 days after the unit is rented
False and misleading advertising by the licensees
A violation only if callers are in a protected class
questions.explanation: Advertising a unit the firm knows is unavailable to lure inquiries is bait advertising, which is false and misleading and can lead to licensing discipline. No grace period applies, and the conduct is improper whoever responds. The fair housing angle is a separate question.

questions.q: A listing for a 24-unit apartment building in Albany says "No Section 8." Which statement is correct?
options: It violates the state's lawful-source-of-income protection
It is lawful because only NYC protects voucher holders
It is lawful if the landlord's broker placed the ad
It is lawful if the rule is applied to every applicant
questions.explanation: Since 2019, the NYS Human Rights Law has protected lawful source of income, including housing vouchers, statewide, so this ad is discriminatory. Applying the exclusion to everyone is still discrimination, and a broker who places the ad shares the liability.

questions.q: A salesperson is the landlord's agent on a New York City rental. Which sequence meets the required disclosure timing?
options: Application and screening; DOS-1735; fee disclosure; lease signing
DOS-1735; lease signing; fee disclosure; application and screening
Fee disclosure; application and screening; lease signing; DOS-1735
DOS-1735; application and screening; fee disclosure; lease signing
questions.explanation: The agency disclosure comes at the first substantive contact. Next come the application and screening. The FARE itemized fee disclosure must be signed before the lease is signed. Giving DOS-1735 after the application, or the fee disclosure after the lease, misses the required timing.

questions.q: At lease signing, a tenant gives the landlord's salesperson a check payable to the brokerage for first month's rent and the security deposit, both to be passed on to the landlord. What should happen to the check?
options: The salesperson deposits it in her personal account for the landlord
The broker deposits it in a special escrow account within 3 business days
The salesperson holds it uncashed until the lease term begins
The broker deposits it in the firm's operating account for the landlord
questions.explanation: Money held for others is trust money. The broker must deposit it in a separate special account within three business days and account for it promptly. Putting it in a personal or operating account is commingling, and holding the check indefinitely fails to protect the funds.

questions.q: A deal sheet shows an accepted price of $1,150,000, a mortgage of $920,000, and the customary NYC 10% contract deposit. What are the loan-to-value ratio and the contract deposit?
options: 80% LTV; $115,000 deposit
80% LTV; $230,000 deposit
20% LTV; $115,000 deposit
80% LTV; $92,000 deposit
questions.explanation: LTV = $920,000 ÷ $1,150,000 = 80%. Deposit = 10% × $1,150,000 = $115,000. $230,000 is the full 20% down payment, 20% is the equity share rather than LTV, and $92,000 takes 10% of the loan instead of the price.
questions.citation: LTV = loan ÷ price or appraised value (lower); customary NYC contract deposit

questions.q: A deal sheet shows an $875,000 sale with a 5% commission split 50/50 between the listing and cooperating brokerages. The buyer's salesperson works at the cooperating firm on a 60/40 split in her favor. What does she earn?
questions.explanation: $875,000 × 5% = $43,750. The co-broke half is $43,750 × 50% = $21,875, and her share is $21,875 × 60% = $13,125. $26,250 applies 60% to the whole commission, $21,875 is her firm's entire side, and $8,750 is her broker's 40%.
questions.citation: Commission arithmetic; listing agreement and office compensation plan

questions.q: A $1,240,000 sale carries a 6% commission, split 50/50 with the cooperating broker. The listing salesperson's split with her own broker is 70/30 in her favor. How much does the listing brokerage keep?
questions.explanation: $1,240,000 × 6% = $74,400. The listing side is $74,400 × 50% = $37,200. The brokerage keeps 30%: $37,200 × 0.30 = $11,160. $26,040 is the agent's 70%, $22,320 takes 30% of the whole commission, and $37,200 is the whole listing side.
questions.citation: Commission arithmetic; listing agreement and office compensation plan

questions.q: A cooperating brokerage was offered 2.5% of the sale price and receives a $15,000 commission check at closing. What was the sale price?
questions.explanation: Price = $15,000 ÷ 0.025 = $600,000. $300,000 divides by 5%, a total commission the stem doesn't give. $1,200,000 halves the 2.5% again, and $750,000 divides by 2%.

questions.q: A listing agreement pays the listing brokerage 3% and offers the buyer's brokerage 2.5% on a $720,000 sale. What does the seller pay in total commission, and what does the cooperating broker receive?
options: $39,600 total; $19,800 to the co-broke
$21,600 total; $18,000 to the co-broke
$36,000 total; $18,000 to the co-broke
$39,600 total; $18,000 to the co-broke
questions.explanation: Total: $720,000 × 5.5% = $39,600. Co-broke share: $720,000 × 2.5% = $18,000, and the listing side gets $21,600 (3%). $19,800 wrongly splits the total 50/50, $21,600 is only the listing side, and $36,000 assumes a 5% total.

questions.q: The buyer's side of a $560,000 sale pays 2.5%. The buyer's brokerage owes another licensed broker a 25% referral fee on its side. The buyer's salesperson is then paid 50% of what her firm keeps. What does she earn?
questions.explanation: Side: $560,000 × 2.5% = $14,000. Referral: $14,000 × 25% = $3,500, which leaves $10,500. Her 50%: $10,500 × 0.5 = $5,250. $7,000 ignores the referral, $10,500 is the firm's net, and $3,500 is the referral fee.
questions.citation: Commission arithmetic; RPL § 442 (fees shared only with licensed brokers)

questions.q: In a typical New York City residential sale, who holds the buyer's contract deposit after the contract is signed?
options: The listing broker, in its operating account
The seller, who may use it for moving costs
The seller's attorney, as escrow agent
The buyer's lender, until the loan closes
questions.explanation: In NYC practice, the seller's attorney usually holds the down payment in escrow under the contract's escrow terms until closing or a proper release. It is not the seller's money to spend, and a broker may not put trust funds in an operating account.
questions.citation: Customary NYC contract practice; escrow terms of the contract of sale

questions.q: A buyer's offer on a Manhattan condo has been accepted. She asks whether New York law requires her to put down a 10% contract deposit. What is the best answer?
options: No; 10% is customary, and the amount is negotiable
Yes; state law requires 10% on all home contracts
Yes; lenders require exactly 10% before a commitment
No; state law caps contract deposits at 5% of price
questions.explanation: The 10% deposit is NYC custom, not a statute. The parties may agree to a different amount, often outside NYC, and the deal sheet simply records what was agreed. No law sets a 10% requirement or a 5% cap.
questions.citation: Customary NYC practice; contract terms control

questions.q: After the listing agent sends out the deal sheet in a typical New York City sale, who ordinarily prepares the first draft of the contract of sale?
options: The buyer's attorney
The seller's attorney
The listing salesperson
The buyer's mortgage lender
questions.explanation: In NYC the seller's attorney drafts the contract from the deal sheet, and the buyer's attorney reviews it, does due diligence, and negotiates riders. The salesperson supplies the deal terms but does not draft the contract, which is legal work.
questions.citation: Customary NYC practice; Judiciary Law § 478 (practice of law)

questions.q: A buyer's agent fills out a deal sheet that will go to both attorneys and the listing side. In the notes, she writes that her client 'could go higher if needed.' What is the problem?
options: Nothing, because a deal sheet is only an internal record
Nothing, because the price has already been agreed to
It is a problem only if the seller signs the deal sheet
It reveals the client's confidential negotiating position
questions.explanation: A deal sheet goes to the other side, and terms can be renegotiated later, for example after an inspection. Revealing the buyer's willingness to pay more breaches the agent's fiduciary duty of confidentiality. The deal sheet is not a private office memo.
questions.citation: Fiduciary duty of confidentiality; RPL § 443 (buyer's agent duties)

questions.q: A salesperson is preparing a deal sheet for an accepted offer on a co-op apartment. Which contingency is standard for a co-op purchase but not for a typical house sale?
options: Approval of the deed by the county clerk
Approval of the price by the Department of State
Approval of the purchaser by the co-op board
Approval of the sale by the seller's lender
questions.explanation: A co-op buyer acquires shares and a proprietary lease, so the board must approve the purchaser, and the deal sheet should flag board approval. A co-op sale has no deed to record, and DOS does not approve prices.
questions.citation: Customary co-op contract practice; co-op proprietary lease and bylaws

questions.q: An office manager tells a salesperson to write 6% on every deal sheet because 'that's the board rate in this area.' What is the correct response?
options: Commissions are negotiable; a set area rate raises antitrust issues
6% is the maximum commission allowed under New York license law
The board rate controls unless the seller objects to it in writing
The rate is fixed each year by the Department of State's rules
questions.explanation: Each commission is negotiated between the broker and the client. Brokers who agree on or enforce a standard area rate risk price-fixing liability under antitrust law. Neither DOS nor license law sets or caps commission rates.
questions.citation: Sherman Antitrust Act; NY Donnelly Act (GBL § 340)

questions.q: Before closing, the cooperating broker's office asks the selling salesperson where to send her share of the commission. What is the proper answer?
options: Pay me directly, since my license permits it
Pay me directly if my broker consents in writing
Pay my brokerage; I can be paid only through my broker
Pay the seller's attorney, who will forward it to me
questions.explanation: A salesperson may receive compensation only from her own associated broker. The cooperating firm pays her brokerage, which then pays her under their split. Her broker's consent does not allow direct payment.

questions.q: Under RESPA Section 8, which payment is prohibited?
options: A title agent paying a salesperson $200 for each buyer referred to the title agent
A buyer paying the closing attorney's fee for legal services actually performed
A seller paying the listing broker's agreed commission
A lender paying an appraiser for an appraisal actually completed
questions.explanation: RESPA § 8 bans kickbacks and fees for referrals of settlement business in federally related mortgage loans. Payment for goods or services actually performed is allowed. Calling a referral fee "marketing" does not fix it.

questions.q: A brokerage owns part of a title agency and wants to refer its buyers there. Under RESPA, this affiliated business arrangement is lawful only if the brokerage:
options: Requires all its buyers to use the affiliate so it can keep closing costs low and consistent
Is paid a flat fee by the affiliate for each referral that closes, as long as the fee is disclosed
Discloses the relationship and estimated charges, does not require its use, and receives only an ownership return
Tells the buyer about its ownership interest in the title agency verbally, but only after the closing has been completed
questions.explanation: An affiliated business arrangement needs written disclosure at or before the referral, no required use (with narrow exceptions), and nothing of value to the referrer beyond a return on the ownership interest.

questions.q: A seller insists, as a condition of the sale, that the buyer purchase title insurance from a particular title company. Under RESPA, this is:
options: Allowed, as long as the requirement is clearly written into the contract of sale that both parties sign
Prohibited, because a seller may not require the buyer to use a particular title insurer
Allowed, if the seller agrees to pay half of the title insurance premium
Required, because the seller chooses the title insurer
questions.explanation: RESPA § 9 bars a seller from requiring, directly or indirectly, as a condition of sale that the buyer buy title insurance from a particular company in a federally related mortgage transaction.

questions.q: Under TRID, when must the lender deliver or mail the Loan Estimate?
options: At least 3 business days before consummation of the loan
Within 10 business days after the lender's appraisal of the property has been completed
At the closing table, along with the note and the mortgage
Within 3 business days after receiving the consumer's loan application
questions.explanation: The Loan Estimate is due within 3 business days after the creditor receives an application (the six items: name, income, SSN, property address, estimated value, loan amount). The 3-days-before-consummation rule applies to the Closing Disclosure.

questions.q: Under TRID, the borrower must receive the Closing Disclosure:
options: Within 3 business days after receiving the loan application
At least 3 business days after consummation of the loan
On the day of closing, before signing
At least 3 business days before consummation of the loan
questions.explanation: The Closing Disclosure must be received at least 3 business days before consummation so the borrower can compare it with the Loan Estimate. Mixing it up with the Loan Estimate timing is the classic trap.

questions.q: A borrower receives her Closing Disclosure on a Monday. No federal holidays fall that week. Under TRID, the earliest day the loan may be consummated is:
options: Monday
Thursday
Tuesday
the following Monday
questions.explanation: The CD must be received at least 3 business days before consummation. Counting Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday as the three days, consummation may occur Thursday.

questions.q: After the Closing Disclosure is delivered, which change requires a corrected CD AND a new 3-business-day waiting period?
options: The seller agrees to a $1,000 credit to the buyer for a repair
The recording fee rises by $15
The loan product changes from a fixed-rate to an adjustable-rate loan
The closing time is moved from the morning to the afternoon of the same day
questions.explanation: Only three changes restart the waiting period: the APR becomes inaccurate beyond tolerance, the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added. Other changes need a corrected CD at or before closing, but no new wait.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a typical residential closing in New York?
options: Buyer and seller usually each have an attorney, who attend the closing with or for their clients
A neutral escrow company closes the sale by mail, and attorneys are rarely involved
The listing salesperson prepares the deed and conducts the closing on behalf of both parties
The county clerk conducts the closing at the clerk's office and transfers title
questions.explanation: New York is an attorney-closing state: buyer's and seller's attorneys, the lender's attorney, and often a title closer attend. Salespersons may attend but cannot draft deeds or give legal advice. The county clerk only records documents afterward.
questions.citation: NY Judiciary Law § 478 (practice of law); NY RPL Article 12-A

questions.q: At closing, the buyer's $40,000 earnest money deposit held in escrow is entered on the closing statement as a:
options: Credit to the buyer only
Debit to the buyer only
Credit to the seller and debit to the buyer
Debit to the seller only
questions.explanation: The deposit is money the buyer already paid toward the price, so the buyer is credited. It is not a seller credit because the purchase price (seller credit) already includes it.

questions.q: On a closing statement, the purchase price is shown as:
options: A credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller
A debit to both the buyer and the seller
A debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
A credit to both the buyer and the seller
questions.explanation: The buyer owes the price (debit), and the seller receives it (credit). Most items are double entries like this; the buyer's new loan and the seller's loan payoff are single entries.

questions.q: At closing, the seller's existing mortgage balance of $210,000 is paid off. On the closing statement this is a:
options: Credit to the seller only
Debit to the seller only
Debit to the buyer only
Debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: The payoff is the seller's obligation, paid out of the seller's proceeds, so it is a seller debit. The buyer is not involved, so it is a single entry. The buyer's new loan, by contrast, is a buyer credit only.

questions.q: Annual property taxes of $7,300 are paid in arrears and have not been paid for the current calendar year. Closing is May 1; the buyer owns the closing day. Using a 365-day year, what is the proration?
options: $2,400 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$4,900 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$2,420 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$2,400 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: $7,300 ÷ 365 = $20 per day. Seller's days: Jan 1–Apr 30 = 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 = 120. $20 × 120 = $2,400. The seller used those days but has not paid, and the buyer will pay the bill later, so seller debit/buyer credit.

questions.q: The seller paid the full $3,650 calendar-year tax bill in advance. Closing is October 1; the buyer owns the closing day. Using a 365-day year, what is the proration?
options: $920 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$2,730 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$910 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$920 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
questions.explanation: $3,650 ÷ 365 = $10 per day. Buyer's days: Oct 1–Dec 31 = 31 + 30 + 31 = 92. $10 × 92 = $920. The seller prepaid the buyer's share, so the buyer reimburses: seller credit/buyer debit.

questions.q: A house outside New York City sells for $425,000. What is the New York State real estate transfer tax, and who normally pays it?
options: $1,700, paid by the buyer
$1,700, paid by the seller
$4,250, paid by the seller
$850, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: The rate is $2 for each $500 (or fraction) of consideration: $425,000 ÷ 500 = 850 units × $2 = $1,700. The grantor (seller) normally pays; the buyer is secondarily liable if the seller does not pay.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a single-family home for $1,200,000. The additional 1% ("mansion") tax is:
options: $2,000, paid by the buyer
$12,000, paid by the seller
$12,000, paid by the buyer
$2,000, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: The mansion tax is 1% of the full consideration when residential consideration is $1 million or more, and the grantee (buyer) pays: $1,200,000 × 1% = $12,000. Taxing only the $200,000 above $1 million is the trap.

questions.q: Who customarily pays New York's mortgage recording tax on a buyer's new purchase-money mortgage?
options: The borrower (buyer), based on the amount of the mortgage debt
The seller, based on the full purchase price of the property
The broker, out of the commission
The county clerk, as an expense of recording the mortgage
questions.explanation: The mortgage recording tax is calculated on the secured debt, not the sale price, and is generally paid by the borrower. On some residential loans the lender pays a portion, but the borrower bears the main charge.

questions.q: A title search shows an old, unpaid judgment against the seller. Before closing, the seller's attorney should generally:
options: Have the judgment paid or otherwise cleared so the title company removes the exception
Ignore it, since a judgment lien is automatically released when the property is sold
Ask the buyer to take title subject to the judgment as part of the purchase price
Have the listing salesperson sign an affidavit stating that the judgment is invalid
questions.explanation: Title exceptions such as judgments, open mortgages, and liens must be cleared (paid at closing, satisfied, or bonded) to deliver the marketable, insurable title the contract requires. A sale does not wipe out a recorded judgment lien.
questions.citation: NY CPLR § 5203 (judgment liens); title insurance practice

questions.q: A new survey shows the neighbor's garage extends two feet onto the seller's lot. This finding is an example of:
options: A special assessment the buyer must pay
An easement in gross held by the utility company
An encroachment that may affect marketable title
A defect that title insurance always covers without exception
questions.explanation: A survey shows boundaries, improvements, and encroachments. An encroachment can make title unmarketable, and title policies often take a survey exception unless a survey is provided.
questions.citation: NY RPL (marketable title); title insurance practice

questions.q: The buyer's final walk-through just before closing is mainly meant to:
options: Start a new inspection period that allows the buyer to cancel the contract for any reason before closing
Confirm the property is in the agreed condition and that required repairs or vacancy are complete
Measure the home's rooms so the lender's appraiser can finish the appraisal report
Let the salesperson and the buyer renegotiate the final purchase price before signing
questions.explanation: The walk-through checks that the property is in the condition the contract requires (repairs done, fixtures left, broom-clean, vacant) as of closing. It does not create a new contingency.

questions.q: After a New York closing outside NYC, the deed is recorded with the county clerk along with the transfer tax return (TP-584) and the real property transfer report (RP-5217). Recording the deed primarily:
options: Transfers title, since a New York deed is void until it is recorded
Lets the buyer avoid the transfer tax
Replaces the need for title insurance
Gives constructive notice of the buyer's ownership to everyone
questions.explanation: Title passes on delivery and acceptance of the deed. Recording protects the buyer by giving public (constructive) notice and priority under New York's race-notice recording act.
questions.citation: NY RPL § 291 (recording act); NY Tax Law § 1409 (TP-584)

questions.q: Who is generally responsible for filing IRS Form 1099-S to report the gross proceeds of a real estate sale?
options: The buyer's homeowners insurance company, which insures the property
The listing salesperson personally, as the licensee who procured the buyer and earned the commission
The local assessor, which records the sale on the assessment roll
The person responsible for closing, such as the settlement or closing attorney
questions.explanation: IRC § 6045(e) requires the "real estate reporting person", usually the person responsible for closing, to report the seller's gross proceeds on Form 1099-S. Some main-home sales are exempt when the seller certifies they qualify.

questions.q: A foreign seller sells a New York investment property for $1,500,000. No reduced rate or exemption applies. Under FIRPTA, how much must the buyer withhold?
options: $0, because the seller's broker handles the tax
questions.explanation: FIRPTA makes the buyer the withholding agent. The standard rate is 15% of the amount realized: $1,500,000 × 15% = $225,000. The buyer can be liable if it fails to withhold.

questions.q: Which of the following transactions is NOT covered by RESPA?
options: An FHA-insured purchase loan on an owner-occupied three-family home
A home equity second mortgage on an owner-occupied single-family home
An all-cash purchase of a single-family home with no mortgage financing
A conventional refinance of a condominium unit occupied by its owner
questions.explanation: RESPA applies to federally related mortgage loans secured by one-to-four-family residential property, including refinances and subordinate-lien loans. An all-cash purchase involves no mortgage loan at all, so RESPA does not reach it; the trap is assuming a second mortgage falls outside the law.
questions.citation: RESPA, 12 U.S.C. §2602(1); Regulation X, 12 CFR §1024.2 and §1024.5

questions.q: Which payment is permitted under RESPA Section 8?
options: A listing broker sharing its commission with the cooperating broker who found the buyer
A mortgage lender sending a salesperson a $100 gift card for each buyer who closes a loan
A title agency paying for a broker's office party because the broker sends it most closings
A homeowner's insurance agent paying a salesperson a flat fee for every buyer referred
questions.explanation: Section 8(c) expressly exempts payments made under cooperative brokerage and referral arrangements between real estate agents and brokers. Gift cards, parties, or flat fees given because of settlement-service referrals are prohibited things of value, whatever form they take.

questions.q: A mortgage company pays a brokerage $1,500 a month under a 'marketing services agreement.' The payment rises whenever the brokerage's agents refer more buyers to the lender, and the brokerage performs little actual marketing. Under RESPA, this arrangement is:
options: Lawful, because the payment is labeled as a fee for marketing services
Lawful, as long as each referred buyer signs a disclosure of the arrangement
Lawful, because the payment goes to the brokerage rather than to its agents
Unlawful, because the payment is really compensation for settlement referrals
questions.explanation: RESPA looks at substance, not labels: a payment that tracks referral volume and is not reasonably related to services actually performed is a kickback. Disclosing it to buyers does not make a prohibited referral payment lawful.

questions.q: A buyer learns that her lender paid her salesperson a fee for steering her to the loan. In a private lawsuit under RESPA Section 8, she may recover up to:
options: The amount of the referral fee the salesperson actually received
Three times the amount of any charge she paid for the settlement service
The full amount of all closing costs shown on her Closing Disclosure
Double the referral fee, plus mandatory rescission of the mortgage loan
questions.explanation: Violators of Section 8 are jointly and severally liable to the borrower for three times the charge paid for the settlement service involved, plus court costs and attorney's fees. Section 8 violations also carry criminal penalties of up to $10,000 and one year in prison.

questions.q: A brokerage that owns 30% of a mortgage company refers a buyer to that company. Under RESPA, when must the brokerage give the buyer the Affiliated Business Arrangement Disclosure?
options: At the closing table, along with the Closing Disclosure
Within 3 business days after the buyer applies for the loan
At or before the time the referral is made to the buyer
Only if the buyer asks whether the companies are related
questions.explanation: The person making the referral must give the affiliated business disclosure at or before the time of the referral, so the buyer can shop knowing of the ownership tie. The 3-business-day period is the Loan Estimate deadline, a different rule.

questions.q: Under RESPA's affiliated business rules, a lender may require a borrower to use a particular provider chosen by the lender only for which service?
options: Homeowner's insurance written by an affiliated insurance agency
Title insurance issued through an affiliated title agency
A survey performed by an affiliated land surveying firm
An appraisal ordered by the lender to protect its own interest
questions.explanation: Regulation X allows a lender to require the use of an attorney, credit reporting agency, or real estate appraiser chosen to represent the lender's interest. Requiring the use of an affiliated insurer, title agency, or surveyor defeats the affiliated business exemption.

questions.q: A borrower's escrow account pays $6,000 a year for property taxes and $1,800 a year for homeowner's insurance. Under RESPA, the maximum cushion the servicer may require is:
questions.explanation: Annual disbursements are $6,000 + $1,800 = $7,800, and the cushion may not exceed one-sixth of that: $7,800 ÷ 6 = $1,300, which equals two months of the $650 monthly escrow payment. $650 is only one month, and $1,950 or $2,600 would be three or four months.

questions.q: A servicer's annual escrow analysis shows a $140 surplus in the account of a borrower who is current on payments. Under RESPA, the servicer must:
options: Keep the surplus as an added cushion for next year's tax bill
Refund the surplus to the borrower within 30 days of the analysis
Hold the surplus until the loan is paid off or the home is sold
Apply the surplus to principal only if the borrower asks in writing
questions.explanation: When an escrow analysis shows a surplus of $50 or more and the borrower is current (payments received within 30 days of the due date), the servicer must refund it within 30 days of the analysis. Only a surplus under $50 may instead be credited against the next year's escrow payments; the cushion itself is capped at one-sixth of annual disbursements.

questions.q: When the servicing of a mortgage loan is transferred, RESPA generally requires the old servicer to notify the borrower:
options: At least 30 days before the effective date of the transfer
Within 30 days after the new servicer receives the loan file
At least 15 days before the effective date of the transfer
Within 60 days after the borrower's next payment comes due
questions.explanation: The transferor servicer must give notice at least 15 days before the transfer's effective date, and the new servicer must give notice within 15 days after it (the two may send one combined notice at least 15 days before). Sixty days is the separate late-payment protection period.

questions.q: After her loan's servicing is transferred, a borrower mails her next payment on time to the old servicer by mistake. During the 60 days after the transfer, the new servicer:
options: May charge a late fee but may not report the payment as late
May treat the payment as late once the grace period has passed
Must return the payment and demand that she promptly resend it
May not treat the timely payment as late or impose a late fee
questions.explanation: For 60 days after the effective date of a servicing transfer, a payment received by the old servicer on or before its due date may not be treated as late for any purpose, including late fees. A transfer changes where payments go, not the loan's terms.

questions.q: Under TRID, a lender has received an 'application,' which starts the Loan Estimate clock, once it has six pieces of information. Which is NOT one of the six?
options: Two years of the borrower's federal tax returns
The borrower's name and Social Security number
The address of the property securing the loan
The property's estimated value and loan amount
questions.explanation: The six items are the consumer's name, income, Social Security number, property address, estimated property value, and loan amount sought. A lender cannot delay the Loan Estimate by first demanding documents such as tax returns.

questions.q: Before a consumer receives the Loan Estimate and indicates an intent to proceed, the lender may charge the consumer only:
options: An application fee and an appraisal deposit
A bona fide and reasonable credit report fee
A rate-lock fee to hold the quoted interest rate
Any fee the consumer agrees to pay in writing
questions.explanation: Until the consumer has received the Loan Estimate and said she wants to proceed, the only fee a lender may impose is a bona fide and reasonable charge for obtaining her credit report. Application, appraisal, and rate-lock fees must wait.

questions.q: In addition to the 3-business-day delivery rule, TRID requires the lender to deliver or mail the Loan Estimate:
options: At least 10 business days before the appraisal is ordered
No later than the day the buyer signs the contract of sale
No later than 7 business days before consummation of the loan
At least 3 business days before the Closing Disclosure is sent
questions.explanation: The Loan Estimate must go out within 3 business days of application and also no later than the seventh business day before consummation. The contract signing and the appraisal order do not control its timing.

questions.q: A borrower wants to close two days after receiving her Closing Disclosure. Under TRID, the 3-business-day waiting period may be waived only if:
options: The buyer and seller both sign an addendum to the contract of sale
The lender's attorney approves the waiver at the closing table
The interest rate is locked and the APR has not changed at all
She has a bona fide personal financial emergency and gives a written waiver
questions.explanation: Only the consumer can waive the waiting period, and only for a bona fide personal financial emergency described in a dated, signed written statement (not a preprinted form). Contract addenda or attorney approval cannot shorten it.

questions.q: A lender mails the Closing Disclosure on a Monday, and there is no proof the borrower received it earlier. No federal holidays fall in the next two weeks. Under TRID, the earliest the loan may be consummated is:
options: Thursday of the same week
Monday of the next week
Saturday of the same week
Tuesday of the next week
questions.explanation: A mailed CD is presumed received 3 business days after mailing, and for this rule business days are every day except Sundays and federal holidays: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, so receipt is Thursday. Consummation may occur on the third business day after receipt: Friday, Saturday, Monday. Skipping Saturday gives the wrong answer of Tuesday.

questions.q: After the borrower receives the Closing Disclosure, which change requires a corrected CD but does NOT start a new 3-business-day waiting period?
options: A prepayment penalty is added to the loan's terms
The APR on the fixed-rate loan rises by 0.25 percentage point
The loan changes from a fixed rate to an adjustable rate
The settlement agent's fee rises $150 and the APR stays accurate
questions.explanation: Only three changes restart the wait: the APR becomes inaccurate (more than 1/8 percentage point for a regular loan), the loan product changes, or a prepayment penalty is added. Other changes, like a modest fee increase, need only a corrected CD at or before consummation.

questions.q: Under TRID's tolerance rules, which charge may NOT increase at all from the Loan Estimate to closing?
options: The lender's origination charge
Prepaid interest on the new loan
The homeowner's insurance premium
Initial deposit to the escrow account
questions.explanation: Charges paid to the creditor or its affiliates, such as the origination charge, carry zero tolerance, as do transfer taxes and services the consumer may not shop for. Prepaid interest, insurance premiums, and escrow deposits may change without a tolerance limit as long as they were estimated in good faith.

questions.q: A borrower allowed to shop for title services picks a provider from the lender's written list. Under TRID, that provider's charges fall into which tolerance category?
options: Zero tolerance; the charge may not increase at all
No tolerance limit; any increase is acceptable
10% cumulative tolerance, together with recording fees
15% tolerance, measured separately for each fee
questions.explanation: Recording fees and shoppable third-party services obtained from a provider on the lender's list are grouped together, and their total may rise no more than 10% over the Loan Estimate. The 10% test is cumulative, not fee by fee.

questions.q: A borrower who was allowed to shop ignores the lender's list and hires a title provider she found on her own. If that provider's fees exceed the Loan Estimate, the lender:
options: Must refund any amount above the original estimate
Must refund any amount over 10% of the estimate
Must issue a new Loan Estimate and restart the clock
Is not subject to a tolerance limit for those fees
questions.explanation: When the consumer shops and chooses a provider not on the lender's written list, those charges have no tolerance limit; they need only be estimated in good faith. The 10% bucket applies only to providers chosen from the list.

questions.q: At closing, the lender's zero-tolerance fees exceed the Loan Estimate by $400. To cure the tolerance violation, the lender must:
options: Cancel the loan and re-disclose all terms to the borrower
Refund the $400 excess no later than 60 days after consummation
Pay the borrower three times the excess as a statutory penalty
Credit the $400 against the borrower's first monthly payment
questions.explanation: A tolerance violation is cured by refunding the excess to the consumer within 60 days after consummation, with a corrected Closing Disclosure. Treble damages are a RESPA Section 8 remedy, not the TRID cure.

questions.q: Which loan is NOT subject to the TRID Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure rules?
options: A 30-year fixed-rate loan to buy a single-family home
An FHA-insured loan to buy an owner-occupied two-family home
A reverse mortgage taken out by a 70-year-old homeowner
A conventional refinance of an owner-occupied condominium
questions.explanation: TRID covers most closed-end consumer mortgages secured by real property, including purchase loans and refinances. Reverse mortgages, home equity lines of credit, and loans on mobile homes not attached to land are excluded and use other disclosures.

questions.q: A foreign seller sells a Westchester home for $850,000 to a buyer who signs a statement that she will live in it as her residence. No withholding certificate was obtained. Under FIRPTA, the buyer must withhold:
questions.explanation: When the buyer will use the home as a residence and the price is over $300,000 but not over $1,000,000, the rate drops to 10%: $850,000 × 10% = $85,000. $127,500 applies the full 15% rate, and $0 applies only when the price is $300,000 or less.

questions.q: A nonresident alien sells a condominium for $280,000. The buyer, a U.S. citizen, will live in it for most of each of the next two years. Under FIRPTA, the buyer's required withholding is:
options: $42,000, which is 15% of the sales price
$28,000, which is 10% of the sales price
$14,000, which is 5% of the sales price
$0, because the residence exemption applies
questions.explanation: No withholding is required when the buyer acquires the property as a residence and the amount realized is $300,000 or less. A residence means the buyer or family plans to live there at least 50% of the days it is used in each of the first two 12-month periods.

questions.q: At closing, a seller who is a U.S. citizen signs a certification of non-foreign status that states his name, address, and taxpayer identification number. As a result, the buyer:
options: Must still withhold 10% until the IRS confirms citizenship
Generally need not withhold any tax under FIRPTA
Must withhold 15% but may claim a refund later
Must withhold only from the seller's net profit
questions.explanation: A signed non-foreign certification with the seller's TIN relieves the buyer of FIRPTA withholding unless the buyer knows it is false. FIRPTA targets foreign sellers; withholding is never based on net profit.

questions.q: A foreign investor sells a rental house for $600,000, realizing a $200,000 gain. The buyer will keep renting it out, and no exemption or withholding certificate applies. FIRPTA withholding is:
questions.explanation: FIRPTA withholding is 15% of the amount realized (the gross price), not the gain: $600,000 × 15% = $90,000. $30,000 wrongly applies 15% to the gain, and $60,000 uses the 10% rate available only when the buyer will live there.

questions.q: If no closing attorney or settlement agent is responsible for a residential closing, which party is next in line under IRS rules to file Form 1099-S?
options: The buyer's mortgage lender
The seller's real estate broker
The buyer's real estate broker
The buyer of the property
questions.explanation: The reporting order is the person responsible for closing, then the mortgage lender, then the seller's broker, then the buyer's broker, and finally the buyer. A broker files only when there is no closing agent and no lender.

questions.q: A married couple sells their principal residence for $460,000 and gives the closing attorney a written certification that the entire gain is excludable from income. The closing attorney:
options: Must file Form 1099-S reporting only the couple's net gain
Must file Form 1099-S reporting the full $460,000 price
Must withhold estimated tax and report it on Form 1099-S
Is generally not required to file Form 1099-S for this sale
questions.explanation: A principal-residence sale of $500,000 or less for a married couple ($250,000 for a single seller) is exempt from 1099-S reporting when the sellers give the required written certification. When a 1099-S is filed, it reports gross proceeds, never net gain.

questions.q: A father deeds his upstate house to his daughter as a gift, and no consideration is paid. Regarding Form TP-584:
options: It is not needed, because no transfer tax is owed on a gift
It must still be filed with the deed, claiming the exemption
It is filed only if the county assessor later requests it
It replaces the deed, so the deed itself is not recorded
questions.explanation: The grantor and grantee must jointly file a transfer tax return for each conveyance whether or not tax is due, so a gift deed still needs a TP-584 showing the exemption. The county clerk will not record the deed without it.

questions.q: A New York State agency, which is exempt from the real estate transfer tax, sells surplus land to a private developer for $900,000. Who must pay the NYS transfer tax?
options: No one, because the seller's exemption covers the whole sale
The state agency, because the seller always owes the tax
The developer, because the grantee pays if the grantor is exempt
The county clerk, out of the recording fees it collects
questions.explanation: The grantor normally pays the transfer tax, but when the grantor is exempt or fails to pay, the duty shifts to the grantee. The seller's exemption is personal and does not make the conveyance itself tax-free.

questions.q: The RP-5217 Real Property Transfer Report filed with a deed in New York is used mainly to:
options: Calculate and pay the state's real estate transfer tax
Certify that the seller is not a foreign person under FIRPTA
Give the buyer's lender proof that the mortgage was recorded
Supply sales data used to oversee and equalize assessments
questions.explanation: The RP-5217 reports the sale's details so state and local officials can track sales prices, compute equalization rates, and review assessments. Transfer tax is reported and paid on the TP-584, not the RP-5217.
questions.citation: NY Real Property Law §333(1-e); Real Property Tax Law §574

questions.q: A deed for a house on Staten Island is ready to be recorded. Where is it recorded?
options: With the Richmond County Clerk, though the NYC-RPT is still prepared in ACRIS
With the Office of the City Register, the same as for a Brooklyn property
With the NYS Department of State's Division of Licensing Services
With the NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, which records NYC deeds
questions.explanation: The NYC Department of Finance's Office of the City Register records deeds for Manhattan, the Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens through ACRIS, but Staten Island deeds are recorded with the Richmond County Clerk. The NYC transfer tax return is still prepared through ACRIS for all five boroughs.
questions.citation: NYC Department of Finance, ACRIS and property recording rules; Richmond County Clerk

questions.q: A one-family house in Queens sells for $750,000. What New York City Real Property Transfer Tax is due?
questions.explanation: For a residential sale above $500,000 the 1.425% rate applies to the full price, not just the excess: $750,000 × 1.425% = $10,687.50. $8,562.50 wrongly splits the price into tiers, and $3,000 is the separate NYS transfer tax ($750,000 ÷ 500 × $2).

questions.q: A Florida resident sells a vacation home in the Catskills. Before the deed can be recorded, the seller generally must:
options: Obtain a FIRPTA withholding certificate from the IRS
File Form 1099-S with the county clerk at recording
Pay estimated NYS income tax on the gain using Form IT-2663
Register with the Department of State as a nonresident owner
questions.explanation: A nonresident individual selling New York real property must compute and pay estimated state income tax on the gain with Form IT-2663 when the deed is recorded. FIRPTA applies to foreign persons, not to U.S. citizens who live in another state.

questions.q: A Rochester home sells for $412,300. Using New York's rate of $2 for each $500 of consideration or fraction thereof, the transfer tax reported on Form TP-584 is:
questions.explanation: $412,300 ÷ $500 = 824.6, and any fraction counts as a full unit, so 825 units × $2 = $1,650. $1,649.20 applies a straight 0.4%, $1,648 drops the fraction, and $825 forgets to multiply by $2.

questions.q: In a typical downstate New York home sale, once the offer is accepted the formal contract of sale is usually first drafted by:
options: The seller's attorney, who then sends it to the buyer's attorney
The listing salesperson, using the brokerage's standard form
The buyer's attorney, after reviewing the title report
The title company's closer, at the request of the lender
questions.explanation: In attorney-driven downstate practice the seller's attorney drafts the contract and sends it to the buyer's attorney for review and negotiation; the licensee's role ends with the memorandum of the deal. The title report comes later, after the contract is signed.
questions.citation: New York attorney-closing practice; Judiciary Law §478 (unauthorized practice of law)

questions.q: In a New York attorney-driven closing, which party typically orders the title search and title insurance commitment for the buyer?
options: The seller's attorney, as part of preparing the deed
The buyer's attorney, after the contract is signed
The listing broker, once the contract is fully signed
The lender's appraiser, when inspecting the property
questions.explanation: The buyer's attorney orders title so the buyer's own advocate can review exceptions and demand that the seller clear them before closing. The seller's attorney prepares the deed but does not order the buyer's title insurance.

questions.q: At a New York closing, the bank attorney who prepares and supervises the mortgage documents represents:
options: The lender, even though the buyer usually pays the fee
The buyer, because the buyer pays that attorney's fee
Both buyer and lender, acting as a neutral escrow agent
The seller, whose old loan is being paid off at closing
questions.explanation: The lender's (bank) attorney represents only the lender, making sure its loan documents are signed and its conditions met, even though the borrower is typically charged the fee. The buyer needs her own attorney for advice.

questions.q: Which duty is typically handled by the title closer at a New York closing?
options: Negotiating last-minute price credits for the buyer
Collecting title charges and taking documents for recording
Preparing the deed and the seller's closing statement
Advising the seller whether the payoff figure is correct
questions.explanation: The title closer represents the title company: collecting the premium, recording fees and taxes, and payoff funds, clearing title exceptions, and taking the deed, mortgage, and tax forms for recording. Drafting the deed and advising clients are attorney work.
questions.citation: New York attorney-closing practice; NY Insurance Law Article 64 (title insurance)

questions.q: At closing, the seller's attorney offers to hand the listing salesperson a check for her share of the commission directly from the seller's proceeds. Under New York law, the salesperson:
options: May accept it if her broker gives oral consent at the closing
May accept it if the amount matches the listing agreement
May accept compensation only from her own supervising broker
May accept it if the buyer's attorney witnesses the payment
questions.explanation: A salesperson may receive compensation only from the licensed broker with whom she is associated. The full commission goes to the broker, who then pays her share; consent or matching amounts do not change this.

questions.q: The buyer is financing the purchase with a new $416,000 mortgage loan from a bank. On the closing statement, the new loan is entered as a:
options: Credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller
Debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
Credit to the buyer only
Debit to the buyer only
questions.explanation: The new loan is money the buyer brings to closing from a third party, so it reduces what the buyer owes and is a buyer credit only. The seller receives the full price regardless of how the buyer pays, so the loan never appears on the seller's side.
questions.citation: General closing statement practice (debits and credits)

questions.q: The seller agreed to pay the listing broker a commission of 6% of the $585,000 sale price. How does the commission appear on the closing statement?
options: $35,100 debit to the seller only
$35,100 debit to the seller and credit to the buyer
$35,100 debit to the buyer only
$17,550 debit to each of the buyer and seller
questions.explanation: $585,000 × 6% = $35,100. The commission is a cost the seller agreed to pay a third party, so it is a single debit to the seller; the buyer receives nothing, so there is no matching buyer credit.
questions.citation: General closing statement practice; listing agreement

questions.q: At closing, 200 gallons of heating oil remain in the seller's tank, and the contract says the buyer pays for it at $3.80 per gallon. The closing statement should show:
options: $760 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$760 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$380 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$760 credit to the buyer only
questions.explanation: 200 gal × $3.80 = $760. The seller paid for oil the buyer will burn after closing, so the buyer reimburses the seller: seller credit, buyer debit. Reversing the entries treats it like an unpaid bill, which it is not.
questions.citation: General proration practice; contract of sale

questions.q: A seller of a two-family house collected the tenant's $2,400 rent for June (30 days) on June 1. Closing is June 21 and the buyer owns the closing day. What is the rent proration?
options: $1,600 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$800 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$1,600 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$800 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
