questions.explanation: $2,400 ÷ 30 = $80 per day. The buyer owns June 21–30, which is 10 days: $80 × 10 = $800. The seller already pocketed rent belonging to the buyer, so it is a seller debit and buyer credit; $1,600 is the seller's own 20 days.
questions.citation: General proration practice (rents collected in advance)

questions.q: A seller of a small apartment building holds two tenants' security deposits of $1,800 each. At closing the deposits are turned over to the buyer. The closing statement shows:
options: $3,600 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$3,600 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$3,600 debit to the buyer only
Nothing, since deposits belong to the tenants
questions.explanation: 2 × $1,800 = $3,600. The buyer takes on the duty to return the deposits, so the seller hands over that money: seller debit, buyer credit. The deposits do belong to the tenants, which is exactly why the new owner who must refund them receives them.
questions.citation: NY General Obligations Law §7-105 (transfer of security deposits on conveyance)

questions.q: To settle an inspection issue, the seller agreed to give the buyer a $6,000 credit at closing toward the buyer's costs. On the closing statement this is a:
options: Debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
Credit to the buyer only
Debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer
Debit to the seller only
questions.explanation: A seller concession moves money from seller to buyer, so it is a double entry: seller debit, buyer credit. A single seller debit would describe money paid to an outsider, such as a commission, not money passing to the buyer.
questions.citation: General closing statement practice; contract of sale

questions.q: The buyer's lender requires an initial deposit into the buyer's new escrow account for future property taxes and homeowners insurance. On the closing statement, this deposit is a:
options: Debit to the buyer only
Credit to the buyer only
Debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
Credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
questions.explanation: The initial escrow deposit is the buyer's money paid to the buyer's own lender, so it is a buyer debit only. It is not a proration between the parties, so nothing appears on the seller's side.
questions.citation: General closing statement practice; RESPA escrow account rules

questions.q: Which item normally appears ONLY on the buyer's side of the closing statement?
options: The purchase price of the property
A proration of prepaid property taxes
Transfer of tenants' security deposits
The premium for the owner's title policy
questions.explanation: The owner's title insurance premium is paid by the buyer to a third party, so it is a single buyer debit. The price, tax prorations, and security deposit transfers all move money between buyer and seller and therefore appear on both sides.
questions.citation: General closing statement practice; NY custom (buyer pays title insurance)

questions.q: Annual property taxes of $5,400 for the calendar year are paid in arrears and are still unpaid. Closing is March 16, and the seller owns the days through March 15. Using a 360-day year (30-day months), the proration is:
options: $1,125 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$4,275 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$1,125 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$4,275 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: $5,400 ÷ 360 = $15 per day. Seller's period = January 30 + February 30 + March 15 = 75 days; 75 × $15 = $1,125. The buyer will pay the whole bill later, so the seller pays for its share now: seller debit, buyer credit. $4,275 is the buyer's own share.
questions.citation: General proration practice (expenses paid in arrears)

questions.q: The seller paid the full $9,125 school tax for the July 1–June 30 fiscal year. Closing is February 1 in a non-leap year, and the buyer owns the closing day. Using a 365-day year, the proration is:
options: $5,375 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$3,750 credit to the seller, debit to the buyer
$3,750 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
$5,375 debit to the seller, credit to the buyer
questions.explanation: $9,125 ÷ 365 = $25 per day. Buyer's period, Feb 1–June 30 = 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 30 = 150 days; 150 × $25 = $3,750. The seller prepaid the buyer's share, so seller credit, buyer debit. $5,375 is the seller's own 215 days, a common trap when the fiscal year is read as a calendar year.
questions.citation: General proration practice (expenses paid in advance)

questions.q: Price $520,000; buyer's deposit held in escrow $52,000; new loan $416,000; buyer's closing costs $14,300; and a $1,250 tax proration credited to the buyer. How much must the buyer bring to closing?
questions.explanation: Buyer debits: $520,000 + $14,300 = $534,300. Buyer credits: $52,000 + $416,000 + $1,250 = $469,250. Cash due = $534,300 − $469,250 = $65,050. $67,550 treats the proration as a debit, and $117,050 forgets the deposit already paid.
questions.citation: General closing statement practice (buyer debits minus credits)

questions.q: A seller outside NYC sells for $640,000. Charges: 5% commission, $310,000 mortgage payoff, NYS transfer tax, and $2,500 in other seller costs. The seller receives a $1,800 tax proration credit. What are the seller's net proceeds?
questions.citation: NY Tax Law §1402 (transfer tax); general closing statement practice

questions.q: Before closing, the seller's attorney requests a payoff letter from the seller's mortgage lender. The payoff letter's main purpose is to state:
options: The loan balance shown on the seller's last monthly statement
The exact amount to retire the loan through a date, plus per diem interest
The amount the buyer's lender will lend against the property
The interest the seller paid for the year, for income tax purposes
questions.explanation: A payoff letter gives the total needed to satisfy the loan (principal, accrued interest, and fees) good through a stated date, with a per diem figure for later days. A monthly statement balance omits interest accrued since the last payment, so paying it would leave the lien open.

questions.q: A payoff letter shows $212,400 due through June 1, with per diem interest of $34.50 for each day after. The payoff funds will reach the lender 14 days later. What payoff amount is debited to the seller?
questions.explanation: 14 days × $34.50 = $483; $212,400 + $483 = $212,883. $212,400 ignores interest accruing after the good-through date; $212,917.50 counts 15 days and $213,435 adds a full 30 days of interest.
questions.citation: General closing practice (mortgage interest paid in arrears; payoff per diem)

questions.q: A one-family house in Queens sells for $750,000. What is the New York City Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT), and who customarily pays it?
options: $10,687.50, paid by the seller
$8,562.50, paid by the seller
$10,687.50, paid by the buyer
$13,687.50, paid by the seller
questions.explanation: Because the residential price exceeds $500,000, the 1.425% rate applies to the full price: $750,000 × 1.425% = $10,687.50, customarily a seller cost. $8,562.50 wrongly applies 1.425% only to the excess over $500,000; $13,687.50 adds the $3,000 NYS transfer tax, which is a separate tax.

questions.q: A Brooklyn condo resale closes at $450,000 with no exemptions. Following NY custom, what is the seller's combined NYS transfer tax and NYC RPTT?
questions.explanation: NYS: $450,000 ÷ 500 = 900 units × $2 = $1,800. NYC RPTT at $500,000 or less: $450,000 × 1% = $4,500. Total = $6,300. $8,212.50 wrongly uses the 1.425% rate, which applies only above $500,000.
questions.citation: NY Tax Law §1402; NYC Administrative Code §11-2102

questions.q: A house in Erie County sells for $412,300. What is the NYS real estate transfer tax?
questions.explanation: $412,300 ÷ $500 = 824.6, and any fractional $500 counts as a full unit, so 825 units × $2 = $1,650. $1,649.20 multiplies by 0.4% without rounding up; $1,648 drops the fraction; $4,123 uses 1%.

questions.q: A buyer contracts to purchase a residence outside NYC for exactly $1,000,000. Regarding the additional 1% ("mansion") tax:
options: No tax is due, since the price does not exceed $1 million
$10,000 is due, paid by the seller
$10,000 is due, paid by the buyer
$4,000 is due, paid by the buyer
questions.explanation: The mansion tax applies to residential consideration of $1 million or more, so exactly $1,000,000 × 1% = $10,000, and it is the buyer's tax. $4,000 is the seller's NYS transfer tax on the same price ($1,000,000 ÷ 500 × $2).

questions.q: A buyer pays $450,000 for a house and finances $360,000. Assume the borrower's share of the mortgage recording tax is 1.05% of the loan (the lender pays its own separate share) and ignore any deductions. What is the borrower's tax, and who customarily pays it?
options: $4,725, paid by the buyer
$3,780, paid by the buyer
$3,780, paid by the seller
$945, paid by the buyer
questions.explanation: Mortgage recording tax is based on the debt secured, not the price: $360,000 × 1.05% = $3,780, a borrower (buyer) cost. (On 1–6 family homes the lender pays the 0.25% special additional tax, so the borrower's share is not the whole tax.) $4,725 applies the rate to the $450,000 price; $945 applies it to the $90,000 down payment.
questions.citation: NY Tax Law Article 11 (§253 mortgage recording tax)

questions.q: In a typical New York resale, which closing cost is customarily paid by the BUYER?
options: The NYS real estate transfer tax
The lender's title insurance premium
The fee to record the seller's satisfaction
The listing broker's agreed commission
questions.explanation: In New York the buyer customarily pays for title insurance, including the lender's policy the buyer's lender requires. The transfer tax, recording the satisfaction of the seller's old mortgage, and the listing commission are seller costs.
questions.citation: NY closing custom; contract of sale allocation controls

questions.q: In a typical NYC resale of a $1.1 million co-op apartment, each of the following is customarily paid by the seller EXCEPT:
options: The NYS real estate transfer tax
The NYC real property transfer tax
The additional 1% mansion tax
The payoff of the seller's share loan
questions.explanation: The 1% mansion tax on residential transfers of $1 million or more is the buyer's tax. The NYS transfer tax, the NYC RPTT, and paying off the seller's own loan are customarily seller obligations.
questions.citation: NY Tax Law §§1402, 1402-a; NYC Administrative Code §11-2102

questions.q: At closing, the seller's lender receives full payoff of a residential mortgage. Under New York law, within how many days must the lender present a satisfaction of mortgage for recording?
options: 10 days
60 days
90 days
30 days
questions.explanation: The mortgagee must execute a satisfaction and arrange for it to be presented for recording within 30 days after payoff, with statutory damages to the mortgagor ($500, rising at 60 and 90 days) for failing to do so. The 60- and 90-day marks are penalty escalation points, not the deadline.

questions.q: At the final walk-through, the buyer finds that a built-in dishwasher included in the contract has been removed. Closing is in two hours. What is the best course for the buyer's salesperson?
options: Promise the buyer a credit from the brokerage to save the deal
Tell the buyer to close and sue the seller in small claims afterward
Have the buyer refuse to close and keep the deposit as damages
Report it at once to the buyer's attorney to negotiate a remedy
questions.explanation: The missing fixture is a contract issue for the attorneys, who can negotiate a credit, a replacement, or an escrow holdback before the deed is delivered. A salesperson should not promise money, give legal advice on suing, or tell the buyer to walk away and claim the deposit.
questions.citation: General closing practice; contract of sale (fixtures)

questions.q: The seller's moving truck is delayed, and the seller asks to stay in the house for 10 days after closing. If the buyer agrees, the safest approach is:
options: A verbal promise from the seller, confirmed by both salespersons
A written post-closing possession agreement with money held in escrow
Delaying recording of the deed until the seller moves out
Letting the seller keep a set of keys until the movers arrive
questions.explanation: Attorneys normally prepare a written possession agreement setting a move-out date, a daily use charge, and an escrow holdback from the seller's proceeds that is released when the seller leaves. Delaying recording only exposes the buyer's title to intervening liens and does nothing to secure vacancy.
questions.citation: General closing practice (post-closing occupancy and escrow holdbacks)

questions.q: Two days before closing, before title or possession has passed, a fire destroys a material part of the house through no fault of the buyer. Under New York's Uniform Vendor and Purchaser Risk Act, absent a contrary contract term:
options: The seller cannot enforce the contract, and the buyer may recover the deposit
The buyer must close at the contract price and claim against its own insurer
The buyer must close, but the price is reduced by half
The seller may keep the deposit because the buyer signed the contract
questions.explanation: When neither title nor possession has passed and a material part is destroyed without the purchaser's fault, the seller cannot enforce the contract and the purchaser may recover any money paid. Risk shifts to the buyer only once title or possession transfers.

questions.q: The buyer's title report shows a $9,000 judgment against "Robert Allen." The seller is Robert J. Allen, a different person with a similar name. The usual way to clear this objection is:
options: Paying the judgment in full from the seller's proceeds
Starting a quiet title action before closing
Asking the judgment creditor to change its records
A seller affidavit of non-identity accepted by the title insurer
questions.explanation: For a same-name judgment, the seller signs an affidavit showing he is not the judgment debtor (with identifying details), and the title company then omits the exception. Paying a stranger's debt is unnecessary, and a quiet title action is far more than this routine objection requires.

questions.q: The title search shows a 2009 mortgage that a prior owner paid off, but no satisfaction was ever recorded. To clear this objection, the seller's attorney should generally:
options: Get a satisfaction recorded or other proof of payment the insurer accepts
Ignore it, because a mortgage over ten years old expires automatically
Have the buyer take title subject to the open mortgage
Ask the county clerk to remove the mortgage from the index
questions.explanation: An unsatisfied mortgage of record clouds title until a satisfaction is recorded or the title insurer accepts other proof of payment and removes the exception. A recorded mortgage does not simply expire after ten years, and the clerk cannot remove a recorded instrument on request.
questions.citation: NY RPL §321 (discharge of mortgage of record); general title practice

questions.q: At closing, a small mechanic's lien appears that the seller disputes and cannot discharge today. The parties still want to close. A common solution is:
options: Have the buyer pay the lien and deduct it from the commission
Close and leave the lien for the buyer to contest later
A title company escrow holdback from the seller's proceeds
Postpone recording of the deed until the lien expires
questions.explanation: The title company can hold back enough of the seller's proceeds (often more than the lien amount) in escrow and insure over the lien, releasing the funds when it is resolved. Delaying recording leaves the buyer unprotected and does not affect the lien.
questions.citation: General title practice (escrow/holdback to insure over liens)

questions.q: Just before closing, the title closer runs a bring-down (continuation) search. Its purpose is to:
options: Confirm the survey still matches the property's boundaries
Verify the buyer's credit has not changed since loan approval
Recompute the tax prorations using the final bill
Find liens or conveyances recorded since the original search
questions.explanation: The original title search may be weeks old, so a bring-down search updates it to the closing date to catch new judgments, liens, or deeds. Surveys, credit, and prorations are handled separately.

questions.q: In an escrow closing, as distinguished from a table closing:
options: A neutral escrow agent holds the deed and funds until all conditions are met
The buyer and seller sit together and exchange the deed and checks
The seller delivers the deed to the buyer before the loan is approved
The broker holds the deed in the brokerage's escrow account
questions.explanation: In an escrow closing, the parties deposit the deed, funds, and documents with a disinterested escrow agent, who completes the transaction once every condition is met, so the parties need not meet. Sitting together to exchange documents describes the table closing customary in New York.
questions.citation: General closing practice (escrow vs. table closings)

questions.q: A seller has relocated to Arizona and cannot attend the closing in Westchester. Which arrangement lets the sale close without the seller present?
options: The listing salesperson signs the deed for the seller at closing
The seller mails a signed deed directly to the buyer to record
The buyer's attorney signs the seller's name on an unsigned deed
Seller signs the deed in advance; an attorney holds it in escrow
questions.explanation: The seller can sign and acknowledge the deed in advance and deliver it to an attorney or escrow agent to be released only when the buyer's funds arrive (or appoint an attorney-in-fact by a proper power of attorney). Mailing the deed straight to the buyer risks delivery without payment, and an unauthorized signature is a forgery.
questions.citation: NY RPL §291 (acknowledgment required for recording); general escrow practice

questions.q: As between the seller and buyer, title to the property passes when the deed is:
options: Signed by the grantor in front of a notary
Delivered by the grantor and accepted by the grantee
Recorded with the county clerk by the title company
Reviewed and approved by the buyer's lender
questions.explanation: A deed transfers title upon delivery by the grantor and acceptance by the grantee during the grantor's lifetime. Signing alone does not pass title, and recording protects the buyer against later third parties but is not needed between the parties.
questions.citation: General conveyancing law (delivery and acceptance); NY RPL §291

questions.q: Which is NOT required for a deed to transfer title from seller to buyer between the two of them?
options: Recording of the deed in the county clerk's office
The grantor's signature on the deed
Delivery of the deed to the grantee
Acceptance of the deed by the grantee
questions.explanation: Signature, delivery, and acceptance are what make the conveyance effective between the parties. Recording gives constructive notice to the world and protects against later purchasers, but an unrecorded deed is still valid between grantor and grantee.

questions.q: A seller closes with Buyer 1, who delays recording the deed. A week later the seller fraudulently sells the same house to Buyer 2, who pays value, has no notice of the first sale, and records first. Under New York's recording act:
options: Buyer 1 prevails because that deed was delivered first
Buyer 2 prevails as a good-faith purchaser who recorded first
The two buyers share title as tenants in common
The sale to Buyer 2 is void, and the seller keeps the price
questions.explanation: New York is a race-notice state: an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith purchaser for value who records first. Buyer 1 is left with a claim against the seller (and any title insurer), which is why prompt post-closing recording matters.

questions.q: On closing morning, the buyer receives an email that appears to be from the attorney's office with new wiring instructions for the down payment. The buyer's salesperson should advise the buyer to:
options: Wire the funds promptly so the closing is not delayed
Reply to the email asking whether the change is real
Call the attorney at a known number to verify before wiring
Call the phone number listed in the new email to confirm
questions.explanation: Last-minute changes to wiring instructions are a classic wire-fraud sign. Verification must use an independently known phone number; replying to the email or calling the number it lists may reach the criminal.

questions.q: At closing, a salesperson asks the seller's attorney to write her share of the commission as a check payable directly to her. The attorney should:
options: Pay the commission to the brokerage, which then pays the salesperson
Pay the salesperson directly if the broker gives verbal approval
Split the commission check between broker and salesperson
Pay the salesperson directly since she procured the buyer
questions.explanation: A salesperson may be paid compensation only by the broker she is licensed with. The commission is paid to the brokerage, which then pays the salesperson her split; direct or split checks to the salesperson are not permitted, even with broker approval.

questions.q: A buyer assumes the seller's existing mortgage, which has a $150,000 balance on the closing date. On the closing statement, the assumed balance is entered as a:
options: Debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
Credit to the seller only
Debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer
Credit to the buyer only
questions.explanation: By assuming the loan, the buyer takes over $150,000 of debt the seller would otherwise pay, so it counts toward the price: buyer credit and seller debit. A new loan from a bank, by contrast, is a buyer credit only.

questions.q: A buyer's balance due at a New York closing is $65,050. In what form is it customarily paid?
options: A personal check written at the closing table
Cash brought to the closing in an envelope
A promissory note delivered to the seller
A bank wire or certified or official bank check
questions.explanation: Closing funds are customarily good funds: a wire transfer or a certified or official bank check, since the seller's attorney and lender payoff need money that cannot bounce. Personal checks are generally not accepted for the balance, and a note is seller financing, not payment.

questions.q: Put these steps in their usual order: (1) recording of the deed and mortgage; (2) title report and objections cleared; (3) final walk-through; (4) deed delivered and funds disbursed at closing.
questions.explanation: Title objections are raised and cleared before closing, the walk-through occurs shortly before closing, the deed is delivered and funds disbursed at closing, and the title company records the deed and mortgage afterward. Recording before delivery would be out of order.
